summary.highest_risk: The highest-scored finding so far is the historic eastern Pacific El Niño warmth, with NOAA forecasting a record share of the ocean in marine heatwave conditions, followed by the 2026 Arctic sea-ice minimum and the third-lowest Antarctic winter peak, and crude oil from the grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi reaching Oman's coast.
summary.directional_picture: Coverage is in its first days: these findings come from a global sweep of the last week of news and agency releases, not from the sea-by-sea baseline passes, which begin next. Physical and climate findings dominate the early picture; pollution, fisheries and habitat findings will fill in as the baseline passes run.

cross_cutting.label: Climate signal
cross_cutting.text: Marine heatwave extent, king-tide flooding in South Florida and record-low polar sea ice all point the same way in the same season.

cross_cutting.label: Governance in motion
cross_cutting.text: A NOAA public comment on a Clarion-Clipperton nodule permit and the Nairobi Convention COP12 show seabed and regional-sea governance decisions under way.

records.title: Historic El Niño drives extreme eastern Pacific warmth and a forecast record share of the ocean in marine heatwave
records.description: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center says on 8 October 2026 that El Niño continues to strengthen, with eastern equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures more than 4.0C above average in places. NOAA's marine heatwave forecast gives eastern tropical Pacific heatwave likelihood above 90% through winter 2026-27, and global coverage is forecast to reach 45%. NOAA Fisheries said on 8 October 2026 that the chance of a very strong El Niño in fall and winter 2026-27 is above 83 percent and that the event is expected to last into early spring 2027, with expected effects on West Coast, Pacific Islands, Alaska and Caribbean fisheries and marine life. Copernicus Climate Change Service reported on 14 October 2026 that September 2026 had the highest September sea surface temperature on record for the extra-polar ocean (60S-60N) at 21.05C, against the previous record of 20.92C in 2023, with record September values along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean.

location.name: Eastern tropical Pacific and global ocean
location.detail: Eastern equatorial Pacific El Niño region with global marine heatwave coverage effects

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale ocean heating from a developing El Niño is a physical climate condition.

notes.harm: Heatwave exposure is forecast rather than a documented mortality event; subsurface anomalies above +10C persist in the eastern Pacific (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources documents closures or fishery losses from this event so far (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: NOAA puts 38% of the global ocean in heatwave in August 2026 and forecasts 45% for winter (ref 3).
notes.duration: Copernicus recorded heatwaves over about 82% of the ocean by end of June (ref 2), NOAA forecasts them through winter 2026-27 (ref 3), and C3S says August and September 2026 each set a monthly SST record and El Niño is expected to last into 2027 (ref 6).
notes.significance: CPC has an El Niño Advisory in effect and gives 83% for a historic event in October-December (ref 1).

records.title: Arctic sea ice minimum ties tenth lowest and Antarctic winter peak is third lowest in 2026
records.description: NASA reports the Arctic minimum on 12 September 2026 was about 4.6 million square km, tied for tenth lowest, and the 20 lowest minimums all fall in 2007-2026; the UK Met Office, using another dataset, ranks it 14th lowest at 5.06 million square km. Provisional NSIDC data put the Antarctic winter peak at 17.59 million square km on 14 September, third lowest, and NSIDC reported on 7 October that Antarctic daily extent had been at record lows since 2 October. The Met Office end-of-season report of 14 October 2026 puts September Antarctic extent at 17.76 million square km, third lowest September since 1979, briefly a record low at the end of September, and says Arctic summer 2026 was cool and stormy with the September extent 16th lowest on OSI SAF data.

records.description: Fifteen pygmy killer whales stranded on Ninety Mile Beach in New Zealand's Far North District on 1 October 2026, and at least 12 were found dead. records.title: NOAA public comment on a 65,000 km2 deep-seabed nodule mining application in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone
records.description: NOAA found a consolidated exploration licence and commercial recovery permit application from TMC USA, submitted on 6 February 2026, fully compliant with US deep seabed mining law and opened a 60-day public comment period running to 19 October 2026, with a virtual hearing on 13 October from 3 to 5 p.m. ET. records.title: Nairobi Convention COP12 in Dar es Salaam, on the Convention's 40th anniversary, closes with 15 decisions on Western Indian Ocean governance
records.description: The twelfth Conference of the Parties to the Nairobi Convention met in Dar es Salaam on 6-9 October 2026 with its ten Contracting Parties. Tanzania set priorities including national law and enforcement, coastal ecosystem restoration and marine pollution. UNEP reported on 9 October 2026 that the meeting concluded with 15 decisions, including a regional strategy to combat plastic pollution, a regional contingency plan for major marine pollution incidents, new initiatives for mangroves, seagrasses and coral reefs, and measures on ocean accounting and blue finance; more than 1,600 delegates attended. The full texts of the decisions are not in the cited sources.

records.title: Crude oil leaking from grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi reaches Oman's coast
records.description: The tanker Caroline Bezengi, reported to carry around 800,000 barrels of Russian crude, was disabled near the Al Hallaniyat Islands off Oman and has leaked oil since the summer. Omani authorities put the slick at nearly 400 square kilometres and confirmed oil on mainland beaches at Ras Madrakah in mid-August; Greenpeace estimated about 1,300 square kilometres. As of 8 October 2026 the ship was still stuck on the rocks and still leaking, with no sign yet that the cargo offload had begun.

location.detail: Arabian Sea coast of Oman, off the Hallaniyat archipelago marine reserve; oil reported on the Ras Madrakah shoreline and expected on southern Masirah Island

records.layer_rationale: Crude oil released into coastal waters from a grounded tanker.

notes.harm: Oil reached beaches at Ras Madrakah, affecting up to 40 km of coastline, near a marine reserve created last year for sea turtles; no casualty counts are reported (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure is documented in the opened sources; the vessel lies about 22 nautical miles off the fishing village of Sharbithat (ref 2), and Maritime Executive reports fishing boat activity in the area has resumed as of 8 October (ref 4).
notes.scale: Omani authorities put the slick at nearly 400 sq km around one archipelago and a stretch of mainland coast; Greenpeace's 1,300 sq km estimate is still within one national coast (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Disabled on 8 June and grounded on 30 June (refs 1, 2), the tanker was still leaking on 8 October, so the release has run for about four months (ref 4).
notes.significance: The IMO confirmed monitoring and oil spill contingency planning (ref 2), Oman's emergency committee cleared oil from 12 km of coastline (ref 5), and the IOPC Funds said it would not be involved because the incident likely resulted from an act of war (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Record June 2025 marine heatwave covered 62% of the Mediterranean surface; 2025 was the second-warmest year on record
records.description: Copernicus Marine reported that June 2025 was the warmest June on record for the Mediterranean, with a mean sea surface temperature of 23.86 C, and that a high-intensity marine heatwave affected 62% of the sea surface at the peak. Its annual bulletin ranks 2025 as the second-warmest year, with the whole basin touched by a marine heatwave for the third year running.

notes.livelihoods: None of the four cited sources reports a fishery, port or tourism restriction tied to the 2025 heatwave (refs 1-4).
notes.scale: Heatwave conditions covered up to 62% of the sea surface at the June 2025 peak and 93% of the basin reached strong or higher intensity during the year, a regional-sea extent (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The entire Mediterranean was affected by a marine heatwave at some point in 2025 for the third consecutive year, so the pattern is recurring (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The sources are monitoring bulletins and press releases with no advisory, closure or enforcement action, so no formal-notice credit is given (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Mediterranean surface waters hit an all-time daily record of 28.47 C on 15 August 2024 in the warmest year then on record
records.description: Mercator Ocean, which runs the Copernicus Marine Service, reported that 15 August 2024 was the hottest day on record for Mediterranean surface waters, at a mean 28.47 C, and that surface temperatures had stayed above 28 C since 6 August. The 2025 Copernicus bulletin states that 99% of the basin saw strong or higher marine heatwaves in 2024, and a June 2025 report said the 28.47 C record still stood.

notes.duration: Temperatures stayed above 28 C from 6 August, the longest such spell recorded, within a run of three consecutive years with basin-wide heatwaves (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Greenpeace monitoring finds marine heatwaves down to 40 m and gorgonian and coral damage in Italian marine protected areas
records.description: Greenpeace Italia's Mare Caldo network reported repeated marine heatwaves at all 14 monitored Italian stations in 2025, including a 41-day heatwave at Asinara that reached 3.5 C above the climatological threshold, with heat reaching 30 to 40 m depth. Its earlier report found severe impact on 94% of Paramuricea clavata colonies at 25 m at Portofino, and necrosis or bleaching of gorgonians and the coral Cladocora caespitosa at several sites.

records.title: Venice's MOSE barrier raised 25 times in 2023 and 28 in 2024 as high tides hit a record; study warns it may fail by 2100 in the worst case
records.description: Venice's MOSE storm-surge barrier was raised 25 times in 2023 and 28 times in 2024, 97 times since 2020, while tides above 80 cm reached 219 events in 2024, the most recorded. A 2025 INGV study reported in Il Post found that in the highest-emissions scenario the 3 m sea-lagoon difference MOSE was designed for would be exceeded in 2100.

notes.livelihoods: Port operators say each raising limits port operations and want more involvement in how MOSE is managed (ref 1).
notes.scale: The system protects one lagoon with three inlets; INGV maps flooding of about 139 km2 by 2150 around Lido, Cavallino, Chioggia and the airport (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Tides above 80 cm rose from about 75 events a year around 2000 to 126 around 2020 and then to 219 in 2024, a chronic trend (ref 1).
notes.significance: No court ruling, order or emergency declaration is cited; MOSE operates under state management and critics call procedures provisional (refs 1, 3).

records.description: Spain's Ministry for the Ecological Transition says the Ebro Delta coast suffers erosion worsened by reduced sediment supply, subsidence averaging 3 mm a year, sea-level rise and more intense storms. records.title: Mediterranean acidification has lowered pH by 0.055 to 0.157 units since pre-industrial times, with sparse monitoring and no consistent policy
records.description: A systematic review in Frontiers in Marine Science found Mediterranean pH has fallen by between 0.055 and 0.157 units since pre-industrial times, a wider range than the Atlantic and global ocean, with the Algero-Provencal and Ionian sub-basins least studied. A 2025 GEOMAR-led meta-analysis states the sea is warming faster and acidifying more strongly than the open ocean.

records.title: Boat anchoring put over 50,000 hectares of Posidonia seagrass at risk across the Mediterranean in 2024, WWF reports
records.description: WWF's 2025 report, built on 2024 vessel-tracking (AIS) data, estimates that more than 50,000 hectares of Posidonia oceanica meadows were potentially hit by anchoring and that over 179,000 boats may have anchored on them. Italy ranks first for impacts, followed by Spain and Turkey, with Greece and France also named as hotspots. A 2025 cross-border journalism investigation found that regulations exist in Spain, France and Italy but patrols are limited and violations often go unpunished.

location.detail: Basin-wide AIS analysis; named hotspots include Golfo Aranci (Sardinia, Italy) and the coasts of Spain, Turkey, Greece and France.

notes.harm: WWF describes the 50,000+ hectares as potentially affected in 2024, an AIS-based estimate rather than a surveyed loss, with scars that can take more than 100 years to heal (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or disruption is reported; the WWF figure of over 4 billion euros a year is a valuation of lost ecosystem services, not a livelihood loss (ref 1).
notes.scale: The analysis covers the whole Mediterranean basin, with Italy, Spain and Turkey ranked highest and Greece and France named as hotspots (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Impacts concentrate every May to September, when boat traffic can rise up to fourfold at Golfo Aranci, and the damage is described as lasting a century (ref 1).

records.title: Repeated marine heatwaves kill red gorgonian forests at the Medes Islands and Portofino

Greenpeace Italy's Mare Caldo monitoring recorded severe impact on 94% of P. clavata colonies at 25 m in Portofino in 2024, and bleaching of the coral Cladocora caespitosa at Tavolara and Ventotene.

records.title: Fan mussel Pinna nobilis pushed to ecological extinction in open Mediterranean waters by parasite-linked mass mortality
records.description: A die-off that began in late 2016 and is mainly linked to the parasite Haplosporidium pinnae has spread across all Mediterranean basins, with mortality up to 100% in affected populations. A 2025 review and the EU LIFE PINNA CARE project describe survivors confined mostly to coastal lagoons and deltas; a 2026 study confirmed the parasite in the southern Sea of Marmara from a November 2024 sample.

notes.harm: Mortality has reached up to 100% in affected populations since 2016 and the species is ecologically extinct in open waters (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or coastal-economy disruption is described in the opened sources (refs 1, 2).

notes.duration: The mortality has run since late 2016, and a sample from 23 November 2024 confirmed the parasite in new Marmara waters (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The IUCN lists the species as Critically Endangered and the EU funds a LIFE project of 3.93 million euros to prevent extinction (ref 2).

records.title: Fin whale found alive with deep propeller wounds in the Pelagos Sanctuary in August 2025
records.description: On 13 August 2025 passengers on a whale-watching boat saw a fin whale with multiple deep gashes across its back off Andora, western Liguria, inside the Pelagos Sanctuary. The animal, named Stripes by Tethys, was alive and the injuries were consistent with a recent propeller strike; Italian Coast Guards were alerted. OceanCare and Tethys say collision risk rises with speed, especially above 10 knots, and detected strikes are only a subset.

IFAW cited 13 of 24 strandings on the Greek coast between 1992 and 2016 with clear ship-strike evidence. Greek-owned Arcadia Shipmanagement voluntarily rerouted its ships away from the trench in 2024.

records.description: The GFCM's State of Mediterranean and Black Sea Fisheries 2025 report puts the share of overexploited assessed stocks at 52 percent, the lowest in its time series but still far above a sustainable level. records.title: GFCM does not extend the Mediterranean deep-sea trawl ban from 1,000 m to 800 m depth
records.description: The GFCM bans bottom trawling below 1,000 m. Oceana and MedReAct report that at its November 2025 annual session Mediterranean countries did not extend the ban to 800 m, despite pilot studies in six countries showing ecological benefits with limited or no cost to fisheries. A June 2026 report says the extension would protect about 100,000 km2 and that bamboo coral has nearly collapsed in some areas.

notes.harm: Oceana and MedReAct report bamboo coral (Isidella elongata) has nearly collapsed in some areas from bottom-contact fishing (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The pilot studies found minimal costs for fishers and minimal fishing occurs at these depths, so no fishery loss is reported (ref 2).
notes.scale: The measure covers the whole GFCM Mediterranean area, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: A 2023 GFCM commitment to expand deep-water protection in 2025 was not met, and a proposal is pending for the 2026 annual meeting (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The GFCM Scientific Advisory Committee backed the extension, but the commission did not adopt it, which is a formal process outcome rather than an order (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Invasive silver-cheeked toadfish damages small-scale fishing gear in Cyprus and Greece
records.description: The invasive silver-cheeked toadfish, which entered the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, destroys nets and gear for coastal fishers. Cyprus's fisheries department reports more than 103 tonnes removed since a grant scheme began in June 2024, and Greece is discussing a similar pilot after fishers in Volos reported the fish moving north.

notes.harm: Fishers in Volos report octopus have become much less common where the pufferfish increased, and the species is linked to swimmer incidents, without further detail (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Cyprus says the species damages fishing gear and netting; about 150 professional fishers in eleven groups joined the removal scheme (ref 1).
notes.scale: The invasion spans the eastern Mediterranean from Cyprus to northern Greece (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: The Cyprus grant scheme began in June 2024 and runs to the end of 2029, and the species has spread north over years (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: A formal government grant scheme paying 4.73 euros per kg is in force in Cyprus, with Greece discussing a pilot (ref 1, ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Greece commits to end bottom trawling in marine parks by 2026 and all protected areas by 2030
records.description: At the Our Ocean Conference in Athens in April 2024, Prime Minister Mitsotakis announced that Greece would ban bottom trawling in its national marine parks by 2026 and in all marine protected areas by 2030. The plan includes the Ionian Marine National Park, about 12 percent of Greek territorial waters, and the South Aegean Marine Protected Area, 6.6 percent, with 780 million euros of investment. In July 2026 the government finalised a presidential decree for South Aegean Marine Park I with a complete ban on bottom-towed gear; it still has to go to the Council of State, and an Ionian decree was promised in the coming weeks (ref 3).

notes.scale: The ban covers Ionian and South Aegean parks, about 12 and 6.6 percent of territorial waters (ref 2).
notes.duration: The measures stretch from the April 2024 announcement to 2030, with 2026 as the first deadline (ref 1).
notes.significance: The commitment is a government announcement with a legislated 30 percent protection goal and 780 million euros pledged, and it drew a formal Turkish objection (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Heatwave destroys Thermaic Gulf mussel harvest, second collapse in three years
records.description: July 2024 heatwaves pushed Thermaic Gulf sea temperatures above 30 C, too hot for farmed mussels, and farmers reported a 90 percent drop in the 2024 catch, the second such collapse in three years. All seed for the next season also died, and the Pieria Chamber of Commerce said there would be no production in 2025 and sought state compensation.

notes.livelihoods: All seed for the coming season died, and the chamber forecast no production in 2025; about 100 families in Kymina seek compensation to pay debts (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Invasive blue crab devastates Po Delta clam farming, fishing cooperative revenue down 75 percent
records.description: The Atlantic blue crab has been a major problem in the Po Delta for over two years, cutting commercial clam yields by up to 70 percent in some areas and destroying young clams, with damage in the Emilia-Romagna clam sector reported at no less than 16.8 million euros. Nearly 2.3 million kg of crabs were incinerated with public funds, yet eradication has failed. The Polesine fishermen's consortium reports revenue down 75 percent and membership from about 1,500 to 850.

notes.livelihoods: Revenues of the Polesine fishermen's consortium fell 75 percent to about 15 million euros across 2024-2025 and members dropped from roughly 1,500 to 850 (ref 1).

notes.duration: The problem has run for over two years, since 2023, and eradication failed (ref 1).
notes.significance: The agriculture ministry approved a declaration decree for 2025 aquaculture damages (ref 1) and a commissioner allocated 2.9 million euros in national compensation (ref 2).

records.title: Escaped farmed sea bream and sea bass may mask overfishing of wild Mediterranean stocks, study finds
records.description: A 2024 Scientific Reports study found sea bream landings were significantly correlated with estimated biomass of escaped farmed sea bream entering the wild; no significant overall relationship was found for sea bass. The authors say escapes of gilthead sea bream and European sea bass may mask wild stock overexploitation, confound stock assessments, alter genetic diversity and spread pathogens. A 2023 review of a Greek Aegean farm put escapes at 0 to 2 percent of stock per event, 5 to 8 times a year.

notes.duration: The study links landings regime shifts to the onset of Mediterranean aquaculture, a chronic multi-decade pattern, and the Greek farm records show 5-8 escape events a year (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The evidence is peer-reviewed research with no regulator action or formal notice (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Phosphogypsum dumped into the Gulf of Gabès since 1972, with a sea-discharge suspension reported in October 2025
records.description: Phosphate processing at Gabès in southeastern Tunisia has discharged untreated phosphogypsum into the gulf since 1972. A 2024 peer-reviewed study found that the resulting foam carries uranium, cadmium, arsenic and radionuclides. In October 2025 an industrial-environment expert told the national news agency TAP that the contaminated seabed strip extends about 3 km offshore and that the government had decided to suspend sea discharge.

location.name: Gulf of Gabès (Chatt Essalem and Ghannouch)
location.detail: Gabès governorate, southeastern Tunisia; discharge from the Groupe chimique tunisien phosphate complex near Chatt Essalem and Ghannouch beaches

records.layer_rationale: Industrial phosphogypsum slurry with trace metals and radionuclides is discharged directly into coastal waters.

notes.harm: The 2024 study in the Journal of Hazardous Materials reported uranium 56 mg/kg, cadmium 50 mg/kg, arsenic 30 mg/kg and radium-226 1,169 Bq/kg in phosphogypsum foam, and contaminated marine life on Chatt Sidi Abd Essalam beach (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: A Daraj report says the gulf's fish species fell from over 270 to about 50, but attributes the figure to no named source, so only a limited livelihood impact is scored (ref 4).
notes.scale: The contamination described is one gulf, with a seabed strip about 3 km wide off Chatt Essalem and Ghannouch (ref 3).
notes.duration: Untreated dumping into the sea began in 1972 and was still continuing when the October 2025 suspension was reported (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A scientific committee recommended an immediate halt to sea dumping and the government approved reclassifying phosphogypsum on 5 March 2025 (ref 2); the October 2025 suspension rests on one TAP-based report (ref 3), so a formal notice rather than an enforcement order is scored.

population_affected.note: No population figure for the coastal communities is given in the cited marine-pollution sources.

records.title: Mar Menor lagoon: chlorophyll rebound in summer 2025 and anoxic bottom water after the October flood
records.description: The IEO-CSIC BELICH monitoring team reported in July 2025 that chlorophyll in the Mar Menor was about five times higher than two years earlier and that light reaching the bottom had fallen from 23.5% to 5.8%. After the October 2025 'Alice' flood, oxygen in the southern lagoon fell below 2 mg/L by 19 October and a deep anoxic layer formed, with fauna moving toward the surface. In early 2026 the lagoon also held more invasive Caulerpa algae than in previous years, with 1,158 tonnes removed in January.

location.name: Mar Menor coastal lagoon
location.detail: Region of Murcia, southeastern Spain; lagoon of about 135 km2 separated from the Mediterranean by the La Manga sandbar

records.layer_rationale: Decades of nutrient loading drive phytoplankton blooms and oxygen depletion in the lagoon.

notes.harm: BELICH scientists reported a near-anoxic deep layer in the south after the Alice flood, with oxygen below 2 mg/L by 19 October 2025 and fauna fleeing toward the surface (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: Los Alcázares received permission to hand-remove Caulerpa at three beaches (Los Narejos, Carrión, La Concha), and the algal sludge deters swimmers (ref 5).
notes.scale: The problem is confined to one lagoon of about 135 km2 (ref 6).
notes.duration: The ecosystem has been in crisis since the 2016 collapse, with a new low-oxygen episode in October 2025 and a chlorophyll rebound from July 2025 (refs 2, 4, 5).
notes.significance: The Belich team convened a crisis cabinet in October 2025 (ref 3) and the national Secretary of State for the Environment briefed the regional minister in July 2025 (ref 2), without a declared emergency.

population_affected.note: No population figure appears in the cited monitoring reports.

records.title: Spanish courts convict farmers for nitrate-laden desalination discharges into the Mar Menor
records.description: In September 2024 a Campo de Cartagena farmer admitted discharging about 68,061 m3 of nitrate-rich water from an unauthorised desalination plant into the Mar Menor in 2015-2017 and received a one-year suspended sentence. A second conviction followed in September 2025 for a Torre Pacheco farm manager, with about 118,000 euros in fine and compensation. A later case, the first with the lagoon's own legal representatives, ended in a plea deal; the prosecutor said dozens more trials are scheduled.

records.title: Large mucilage event across the northern Adriatic in summer 2024
records.description: Mucilage aggregates from large algal blooms spread along the Croatian, Slovenian and Italian Adriatic coasts from late June 2024, with aggregates more than 20 km long recorded off Istria. A regional agency oceanographer said the bloom began off Croatia and Slovenia and reached Italy by current, and Italian coastal officials reported tourist and fishing disruption. Later peer-reviewed work linked the event to warm water and sudden freshwater inflow from the Po River.

location.name: Northern Adriatic (Gulf of Trieste to Romagna and Istria)
location.detail: Mucilage reported from Abruzzo to the Marche, Veneto, Trieste and the Romagna Riviera in Italy, and along the Slovenian and Istrian coasts

records.layer_rationale: Nutrient-rich river water and warm conditions drive bloom and mucilage formation in the Adriatic.
secondary_drivers: Po River freshwater and nutrient input

notes.harm: The mucilage is non-toxic but plankton diversity inside it was lower than in typical blooms, and it can smother benthos and clog nets (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Hotel and beach-club pools were crowded as bathers avoided the sea, damaged boats and nets were reported, and farm-food association Unci asked for a crisis unit and earlier fishing closures (ref 1).
notes.scale: Italian, Slovenian and Croatian coasts were affected, from Abruzzo to Trieste and Istria (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Reports began in early July and became frequent in August 2024, easing by mid-August with the end expected at the first autumn storms (ref 1).
notes.significance: Only agency commentary from Arpae's Daphne unit and later studies were found; no formal advisory or enforcement was identified (refs 1-3).

population_affected.note: No count of affected people appears in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Mucilage aggregates ranged from formations over 20 km long to patches under 20 m (Ruđer Bošković Institute, Jan 2026).

records.title: Damaged Russian LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz drifts and is later anchored off Libya with fuel oil aboard
records.description: The LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz was hit by explosions and fire on 2-3 March 2026 and abandoned. It drifted unmanned between Malta and Libya carrying LNG, an estimated 450 tonnes of heavy fuel oil and 250 tonnes of diesel; five EU governments asked the Commission to activate the EU civil protection mechanism. Libyan tow attempts failed and the ship was anchored off Benghazi in late April; no oil spill had been confirmed as of 4 May 2026.

notes.livelihoods: Malta reportedly barred vessels within 7 km (ref 1) and Libya's ports authority told ships to stay at least 5 nautical miles away (ref 4).
notes.scale: Italy, Spain, Malta, Greece and Cyprus wrote to the Commission about a Mediterranean-wide ecological risk (ref 1).
notes.duration: The vessel was abandoned on 3 March 2026 and was still anchored with unresolved cargo and fuel on 4 May 2026 (refs 2, 5).
notes.significance: Five governments formally requested EU civil protection activation (ref 1), Libya ran a national emergency response and Cedre advised EMSA, DG ECHO and REMPEC (refs 2, 6).

records.title: Untreated sewage from Gaza's collapsed wastewater system flows into the Mediterranean
records.description: UNEP's June 2024 preliminary assessment found that all five of Gaza's wastewater treatment plants had shut down and that untreated sewage was reaching beaches and coastal waters with pathogens, nutrients, microplastics and hazardous chemicals. A UNEP spokesperson cited high chlorophyll and suspended organic matter in coastal waters. Oxfam reported in February 2025 that about 130,000 m3 of untreated sewage a day was contaminating the sea, with 73 of 84 sewage pumping stations destroyed.

notes.scale: The pollution covers the Gaza coastline and drifts north toward Israeli beaches (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Mediterranean plastic waste above 200,000 tonnes a year as Barcelona Convention parties adopt the Cairo Declaration
records.description: The IISD summary of the 24th meeting of the Barcelona Convention parties (Cairo, 2-5 December 2025) says more than 200,000 tonnes of plastic waste are dumped into the Mediterranean each year. Parties adopted the Cairo Ministerial Declaration, committing to eliminate harmful single-use plastics by 2030, while draft references to the entire lifecycle of plastics were dropped. The Union for the Mediterranean earlier estimated 570,000 tonnes a year and about 7% of the world's microplastics in the sea.

notes.duration: Plastic input is chronic and, on business-as-usual, projected to quadruple by 2050 per the UfM (ref 2).
notes.significance: COP 24 adopted the Cairo Ministerial Declaration and the 2026-2035 strategic decisions, a treaty action (ref 1).

records.title: Satellite study flags the Mediterranean among the oceans' highest concentrations of chronic oil slicks from ships
records.description: SkyTruth's global satellite estimate, released 23 September 2026 from 2023-2025 imagery, places the Mediterranean among the areas with the highest oil-slick concentrations and finds three of the ten most polluted Important Marine Mammal Areas there. In the Spanish Mediterranean cetacean migration corridor MPA, analysts hand-labelled 45 true slicks, all from vessels, tracing 20 vessels. The regional response centre REMPEC has estimated 1,500 to 2,000 operational oil spills a year in the basin.

records.layer_rationale: Chronic operational oil discharges from ships along busy routes.

notes.harm: SkyTruth says slicks overlap three of the ten most polluted Important Marine Mammal Areas, a potential harm to cetaceans without measured impacts (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the sources reports closures or lost fishing from these slicks (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: The Mediterranean is named among the highest-concentration regional seas (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The analysis covers 2023-2025 and REMPEC describes operational spills as a continuing source (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: REMPEC's study under the Barcelona Convention framework estimates 1,500-2,000 operational spills a year (ref 3); no enforcement action is cited.

records.title: Ship strikes on fin and sperm whales in the north-western Mediterranean PSSA, where the IMO speed measure is voluntary
records.description: The IMO designated the north-western Mediterranean a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area in July 2023 because ship strikes are the main human-caused cause of death for fin and sperm whales there. The associated 10 to 13 knot speed reduction is a recommendation, not a requirement. In August 2025 whale-watchers and Tethys researchers reported a live fin whale with deep propeller wounds off western Liguria inside the Pelagos Sanctuary.

location.name: NW Mediterranean PSSA (Pelagos Sanctuary)
location.detail: Waters between Valencia and Genoa, including the Pelagos Sanctuary (France, Italy, Monaco) and the Spanish Mediterranean Cetacean Migration Corridor

records.layer_rationale: Vessel collisions are documented as the leading human-caused mortality for two endangered whale populations.

notes.harm: ACCOBAMS document SC16/Doc18 states ship strikes are the primary human-induced mortality for the two species, and Tethys reported a live fin whale with deep propeller gashes on 13 August 2025 (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The IMO associated protective measures are recommendatory, so no route or speed restriction binds shipping (refs 4, 5).
notes.scale: The PSSA spans the waters between Valencia and Genoa, a regional-sea area (ref 3).
notes.duration: The 2023 IMO designation rests on decades of records; the ACCOBAMS paper cites fatal strike records from 1971 to 2001 and 2023 traffic data (ref 3).
notes.significance: IMO MEPC designated the PSSA by Resolution MEPC.380(80) on 7 July 2023 (refs 3, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Commercial vessels in the PSSA sailed more than 80% of their 2023 distance at average speeds above 10 knots, per the AIS analysis in ACCOBAMS document SC16/Doc18 (ref 3).

The measures are voluntary, so no direct cost to carriers is documented (ref 4).

records.title: Mediterranean SOx emission control area applies from May 2025 while regional bodies work on consistent enforcement
records.description: The Mediterranean became a MARPOL Annex VI sulphur emission control area on 1 May 2025, with a 0.10% fuel sulphur limit against 0.50% elsewhere. UNEP/MAP projected a large cut in sulphur oxide emissions. REMPEC, the regional marine pollution centre, said in August 2025 that attention should turn to consistent enforcement and ran a September 2025 training webinar on inspections and on ratification of MARPOL Annex VI by beneficiary countries.

location.name: Mediterranean Sea SOx ECA
location.detail: Whole Mediterranean Sea; proposed by the 21 Barcelona Convention states and the EU and adopted by the IMO MEPC

records.layer_rationale: Ship exhaust sulphur oxides and particulate matter are the regulated air pollutants.

notes.harm: UNEP/MAP estimated the measure would avoid about 1,100 premature deaths and 2,300 childhood asthma cases a year, a projected rather than measured health burden (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The rule sets a fuel limit and no port or route is closed; REMPEC records no restriction on trade (ref 2).
notes.scale: The control area covers the whole Mediterranean Sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 0.10% limit has applied since 1 May 2025 and is permanent under MARPOL Annex VI (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: IMO MEPC 79 adopted the designation on 15 December 2022, with effect from 1 May 2025 (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The ECA requires fuel of at most 0.10% m/m sulphur from 1 May 2025, against 0.50% outside it; UNEP/MAP projected a 78.7% cut in SOx emissions (ref 1).

records.title: Barcelona and its port agree to cut cruise terminals from seven to five as cruise traffic grows
records.description: In July 2025 Barcelona City Council and the Port of Barcelona signed a protocol to reduce cruise terminals from seven to five by 2030, cutting maximum daily cruise capacity from 37,000 to 31,000 passengers. The port will rebuild a 610 metre quay section so ships can connect to shore power. Barcelona handled 3.65 million cruise passengers in 2024.

notes.duration: Passenger numbers rose about 20% from 2018 to 2024 and works run from 2026 to 2030 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: New offshore gas leases around Crete, including Chevron and HELLENiQ in February 2026, and cetacean concerns in the Hellenic Trench
records.description: On 16 February 2026 Chevron and HELLENiQ ENERGY signed lease agreements for four Greek offshore blocks, two of them south of Crete, subject to ratification by the Greek Parliament; Naftemporiki reports seismic surveys planned for autumn 2026. Separately, a 2021-2022 survey by the University of Exeter, Greenpeace Greece and the Pelagos Cetacean Research Institute found at least four cetacean species in the Hellenic Trench year-round, in the area of the earlier ExxonMobil and HELLENiQ blocks west and southwest of Crete, where 2D seismic work ended in February 2023. The opened sources do not state whether the new blocks overlap the surveyed habitat.

records.title: Mediterranean marine protected areas cover 9% of the sea, 0.07% strictly protected, far short of 30% by 2030

records.title: Mass coral bleaching and die-off at Con Dao after 32 C seawater in 2024
records.description: Con Dao National Park and the Institute of Oceanography surveyed the archipelago in early June 2024 and found 80 to 100% of eastern reefs and up to 70% of western reefs bleached, with about 20% and 10% dead respectively. Seawater at Hon Tai was measured at 32 C, above the 24 to 30 C range corals normally tolerate. The park board proposed limiting seafood harvesting, swimming and diving for three months and postponing coral restoration.

records.title: MT Terranova fuel-oil tanker sinking oils the Manila Bay coast of Bataan, Cavite and Bulacan
records.description: The Philippine tanker Terranova capsized in heavy weather during Typhoon Gaemi on 25 July 2024 with 1,468,896 litres of fuel oil, and one crew member died. records.title: Summer bottom-water hypoxia and high nutrient levels persist in the Pearl River Estuary
records.description: Research in the lower Pearl River Estuary finds bottom waters turn hypoxic under stratification, with about 65% of the oxygen-consuming organic matter coming from algal growth and 35% from land. Hong Kong's Environmental Protection Department reports that nutrient compliance in its waters is limited by high background levels from the estuary, and China's 2025 marine bulletin lists estuarine hypoxia as a continuing risk.

notes.harm: A July 2014 cruise found bottom waters hypoxic at both sampling legs, with oxygen near 30 µmol/kg at one station (ref 3); a 2024 study measured sediment oxygen uptake averaging about 41 mmol per square metre per day (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Hong Kong recorded 13 red tide incidents in 2023 but no red-tide fish kill (ref 2), so no fishery disruption is documented in the cited sources.
notes.scale: The studied hypoxic area is the lower estuary (10 to 70 m depth) shared by Guangdong and Hong Kong waters, a regional coastal sector (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Hypoxia was documented on a July 2014 cruise (ref 3) and a December 2024 paper still models its development in the same estuary (ref 1); China's 2025 bulletin lists estuarine hypoxia as a continuing national risk (ref 4).
notes.significance: EPD's annual compliance reporting gives Deep Bay 53% water quality objective compliance and total inorganic nitrogen 70% in 2023 (ref 2), and China's Ministry of Natural Resources bulletin of 8 June 2026 flags estuarine hypoxia nationally (ref 4).

records.description: Four of the eight subsea cables serving Vietnam (SJC2, AAE-1, AAG and IA) were reported faulty in August 2026, affecting about 30% of the country's international internet traffic according to Light Reading. records.title: Record 2023 Caribbean marine heatwave began one to two months early and was followed by coral die-offs across the wider Caribbean
records.description: NOAA and University of Queensland scientists reported in December 2023 that extreme marine heatwaves covered the wider Caribbean, with record heat stress that started one to two months earlier than usual and lasted longer. A 2024 field study reported abnormal heat of 1 to 3 C above normal from March 2023, lasting more than five months in parts of the region, and a May 2026 study found most surveyed Caribbean sites had tipped into net reef erosion.

location.name: Wider Caribbean Sea (regional)
location.detail: Wider Caribbean including Florida-adjacent waters; longest heat stress reported around Jamaica, Haiti, Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica (ref 3)

records.layer_rationale: A basin-scale sea-surface heat anomaly is a physical climate event, with reef damage as its downstream effect.

notes.harm: NOAA's Coral Reef Watch coordinator said high mortality of staghorn and elkhorn corals had been reported in Florida, Puerto Rico and Mexico, and a study reported 60 to 100% of reef bleached in some areas with many patches dead (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources reports a fishery, tourism or port restriction tied to the 2023 heatwave itself (refs 1-5).
notes.scale: NOAA said nearly all reef regions in the wider Caribbean were exposed to about double the heat stress expected to cause mortality, a regional-sea extent (ref 1).
notes.duration: Abnormal heat lasted more than five months in parts of Haiti, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica, the longest on record there, which is months rather than a year (ref 3).
notes.significance: The finding rests on NOAA's report with the University of Queensland and Coral Reef Watch heat-stress products, which is an agency notice but no enforcement or declaration (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: NOAA: nearly all coral reef regions in the wider Caribbean, including Florida, were exposed to about double the heat stress expected to cause mortality (ref 1).

records.title: May to late-autumn 2023 ocean heat wave bleached reefs along Belize's barrier reef tract
records.description: A marine heat wave that began in May 2023 pushed water temperatures to about 32 C and kept them high until late autumn along an almost 200-mile stretch of Belize's barrier reefs and atolls. Belize's Fisheries Department confirmed bleaching in late June 2023 and ran monitoring surveys in marine reserves through November 2023.

notes.livelihoods: The opened sources report no closure or restriction on fishing or tourism tied to the heat wave (refs 1-3).

records.title: Hurricane Beryl's storm surge and winds devastated Carriacou, Petite Martinique and the Grenadines in July 2024
records.description: Beryl struck Carriacou as a Category 4 hurricane on 1 July 2024. Grenada's Meteorological Service reported 99% of buildings on Carriacou damaged or destroyed, and the NHC puts damage at USD 218 million for Grenada and USD 231 million for St. Vincent and the Grenadines.

records.description: Barbados's Coastal Zone Management Unit said in June 2026 that beaches that should be building were eroding, and attributed it to large pulses of South American river water raising water levels around the island. records.title: Caribbean surface waters are acidifying, with aragonite saturation falling at La Parguera and the only Caribbean time series left sparse
records.description: A 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science paper reports Caribbean surface aragonite saturation has declined by about 3% since pre-industrial levels and surface acidity rose roughly 10% from 1992 to 2015. La Parguera, Puerto Rico, hosts the only sustained CO2 time series, the CARIACO series off Venezuela was discontinued in 2017, and a Puerto Rico assessment finds aragonite saturation there falling 0.098 units per decade.

notes.harm: The papers report falling aragonite saturation, with La Parguera waters below the 3.7 carbonate-sediment dissolution threshold for up to 90% of the year, but no direct organism loss is documented (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, shellfish or tourism restriction linked to acidification appears in the opened sources (refs 1, 2).

notes.duration: Aragonite saturation at La Parguera has declined by 0.098 units per decade in monitoring since 2009 and surface acidity rose 10% over 1992-2015, so chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The sources are a peer-reviewed paper and a research framework; no regulator action or standard breach is cited, though SDG 14.3.1 reporting is mentioned (ref 1).

records.title: Mesoamerican Reef coral cover falls to 17% after the 2023 to 2024 bleaching, with about 40% of corals severely affected
records.description: The 2024 Healthy Reefs report card, covering 286 sites in Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, found coral cover down from 19% to 17% because of disease and the most severe bleaching on record, with about 40% of corals severely affected. Overall reef health is still rated poor and 62% of sites are poor or critical, although herbivorous and commercial fish biomass rose after stronger enforcement. Severe mortality at several iconic sites occurred after the survey ended, so the cover figure understates the loss.

location.detail: Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System along the western Caribbean coasts of Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, about 1,000 km long; the report card covers 18 subregions.

records.layer_rationale: Habitat loss on a regional reef system driven by thermal stress and disease.

notes.harm: Coral cover fell from 19% to 17% and about 40% of corals were severely affected by the 2023 bleaching, with severe mortality at several iconic reef sites (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited reports document no closure, advisory or lost fishery from the bleaching; they recommend tourism carrying-capacity limits only as a precaution (ref 1).
notes.scale: Monitoring across 286 sites and 18 subregions in four countries, a regional-sea scale rather than a single reef (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: Belize was under a NOAA level 2 alert in August 2023 and the report card, published in November 2024, still records disease and bleaching losses, so the damage spans more than a year (ref 3, ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal regional report card from 42 organisations rates the reef 'poor' overall and asks for a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area designation, but no enforcement order exists (ref 1).

records.title: Largest known Caribbean staghorn coral population at Coral Gardens, Belize, dies out in the 2023 marine heatwave
records.description: Annual quadrat surveys show live Acropora cervicornis at Coral Gardens, Belize, fell to zero between June and December 2023 during a heatwave that reached NOAA Alert Levels 4 and 5. The site held the largest documented extant population of this endangered coral in the Caribbean, with genets over 400 years old. A June 2024 survey found only scattered survivors at depth and on one reef-crest location, while algal cover rose.

notes.livelihoods: The abstract reports no fishery, tourism or closure effect at the site (ref 1).
notes.scale: A single reef site was surveyed, even though it was the largest known staghorn population in the Caribbean (ref 1).
notes.duration: Surveys ran from 2012 to June 2024 and show no recovery a year after the collapse, with algae up 13% and urchins down from 24.1 to 13.6 per square metre (ref 1).
notes.significance: The affected species is formally listed as endangered, and the loss is reported in a peer-presented AGU Fall Meeting abstract (ref 1); no enforcement or treaty action followed.

records.title: Bonaire reefs lose coral to record 2023 bleaching and the first outbreak of stony coral tissue loss disease
records.description: STINAPA Bonaire recorded visible thermal stress on 84% of surveyed coral colonies in 2023, the highest since monitoring began in 2016, and 19% of colonies showed partial or complete bleaching mortality by February 2024. A peer-reviewed study of the same year, after the disease was first sighted in March 2023, found SCTLD-sensitive coral cover on the leeward reefs fell from over 3% in 2014 to about 1% by 2023, nearly zero at City Limits and Klein transects.

notes.livelihoods: The report notes reef tourism earns about 125 million dollars a year on Bonaire but documents no closure or lost income (ref 1).
notes.scale: The surveys cover ten sites on one island's leeward coast (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: Bleaching ran through 2023 with follow-up mortality in February 2024, while SCTLD has been present since March 2023 and was still being tracked in the January 2025 paper (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The park manager STINAPA issued a formal monitoring report in December 2024 and the study was peer reviewed in January 2025, but no enforcement action is reported (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Stony coral tissue loss disease reaches Laughing Bird Caye, Belize, as it sweeps the Mesoamerican Reef
records.description: Stony coral tissue loss disease, first found on the Mesoamerican Reef at Puerto Morelos in July 2018, was detected for the first time in Laughing Bird Caye National Park, Belize, in May 2025. It has spread to 33 Caribbean countries and territories, affects more than 30 reef-building coral species and kills up to 90% of the most susceptible. Its cause is still unknown, and teams in Belize and Honduras treat colonies with antibiotic paste.

notes.significance: Reported by journalists and NGO responders; no regulator order, listing or emergency declaration appears in the sources (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Record sargassum influx buries the Mexican Caribbean coast in 2025, with 73,224 tonnes collected
records.description: The 2025 sargassum season on the Quintana Roo coast was the largest on record for the region, with 73,223.86 tonnes collected against 40,992 in 2024 and 65,646 in 2022. The University of South Florida found the Atlantic sargassum bloom in April 2025 was 40% above the June 2022 all-time high. A UNAM seagrass researcher warns the decomposing mats block light and suffocate seagrass meadows that shelter fish, shrimp and lobster and hold sediment on the beaches.

records.title: Turtle grass cover at Turneffe Atoll, Belize, falls from 65% to 24% and vanishes from shallow transects by 2025
records.description: SeagrassNet monitoring at two sites in Turneffe Atoll Marine Reserve showed Thalassia testudinum cover falling from 65.12% in 2022 to 23.85% in 2025, with seagrass gone entirely from the shallow transects at both sites. records.title: Jamaica holds a six-month conch close season each year after the Pedro Bank conch fishery collapsed
records.description: Jamaica's National Fisheries Authority runs an annual conch close season, 30 August 2025 to 28 February 2026 in the latest cycle, set at the peak spawning period. The measure follows an October 2019 Pedro Bank assessment that led to a 2019 ban and a 2020 closure, a reopening in 2022, and regulations made in 2023 with fines of up to $1 million for fishing in the close season.

records.layer_rationale: A queen conch stock was overfished to collapse and is managed under closed seasons and quotas.

notes.livelihoods: The NFA acknowledged the economic hardship of the closure, and the close season bars catching, selling or processing conch from 30 August 2025 to 28 February 2026 (ref 1, ref 5).

notes.duration: Closures and restrictions run from the 2019 ban through the 2022 reopening to the 2025-26 close season, now an annual measure (ref 4, ref 1, ref 3).
notes.significance: The close season is gazetted yearly and enforced under the Fisheries (Conservation of Queen Conch) Regulations, 2023, with fines up to $1 million or 12 months in jail, and up to $3 million or two years for illegal possession (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Honduran spiny lobster dive fishery has killed hundreds and paralyzed thousands of Miskito divers

records.title: Gulfstream barge bunker fuel spill oils about 15 km of Tobago's coast, with waste and liability still unresolved
records.description: An overturned barge named Gulfstream, towed by the tug Solo Creed, lodged about 200 m off Cove, Tobago, and leaked persistent Bunker Fuel C from 7 February 2024; the Prime Minister called it a national emergency. About 15 km of coastline, including beaches, mangroves, rivers and a reef, was oiled, and Trinidad and Tobago reported the incident to the IOPC Funds. In September 2025 the recovered waste was still stored in pits at Studley Park, the tug had escaped arrest and not been found, and compensation payments were set to run to 2027.

records.title: Venezuela and Trinidad and Tobago dispute oil spills in the Gulf of Paria after a May 2026 release
records.description: Trinidad and Tobago says a spill of about 10 barrels was detected on 1 May 2026 and contained the same day. Heritage Petroleum and the Energy Minister say field checks, Coast Guard and drone reconnaissance found no evidence of large amounts of oil.

records.title: Motagua River plastic and mixed waste again floods Omoa and Puerto Cortes beaches, Honduras
records.description: Each rainy season the Motagua River carries waste from Guatemala about 500 km to the Honduran Caribbean coast, covering beaches at Omoa and Puerto Cortes with plastic, styrofoam, bottles and hospital waste. Honduran officials and a local marine researcher said in September 2025 that the problem has lasted more than eleven years and worsens each winter, while Guatemala says a new river barrier retains 75-80% of floating plastic. Reporting also cites microplastics in regional fish and fishers forced farther offshore.

notes.livelihoods: Fishers say murky water and trash-filled nets force them to fish farther offshore, and tourism losses were estimated at US$2.6 million a month in 2022 (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The debris reaches two countries' coasts and Guatemalan studies cite about 8,500 tonnes of solid waste a year from the basin to the Caribbean (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The marine researcher quoted says the problem has lasted over eleven years and 'every winter is worse' (ref 1).
notes.significance: Officials proposed a bilateral agreement after the 2023 crisis and Guatemala reports a new barrier, but El Heraldo says no firm actions or deadlines followed (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Hakai (2022) cites about 80 families being relocated from Barra del Motagua; no current figure for the coast.

records.title: Recurring crude oil spills foul Lake Maracaibo and the Falcon coast in Venezuela
records.description: Venezuela's western oil region has frequent crude spills from ageing pipelines and facilities that reach Lake Maracaibo, which opens to the Gulf of Venezuela, and the Falcon coast. The NGO Clima 21 counted at least 43 spills from July 2023 to January 2024, 90% in Zulia and Falcon, and oil-coated turtles and birds were rescued. The government reports more than 140,000 tonnes of waste removed and pipeline replacement, but the state publishes no spill volumes.

location.detail: Zulia and Falcon states, western Venezuela, including submarine pipelines near Paraguana; Lake Maracaibo is brackish and connects to the Gulf of Venezuela.

notes.harm: Clima 21 reports 22 oil-coated animals treated in 2023 and a turtle found fully covered in oil in January 2024, and the government reports more than 140,000 tonnes of oily waste removed (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Shrimp catches in Lake Maracaibo were reportedly contaminated, per the Izquierda Diario summary of Observatory of Political Ecology cases (ref 2).
notes.scale: Spills were counted across Zulia (31) and Falcon (29) in 2022 and 90% of 43 spills in mid-2023 to early 2024 were in those two states (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Clima 21 describes the problem as about 100 years of accumulated spills and has seen no significant improvement since 2022 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The government reported more than 150 inspections of plants and industrial sites and a May 2024 sampling plan, which is an official response but no sanction or order is reported (ref 1).

records.title: Record sargassum strandings and hydrogen sulphide alerts on French Antilles and Mexican Caribbean shores
records.description: Sargassum washing ashore in large quantities decomposes and releases hydrogen sulphide and ammonia; in April 2023 the air-quality monitor Gwad'Air issued a red alert at Capesterre, Marie-Galante. Meteo-France forecast 'fort a tres fort' strandings for Guadeloupe and Martinique in April 2026, the port of La Desirade was blocked for several days, and the Atlantic sargassum belt reached a record 40 million tonnes in May 2025 according to the University of South Florida. Quintana Roo expected about 400,000 tonnes ashore in 2025.

location.name: French Antilles and Quintana Roo coasts
location.detail: Guadeloupe (including Marie-Galante and La Desirade), Martinique, and the Mexican Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo.

records.layer_rationale: Decaying sargassum biomass emits hydrogen sulphide and ammonia on shore; the bloom is linked to Atlantic nutrient enrichment, which these sources do not themselves document.

notes.harm: Gwad'Air recorded a red alert for hydrogen sulphide at Capesterre, Marie-Galante, in April 2023, and studies cited link the gases to health risks, while a French health council opinion in 2012 found H2S generally low near stored sargassum (refs 1, 5).
notes.livelihoods: The port of La Desirade was blocked for several days and Quintana Roo tourism suffered (refs 3, 4).
notes.scale: Strandings affect the French Antilles and the Mexican Caribbean coast, two shores of the regional sea (refs 2, 4).
notes.duration: France has run two national sargassum plans since 2018 and a third was announced in May 2025, so the problem is recurring (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Meteo-France issued a red-level 'tres fort' stranding warning for Martinique in April 2026 and Gwad'Air a red alert in 2023 (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: A 2018 Lancet letter reported more than 11,000 acute toxicity cases over eight months in Martinique and Guadeloupe (ref 1); no current-year figure was found.

key_measure.text: Gwad'Air issued a red alert at Capesterre, Marie-Galante, on 18 April 2023 for hydrogen sulphide from rotting sargassum (Environmental Health News, 24 April 2024).

Tourism in Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Cozumel is being hurt (ref 4).

records.title: Repeated fish die-offs from low oxygen in the Cienaga Grande de Santa Marta lagoon complex
records.description: Fishers and the regional authority Corpamag reported fish dying in the Cienaga Grande de Santa Marta from February 2024, with mojarra and robalo found floating, and attributed it to drought and heat linked to El Nino and low dissolved oxygen. A later undated report describes a further die-off, fishers digging a provisional canal to bring in freshwater, and a dispute with Corpamag over the work. Corpamag warned that decomposing fish pollute the water and can cause disease.

notes.scale: The die-offs are in one lagoon complex, with related events elsewhere in the sources (ref 1).

records.title: Marine litter in Roatan's mangroves and reefs fed by Honduran rivers and the Motagua
records.description: A November 2024 paper in the Gulf and Caribbean Fisheries Institute proceedings measures marine litter in Roatan's mangrove forest and examines litter in the gut of a dead American crocodile, noting thousands of tons of plastic reach the western Caribbean each year from the Motagua River and Honduran rivers. A March 2025 volunteer clean-up led by Waste Free Oceans with BICA and Roatan Marine Park removed over 1.71 tonnes of waste from beaches, mangroves and underwater sites. BICA says mismanaged solid waste in the Bay Islands threatens coastal ecosystems and health.

records.title: Guyana Court of Appeal overturns order for an unlimited Exxon guarantee covering Stabroek Block oil spills
records.description: On 7 May 2026 Guyana's Court of Appeal unanimously set aside a 2023 High Court order requiring ExxonMobil Guyana to provide an unlimited parent-company guarantee for spill liability under the Liza Phase 1 permit. The appeal court held that liability and financial assurance are distinct and that the Environmental Protection Agency may set a defined guarantee; ExxonMobil had offered a US$2 billion guarantee. The case was brought by two citizens, who argued the permit required unlimited assurance.

records.title: International Seabed Authority Council ends July 2026 session in Kingston without adopting the deep-sea mining code
records.description: The ISA Council ended Part II of its 31st session in Kingston, Jamaica, on 24 July 2026 without adopting the exploitation regulations known as the Mining Code. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence reported that environmental safeguards, liability, inspection and benefit-sharing remain unresolved and that experts expect talks to run three to four more years. records.title: Ocean Foundation warns of spill-liability gap as aging sanctioned tanker transits the Caribbean toward Venezuela

records.title: Hurricane Helene's record storm surge devastated Florida's Big Bend and flooded Tampa Bay
records.description: NHC's final report puts Helene's storm-surge inundation at 12 to 16 ft above ground from Keaton Beach to Steinhatchee, where about 80% of buildings were destroyed. The NOS gauge at Cedar Key read 9.30 ft above MHHW, the highest since 1914 and above the Idalia record of 6.89 ft a year earlier, and St. Petersburg reached a record 6.31 ft. Storm surge caused 14 deaths, all in Florida.

records.title: Hurricane Isaias brought storm surge to the Alabama and western Florida Panhandle coast in October 2026
records.description: Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of 9 October 2026 as a Category 2 hurricane with 105 mph winds, after a storm surge warning covered Dauphin Island to the Suwannee River. Forecasts ahead of landfall ranged up to 9 ft of surge, and NHC's overnight update lowered the Florida forecast to 2 to 4 ft; news reports describe surge overtopping fences and beach walkways in Destin. These are preliminary news reports and NHC has not yet issued a post-storm report.

records.title: Tulane-led study says relative sea-level rise in coastal Louisiana may be three times the global average
records.description: A Nature Sustainability study led by Tulane geologist Torbjorn Tornqvist, reported on 5 May 2026, says sea-level rise in coastal Louisiana may be about three times the global average because the land is subsiding. It finds that nearly all of Louisiana's coastal zone has lost residents since 2000, especially after major hurricanes, and urges planning now for relocation. The Gulf is expected to reach an ancient shoreline about 30 miles north of New Orleans, with no timeline given. The state's Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority chairman disputed the study on 27 May 2026.

notes.livelihoods: Nearly all of Louisiana's coastal zone has lost residents since 2000, which the researchers read as depopulation already under way (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The finding covers Louisiana's whole coastal zone (ref 2).
notes.duration: Subsidence-driven relative sea-level rise is chronic, and the population decline spans 2000 to 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study and news coverage, disputed by the state coastal agency chairman and New Orleans mayor in opinion remarks, with no regulatory notice or order in the cited pages (refs 1, 2, 4).

population_affected.note: The coverage gives no population count, only that nearly all coastal-zone areas lost residents since 2000.

records.title: Galveston's relative sea level is rising fast because of subsidence
records.description: A peer-reviewed study of the Galveston Pier 21 tide gauge found about 0.7 m of relative sea-level rise since 1909, with groundwater-driven aquifer compaction accounting for up to 85% of it, and projects another 1.9 m by 2100. A 2024 National Wildlife Federation study, as reported in March 2025, found about 8 inches of rise in 14 years at Galveston. NOAA data show Galveston Pier had 23 high-tide flood days in the 2023-24 year, more than predicted.

records.description: NOAA's high-tide flooding outlook reports Eagle Point, Texas, had 28 flood days in the 2023-24 meteorological year and Galveston Pier 23 days, while four eastern Gulf stations set records, including St. Petersburg with 6 days; Clearwater Beach had 7. records.title: Galveston Bay's proposed storm-surge barrier has $500,000 in federal funding against a $21 billion federal share
records.description: The Coastal Texas Project, known as the Ike Dike, would put gates across the mouth of Galveston Bay flanked by dunes. As of December 2025 the federal government had appropriated $500,000 for a small component against a $21 billion federal share, while Texas had appropriated $950 million to the Gulf Coast Protection District. Design contracts were approved for the gates and the dunes, and the Army Corps says design could take two to five years and construction 10 to 15 more.

records.title: Sea-level rise could flood 581,000 to over 800,000 hectares of Mexico's Gulf and Caribbean coast by 2100

records.title: Gulf of Mexico acidification is documented but has no long-term basin time series
records.description: A 2025 paper from a US-Mexico-Cuba summit states that acidification is occurring in the open Gulf and estuaries but that no long-term time series exists for the Gulf, with gaps in nearshore, deep and karst waters. A 2018 study at the Flower Garden Banks found decreases in subsurface pH and aragonite saturation larger than in other tropical and subtropical waters. USGS started a 2025 analysis of acidification monitoring at Gulf Islands and Padre Island National Seashores.

records.title: Record 2023 heatwave bleached every monitored Florida Keys coral and killed up to 43% of tracked colonies on inshore reefs
records.description: Summer 2023 was the most severe marine heatwave on record for Florida's coral reef; a peer-reviewed study of over 4,200 brain and boulder coral colonies at nine reefs found 100% bleaching. Offshore reefs lost almost no tracked colonies, but at two inshore reefs 43.1% (Newfound Harbor) and 30% (Cheeca Rocks) of colonies died completely, and the authors report branching Acropora corals and inshore octocorals locally extinct at most sites. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) calls it the worst bleaching event ever recorded in Florida.

location.name: Florida Keys reef tract (Keys National Marine Sanctuary)
location.detail: United States, Florida Keys from Key Largo to the Dry Tortugas; the Keys sit at the Gulf of Mexico / Straits of Florida boundary.

records.layer_rationale: Habitat loss and coral mortality driven by thermal stress on a reef tract.

notes.harm: Newfound Harbor lost 43.1% of tracked colonies completely and Cheeca Rocks 30%, and Acropora corals were locally extinct at most sites (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited study and FWC page describe no fishery, dive-site or beach closure tied to the bleaching, so no disruption is scored (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: FWC lists the Keys, Dry Tortugas, Marquesas and southern Miami-Dade among the most heavily impacted areas, and the study monitored nine reefs (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: FWC places heat from mid-July with water not cooling until October 2023, and recovery lesions were still reported on Orbicella faveolata afterwards (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: FWC's agency page records it as the worst bleaching event ever recorded in Florida and NOAA reported the 2023 heat as unlike any other in the region's recorded history (refs 2, 3); no regulatory action is cited.

records.title: Fewer than 22% of outplanted staghorn and under 5% of elkhorn corals survived the 2023 heatwave at Mission: Iconic Reefs sites
records.description: NOAA's Mission: Iconic Reefs assessment, reported in early 2024, found that fewer than 22% of about 1,500 outplanted staghorn corals and fewer than 5% of about 1,000 outplanted elkhorn corals remained alive across five of the seven restoration sites. Looe Key Reef had no live staghorn or elkhorn in the sampled areas, and live staghorn persisted only at the two northernmost reefs. NOAA has since shifted restoration toward heat-tolerant stock and massive brain and boulder corals.

records.title: Rice's whale, about 51 left, loses Gulf vessel-speed protections while NOAA's 2025 opinion finds extinction risk
records.description: The Rice's whale, found only in the Gulf, numbers about 51 animals (2022 stock assessment). NOAA denied a 10-knot vessel-speed petition in October 2023, the Fifth Circuit removed habitat protections from Lease Sale 261 in November 2023, and in February 2025 new rules dropped a recommendation that large vessels slow down in its habitat. NOAA's revised May 2025 biological opinion found that, without precautionary measures, oil and gas activities could lead to extinction, and Earthjustice sued in May 2025.

notes.scale: The whale's range covers the northern Gulf of Mexico, a regional sea, mostly in the northeastern Gulf (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 2020 opinion was vacated in August 2024 and the revised one issued May 2025, while the critical habitat final decision is delayed to July 2027 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The species is ESA-listed as endangered, the Fifth Circuit ruled on 14 November 2023 and a federal court vacated the 2020 opinion (refs 1, 4).

records.title: Kemp's ridley nests hit records on the Texas coast, 449 in 2025 and over 650 in 2026, yet the species remains critically endangered
records.description: Texas recorded 449 Kemp's ridley nests in 2025, a state record, and more than 650 in 2026, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The National Park Service says the species remains critically endangered, nesting has not met recovery targets since growth stalled after 2009, and Mexico has left some nests to incubate unprotected on the beach since 2004. records.title: Study links Bonnet Carré Spillway openings to dolphin skin lesions and strandings in the Mississippi Sound; coalition sues Army Corps
records.description: A peer-reviewed study of 2010 to 2021 data found that the prevalence of common bottlenose dolphins with skin lesions in the western Mississippi Sound, and the frequency of stranded dolphins across the Sound, were significantly related to Bonnet Carré Spillway discharge. The Corps diverted 6.4 trillion gallons in 2011 and 10.07 trillion gallons in 2019. In January 2024 the Mississippi Sound Coalition sued the Army Corps, alleging the 2019 opening killed many resident dolphins without a Marine Mammal Protection Act take permit.

location.name: Mississippi Sound
location.detail: United States, Mississippi and Alabama coast, Lake Borgne and Biloxi Marsh to Dauphin Island; discharge comes from the Bonnet Carré Spillway in Louisiana.

records.layer_rationale: Mortality and disease in marine mammals linked to river diversion freshwater.

notes.harm: The study found lesion prevalence and stranding frequency significantly related to spillway discharge, and the 2018-2019 stranding relationship highly significant (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The coalition alleges the 2019 opening severely harmed the Sound's oyster population, an allegation in a complaint and not a finding (ref 2).
notes.scale: The effect is mapped across one sound along the Mississippi and Alabama coast (ref 1).
notes.duration: Diversions in 2011, 2019 and lower-discharge years coincided with lesions and strandings across 2010 to 2021, a recurring pattern (ref 1).
notes.significance: A complaint was filed on 22 January 2024 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi under the Marine Mammal Protection Act; no ruling is cited (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The prevalence of dolphins with skin lesions in the western Mississippi Sound was significantly related to Bonnet Carré Spillway discharge, not to coastal stream discharge.

records.title: Gulf shrimp fleet shrinks under record-low dockside prices as NOAA moves to extend the permit moratorium
records.description: NOAA says Gulf shrimp stocks are healthy but profitability and effort keep declining, with valid Gulf shrimp permits down from 1,933 in 2008 to 1,287 in 2024, and in September 2026 the Louisiana Shrimp Association asked the administration to limit imports. Reports in August and September 2026 describe shrimp selling for 50 to 60 cents a pound against diesel near 5 dollars a gallon. Federal disaster requests from Louisiana and Alabama in 2023 were listed by NOAA as withdrawn or ineligible.

notes.duration: NMFS ties the effort decline to fuel costs and import-driven price drops seen since the early 2000s, and the permit moratorium dates to 2006 (ref 1).

records.description: Florida's wildlife commission voted in November 2025 to reopen Apalachicola Bay to limited oyster harvest from 1 January 2026, ending a closure that began in 2020 after the fishery collapsed in 2013. records.title: Campeche and Yucatan Octopus maya catches fall short: Campeche down in 2024, red tide in 2025, weak start to 2026

records.title: Gulf hypoxic zone off Louisiana and Texas measured at 6,705 sq mi in 2024, 4,402 in 2025 and 1,332 in 2026
records.description: NOAA-supported summer cruises led by LUMCON measured the bottom-water low-oxygen zone off Louisiana and Texas at about 6,705 square miles in July 2024, 4,402 in July 2025 and 1,332 in July 2026. The 2026 zone came in far below the June forecasts of 7,027 (NOAA) and 7,532 (LSU) square miles; GCOOS attributes the small size to below-average river discharge and Tropical Storm Bertha mixing the water column. The Hypoxia Task Force goal is a five-year average below 1,900 square miles by 2035; the average stood at 4,755 after the 2025 measurement.

location.name: Louisiana-Texas continental shelf
location.detail: Bottom waters of the northern Gulf shelf off Louisiana and Texas, fed by the Mississippi-Atchafalaya river basin nutrient load.

records.layer_rationale: Agricultural nutrient runoff drives algal growth whose decay strips oxygen from bottom water each summer.

notes.harm: NOAA defines the zone as seafloor water at 2 mg/L oxygen or less; in 2025 about 2.8 million acres of habitat were unavailable to fish and bottom-dwelling species (ref 6).
notes.livelihoods: LSU says low oxygen stresses or kills fish, shrimp and crabs, and NOAA says it drives fish and shrimp out of the area (refs 2, 5); no closure is documented in the cited pages.
notes.scale: The zone covers shelf bottom waters off Louisiana and Texas, a national coastline segment rather than the whole Gulf (ref 4).
notes.duration: Measured every summer since 1985 (38 years of measurement by 2024, 40 by 2026) (refs 7, 3), so chronic and recurring.
notes.significance: The Mississippi River/Gulf Hypoxia Task Force has a formal goal of a five-year average below 1,900 sq mi by 2035; the 2025 average of 4,755 sq mi is more than twice that (ref 5).

records.title: Main Pass Oil Gathering pipeline released 1.1 million gallons of crude; record $9.6 million penalty proposed
records.description: An 18-inch subsea pipeline of the Main Pass Oil Gathering system released about 1.1 million gallons of crude oil on 15 November 2023 in Louisiana state waters southeast of Venice. The NTSB found a fitting lost its seal after geohazard-driven pipeline movement and that the control room did not shut the system down despite leak indications. PHMSA issued a notice of probable violation on 31 December 2025 and proposed a $9,622,054 civil penalty, which it calls the largest ever proposed in a pipeline safety case; the operator disputes parts of it.

records.title: Karenia brevis red tide bloom after Hurricane Milton spread over 200 miles of Florida's southwest Gulf coast
records.description: A Karenia brevis bloom that began near Tampa Bay after Hurricane Milton in October 2024 stretched more than 200 miles from Tampa Bay to Key West by early February 2025, with Lee and Charlotte counties at its centre. Local health departments advised against more than a dozen beaches, and dead fish, eels and a few sea turtles washed ashore between Sarasota and Key West. WGCU reported the bloom had dissipated by mid-March 2025, and FWC reported only background to very low K. brevis levels on 9 October 2026.

records.title: Court finds Lease Sale 259 review inadequate on Rice's whale and climate; Interior reaffirms the sale in 2026
records.description: In March 2025 the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia held that BOEM's environmental review for Gulf Lease Sale 259 (March 2023) did not adequately assess greenhouse gas emissions or impacts on the Rice's whale, and ordered briefing on remedy. In February 2026 BOEM issued a Record of Decision reaffirming Lease Sales 259 and 261 on their original terms, relying on a new programmatic EIS; the remedy question and the stayed Lease Sale 261 challenge remain open.

records.title: Mandated Gulf lease sales BBG1 to BBG3 have run and a fourth (BBG4) of about 80 million acres is proposed at a 12.5% royalty
records.description: Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21) BOEM must hold 30 Gulf of America lease sales, the first of which (BBG1, December 10, 2025) drew $300.4 million in high bids on 181 blocks and the second (BBG2, March 11, 2026) $47.0 million on 25 blocks. A Congressional Research Service report says the whale-habitat exclusion and 10-knot vessel terms proposed for Lease Sale 261 are not part of these mandated sales. On 9 October 2026 the Marine Minerals Administration proposed a fourth sale, BBG4, offering 15,104 blocks over about 80.4 million acres, with bids opening on 10 March 2027 and a comment deadline of 8 December 2026. Baird Maritime reports the first three sales (December 2025, March 2026, August 2026) brought $430 million in combined high bids.

notes.significance: Each sale follows a formal Notice of Sale; the BBG2 final notice was published in the Federal Register on February 5, 2026 (ref 4).
