records.title: Louisiana federal court rules against NMFS jeopardy finding for Rice's whale and oil and gas vessels
records.description: NMFS's May 20, 2025 biological opinion on Gulf oil and gas activities found jeopardy to the Rice's whale, a species NMFS's 2022 assessment put at 51 individuals, with an alternative focused on vessel monitoring technology. On January 23, 2026 the Western District of Louisiana granted summary judgment to Louisiana, the American Petroleum Institute and Chevron, holding the jeopardy determination and alternatives violated the ESA and APA; remedy briefing was ordered and a parallel Maryland case by environmental groups is pending.

notes.harm: NMFS's 2025 opinion found oil and gas vessel operations likely to jeopardize the whale through strike risk; the court record quotes the bureaus' assessment that neither of two known strikes was attributed to oil and gas activity, so harm is potential (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Industry groups warned a gap in the opinion could halt nearly all Gulf offshore operations, but no shutdown occurred in the cited sources (ref 2).
notes.scale: The whale occurs only in the Gulf, where NMFS places it along the 100 to 400 m shelf break; the 2022 estimate was 51 animals (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Litigation over the biological opinions began with a 2020 suit and the 2024 Maryland vacatur, and the Louisiana ruling came on January 23, 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Judge James Cain Jr. granted summary judgment on January 23, 2026 against NMFS's jeopardy determination and parts of its incidental take statement (ref 1).

records.title: More than 2,700 Gulf wells and 500 platforms overdue for decommissioning, with bonds far below estimated costs
records.description: A January 2024 GAO audit found that as of June 2023 more than 2,700 wells and 500 platforms in the Gulf were overdue for decommissioning under BSEE deadlines, while BOEM held about $3.5 billion in supplemental bonds against estimated costs of $40 to $70 billion. All four GAO recommendations remained open per GAO's page, and Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas sued over BOEM's 2024 financial assurance rule.

notes.scale: GAO counted more than 2,700 wells and 500 platforms overdue across Gulf leases, over 75% of end-of-lease and idle infrastructure (ref 1).
notes.duration: Operators missed the one-year deadline for over 40% of wells and 50% of platforms on leases that ended 2010 to 2022 (ref 1).
notes.significance: GAO issued four recommendations that Interior accepted, and as of March 2026 all four were still open (ref 1).

population_affected.note: The audit counts wells and platforms rather than people.

key_measure.text: As of June 2023, more than 2,700 wells and 500 platforms in the Gulf were overdue for decommissioning, and BOEM held about $3.5 billion in supplemental bonds against $40 to $70 billion in estimated costs (GAO-24-106229).

records.title: Gulf's only offshore wind lease off Lake Charles cancelled in 2026 after the second sale was called off
records.description: BOEM's first Gulf offshore wind auction on August 29, 2023 produced one lease, OCS-G 37334 off Lake Charles, Louisiana, won by RWE with a $5.6 million bid; the Galveston areas drew no bids and a second sale was cancelled in July 2024 for lack of competitive interest. On August 4, 2026 Interior cancelled and rescinded the lease under a settlement in which RWE relinquished its U.S. leases for $1.22 billion.

records.title: Dredging spills for CP2 LNG terminal coat oyster reefs in Calcasieu Lake, Louisiana
records.description: An August 4, 2025 dredge sediment release tied to Venture Global's CP2 LNG construction put an estimated 9,000 to 18,000 cubic yards of material south of the No-Name Weir into Calcasieu Lake, according to a fishers' petition; Louisiana wildlife officials confirmed sediment on public oyster reefs and elevated mortality, without directly attributing it to the company. Litigation followed, and on August 25, 2026 the D.C. Circuit upheld FERC's approval of CP2, finding a moderate but not significant effect on commercial fishing.

location.name: Calcasieu Lake (Big Lake) and No-Name Weir
location.detail: Cameron Parish, southwest Louisiana, next to the existing Calcasieu Pass LNG terminal; CP2 is planned at up to 28 million tonnes per year of LNG.

records.layer_rationale: Sediment smothering of oyster reefs and marsh in a coastal estuary from LNG terminal dredging.

notes.harm: Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries confirmed in September 2025 sediment deposits on several public oyster reefs and elevated mortality near the weir, and the Cameron Parish Port said mud filled more than 260 acres of vegetated marsh (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Twenty commercial fishers and seafood businesses sued on July 30, 2026 alleging business losses, and an oyster farm alleges the spill destroyed its crop; the allegations are unproven (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The documented effects are in one lake and its adjacent marsh near the terminal site (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The petition lists failures on August 4, 2025, December 17, 2025, January 16, 2026 and February 14, 2026, about six months of recurring incidents (ref 2).
notes.significance: A Calcasieu Parish judge ordered scientific testing on April 14, 2026 and the D.C. Circuit ruled on August 25, 2026 on FERC's approval of CP2 (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: The sources count fishers in a suit (20 plaintiffs) but report no affected-population figure.

key_measure.text: Dredged sediment spilled south of the No-Name Weir on August 4, 2025, releasing an estimated 9,000 to 18,000 cubic yards into Calcasieu Lake, per the fishers' court petition.

records.title: Court vacates Rio Grande LNG approval in 2024; FERC's 2025 remand order is challenged again
records.description: On August 6, 2024 the D.C. Circuit vacated FERC's remand authorization for the 27 million tonne per year Rio Grande LNG terminal at the Port of Brownsville, Texas, because FERC should have prepared a supplemental EIS; petitioners had argued FERC failed to weigh environmental justice and greenhouse gas impacts. FERC issued an Order on Remand on August 29, 2025, and on December 15, 2025 the South Texas Environmental Justice Network, the City of Port Isabel and the Sierra Club petitioned the D.C. Circuit to set it aside.

notes.significance: The D.C. Circuit vacated the authorization on August 6, 2024 and a new petition (No. 25-1284) was filed on December 15, 2025 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Louisiana cancels the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion after permit suspension, leaving land loss unaddressed
records.description: The Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, intended to divert Mississippi River water and sediment into the Barataria Basin and build land, was cancelled on July 17, 2025, announced by Louisiana's coastal authority and the Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group, after the Army Corps suspended its permit. More than $600 million had been spent without completing the project; the basin has lost roughly 432 square miles of land since 1932 and the state has pivoted to a smaller diversion at Myrtle Grove.

location.name: Barataria Basin and Barataria Bay
location.detail: Southeast Louisiana, Jefferson and Plaquemines parishes; the diversion was designed to divert up to 75,000 cubic feet of river water per second.

records.layer_rationale: A government decision to end a coastal restoration project amid permitting, cost and fisheries disputes.

notes.harm: The basin has lost roughly 432 square miles of land since 1932 per ASCE, and the 2022 EIS projected up to about 17,300 acres of new land by 2050 that will not be built (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Oyster and brown shrimp concerns drove opposition, but no fishery closure from the diversion is documented, since it was never completed (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: The cancellation concerns one basin project, while the land loss it targeted is basin-scale along coastal Louisiana (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Land loss has run since 1932 and the project spanned construction from August 2023 to cancellation in July 2025 (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Army Corps suspended the project's permit and the trustees cut the authorized budget from $2.26 billion to $618.52 million on July 17, 2025 (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure appears in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The authorized budget was reduced from $2.26 billion to $618.52 million, reflecting funds already spent, as the project was cancelled on July 17, 2025 (Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group, as reported by Fox 8).

records.title: Crude oil spill from Dos Bocas marine terminal fouls Tabasco beaches and halts fishing in May 2025
records.description: From May 4, 2025 residents and fishermen in Paraíso, Tabasco reported tar and crude on beaches near Mexico's Dos Bocas marine terminal, with beaches closed along nearly 17 km of coast, fish deaths reported and fishing paralyzed. Mexico's environmental safety regulator ASEA confirmed the spill came from the Dos Bocas marine terminal and asked Pemex for a detailed report on its causes; oil also reached mangroves and the Mecoacán lagoon, per local reports.

location.detail: Paraíso, Tabasco, southern Gulf of Mexico (Bay of Campeche), next to the Olmeca (Dos Bocas) refinery; Spanish-language sources.

records.layer_rationale: Hydrocarbon release from a marine oil terminal contaminating coast, mangroves and fisheries.

notes.harm: Residents reported dead sábalo, jurel and bonito and effects on oyster larvae and pelicans, and tar reached mangroves and the Mecoacán lagoon, but findings by authorities were not found (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Public beaches were closed for nearly 17 km of coast and fishing was paralyzed, per local reports (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The affected stretch is one coastal municipality's shoreline and an adjoining lagoon (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The reports describe the first days after May 4, 2025, and no later duration is documented in the pages opened (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: ASEA, an agency of Mexico's environment ministry, began a supervision of Pemex and requested a detailed report on causes (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: Local reports describe fishers, restaurants and beach services affected but give no count.

records.title: Corpus Christi Ship Channel deepening for supertankers would dredge 46 million cubic yards into the Gulf
records.description: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority has applied to deepen the ship channel from 54 to about 75 feet so fully laden very large crude carriers can load, extending the entrance channel into the Gulf (a roughly 10-mile extension in the draft EIS; the Corps' 2019 notice described 13.8 miles of deepening); the Army Corps' June 2022 draft EIS puts new-work dredging at about 46 million cubic yards. A 2026 conference abstract by a University of Texas marine scientist flags larval-recruitment and brine-discharge concerns, and no permit decision was found in the sources opened.

location.detail: Nueces County, Texas, from Harbor Island through Aransas Pass into the Gulf; the port exports about 2.4 million barrels of oil per day (UT Marine Science Institute abstract).

notes.harm: The draft EIS lists direct inshore impacts including 16.61 acres of tidal wetlands and 6.88 acres of seagrass, and an abstract flags risk to larval recruitment, a potential harm (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or route restriction is documented; the project would enlarge rather than restrict shipping (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Effects are centred on one channel and adjacent bays, though the entrance channel would extend roughly 10 miles into the Gulf (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The application was filed January 3, 2019 and the draft EIS appeared in June 2022, with the issue still discussed in May 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A Corps Draft Environmental Impact Statement and a FAST-41 permitting track are formal federal processes, but no decision was found (ref 1).

population_affected.note: The EIS and abstract give no population figure.

records.title: Record northeast Pacific marine heatwave rivals the Blob and persists off the US West Coast into 2026
records.description: NOAA Fisheries reports that a marine heatwave first tracked in May 2025 reached a record average northeast Pacific temperature of 20.6 C on 9 September 2025 and has dominated West Coast waters since, strengthening again after weakening in autumn. NOAA says its ecological impact has so far been much less than the 2013 to 2016 Blob, but harmful algal blooms, reduced salmon ocean survival and unusual species locations are being tracked. The tracker records 2026 daily sea-surface temperature records at some California Current sites.

location.name: California Current and offshore northeast Pacific
location.type: Marine heatwave footprint (open coast and offshore)
location.detail: US West Coast from Southern California to Alaska and British Columbia, extending offshore across the North Pacific; Oregon and Washington nearshore waters largely spared in 2025.

records.layer_rationale: A physical ocean-temperature anomaly driven by persistent atmospheric conditions.

notes.harm: NOAA says the event has had much less ecological impact than the Blob so far, but is tracking harmful algal blooms that sicken marine mammals and reduced salmon ocean survival (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: NOAA lists shellfish fishery closures from harmful algal blooms as a possible consequence and notes lower salmon survival (ref 1); no specific closure is cited, so limited.
notes.scale: NOAA Blobtracker put the early September 2025 footprint near 3 million square miles, reaching from Kamchatka to California (ref 3), so basin-scale.
notes.duration: Tracked since May 2025; NOAA says it has dominated West Coast waters since summer 2025 and strengthened again after receding in October and November (ref 1); the tracker was updated in September 2026 with the heatwave still expanding (ref 2).
notes.significance: NOAA Fisheries published a formal feature story and maintains an operational tracker designating the event NEP25A (refs 1, 2); no emergency declaration cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: On 9 September 2025 the northeast Pacific reached its highest average temperature on record, 20.6 C (about 69 F), nearly half a degree warmer than any previous record (NOAA Fisheries).

records.title: Recurring Gulf of Alaska marine heatwaves weaken nutrient-carrying eddies; a new heatwave formed offshore in May 2026
records.description: A Brown University study summarised by NOAA Climate.gov found that marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Alaska have become more frequent since 2013 and weaken coastal circulation and eddies that carry nutrients to phytoplankton. NOAA's heatwave tracker reports that a second 2026 feature, NEP26A, formed in the offshore Gulf of Alaska in May 2026, and NOAA noted unusual tuna catches in Alaska in autumn 2025.

records.title: Surf and bluff erosion repeatedly close the LOSSAN rail line at San Clemente and threaten the Del Mar bluffs
records.description: The coastal rail line through San Clemente has faced repeated closures over five years from surf on one side and fragile bluffs on the other; emergency work in April 2025 halted trains for about six weeks, and high surf eroded ballast again in June and July 2026. The city faces a sand deficit of about 3 million cubic yards, and officials are studying moving the line inland. At Del Mar, about 1.7 miles of track follows a fragile bluff and stabilization is underway.

location.detail: Orange and San Diego counties, southern California; 7 miles of low-lying track at San Clemente and about 1.7 miles on the Del Mar bluffs.

notes.scale: The documented damage is a localized stretch of coast: 7 miles at San Clemente and about 1.7 miles at Del Mar (ref 2).
notes.duration: AP says closures have recurred over the past five years (ref 1); a king tide eroded ballast on 16 June 2026 and surf did so in late July 2026 (ref 2).
notes.significance: AP reports California's recent emergency declaration for the line (ref 1); OCTA ordered emergency stabilization of four vulnerable areas (ref 3).

records.title: Pacifica pier closed and cafe demolished as seawall fails; local emergency declared over coastal erosion
records.description: The Pacifica Municipal Pier closed indefinitely in June 2026 after structural cracking at the seawall connection, and the city demolished the Chit Chat Cafe at its entrance. The city council declared a local emergency, and the city says erosion had already forced demolition of three apartment buildings. Rep. Sam Liccardo says $50 million for the more than $80 million seawall project was revoked in 2025, and Pacifica has received no funding for it.

records.title: Quinault Nation relocates Taholah lower village uphill from sea-level rise, storm surge and tsunami risk
records.description: The Quinault Indian Nation is moving its two villages at the Quinault River mouth about a mile uphill because of rising seas, flooding, storm surge and tsunami risk. The relocation is estimated to cost about $100 million; a $25 million federal grant and HUD housing funds for six elder homes were announced in 2022 and 2024. The tribe says relocating a whole village will take a long time.

records.title: Record king tides and storm flood Highway 101 and Marin communities in San Francisco Bay, January 2026
records.description: On 3 January 2026 record king tides combined with a storm to flood a 15-mile stretch from the Sausalito area to San Rafael, closing Highway 101 exits and trapping cars in water 3 to 4 feet deep. KQED reports hundreds of structures were affected and the tide reached a 28-year high at the San Francisco gauge. An $18 million federal grant for a neighborhood sheet-pile wall has been paused for months.

records.title: Aging coastal levees at Stanwood and Grays Harbor face king-tide flood risk as federal funding stalls
records.description: A January 2026 king tide gouged a half-mile of the century-old levee at Stanwood on Skagit Bay, and emergency repairs were funded in July 2026 with $1.75 million. At Grays Harbor, a planned 11-mile levee for Aberdeen and Hoquiam awaits promised federal funds after FEMA cancelled its BRIC program in April 2025 and a federal judge ordered it restored. NOAA researchers put the chance of a very strong El Nino by autumn 2026 at 80 percent, which UW oceanographer Ian Miller says can raise Pacific Northwest sea levels.

notes.harm: Waves and wind gouged a half-mile of the Stanwood outer levee in January 2026; a 2022 county study estimates failure could displace 1,100 people and damage $480 million of buildings (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or fishery restriction is reported; the levees are protective projects not yet built or repaired (ref 1).
notes.scale: The two sites span Puget Sound and the Washington outer coast, covering about 5,000 Grays Harbor properties and Stanwood (ref 1).
notes.duration: Grays Harbor cities have sought levees since the 2015 floods, and the Stanwood levee is about a century old (ref 1).
notes.significance: A federal judge ordered FEMA's cancelled BRIC program restored in December 2025, and Stanwood repairs received emergency approvals (ref 1).

records.title: Near-bottom hypoxia now covers up to 56 percent of the Oregon and Washington shelf in strong upwelling years
records.description: A 2024 Scientific Reports study found near-bottom hypoxia over about 15,500 square kilometres, nearly half the shelf inshore of 200 metres, in summer 2021, with the hypoxic share up from an average of about 2 percent in 1950 to 1980 and 24 percent in 2009 to 2018. Researchers tie the trend to stronger upwelling winds under climate change. NOAA notes hypoxic zones are increasingly forming on Dungeness crab and other fishing grounds.

location.name: Oregon and Washington continental shelf
location.detail: Near-bottom waters inshore of the 200 m isobath off Oregon and Washington, with a mid-shelf band extending 450 km along north-central Oregon and Washington.

records.layer_rationale: Declining dissolved oxygen is a physical ocean-chemistry change with ecosystem effects.

notes.harm: Barth et al. measured oxygen below the harmful 61 micromoles per kilogram threshold across 15,500 square kilometres in 2021 (refs 1, 2); the Daily Astorian reported fish and crab trapped and dying (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: NCCOS says hypoxic zones are forming on once-productive fishing grounds and the Oregon Dungeness fishery averages $39.5 million a year (ref 3); the Quinault Nation closed crab season early in 2018 (ref 5).
notes.scale: The hypoxic band spans the shelf from Oregon into Washington, about 450 km along the coast (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Oxygen maps from 1950 show a steady decline, and hypoxia has formed nearly every summer since 2002 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: NOAA's Integrated Ecosystem Assessment published the finding, and NOAA funded a sensor project from 2018 to 2025 (refs 1, 3); no regulatory action.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The hypoxic fraction of near-bottom shelf water rose from about 2% (1950 to 1980) to 24% (2009 to 2018) and reached 56% in 2021 (Barth et al., Scientific Reports 2024).

records.title: Northern California bull kelp still about 95% lost a decade on, with purple urchin barrens persisting
records.description: Mongabay reported in September 2025 that about 95% of Northern California bull kelp died during the warm-water years of 2013 to 2017 and has not recovered at scale, except in a few coves under intensive restoration. At Casper Cove off Fort Bragg the reporter counted about 120 purple urchins in roughly one square metre, against about 2 per square metre at which kelp thrives. A July 2026 Times-Standard piece repeats a roughly 95% canopy loss since 2014 from Landsat analysis.

location.name: Northern California coast (Sonoma to Humboldt)

records.title: Sunflower sea star still not finally listed three years after the proposed threatened rule, and a lawsuit filed in June 2026
records.description: NOAA Fisheries proposed on 16 March 2023 to list the sunflower sea star as threatened, citing a range-wide decline of 94.3% after the 2013 to 2017 sea star wasting outbreak. NOAA's species page, updated September 2025, still shows the status as proposed. The Center for Biological Diversity sued on 22 June 2026 in the Northern District of California to force a final decision, alleging NMFS missed the 12-month statutory deadline.

records.title: Humpback whale entanglements in Dungeness crab gear delay California's 2025-26 season and reach a record in Oregon
records.description: California confirmed four humpbacks entangled in Dungeness crab gear in 2025 plus four more in unknown gear, and new rules adopted on 21 October 2025 delayed the statewide commercial opener to at least 1 January 2026. A juvenile humpback tangled in two sets of crab gear off Eureka in June 2025 led to closure of the northern zones. An August 2026 report says at least 400 whales were caught in gear off Washington, Oregon and California from 2015 to 2025, and Oregon logged at least four humpbacks in crab gear in 2025.

records.title: H5N1 bird flu kills about 100 northern elephant seals at Año Nuevo, the first detection in the species

records.title: Alaska common murres show no recovery after a heatwave die-off of about 4 million birds
records.description: A study published in Science on 12 December 2024 estimated that the 2014 to 2016 marine heatwave killed about 4 million common murres in Alaska, roughly half the state's population, far above the earlier estimate of about 1 million. Monitoring of 13 colonies in the Gulf of Alaska and eastern Bering Sea found no recovery through 2022. Researchers link the deaths to starvation as Pacific cod, a key prey fish, fell about 80% between 2013 and 2017.

notes.duration: Monitoring from 2016 to 2022 found no signs of recovery (ref 2), so the loss persists years after the heatwave ended.
notes.significance: The evidence is a peer-reviewed study and press coverage (refs 1, 2); the sources record no agency listing or enforcement action.

records.title: California's Fish and Game Commission approves two new tribally co-led marine protected areas, Mishopshno and Point Sal, after voting on 15 petitions
records.description: California's Fish and Game Commission voted on the remaining 15 marine protected area petitions at its 15 and 16 October 2026 hearings. It approved the Mishopshno State Marine Conservation Area at Carpinteria on a 3-2 vote and a 9.18 square mile Point Sal SMCA, the first new MPA approvals in 12 years, and denied or saw withdrawn proposals for Santa Cruz, the Channel Islands, Cabrillo and Catalina. The Department of Fish and Wildlife had recommended denying all petitions; regulations still have to be written and protections may take a couple of years.

location.name: California marine protected area network
location.detail: 124 MPAs along California's roughly 1,100-mile coast; the best-documented petition is the Mishopshno MPA at Carpinteria, Santa Barbara County.

records.layer_rationale: A state decision on whether to strengthen or weaken coastal protected areas.

notes.harm: Some of the 15 pending petitions would weaken existing protections while others would strengthen the network (refs 1, 2); no ecological damage from the pending changes is documented.
notes.livelihoods: Carpinteria's fishing community opposes the Mishopshno MPA as limiting access to a local food source and pastime (ref 1); recreational and commercial fishers told the Commission they have already lost ground to restrictions (ref 3).
notes.scale: The network spans California's roughly 1,100-mile coast and about 16% of state waters (ref 2).
notes.duration: The petition process has run since December 2023 and the Decadal Management Review finished in January 2023 (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Commission voted on 15 October 2026 to approve the Mishopshno SMCA 3-2 and the Point Sal SMCA, a formal decision against the Department of Fish and Wildlife's recommendation (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Roberts Bank Terminal 2 container expansion in the Fraser estuary approved despite findings of significant effects
records.description: Canada approved the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority's Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in 2023 with 370 federal conditions after the federal environment minister concluded it was likely to have significant environmental effects and cabinet found the public interest outweighed them. The project would remove 177 hectares of habitat in an estuary that has already lost 85% of its salmon habitat and could affect biofilm eaten by western sandpipers. Construction was expected to start in 2027, and The Narwhal updated its reporting on 15 May 2026.

records.layer_rationale: Port expansion converting intertidal estuary habitat used by migratory shorebirds and salmon.

notes.harm: The federal assessment found impacts for salmon, wetlands, western sandpipers and southern resident killer whales, and the project removes 177 hectares of habitat; no completed loss yet (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or livelihood closure is documented in the sources; First Nations harvesting and access effects were identified in the assessment (ref 2).
notes.scale: A single estuary site is affected, though the sandpiper population is about 3.5 million with the port saying 17% rely on Roberts Bank (ref 1).
notes.duration: Federal approval came in 2023, construction is expected to start in 2027 and take about six years (refs 1, 2), so the exposure runs for years.
notes.significance: Cabinet approved the project in 2023 with 370 federal conditions and conservation groups challenged it in court (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Cook Inlet belugas remain endangered near 331 animals, about a quarter of the 1979 count
records.description: NOAA Fisheries estimated 331 Cook Inlet belugas (range 290 to 386) from June 2022 aerial surveys, compared with 279 in 2018 and 1,292 in August 1979; the population is listed endangered under the Endangered Species Act. NOAA says it has contracted into the northern inlet in summer, and new surveys in June 2025 were still being analyzed. The recovery plan ranks catastrophic events, cumulative stressors and noise as high concerns.

location.detail: Cook Inlet, Gulf of Alaska coast, near Anchorage and the Kenai Peninsula.

records.layer_rationale: One isolated endangered whale population that has not recovered.

notes.harm: The count fell from 1,292 in August 1979 to 331 in 2022 (ref 1), and NOAA reports a 2.3% decline from 2008 to 2018 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The sources report no fishery closure; subsistence harvest has not been allowed because the population averaged below 350 since listing (ref 3).
notes.scale: A single stock confined to one inlet (ref 2).
notes.duration: The stock fell about 50% between 1994 and 1998 and has not recovered as expected (ref 3).
notes.significance: NOAA listed the population endangered in 2008 and a second five-year review in September 2022 kept that status (refs 1, 3).

records.title: California and southern Oregon ocean salmon closed for three seasons, reopened in 2026 under tight quotas
records.description: The Pacific Fishery Management Council closed ocean salmon fishing off California and southern Oregon in 2023 and 2024 and allowed only six recreational days in 2025, after near-record low Sacramento and Klamath fall Chinook returns. Commerce found fishery resource disasters for the 2023 and 2024 seasons, citing drought, changing ocean conditions and habitat loss. California commercial fishing reopened in spring 2026 with vessel-based trip limits and seasonal harvest guidelines that can close areas early.

records.layer_rationale: Collapse of wild Chinook runs removed a fishery for three seasons.

notes.harm: Sacramento River fall Chinook returned at near-record low numbers in 2022 and the Klamath forecast was the second lowest since 1997 (ref 1); the 2024 closure followed prolonged drought and habitat loss (ref 5).
notes.livelihoods: Commerce found a 100 percent revenue loss against the five-year average for the 2024 salmon fisheries (ref 5), and losses to California coastal economies were estimated above USD 100 million (ref 7).
notes.scale: The closures covered the whole California coast and southern Oregon from Cape Falcon south (ref 1), a national coastline but one coastal region.
notes.duration: Commercial fishing was closed three straight years and recreational fishing had six open days in 2025 (ref 6), with the 2026 season still under early-closure quotas (ref 9).
notes.significance: The Secretary of Commerce issued fishery resource disaster determinations for 2023 (ref 2) and 2024 (refs 4, 5), and NOAA allocated funds in 2026 (ref 8).

records.title: Northern Pacific sardine remains closed to directed fishing under a rebuilding plan, with a stock-merger proposal pending
records.description: NOAA Fisheries' 2025-2026 specifications put northern subpopulation sardine biomass at 30,158 metric tons and prohibit most directed commercial fishing off Washington, Oregon and California, with an annual catch limit of 2,200 tons. Oceana reports that NOAA declared the stock overfished in 2019, won a 2024 court ruling against the first rebuilding plan, and that the Pacific Fishery Management Council in September 2026 advanced a stock definition that would merge the northern and southern subpopulations.

records.title: Deep-ocean DDT and industrial waste dumpsite in the San Pedro Basin off Los Angeles remains under investigation
records.description: Between the 1930s and 1972 Montrose Chemical's DDT acid waste and other industrial waste was dumped in deep basins between Palos Verdes and Santa Catalina Island. Scripps and partner studies report sediment DDT concentrations above those at the nearby Palos Verdes Shelf Superfund site, evidence that much of the DDT was bulk-dumped rather than barrelled, and a 2025 UC Santa Barbara map of hot spots. EPA, NOAA-funded researchers and the Navy are still characterizing the site and no remediation has been decided.

location.name: San Pedro Basin Disposal Site 2
location.detail: Pacific off Los Angeles County, California, roughly halfway between the Palos Verdes Peninsula and Santa Catalina Island at about 1,000 m depth.

records.layer_rationale: Legacy DDT and other chemical waste on the seabed is a chemical contamination problem.

notes.harm: Scripps reports San Pedro Basin sediments with DDT+ concentrations exceeding those at the Palos Verdes Superfund site and UCSB mapped hot spots (refs 1, 4), but no ecological or health harm has been quantified and EPA says risks are still being assessed (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or beach closure tied to the dumpsite is documented; EPA says recreation occurs nearshore and far shallower than the 3,200 ft site and the Palos Verdes Shelf advisories are a separate matter (ref 2).
notes.scale: Scripps mapped more than 36,000 acres of seafloor and the 2021 survey found barrel-sized objects across 135 square miles of the basin, a local rather than regional-sea footprint (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Dumping ran from the 1930s to 1972 (EPA says contaminated disposal in the channel ended in 1975) and most deep sediments show little DDT+ degradation (refs 1, 2, 6).
notes.significance: EPA and partner agencies opened a formal Disposal Site #2 investigation and NOAA awarded Scripps $5.6 million in 2022 and $6 million in 2023 for research, but there is no enforcement or cleanup order (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

records.description: Untreated and partly treated sewage from the Tijuana River watershed in Mexico flows across the border and into the Pacific at Imperial Beach, closing beaches and releasing airborne hydrogen sulfide. EPA and the US section of the International Boundary and Water Commission report expansions and repairs underway, but the problem persists.

records.title: Washington drops Puget Sound nitrogen general permit as 58 treatment plants keep feeding low-oxygen waters
records.description: Ecology says nitrogen from 58 public wastewater treatment plants contributes to low dissolved oxygen in Puget Sound and the Salish Sea, and in 2022 it issued a nutrient general permit to curb it. After legal challenges the Pollution Control Hearings Board invalidated the mandatory permit on 28 February 2025, and on 7 January 2026 Ecology announced it will not reissue it and will address nitrogen through individual plant permits.

records.title: Vancouver's Iona Island plant still gives sewage only primary treatment as Metro Vancouver re-scopes its upgrade
records.description: The Iona Island plant in Richmond, built in 1963, treats wastewater from about 750,000 people and is one of the last primary-only treatment plants in North America. Metro Vancouver's board voted on 3 October 2025 to replace the roughly C$9.9 billion rebuild with a phased C$6 billion upgrade expected to finish by 2039, years after the federal 2030 secondary-treatment requirement.

location.name: Iona Island Wastewater Treatment Plant, Richmond
location.detail: Metro Vancouver, British Columbia, serving the City of Vancouver, parts of Burnaby and Richmond, UBC and the University Endowment Lands.

records.layer_rationale: Discharge of only primary-treated sewage to coastal waters is a pollution issue.

notes.harm: CBC reports the plant provides only primary treatment, removing about half of dissolved organic materials, while secondary treatment removes up to 90% or more of pollutants (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or fishery restriction tied to the plant is mentioned in the cited articles (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Metals and debris from the January 2025 Los Angeles fires washed into Santa Monica Bay
records.description: After the Palisades and Eaton fires, Heal the Bay sampling at ten Santa Monica Bay sites in January and February 2025 found silver, arsenic and zinc above average marine-health limits, with rains carrying metals from burned areas. Los Angeles County lifted its ocean water quality advisory in early April 2025 and later testing found metals below levels posing health risks, but Heal the Bay still lacks regulatory standards to call the water safe and debris and sediment continued to move after storms in winter 2025 to 2026.

In June 2026 a California appeals court upheld an injunction on the repair work, finding the Commission could enforce the Coastal Act where the county declined to act. Critics cite the 2015 Refugio spill from the same pipeline route; Sable states the repairs were completed under a federal consent decree.

records.title: Voluntary ship slowdowns cut vessel noise for Southern Resident killer whales in the Salish Sea, with partial participation
records.description: Vessel noise is a major threat to endangered Southern Resident killer whales. The Vancouver Fraser Port Authority’s ECHO Program runs voluntary slowdowns and a route change in Haro Strait, Boundary Pass, Swiftsure Bank and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Quiet Sound runs one in Admiralty Inlet, Washington. Quiet Sound’s August 2026 report estimates the 2025-26 slowdown cut underwater noise by about 1 dB with 64% participation of piloted transits.

records.title: Revised Canadian catch data raises pressure on Pacific Salmon Treaty renegotiation over Puget Sound Chinook and orca prey
records.description: The Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and Canada, renewed in 2019 for ten years, is being renegotiated. records.title: Oceanfront houses keep collapsing into the surf at Rodanthe and Buxton on Cape Hatteras National Seashore
records.description: Erosion along Hatteras Island has dropped unoccupied oceanfront houses into the Atlantic repeatedly: ten in the four years to September 2024 by the Park Service count, then eight collapses between September 30 and October 3, 2025 after Hurricanes Humberto and Imelda, and four more in Buxton from February 1, 2026. ABC News reported more than two dozen private homes had collapsed since 2020. The National Park Service closes beaches and warns of nail-studded debris after each collapse and knew of no injuries as of the afternoon of September 30, 2025.

location.name: Rodanthe and Buxton, Hatteras Island
location.detail: Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Dare County, North Carolina Outer Banks

records.layer_rationale: Shoreline retreat from waves and storm surge physically removes the land under coastal houses.

notes.harm: Houses were unoccupied and the Park Service reported no bodily injuries on September 30, 2025, but nail-studded debris prompted swimmer and visitor warnings after the 2024 and 2025 collapses (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The beach in front of Buxton was closed in February 2026 and a Rodanthe to Waves stretch was closed after the September 2024 collapse (refs 3, 5, 6).
notes.scale: All collapses are on a few miles of Hatteras Island oceanfront (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.duration: Collapses recur from 2020: ten in four years to September 2024, sixteen between September 16, 2025 and late October, and more in February 2026 (refs 2, 4, 5).
notes.significance: The Park Service issued formal news releases, area closures and a threatened-structures notice after each event (refs 1, 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: More than two dozen privately owned homes along Cape Hatteras National Seashore have collapsed since 2020, sixteen of them since September 16, 2025 (ABC News, October 29, 2025).

records.title: Ocean overwash repeatedly cuts NC Highway 12: Hurricane Erin in 2025 and a 500-foot Pea Island washout in 2026
records.description: Hurricane Erin stayed offshore in August 2025 but its surge and overwash made parts of Highway 12 on Hatteras Island impassable for days, forced about 80,000 people to evacuate Hatteras Island and damaged 56 residential and 4 commercial structures in Buxton, per the National Weather Service. In the late-September 2026 nor'easter, waves broke through dunes near the Pea Island Visitor Center and left about 500 feet of the highway undermined or broken. An Ocracoke Observer editorial counts $105.2 million of NCDOT repairs on NC 12 over 2005-2025.

location.name: NC Highway 12, Hatteras and Ocracoke islands
location.detail: Outer Banks, Dare and Hyde counties, North Carolina: Pea Island, Buxton, Hatteras Village and north Ocracoke

records.layer_rationale: Storm-driven overwash and dune breaching on a barrier island is a physical coastal hazard.
secondary_drivers: Storm surge and swell from offshore storms

notes.harm: Erin damaged 56 residential and 4 commercial structures in Buxton with no injuries or deaths recorded in Dare and Hyde counties (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Highway 12 on Hatteras Island was impassable for multiple days from August 20 until noon on August 23, 2025 and on Ocracoke until August 25 (ref 1).
notes.scale: Impacts cluster on a few miles of road at Pea Island, Buxton, Hatteras Village and north Ocracoke (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The editorial totals NCDOT repair spending of $24.7 million on Ocracoke and $80.5 million on Hatteras over 2005-2025, and the road failed again in September 2026 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The NWS issued a formal county impact narrative and Dare and Hyde counties ordered the first mandatory evacuation for a named storm since Dorian in 2019 (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: About 80,000 visitors and residents evacuated Hatteras Island before Hurricane Erin, and Highway 12 on Hatteras Island did not fully reopen until noon on August 23, 2025 (NWS).

records.title: September 2026 nor'easter causes the worst Jersey Shore erosion and flooding since Sandy
records.description: A rare September nor'easter on September 26-28, 2026 flooded New Jersey beach towns over four consecutive high tides and stripped dunes and beaches. PhillyVoice reported the worst erosion and flooding since Superstorm Sandy in 2012, with Atlantic City's water peaking nearly 8 feet above low tide, about a foot below Sandy, and Brigantine's mayor saying about half the beach was gone. New Jersey declared a state of emergency in eight counties and more than 100,000 customers lost power across the region.

location.name: Jersey Shore, Atlantic City and Brigantine
location.detail: New Jersey coast with impacts to Delaware, Long Island and eastern Massachusetts

records.layer_rationale: Storm surge, breaking waves and high tides eroded beaches and flooded a coastline, a physical coastal hazard.

notes.harm: About half the dunes remain in affected Atlantic City areas with steep drop-offs near Steel Pier, and Brigantine lost about half its beach (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Atlantic City beaches were closed from Friday, some residents were told to evacuate, more than 200 flights were cancelled and island ferries were disrupted (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The storm affected the coast from New Jersey and Delaware to eastern Massachusetts, with 1.04 million homes at moderate or greater surge risk across five states per Cotality (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: The event ran over roughly three days, September 26-28, 2026, with four consecutive high tides of flooding (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency in eight New Jersey counties and the NWS issued a Coastal Flood Warning for the New Jersey and Delaware coast (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Atlantic City's water peaked nearly 8 feet above low-tide level, about a foot below Sandy's peak, in the worst Jersey Shore erosion and flooding since 2012 (PhillyVoice, September 28, 2026).

records.title: Hampton Roads land sinks about twice as fast as the sea rises, and Norfolk high-tide flood days keep climbing
records.description: A Virginia Tech satellite study reported by WHRO found land in parts of Hampton Roads sinking by up to 6 mm per year on top of roughly 3.3 mm per year of global sea-level rise, more than 9 mm of annual land loss relative to the water. NOAA recorded 23 high-tide flood days at Sewells Point (Norfolk) in 2023-24, a station record, and 17 in 2025-26, and projects up to 27 days at Sewells Point for 2026-27.

location.name: Hampton Roads and Norfolk
location.type: Subsiding urban coastal region and tide-gauge location
location.detail: Southeast Virginia: Norfolk, Chesapeake Bay mouth and Hampton Roads cities

records.layer_rationale: Relative sea-level rise from subsidence plus global rise is a physical change in coastal water levels.

notes.harm: The study maps hazard rather than loss: WHRO says land now above water could be submerged within a few decades and gives no flood damage figures (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sewells Point logged 23 high-tide flood days in 2023-24 and 17 in 2025-26, each a day when water exceeded NOAA's flood threshold (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The findings centre on one metropolitan coast and the Sewells Point gauge, though the study covers the US Atlantic coast (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The subsidence data cover 2007-2020 and NOAA flood-day counts are recorded every year, with a station record in 2023-24 and a projection of up to 27 days in 2026-27 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: NOAA's Annual High Tide Flooding Outlook is a formal federal projection naming Sewells Point at up to 27 days for 2026-27 (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Land in parts of Hampton Roads is sinking up to 6 mm per year, so the region sees more than 9 mm of annual land loss relative to the water, about twice the rate waters are rising (WHRO, May 2, 2023).

More than 75% of Mid-Atlantic stations are predicted to meet or exceed their flood-day records in 2026-27 (ref 3).

records.title: Charleston Harbor reaches flood stage 54 times in 2024 as NOAA records a record 17 high-tide flood days
records.description: The Post and Courier counted 54 flood-stage tides at Charleston Harbor in 2024, the calmest year since 2021 yet seventh on the National Weather Service's flood database, with three major floods. NOAA's outlook records a record 17 high-tide flood days at Charleston in the 2023-24 year, and the city's Water Plan projects up to 170 flood events a year by 2050.

location.name: Charleston Harbor
location.detail: Charleston, South Carolina coast

records.layer_rationale: Rising relative sea level and perigean tides flood a coastal city, a physical coastal hazard.

notes.harm: Three of the 2024 floods were major (8 feet or higher) at the harbor gauge, but the sources give no loss or casualty figures (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Floods of 7 feet or more occurred 54 times in 2024, and NOAA's outlook shows a perigean-tide flood on East Bay Street in front of an elementary school (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The counts are for one tide gauge and one city (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Ocean levels are up about a foot in a century and 71 percent of major tidal floods occurred in the last nine years (ref 1).
notes.significance: NOAA's formal annual outlook records a station record of 17 flood days in 2023-24 and the city's Water Plan sets projections of up to 170 flood events a year by 2050 (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Modelling shows ocean acidification could cut sea scallop larval settlement and connectivity in the Mid-Atlantic Bight
records.description: A 2025 peer-reviewed meta-analysis and dispersal model in Estuaries and Coasts projects that acidification-sensitive Atlantic sea scallop larvae would have 17% lower settlement success and over 50% less larval passage between major Mid-Atlantic Bight fishery habitats than insensitive larvae. The authors note no published studies existed on sea scallop larval response to acidification before this work. A Rutgers glider project funded by NJ Sea Grant (2018-2021) was set up to map pH and aragonite saturation in the Bight for sea scallops and surf clams.

location.name: Mid-Atlantic Bight
location.detail: US Atlantic shelf between Cape Cod and Cape Hatteras, scallop and surf clam fishery habitats

records.layer_rationale: Declining aragonite saturation is a chemical change to shelf seawater affecting shell-building larvae.

notes.harm: The model projects 17% lower settlement for acidification-sensitive larvae, a potential rather than observed harm (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The paper calls the scallop fishery economically vital but reports no closure, advisory or landings loss (ref 1).
notes.scale: The dispersal model covers connectivity between major fishery habitats across the Mid-Atlantic Bight (ref 1).
notes.duration: The Rutgers project period was August 2018 to July 2021 and the sources report no multi-year trend result (ref 2).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study and a Sea Grant project are informal for regulatory purposes and no agency notice or listing is cited (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Acidification-sensitive sea scallop larvae had a 17% lower settlement success rate and over 50% less larval passage between major Mid-Atlantic Bight fishery habitats than insensitive larvae in the model.

measures.note: Modelled result of an individual-based dispersal model (ref 1).

measures.note: Reported as 'over 50%' in the abstract; value is the lower bound (ref 1).

signals: Atlantic sea scallops are described as economically vital in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (ref 1).

trend.note: The sources provide a model projection and a 2018-2021 glider mapping project without a measured trend (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Warm Gulf Stream-origin water displaces Labrador water on the Scotian Shelf and in the Gulf of St. Lawrence; Gulf ice hits a record low in 2024
records.description: Fisheries and Oceans Canada's 2024 Atlantic zone summary reports Gulf of St. Lawrence sea ice at a record low and sea-surface temperatures overall second highest since 1982. It says that since about 2010 warmer, saltier water has increasingly replaced cold, fresh Labrador Water, affecting deep-water temperature and oxygen on the Scotian Shelf and in the Gulf, with the influence peaking in 2022. The Canada Water Agency links recent Estuary oxygen declines to more warm, oxygen-poor water at depth carrying a Gulf Stream signature.

secondary_drivers: Shift in Gulf Stream and Labrador Current water supply

notes.harm: DFO reports acidification indicators with overall deterioration and nutrient and zooplankton shifts in 2024, but no mass mortality or contamination (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The opened DFO summaries describe no fishery closure or restriction tied to the warming (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: The 2024 summary covers the whole Atlantic zone including the Scotian Shelf and the Gulf of St. Lawrence (ref 1).
notes.duration: DFO says the water-mass shift has run since about 2010 and peaked in 2022 (ref 1).
notes.significance: These are DFO technical and monitoring reports with no regulatory notice (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: North Atlantic right whale unusual mortality event now covers 176 whales, with about 380 left
records.description: NOAA Fisheries reports that since 2017 elevated numbers of North Atlantic right whales in US and Canadian waters have died (43), been seriously injured (41) or shown sublethal injury or illness (92). The main documented cause is entanglement in fishing gear and vessel strikes. The population estimate rose slightly to 384 at the start of 2024 and 23 calves were born in the 2026 season, but the species remains endangered.

location.name: Western North Atlantic right whale range
location.detail: US east coast from the Southeast calving grounds to the Gulf of Maine, and Canadian waters including the Gulf of St. Lawrence

records.layer_rationale: A protected marine mammal population is declining under human-caused mortality.

notes.harm: NOAA counts 43 dead, 41 seriously injured and 92 sublethally injured or ill right whales in the event, more than 20 percent of the population (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Canada closes fishing grids when right whales are detected, covering snow crab, lobster and other fisheries, which restricts harvesters (ref 4).
notes.scale: The whales range across US and Canadian waters from Florida to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, a regional-sea scale (ref 1).
notes.duration: The event began in 2017 and the NOAA page was still being updated in July 2026 (ref 1).
notes.significance: NOAA declared and maintains a formal Unusual Mortality Event under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The UME covers 176 individual right whales: 43 dead, 41 seriously injured and 92 with sublethal injury or illness; about 380 whales remain, including roughly 70 reproductively active females (NOAA Fisheries, July 2026).

records.title: Canada closes Gulf of St. Lawrence fishing grids when right whales are detected, lifting all 2025 closures in November
records.description: Fisheries and Oceans Canada runs grid-based fishing closures triggered by right whale detections in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, covering snow crab, lobster, whelk and other fisheries. On 2025-11-14 it announced that all prohibited grids would be revoked for the 2025 season, effective 2025-11-15 if no new detections occurred; the measures had been in force since April.

notes.livelihoods: Snow crab, toad crab, rock crab, lobster, whelk and fixed-gear fisheries are prohibited in closed grids, with time to retrieve gear (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The closures apply across the Gulf of St. Lawrence plus Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador regions, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: Measures were in effect from April and revoked on 2025-11-15, about seven months (ref 1).
notes.significance: DFO issues the grid closures and revocations as formal fisheries notices recorded in its Orders Registry (ref 1).

records.title: Florida’s elkhorn and staghorn corals declared functionally extinct after the 2023 marine heatwave
records.description: A Science paper by 47 authors, published 2025-10-23, found that the record 2023 heatwave caused the ninth mass bleaching event on Florida’s Coral Reef and the functional extinction of elkhorn and staghorn coral there. Divers surveyed more than 52,000 colonies at 391 sites: 97.8 to 100 percent died in the Keys and Dry Tortugas, and 37.9 percent offshore southeast Florida.

records.title: Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank lobster stock down 34% from its 2018 peak with overfishing occurring; southern New England stock at record low
records.description: The 2025 ASMFC benchmark stock assessment found the Gulf of Maine/Georges Bank American lobster stock not depleted but down about 34% from its 2018 peak, with overfishing occurring, and the Southern New England stock significantly depleted at its lowest recorded abundance. Maine reported preliminary 2025 landings of about 78.8 million pounds, roughly 7 million pounds below 2024, though dock value stayed above $600 million.

location.name: Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank lobster stock
location.detail: United States waters of the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank, with the Southern New England stock to the south, as assessed by ASMFC.

records.layer_rationale: A commercial stock under fishing mortality above its threshold, so a living-resource issue.

notes.harm: Southern New England abundance averaged about 6 million lobsters in 2021-2023 against an 18 million threshold, the lowest on record, and the Gulf of Maine/Georges Bank stock is down about 34% from 2018 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Maine landings fell to about 78.8 million lb in 2025 with more than 21,000 fewer trips, and the state cites inflation, tariffs and a late molt; no closure was imposed (ref 2).
notes.scale: The finding covers two stock units spanning the Gulf of Maine, Georges Bank and southern New England waters of several US states (ref 1).
notes.duration: Abundance has fallen since the 2018 peak and Maine landings were down again in 2025 after the 2010s boom, a multi-year decline (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: ASMFC accepted the benchmark assessment for management use and its overfishing determination is a formal status finding, but no enforcement order has been issued (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Atlantic mackerel commercial fishery stays closed in Canada as the stock remains in the critical zone
records.description: The Atlantic mackerel stock has been in the critical zone since 2011, with spawning biomass at 35% of the limit reference point in 2024, and the commercial fishery has been closed since 2022. DFO kept the closure for 2025 and 2026 with a small bait and personal-use catch, while harvesters' unions dispute the science and ask for a commercial fishery.

notes.livelihoods: The commercial mackerel fishery has been closed since 2022 and only a 500 t bait and personal-use quota remains, which Newfoundland harvesters say they barely use (refs 1, 4).
notes.scale: The closure applies across all four DFO regions of Atlantic Canada and Quebec (ref 1).
notes.duration: The stock has been in the critical zone since 2011 and the commercial fishery has been closed since 2022 (refs 2, 4).
notes.significance: The Minister ordered the commercial closure to continue for 2025 and 2026 through the management plan, an enforceable decision (ref 1).

records.title: Striped bass remain overfished as the commission rejects a 12% cut and rebuilding by 2029 looks unlikely
records.description: Atlantic striped bass have been overfished since 2019, and the 2024 assessment projected the stock would not rebuild by 2029 without at least a 12% cut in removals. In October 2025 the ASMFC board rejected the coastwide reduction and kept 2026 measures unchanged, citing severe economic consequences, while starting a work group on post-2029 challenges and seven straight years of low Chesapeake Bay recruitment.

location.name: Atlantic coast striped bass stock
location.detail: Coastal states from Maine to North Carolina; the Chesapeake Bay is the main spawning area.

notes.harm: ASMFC states the stock was declared overfished in 2019 and remains overfished, with seven consecutive years of low Chesapeake Bay recruitment (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Existing recreational measures and commercial quotas continue, and the board cited severe economic consequences for not adding a 12% cut (ref 1).
notes.scale: The stock migrates along the Atlantic coast and is managed by coastal states from Maine to North Carolina; a vote of 16 jurisdictions decided the outcome (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Overfished since 2019 with a rebuilding deadline of 2029, so a multi-year, recurring problem (ref 1).
notes.significance: The board formally approved Addendum III in October 2025 but rejected the reduction, so this is a formal management action rather than an enforcement order (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Menhaden quota cut 20% and Chesapeake Bay reduction fishery cap under review
records.description: In October 2025 the ASMFC menhaden board cut the 2026 coastwide catch by 20% to 186,840 metric tons and started an addendum to reduce the 51,000 metric ton Chesapeake Bay cap held by the reduction fishery. In August 2026 the draft addendum advanced to public review with cap cuts of 10% to 50% proposed, a final decision is planned for November, and the operator warns of job losses.

location.detail: Virginia's Chesapeake Bay purse-seine reduction fishery, operating out of Northumberland County, with effects on Maryland bait and pound-net fisheries.

notes.harm: ASMFC found the stock not overfished but fishing mortality above the ecological target, and VIMS calls the science on Bay-specific effects "woefully inadequate"; osprey chicks are starving in parts of the Bay (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Maryland harvested under 10% of its quota in 2024 and bait costs strain its blue crab watermen, while Ocean Harvesters warns of up to 176 jobs at risk in Northumberland County (refs 2, 4).
notes.scale: The dispute centers on a single bay and its purse-seine fleet, though the quota cut applies coastwide (refs 1, 4).
notes.duration: Maryland has struggled to fill its quota since 2017 and the Bay cap debate runs from the October 2025 vote to a November 2026 decision (refs 2, 4).
notes.significance: ASMFC formally cut the 2026 quota and initiated an addendum, which is a formal management process but not yet an enforcement outcome for the Bay (refs 1, 4).

records.title: Illegal elver fishing leads Canada to close the 2024 Maritimes elver fishery, with 169 arrests and 37 charges
records.description: Canada's fisheries minister closed the 2024 commercial elver fishery in the Maritimes on 11 March 2024, citing an immediate threat to public safety and illegal harvesting. DFO arrested 169 people in 2024 and seized 396.3 kg of elvers, including five people from Maine, and 37 people had been charged by December 2024. Maine, by contrast, allocates a fixed 9,688 lb elver quota for 2026.

location.detail: Elver rivers in southwestern Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; Maine's licensed elver fishery is the regulated comparison.

notes.livelihoods: The minister closed the 2024 commercial elver fishery for the season, a restriction on licensed harvesters in the Maritimes (ref 1).

records.title: Revolution Wind: after two stop-work orders and court injunctions, Interior asks a court to remand the project's 2023 construction approval
records.description: Revolution Wind, a 704 MW, 65-turbine wind farm off Rhode Island, received a federal stop-work order in August 2025 and a second 90-day suspension on 22 December 2025, and a federal judge enjoined both so construction could resume. In October 2026 the Interior Department asked a federal court to remand its 2023 construction and operations plan approval so it can re-evaluate the permit, after the final turbine was installed in September 2026 and power began flowing in March 2026. Interior said the request does not signal a change in its approach to offshore wind.

records.description: On 13 July 2024 a GE Vernova blade on a Vineyard Wind turbine about 15 miles southwest of Nantucket failed during testing, and foam and fiberglass debris reached Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard beaches. The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement halted power production and new installation. As of July 2025 its investigation had no completion timetable.

records.title: Container ship Dali strikes Baltimore's Key Bridge, closing the Patapsco shipping channel for about 11 weeks
records.description: On 26 March 2024 the containership Dali lost power and struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge in the Patapsco River at Baltimore, collapsing it and killing six highway workers. The federal shipping channel was fully or partially closed for about 11 weeks while crews removed about 50,000 tons of debris. The NTSB tied the blackout to a loose signal wire in its final report.

location.type: Port shipping channel and bridge collapse site
location.detail: Patapsco River, Baltimore Harbor, Maryland, in the Chesapeake Bay system; the vessel struck Pier 17. Coordinates are approximate.

records.layer_rationale: A vessel casualty that closed a major port channel and disrupted trade.
secondary_drivers: Crew and equipment practices found by investigators

notes.harm: Six highway workers died in the collapse, per the NTSB investigation page (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The 700-foot-wide federal channel was fully or partially closed for about 11 weeks, ships were diverted to other ports and longshore workers had no ships to work (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The impact centered on one port channel in Baltimore Harbor (ref 2).
notes.duration: The bridge was not rebuilt, with reopening targeted for fall 2028 and over 34,000 vehicles a day detoured (refs 3, 1).
notes.significance: The NTSB completed its investigation, with a board meeting on 18 November 2025 identifying the probable cause (refs 1, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The NTSB attributed the Dali's loss of propulsion to a loose signal wire connection at a terminal block caused by improper wire-label banding (NTSB investigation page, ref 1).

measures.note: About USD 100 million per White House officials; Army Corps invoices about USD 75 million and Coast Guard about USD 24 million (ref 3).

signals: Ships were diverted to other ports and longshore workers lost work during the closure (ref 2).
The bridge is estimated to cost USD 1.7 to 1.9 billion to replace (ref 3).

trend.note: The channel reopened in June 2024; bridge reconstruction continues, with reopening targeted for fall 2028 (ref 3).

records.title: Record Coral Sea heat in January to March 2024, the warmest in 400 years
records.description: A peer-reviewed reconstruction found that the January to March 2024 sea-surface temperature in the Coral Sea was the warmest in the 1618 to 2024 record, about 1.73 C above the 1618 to 1899 average. The Bureau of Meteorology reported record-high monthly sea-surface temperatures across the Coral Sea in January and April 2024 and Australian-region waters at their warmest annual average on record. The heat drove the fifth mass bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef in the past ten years.

location.name: Coral Sea and Great Barrier Reef
location.detail: Coral Sea off Queensland, Australia, including the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park

records.layer_rationale: Record sea-surface heat is a physical climate extreme measured in the water column of the Coral Sea.

notes.harm: The Bureau of Meteorology's State of the Climate 2024 lists 2024 as the fifth mass coral bleaching event on the Great Barrier Reef in ten years and says accumulated thermal stress in 2024 was higher than in 2016 (ref 3); AIMS surveys reported the largest single-year coral cover declines on record in the north and south (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources documents a closure, restriction or lost income tied to the 2024 heat itself, so no disruption is scored.
notes.scale: The warmest-in-400-years finding covers the Coral Sea region off Queensland rather than a single reef, so it is scored at the regional-sea level (ref 1).
notes.duration: The reconstructed extreme covers the January to March 2024 window and the Bureau reports record monthly values in January and April, a few months in total (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Bureau of Meteorology issued the record as a formal Annual Climate Statement on 6 February 2025 (ref 2) and the finding was published in Nature (ref 1), but no enforcement or emergency action is cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: January to March 2024 Coral Sea heat extreme was the warmest in 400 years, about 1.73 C above the 1618 to 1899 reconstructed average (ref 1).

measures.name: Coral Sea Jan-Mar 2024 SST anomaly vs 1618-1899 reconstruction
measures.note: Henley et al., Nature, 2024 (ref 1); value read from the paper's results text.

measures.name: Australian-region annual SST anomaly 2024 vs 1961-1990
measures.note: Warmest on record for the region; Bureau of Meteorology annual statement (ref 2).

signals: The Great Barrier Reef underpins reef tourism and fisheries, but the cited sources do not quantify economic losses from the 2024 heat (refs 3, 4).

trend.note: The study reports Coral Sea warming of about 0.09 C per decade over 1900 to 2024 and 0.12 C per decade over 1960 to 2024 (ref 1).

records.title: Second consecutive marine heatwave on the Great Barrier Reef in summer 2024-25
records.description: The Reef Authority, AIMS and CSIRO reported that prolonged above-average water temperatures (marine heatwaves) in December 2024 to March 2025 caused regional coral bleaching in the Far Northern and Northern regions, the sixth mass bleaching event since 2016. Heat stress in the Southern region did not reach levels that warranted aerial bleaching surveys. AAP later reported that Australia's oceans had their warmest 12 months on record in 2024-25.

location.name: Far Northern and Northern Great Barrier Reef
location.detail: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park off Queensland, Australia, mainly Cooktown to Cape York

records.layer_rationale: Prolonged above-average sea temperatures are a physical climate hazard measured against heat stress thresholds.

notes.harm: The Reef Snapshot reports regional coral bleaching in the Far Northern and Northern regions with 41 per cent of 162 inshore and mid-shelf reefs surveyed showing medium to high bleaching, and AIMS reported record annual coral cover declines (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The snapshot and news coverage cited do not document tourism closures, fishery restrictions or lost income, so none is scored.
notes.scale: Bleaching spanned two of the four Marine Park management regions, a regional-sea scale rather than one reef (ref 1).
notes.duration: The event followed the 2023-24 mass bleaching, making the Reef's second back-to-back event, with heat stress accumulating from December 2024 to March 2025 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Reef Authority, AIMS and CSIRO issued a formal end-of-summer Reef Snapshot classifying it as the sixth mass bleaching event since 2016 (ref 1), but no enforcement or emergency declaration is cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Prolonged exposure to higher-than-average water temperatures (marine heatwaves) this summer has caused regional coral bleaching in the Far Northern and Northern regions of the Reef (ref 1).

measures.name: Inshore and mid-shelf reefs with medium to high bleaching prevalence
measures.note: Aerial surveys by AIMS and the Reef Authority, March 2025 (ref 1); bleaching outcome used to document heat impact.

signals: Reef tourism and fisheries depend on reef condition, but the cited sources give no economic loss estimate (refs 1, 3).

trend.note: Back-to-back events in 2023-24 and 2024-25 followed by a smaller 2025-26 event (refs 1, 5).

records.title: King tide breaches Saibai Island sea walls and floods homes in February 2026
records.description: AAP reported that king tides in early February 2026 pushed water on Saibai Island in the Torres Strait about 3.7 metres above average, breaching sea walls, flooding houses and roads and covering the cemetery. Residents said the flooding was more severe than the previous year, and that salt water is seeping into soil and making food harder to grow. The Bureau of Meteorology reports that sea level rise to the north of Australia has been significantly higher than the global average since 1993.

notes.harm: AAP reported water on Saibai about 3.7 metres above average during the king tides, with sea walls breached, water in houses and on roads, and the cemetery underwater (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Residents told AAP that salt water is seeping into soil, making it hard to grow food, that seafood is harder to catch and that communication blackouts add isolation, which are restrictions on food and services rather than displacement (ref 1).
notes.scale: The documented flooding is at a single island community, Saibai, with Boigu named alongside it (ref 1).
notes.duration: The article says monsoon-season king tides recur yearly and are becoming higher each year, and a resident called this year more severe than the last (ref 1).
notes.significance: The cited material is a news report quoting residents with no formal notice, listing or order issued for this specific event (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Federal Court rejects Torres Strait Islanders' sea-level climate claim; appeal listed for July 2026
records.description: On 15 July 2025 the Federal Court of Australia held that the Commonwealth owes Torres Strait Islanders no duty of care over climate change, in Pabai v Commonwealth (No 2) [2025] FCA 796, while accepting that the islanders have suffered and will continue to suffer from sea level rise and extreme events. The applicants' case rested on projected marine inundation and erosion of low-lying islands such as Saibai and Boigu. The applicants appealed, and the Full Federal Court was listed to hear the appeal in Melbourne over four days from 28 July 2026.

location.name: Torres Strait Islands (Saibai and Boigu)
location.detail: Torres Strait Islands, Queensland, Australia; lead applicants from Saibai and Boigu islands

records.layer_rationale: The case concerns exposure of low-lying islands to rising seas, a physical climate impact.

notes.harm: Justice Wigney accepted that Torres Strait Islanders have suffered and will continue to suffer from sea level rise and extreme events if greater action is not taken (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The claim cited coastal erosion, flooding, freshwater contamination and decline in traditional food sources, and the court declined to recognise loss of fulfilment of Ailan Kastom as compensable (ref 1).
notes.scale: The class action is brought for Torres Strait Islanders across the Zenadth Kes island group, a regional rather than single-site claim (ref 1).
notes.duration: The class action was commenced in March 2022, judgment was given in July 2025 and the appeal was listed for hearing from 28 July 2026, so the dispute spans several years (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A Federal Court judgment of 15 July 2025 is a court ruling, and the applicants filed an appeal to the Full Federal Court (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: On 15 July 2025 the Federal Court found the Commonwealth does not owe Torres Strait Islanders a duty of care to protect them from the impacts of climate change (ref 1).

signals: The applicants' alternative case sought predictable funding for seawalls against marine inundation and erosion, which the court also rejected as core government policy (ref 1).

trend.note: The appeal was listed for hearing from 28 July 2026 and no Full Federal Court judgment was found in the cited sources (ref 3).

Justice Wigney noted the law could change through appellate decisions or legislation (ref 2).

records.title: Walande community in South Malaita relocated to the mainland after king tides; seawall failing
records.description: Human Rights Watch reported in March 2025 that the roughly 800 people of Walande, South Malaita, Solomon Islands, moved from an artificial island to the mainland after repeated cyclone and king tide damage, largely at their own expense. Seawater now breaches the 2021 seawall at the new site and is destroying swamp taro land, and some residents are considering moving again. The government adopted Planned Relocation Guidelines in 2022 but has not fully operationalised them.

location.name: Walande, South Malaita
location.detail: Walande, south coast of Malaita, Solomon Islands (map point is the centre of Malaita Island, not the village)

records.layer_rationale: Sea level rise and king tides are driving physical inundation of a coastal community.

notes.harm: HRW reports king tides in 2009 destroyed 16 houses and inundated three quarters of the old island, satellite imagery shows about five hectares near the new site submerged between 2010 and 2024, and the island is now fully submerged (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The whole community of about 800 people was displaced from its island and sea level rise threatens the viability of the swamp taro land it depends on (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The documented impacts concern one village community, Walande, rather than a coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: HRW traces displacement events from Cyclone Namu in 1986 through 2005 and 2009 to the 2021 seawall, partly toppled by September 2024 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The source is an NGO report; the government's 2022 Planned Relocation Guidelines are a policy, not a notice or order about Walande, so no formal action is scored (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: About 800 people, Human Rights Watch (ref 1).

records.title: Cyclone Alfred swell strips beaches and dunes along South East Queensland in March 2025
records.description: The Bureau of Meteorology reported that Severe Tropical Cyclone Alfred, a long-lived Coral Sea system, produced large swell that caused significant coastal erosion along south-east Queensland and north-eastern New South Wales, with an estimated millions of cubic metres of sand scoured and dune escarpments up to 6 metres high. A coastal scientist reported storm surge of up to 0.5 metres above the high tide mark on the Gold Coast, which exposed a buried seawall. Much of the sand sits on offshore sandbars and dunes may take years to recover. Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred eroded about 6 million cubic metres of sand from Gold Coast beaches in March 2025, leaving some sand cliffs about 6 metres high; the mayor said 80% of the beach had gone into the ocean. The council used offshore dredging and dune sand to rebuild beaches. Queensland and the Australian Government later funded a $74 million environmental recovery program that includes beach replenishment.

records.title: Mass coral bleaching strikes the Great Barrier Reef in 2024 and again in 2025
records.description: Aerial surveys in March 2024 confirmed a mass bleaching event, the fifth in eight years, across more than 300 reefs covering about two-thirds of the World Heritage Area. AIMS later reported that the 2024 event had the largest spatial footprint of any bleaching on record, and a smaller event followed in 2025 with medium to high bleaching on 41% of surveyed inshore and mid-shelf reefs in the north and centre. Some reefs have since recovered, for example about 90% of bleached coral at Lady Elliot Island after Cyclone Alfred cooled the water.

records.title: Raine Island green turtles: warm sand skews hatchlings female as egg relocation scales up
records.description: Raine Island, the world's largest green turtle rookery, is producing almost entirely female hatchlings because the sand is too warm for males; a 2018 Current Biology study found 99.1% of juveniles and 86.8% of the whole northern population were female. In summer 2024-25 about 3,000 eggs were moved to the Sir Charles Hardy Islands, and in the following season almost 9,000 eggs were relocated under shade structures that cool the sand by about 1.5 C, with 82% hatching and reaching the sea. Researchers have not yet shown whether relocated hatchlings are as fit as those from untouched nests.
