records.title: Threatened sharks, sawfish and sea snakes caught in Great Barrier Reef gillnet and trawl fisheries as a gillnet ban nears
records.description: Queensland data cited by ABC show 188 fatal interactions with scalloped hammerhead sharks and seven narrow sawfish deaths in the east coast gillnet fishery since February 2024. A gillnet ban in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park takes effect on 1 July 2027, and fishers have funded a review seeking to overturn it. Separately, a mandatory camera rollout on trawlers begins in June 2026, with about 4,000 sea snakes a year reported as trawl bycatch by the Australian Marine Conservation Society.

records.title: Gillnet fishing to be phased out across the Great Barrier Reef by mid-2027, with a funded buyout
records.description: The Queensland and Australian governments announced in November 2023 that gillnet fishing in the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area will end by mid-2027, backed by a A$185 million package that includes about A$90 million in structural adjustment for licence holders. The government says nets entangle threatened dugongs, turtles, dolphins and sawfish. The seafood industry body opposed the decision, and later funding stages for skippers, crew and a gillnet buy-back ran through 2024 and January 2025.

records.title: East coast Spanish mackerel: stock listed depleted in 2023, then Queensland raises catch limits in 2026

A 2025 Queensland assessment put the stock at about 34% of unfished levels, and the government lifted the commercial limit to 250 tonnes from 1 February 2026 and doubled the recreational boat limit. The Australian Marine Conservation Society called the changes short-sighted and risky.

records.title: Reef Water Quality Report Card 2023-2025 shows progress on sediment and nitrogen but rising pesticide risk and poor inshore seagrass and water quality
records.description: The joint Australian and Queensland Reef Water Quality Report Card for 2023-2025, released on 13 August 2026, reports progress towards all water quality targets and a met particulate phosphorus target. Press coverage of the card adds that pesticide risk rose slightly from its 2021 result and that inshore seagrass and marine water quality were rated poor. The card is the final one under the Reef 2050 Water Quality Improvement Plan, which is replaced by a Catchment Water Quality Strategy, and Australia must report to UNESCO on water pollution by the end of 2028.

notes.harm: Marine water quality and seagrass condition fell and were both rated poor in the 2023-2025 card, and pesticide risk rose slightly from 2021 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or tourism restriction is cited; the Queensland statement describes the reef as supporting about 77,000 jobs and A$9 billion a year without reporting disruption (ref 1).
notes.scale: The card covers all Great Barrier Reef catchments and the inshore marine park, a national coastline rather than a single site (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The Marine Monitoring Program reported years of deteriorating inshore water quality trends before improving in 2022-2023, and some indicators still miss guideline values (ref 4); pollution is chronic.

records.title: Cyclone Jasper and Kirrily flood plumes smother inshore reefs, seagrass and mangroves along 700 km of the Great Barrier Reef coast
records.description: Record rain from Cyclone Jasper (landfall 13 December 2023) and Cyclone Kirrily sent flood plumes more than 700 km along the Great Barrier Reef coast, carrying sediment, nutrients and pesticides. A year later James Cook University surveys found every observed intertidal fringing reef smothered by mud and severe mangrove damage, and the Wet Tropics report card recorded all coral lost on the southern reef at Snapper Island.

notes.scale: Plumes stretched more than 700 km along the coastline and reached some mid and outer reefs, around 20,000 GL of freshwater (ref 3).
notes.duration: Mud still smothered inshore reefs a year after landfall, with scientists expecting recovery to take years and mangrove sediment release over five to six years (ref 4).
notes.significance: Evidence is scientific monitoring and a regional report card, with no enforcement or notice cited (refs 3, 5).

records.title: Reef catchment fertiliser use falls and end-of-catchment nitrogen declines, but many cane and grain growers still doubt the science behind the reef regulations
records.description: A 2026 pair of CSIRO and James Cook University studies found synthetic nitrogen and phosphorus fertiliser use fell by up to 25 to 50 per cent across most Great Barrier Reef catchments over one to two decades, and water quality improved at 75 per cent of nine monitored sites over about 40 years. A government review of the 2019 Reef protection regulations, reported in March 2024, found improving compliance but that 40 per cent of surveyed farmers rated the evidence for the rules as weak.

location.name: Sugarcane and grazing catchments of the Great Barrier Reef
location.detail: Queensland reef catchments from Cape York to Burnett-Mary; dissolved inorganic nitrogen from cane land is a driver of inshore reef water quality.

records.layer_rationale: Fertiliser nitrogen and phosphorus runoff drives nutrient enrichment of reef waters, and the finding tracks both the load and the regulation.

notes.harm: Excess nutrients from catchment runoff are linked to algal growth that stresses inshore coral and seagrass, but the sources show improving, not damaging, trends (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or restriction on reef users is cited; the regulations restrict farm practices rather than reef use (ref 2).
notes.scale: The studies cover all Great Barrier Reef river catchments, an area about the size of New Zealand (ref 1).
notes.duration: Fertiliser records span 100 years and water quality records almost 40 years, and the Reef regulations have been in force since 2019 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Queensland's Reef protection regulations are enforceable law and a formal review of them was published in March 2024 (ref 2).

records.title: Prony Resources nickel plant spills ore pulp, sulphur-basin sediment and heavy fuel oil near Baie Nord and Prony Bay, New Caledonia
records.description: The Prony Resources nickel and cobalt plant in southern New Caledonia had three reported spills in about two and a half years: roughly 7 m3 of sediment from the sulphur basin toward Baie Nord creek in November 2023, a thickened ore pulp spill into the same creek on 20 February 2025, and tens of litres of heavy fuel oil into Prony Bay on 3 March 2026. After the February 2025 spill the Southern Province ordered additional measures including six months of creek water-quality monitoring, and for the March 2026 spill it said it would inspect and could set reinforced measures.

notes.duration: Spills were reported in November 2023, February 2025 and March 2026, a recurring pattern (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.title: World Heritage Committee keeps Great Barrier Reef off the In Danger list in 2026 but sets new conditions after 2025 'utmost concern'
records.description: At its 2025 session the World Heritage Committee noted with utmost concern the Reef's continued deterioration due largely to climate change and regretted that 2025 water quality targets were missed. At its 2026 session in Busan it again did not list the property as In Danger, but asked Australia for further water quality, gillnet-phase-out, dredge-spoil and climate actions, with progress reports due in 2028 and 2029. The Queensland Government says it has delivered UNESCO's recommendations since 2022. In July 2025 the World Heritage Committee ordered a full review of Great Barrier Reef management, with a State of Conservation report due in early 2026. A draft decision released on 3 July 2026 recommends against an 'in danger' listing and credits Australia's work on water quality and other pressures, but expresses 'utmost concern' about declining coral cover after the 2024 and 2025 bleaching events. Progress reports are due in December 2028 and 2029.

records.layer_rationale: The finding is a treaty-body review of how the World Heritage Convention is being met for the reef.

notes.harm: Decision 47 COM 7B.2 notes with utmost concern continued deterioration of the property due largely to climate change, citing mass bleaching including the 2023/2024 event (ref 1); decision 48 COM 7B.69 notes with utmost concern declining hard coral cover (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or loss of income is cited in the decisions; the Queensland statement says the Reef supports around 77,000 jobs and A$9 billion a year, which the In Danger question puts at reputational risk rather than disruption (ref 3).
notes.scale: The decisions concern the whole property, which runs along the Queensland coast, so the scale is a coastline-wide protected area rather than one reef (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The Committee has reviewed the property repeatedly (decisions 45 COM 7B.13, 46 COM 7B.62, 47 COM 7B.2 and 48 COM 7B.69) and sets reporting dates to 1 December 2029 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Two Committee decisions in 2025 and 2026 set formal requests and deadlines (1 February 2026, 1 December 2028, 1 December 2029) and the 2026 session decided not to list the property In Danger (refs 1, 2, 3, 4).

records.title: Compulsory pilotage lapses in Hydrographers Passage: 2022 near-grounding report and a June 2025 bulk carrier entry without a pilot
records.description: The ATSB's report on the 2022 Rosco Poplar near-grounding (released July 2024) found the ship came within 200 m of Bond Reef after a GPS fault and that the check pilot system did not reliably assure pilot competency. On 8 June 2025 Maritime Safety Queensland reported that the bulk carrier Leyla Aksoy entered the Hydrographers Passage compulsory pilotage area without a pilot; the vessel was turned back, detained by AMSA and its master was prosecuted by GBRMPA, according to the state agency.

location.detail: About 130 km off Mackay, Queensland, in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park; ships bound for Queensland ports

records.layer_rationale: Navigation-safety compliance and regulator oversight of a shipping route through a protected marine park.

notes.harm: The 225 m Rosco Poplar came within 200 m of Bond Reef, where normal clearance was about 1,500 m, but no grounding is reported (ref 2); the 2025 vessel was kept 'well clear' of the outer edge of the reef (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The 2025 ship was ordered out of the compulsory pilotage area, later detained in Townsville by AMSA, and admitted only after embarking a pilot (ref 1).
notes.scale: Both events concern a single passage, Hydrographers Passage, rather than a sea-wide problem (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The two events are three years apart (4 May 2022 and 8 June 2025), and AMSA is reviewing coastal pilotage (ref 2).
notes.significance: The ATSB issued a safety recommendation to AMSA on its check pilot framework (ref 2), and MSQ says GBRMPA successfully prosecuted the ship's master in the Federal Court (ref 1).

records.title: Port Vila cruise berth out of use after December 2024 earthquake; tender-only calls resume in mid-2025
records.description: A magnitude 7.3 earthquake in December 2024 damaged Port Vila's wharf and cruise facilities and cruise lines stopped calling for about six to eight months. Vanuatu's government arranged a temporary tendering point at the Port Vila seafront, the first call came in June 2025, and Carnival Adventure's 8 August 2025 call was described as the first cruise visit in eight months. The main docking facilities were still under repair in August 2025.

records.title: Solwara 1 seabed mining licences revived by Deep Sea Mining Finance in PNG's Bismarck Sea; Melanesian leaders adopt moratorium
records.description: In August 2023 PNG's Mining Minister told parliament that Nautilus Minerals was extending its three Solwara 1 licences and planned to return; the project's owner, Deep Sea Mining Finance, said it holds full rights. Melanesian Spearhead Group leaders adopted a moratorium on deep-sea mining in their territorial waters on 24 August 2023, and PNG's Prime Minister said on 28 August that Solwara 1 cannot go ahead until technology and studies show it can be done sensitively. A US Congressional Research Service note updated August 2025 reports DSMF exploratory work near Solwara 1 in August 2024.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery or community closure is reported in the sources (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: A single licence area in the Bismarck Sea is involved (ref 1).
notes.duration: Nautilus received its licence in 2011, went bankrupt in 2019 and the revival was reported in 2023 and again as exploratory work in August 2024 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Melanesian Spearhead Group adopted a moratorium in the Udaune Declaration on 24 August 2023 and PNG's Prime Minister said on 28 August 2023 PNG would follow the Pacific majority (ref 1); no PNG law specific to seabed mining existed per MP Allan Marat (ref 1).

records.title: Vanuatu moves to secure maritime zones against sea-level rise after the ICJ climate opinion and the Forum's 2021 declaration
records.description: In August 2021 Pacific Islands Forum leaders declared that maritime zones notified to the UN would be maintained without reduction notwithstanding climate change-related sea-level rise. After the International Court of Justice delivered its climate advisory opinion in July 2025, following a Vanuatu-led initiative, Vanuatu's Climate Change Minister said at the Forum Leaders Meeting in September 2025 that Vanuatu would secure maritime zones 'so that rising seas cannot erase them' and fold the opinion into its NDC.

records.title: Marine heatwave alerts over the Bay of Bengal and Andaman waters, strongest around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
records.description: India's ocean information service INCOIS issued a marine heatwave alert in April 2026 covering six Indian Ocean basins; as of 20 April about 19% of the Bay of Bengal was under Watch and 3% under Alert, with the strongest warming around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands toward Myanmar and Thailand. A peer-reviewed analysis of 1982 to 2021 satellite data found marine heatwave events in the central bay are becoming more frequent, with more than five a year in the last decade.

records.title: Ghoramara Island in the Sundarbans has lost about half its area to erosion and rising seas
records.description: Satellite studies cited by India Water Portal show Ghoramara Island in the Hooghly estuary shrinking from about 7.2 sq km in 1972 to 3.6 sq km in 2022, with a projected 2.6 sq km by 2032, and a second study reports 8.145 sq km in 1990 falling to 3.59 sq km in 2024. Embankments around the island have repeatedly failed and relocation of residents has been ad hoc.

notes.livelihoods: About 3,000 people were displaced in 2016, and Sahapedia records a fall from about 40,000 residents to roughly 5,000 at the 2011 census (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Seasonal low-oxygen zone off the Godavari mouth intensifies each fall in the Bay of Bengal
records.description: A 2024 Frontiers in Marine Science study using Biogeochemical-Argo floats found an intense, shallow oxygen minimum zone off the Godavari River mouth at roughly 40 to 200 m that rises toward the surface and intensifies in fall. The authors attribute it to river-delivered nutrients, coastal upwelling and decomposition of the resulting organic matter, and warn that changes in riverine input could affect the coastal ecosystem. A 2024 peer-reviewed study of Argo float data found that Godavari River discharge drives nutrient enrichment, a plankton bloom and oxygen loss that shoals an intense oxygen minimum zone at roughly 40 to 200 m depth in the western Bay of Bengal each fall. Oxygen in the upper layer of the study box fell from about 3 ml/L in May to about 0.1 ml/L in October. The authors caution that the sample of floats is small.

records.title: Great Nicobar transshipment port and 130 sq km forest diversion cleared by the National Green Tribunal at the Galathea Bay leatherback nesting coast
records.description: On 16 February 2026 India's National Green Tribunal dismissed the coastal-zone challenges to the Rs 80,000 crore Great Nicobar project, which includes an international container transshipment terminal at Galathea Bay, a nesting ground for giant leatherback turtles that the reports say also holds corals and mangroves. The Tribunal accepted the Zoological Survey of India's suggestion that scattered corals can be translocated and ordered full compliance with the clearance conditions. Critics say the clearance rests on deference to government reports rather than a merit review, and the case remains contested. India plans an International Container Transshipment Port at Galathea Bay on Great Nicobar Island, designed to reach 16 million TEU in its final phase. In February 2026 the National Green Tribunal's eastern zonal bench upheld the project's environmental clearance, while critics cite coral, leatherback turtle and seismic risks. A detailed project report was prepared in December 2025 and a tender was reported as likely by July 2026; this record has not confirmed that a tender was issued.

records.title: More than 1,000 dead olive ridley turtles wash ashore on Chennai's beaches in January 2025
records.description: Over 1,000 dead olive ridley turtles washed up along Chennai's coast over several weeks of January 2025, including 346 recorded by volunteers on the 13 km between Neelankarai and Marina Beach, the highest monthly toll for the city. Conservationists pointed to drowning in trawler nets and trawlers working inside the five nautical mile limit; the official post-mortem had not been released at the time of reporting. The National Green Tribunal's southern bench warned of a complete trawling ban in the nesting season and the Fisheries Department mandated turtle excluder devices.

secondary_drivers: Illegal trawling inside the coastal limit

notes.harm: More than 1,000 olive ridley carcasses washed up on the Chennai coast within weeks, 346 of them on one 13 km stretch in January 2025 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The Fisheries Department mandated turtle excluder devices for trawlers and began patrols inside five nautical miles, and fishers said enforcement and subsidy withdrawal hit them (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The deaths were counted along the Chennai coastline, with the volunteer count covering a 13 km stretch (ref 1).
notes.duration: The die-off was concentrated in a few weeks of January 2025, though experts note olive ridleys die every year and only about 20 percent of dead turtles wash ashore (ref 1).
notes.significance: The National Green Tribunal's southern bench took up the deaths and warned of a complete trawling ban during nesting season, a formal notice rather than a ruling (ref 1).

records.title: Record olive ridley arribada of about 700,000 turtles at Rushikulya in February 2025
records.description: Odisha forest officials counted 698,718 olive ridley turtles nesting at Rushikulya between 16 and 23 February 2025, surpassing the 637,000 recorded in 2023, and scientists who have monitored the site for 20 years called it the biggest arribada they have documented. The beach is not a protected area and was guarded by forest staff and villagers, and scientists said the population appears healthy, while noting coastal erosion and development as continuing concerns. The site had no arribada in 2024.

notes.livelihoods: The reports describe fencing and patrols of the beach by forest staff and villagers but no fishery or livelihood restriction (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The arribada occurred on a single 5 km beach at Rushikulya, spreading over about nine km in 2025 (ref 1).
notes.duration: The mass nesting ran about eight days from 16 to 23 February, with hatching expected about 45 days later (ref 1).
notes.significance: The sources are agency counts and scientist comments; no notice, listing or order was issued, and the beach is not a protected area (ref 2).

records.title: Gahirmatha mass nesting fails in 2026 as erosion pushes the olive ridley rookery 14 km north
records.description: Gahirmatha beach in Odisha, described as the world's largest olive ridley rookery, saw no synchronised mass nesting in the 2026 season, with only sporadic nesting reported between the Devi and Dhamra river mouths. A satellite study of 1990 to 2022 found the nesting ground has shifted about 14 km northwards because of coastal erosion, with the highest erosion in 2020-21 coinciding with a roughly 50 percent fall in mass nesting. Experts quoted attribute the 2026 absence to changing ecological conditions and climate change, and the cause has not been established.

notes.livelihoods: Fishing and motorised boating are restricted within 20 km of the coast from Dhamra to the Devi river each year from 1 November to 31 May (ref 1).
notes.scale: The affected area is one rookery, the Gahirmatha beach and adjacent shore in Kendrapara district (ref 1).
notes.duration: The erosion study spans 1990 to 2022 and mass nesting was low in 2023 and 2024 as well, at 31,115 and 66,933 turtles per the Forest Department figures cited (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Gahirmatha was declared a marine sanctuary in 1997 and carries the annual fishing restriction, a formal protected-area regime in place (ref 1).

records.title: Coral bleaching across Thailand's Andaman marine parks closes Phi Phi dive and snorkel sites for almost a year
records.description: Thailand's Department of National Parks reported coral bleaching in 19 marine park areas between 2 April and 8 May 2024, 11 of them on the Andaman Sea coast including Similan, Surin, Phi Phi, Lanta and Phetra, with more than 80 percent bleaching at Pling Island in Sirinat National Park. The Hat Noppharat Thara-Mu Ko Phi Phi National Park closed several dive and snorkel sites on 13 May 2024 and reopened ten sites in April 2025 after assessments showed strong recovery, while the west side of Koh Gai stayed closed.

records.title: Dugongs die as seagrass collapses on Thailand's Andaman coast, with starvation behind at least 40 percent of 2024 deaths
records.description: Thailand's Department of Marine and Coastal Resources recorded an average of 42 dugong deaths a year in 2023 and 2024, more than double the 2019 to 2022 rate, and autopsies indicated at least 40 percent of 2024 deaths were likely starvation. Seagrass cover at Hat Chao Mai National Park and Koh Libong in Trang, which held over 75 percent of the Andaman population in 2017, fell by up to 70 percent between 2020 and 2024. A WWF Thailand and department fact-finding mission took place on 19 to 25 January 2025 and the department adopted an emergency strategy including supplemental feeding.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery or tourism closure is documented; the department prefers co-management with fishers and tour operators over forbidden zones, with go-slow zones only proposed (ref 1).
notes.scale: Losses span the Andaman coast provinces of Trang, Krabi, Phuket and Phang Nga, a national coastline, which held an estimated 273 Thai dugongs in 2022 (ref 1).
notes.duration: Seagrass decline runs from 2020 to 2024 and deaths remained elevated in 2025, with 12 recorded by 9 April (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal WWF Thailand and department fact-finding mission on 19 to 25 January 2025 and a department emergency strategy followed (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Bangladesh limits visitors to Saint Martin's Island, then bars tourist vessels for nine months in 2026 to protect its coral
records.description: Bangladesh's government announced in October 2024 that tourism to Saint Martin's Island, the country's only coral island, would be limited because visitor pressure was polluting the island and stressing its coral, citing that only 41 percent of coral remains. On 1 February 2026 tourist vessels were barred for nine months after a shortened 2025-26 season. The Department of Environment reported healthier reefs, returning sea turtles and more sea snails in 2025, while tour operators and residents warned of lost income.

records.title: Erosion shrinks Bangladesh's Sundarbans mangrove forest at nine forest-office sites while modelling projects up to 80 percent loss in the Indian part
records.description: A March 2025 report found erosion damaging nine sites in the East Sundarbans Division of Bangladesh, taking jetties, patrol posts, cyclone shelters and freshwater ponds, with geo-bag protection failing to stop it and budget limits blocking work elsewhere. A World Bank figure cited in the report puts the combined Sundarbans area at 11,506 sq km in 2016 against 11,904 sq km in 1904 to 1924. A 2023 modelling study projects the Indian Sundarbans could lose 42 to 80 percent of its mangrove area by 2100 under current management.

records.title: Chilika's Irrawaddy dolphin count stays flat at 159 in the January 2026 census
records.description: The Odisha Forest Department's 20 January 2026 census counted 765 dolphins of six species along the state's coast, but only 159 Irrawaddy dolphins in Chilika Lake, a number reporters describe as flat for two years. Experts attribute the stagnation to slow breeding and habitat stress from large prawn gheries and nylon fishing nets. Chilika hosts the largest known single-habitat Irrawaddy dolphin population in the world.

location.name: Chilika Lake, Odisha
location.detail: Brackish coastal lagoon connected to the Bay of Bengal, Odisha, India; a Ramsar site.

records.layer_rationale: Stalled recovery of a lagoon dolphin population under fishing and aquaculture pressure.

notes.harm: The Irrawaddy count of 159 shows no growth, and prawn gheries and nylon nets are named as habitat stress, but no mass mortality is documented (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery restriction is described in the cited census reports (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The population sits in one lagoon, Chilika Lake (ref 2).
notes.duration: The count was 154 Irrawaddy dolphins in the January 2023 survey and 159 in 2026, so the population has been stagnant over several years (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The Irrawaddy dolphin is listed Endangered by the IUCN according to the lake's reference entry, and the Forest Department runs an annual formal census (refs 1, 4).

population_affected.note: Irrawaddy dolphins counted in Chilika on 20 January 2026 (refs 1, 2).

key_measure.text: 159 Irrawaddy dolphins counted in Chilika in the 20 January 2026 census; the population is described as stable with no significant growth (ClimateFactChecks, 13 Feb 2026).

records.title: Horseshoe crab spawning sites on Odisha's coast decline, with a scientist warning of local extinction within 8 to 10 years
records.description: Scientists wrote to the central and Odisha governments in 2023 that horseshoe crab breeding grounds on the Balasore and Kendrapara coast were shrinking, with one estuary falling from about 8,000 sq m to 25 to 30 sq m. In June 2026 a former National Institute of Oceanography scientist warned the Odisha population could vanish within 8 to 10 years, citing a 73 percent decline between 1988 and 2006 and threats from coastal development, pollution, beach modification and net capture. The species is protected under Schedule IV of India's Wildlife Protection Act and no concrete ground action was reported in 2023.

location.detail: Northeast Odisha coast, India, including the Balaramgadi area near Chandipur in Balasore district.

notes.harm: A fall from about 8,000 sq m to 25 to 30 sq m of good breeding estuary was reported, and a 73 percent decline from 1988 to 2006 is cited (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The scientist urges community-based conservation rather than blanket fishing bans, and no restriction on fishers is described (ref 2).
notes.scale: The reports concern spawning sites along the Balasore and Kendrapara coast of Odisha (ref 1).
notes.duration: Decline is documented from 1988 to 2006, scientists reported shrinking sites in 2023 and a new warning came in 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The species has been in Schedule IV of the Wildlife (Protection) Act since 2009 but scientists' letters of March and July 2023 received no reported action (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Not applicable; wildlife population.

key_measure.text: Odisha could lose its horseshoe crab population within eight to ten years if present trends continue; a 73 percent decline was estimated from 1988 to 2006 (Orissa Post, June 2026).

records.title: Small-scale 2023-24 coral bleaching hits South Andaman reefs during the fourth global bleaching event
records.description: India's Ministry of Earth Sciences told Parliament on 4 December 2024 that the fourth global coral bleaching event affected the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, with small-scale bleaching observed in the Andaman region only, especially South Andaman, and put 2023-24 bleaching at 15 to 18 percent in the South Andaman Islands. It attributed the bleaching to higher sea surface temperature linked to El Nino and said most reefs recovered, with studies continuing. The Zoological Survey of India has mapped 143.46 sq km of Andaman reefs outside protected areas.

records.title: Bangladesh hilsa output falls for a second year as bans, blocked migration routes and overfishing fail to rebuild the stock
records.description: Bangladesh's national hilsa production fell from 571,000 tonnes in FY2022-23 to 529,000 tonnes in FY2023-24, and the July to August 2025 catch was 29,519 tonnes against 40,291 tonnes a year earlier. The Department of Fisheries found hilsa migration blocked at 17 points in the Meghna-Tentulia estuary system, and the government ran a 22-day brood-fish ban in October 2025 and an eight-month ban on juvenile hilsa from 1 November 2025. Officials and researchers cite overfishing, fine-mesh nets, siltation, pollution and low rainfall.

location.detail: Northern Bay of Bengal, Meghna-Tentulia estuary, Barguna and Kalapara coast, Bangladesh

records.layer_rationale: A single commercially central fish stock is declining under harvest pressure and habitat change.

notes.harm: Production fell from 571,000 t to 529,000 t and the July-August 2025 catch dropped by about 27 percent year on year; no formal stock assessment is cited, so harm is scored as limited (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Catching, selling and storing hilsa is banned for 22 days in October and juvenile hilsa under 25 cm are banned for eight months, with penalties of up to two years in prison (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The reports describe one species, hilsa, in Bangladesh's rivers, estuaries and coastal waters (ref 1).
notes.duration: Output has fallen since the FY2022-23 peak and the juvenile ban runs 1 November 2025 to 30 June 2026, with brood-fish bans around the Ashwin full and new moons since 2008 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock press release set the juvenile ban under the Protection and Conservation of Fish (Amendment) Ordinance 2025 (ref 2).

population_affected.note: The cited articles give no count of hilsa fishers affected.

records.title: Bangladesh moves its Bay of Bengal fishing ban to 15 April to 11 June, shortening it to 58 days to match India's closure
records.description: From April 2025 Bangladesh replaced its 65-day marine ban (20 May to 23 July, in place since 2015) with a 58-day ban, 15 April to 11 June, after fishing communities asked to align it with India's closure so Indian trawlers could not fish while Bangladeshi boats were barred. The same window was repeated in 2026, with rice relief for registered fishers and calls for stronger patrols against foreign vessels.

notes.livelihoods: All marine fishing in Bangladeshi waters stops for 58 days; Barishal's fisheries office requested rice aid for 2,869 registered fishers and in 2026 Bhola fishers asked for aid in the first week and a pause on NGO loan repayments (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The closure covers all of Bangladesh's Bay of Bengal waters, a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: The earlier 65-day ban ran annually since 2015 and the 15 April to 11 June window was repeated in 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A formal ministry closure notice with a joint enforcement push by the Fisheries Department and local administrations (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Bangladesh's 2025 Nansen survey and falling sea catch point to overfishing by industrial trawlers in the Bay of Bengal
records.description: Preliminary results of the August to September 2025 RV Dr Fridtjof Nansen survey showed an overall decrease in fish stocks in Bangladesh's waters, which the fisheries adviser attributed to overfishing, illegal fishing and harmful nets. Department of Fisheries data show sea fish production fell from 706,000 tonnes in 2021-22 to 628,000 tonnes in 2023-24, with shrimp down almost 44 percent. The government has frozen new shrimp trawler licences and is piloting satellite trackers.

notes.harm: The 2025 Nansen survey's preliminary findings showed an overall decrease in fish stocks, and sea fish production fell by about 78,000 t between 2021-22 and 2023-24 (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No new shrimp trawler licences will be issued and existing ones are not renewed until 2028; fishers report six to seven months of poor harvest and mounting debt (ref 2).
notes.scale: The survey and production data cover Bangladesh's whole marine fishery, a national coastline (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Production has fallen in each year from 2021-22 to 2023-24 and shrimp harvests have declined since 2019 per a fisher quoted (ref 2).
notes.significance: The fisheries adviser presented the survey to the public and announced tighter trawler licensing and tracker pilots (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No fisher count is given; Cox's Bazar has more than 5,000 wooden boats (ref 2).

records.title: India and Bangladesh detain each other's fishers across the northern Bay of Bengal boundary, with court cases in Bagerhat
records.description: Bangladesh's navy detained 14 and then 9 Indian fishers with two trawlers in October 2025; a Bagerhat court acquitted all 23 on 20 January 2026 and they were released on 27 January for handover at the maritime boundary. In December 2025 the Indian Coast Guard detained 35 Bangladeshi fishers on two trawlers in the Bay of Bengal, part of a two-month pattern of such detentions.

notes.duration: Indian Coast Guard detentions were described as a two-month pattern to December 2025 and Bangladesh's cases ran October 2025 to January 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A Bagerhat court acquitted all 23 on 20 January 2026 of charges filed under the Marine Fisheries Act, and the Home Ministry ordered repatriation (ref 1).

records.title: Sri Lankan navy arrests of Tamil Nadu fishers in the Palk Strait continue, with 346 detained in 2025 and bottom trawling at the centre of the dispute
records.description: Sri Lanka's navy said it arrested 346 Indian fishers and seized 44 trawlers in 2025, and further arrests followed in 2026. Rameswaram fishers struck in February 2025 after 32 were detained on 23 February; northern Sri Lankan fishers say Indian bottom trawlers scrape the seabed in their waters. A Joint Working Group on fisheries has not delivered a settlement. The Sri Lankan Navy arrested 10 Indian fishermen off Delft Island in January 2026, and by April 102 fishermen and 15 trawlers had been arrested that year, according to the Navy as reported by PTI. A further nine were arrested on 22 July 2026. The Navy said it arrested about 346 Indian fishermen and seized 44 trawlers in 2025; the arrests are a long-standing India-Sri Lanka dispute over a shared fishing ground.

records.title: Odisha's seven-month fishing ban around Olive Ridley nesting beaches leaves about 11,000 fishing families on one-time aid, with enforcement gaps
records.description: Odisha bans sea fishing within 20 km of the Dhamra, Devi and Rushikulya river mouths from 1 November to 31 May, and year-round in the Gahirmatha Marine Sanctuary, to protect nesting Olive Ridley turtles. About 11,000 families get a one-time Rs 15,000 payment that their union calls too low. The Orissa High Court earlier directed the state to enforce the ban after observing turtles dying in trawler nets and from propellers.

notes.duration: The ban recurs every season; 2024-25 ran 1 November 2024 to 30 May 2025 and the 2025-26 ban began 1 November 2025 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: US tariffs of about 58 percent hit Andhra Pradesh's farmed shrimp sector in 2025, before a February 2026 cut to 18 percent
records.description: After the US raised duties on Indian shrimp in 2025, effective tariffs reached about 58 to 60 percent, and Crisil projected a 15 to 18 percent fall in India's shrimp export volume. Andhra Pradesh, which supplies about 60 percent of India's shrimp export volume, reported processing unit closures and procurement price cuts of 10 to 20 percent. A February 2026 trade deal cut the reciprocal tariff on Indian shrimp from 25 to 18 percent and removed a 25 percent penalty tariff.

notes.harm: No ecological or health harm is cited; the reports are about export revenue, farm investment and jobs (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Dozens of processing units shut, each employing about 400 workers, and some farmers switched to other crops or poultry (ref 2).
notes.scale: The sector is concentrated in Andhra Pradesh but the duties apply to national shrimp exports to the US, which took 311,948 t in 2024-25 (ref 1).
notes.duration: Duties of about 50 percent or more were in force from late August 2025 until the 2 February 2026 trade deal, several months in all (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A US tariff order and later bilateral trade deal changed the duty rate, with Indian GST relief from 22 September 2025 (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Banned antibiotic residues in Indian shrimp exports are traced mainly to Andhra Pradesh farms, with a 43 percent rejection rate in 2025
records.description: India's seafood export authority MPEDA reported in January 2026 that antibiotic residues in export consignments were traced to more than 40 farms in four states, 74 percent of them in Andhra Pradesh. The drugs controller wrote to all states on 3 June 2026 asking how the ban on chloramphenicol and nitrofurans is enforced, citing a 43 percent rejection rate in 2025 by the EU, USA and Japan. US FDA recorded 93 shrimp refusals tied to veterinary drug residues in 2025.

notes.scale: Traced farms span four states, with Andhra Pradesh 74 percent, Odisha 13 percent, West Bengal 8.7 percent and Gujarat 4.3 percent (ref 1).
notes.duration: MPEDA first flagged the issue in May 2023 and residues were still detected in 2025 and 2026 (ref 1).

records.title: Thailand's Fisheries Act amendments would reopen night fishing with fine-mesh nets and ease at-sea transshipment while Andaman stocks recover
records.description: A bill amending Thailand's 2015 fisheries ordinance would allow night fishing with nets of mesh below 2.5 cm beyond 12 nautical miles, and, according to the Environmental Justice Foundation, change rules on transferring catch between boats at sea. The Thai Sea Watch Association and the Environmental Justice Foundation warn it risks another EU yellow card, issued in 2015 and lifted in 2019, and fishers say it would undo the recovery of stocks including in the Andaman Sea. The Department of Fisheries says it would raise catches of anchovies, whose Andaman season runs May to July.

notes.harm: Critics warn fine-mesh nets under 2.5 cm catch larvae and juveniles; no measured damage is cited because the opened sources do not show the bill in force (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or loss is reported; fishers' federations protested outside parliament on 27 January and 7 February 2025 (ref 2).
notes.scale: The bill is national and covers Thai waters, with the Andaman Sea named as one recovering area (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The lower house passed the bill, the Senate accepted it in principle on 13 January 2025 and a special committee was studying it in February and March 2025 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A formal bill in the Senate that senators said the EU was watching, per the committee chair Tawat Suraban (ref 1).

population_affected.note: The Department of Fisheries cited over two million jobs in 2,500 fishing villages as of 2018, not an affected-population count (ref 2).

records.title: Refinery oil from Cyclone Michaung floods reached Ennore Creek and the Bay of Bengal; Rs 73.68 crore compensation order under challenge
records.description: Floodwater from Cyclone Michaung on 3 to 4 December 2023 carried oil from the Chennai Petroleum Corporation (CPCL) refinery area into the Buckingham Canal and Ennore Creek, and oil reached coastal waters and the Pulicat backwaters. The Indian Coast Guard put the slick at about 20 sq km, and an IIT Madras assessment filed with the National Green Tribunal estimated 517 tonnes of oil in the environment after clean-up, plus 393 tonnes removed by CPCL. records.title: Record June 2023 marine heatwave across the North Sea and northwest European shelf
records.description: A Met Office-led study found the northwest European shelf average ran 2.9 C above the June norm for 16 days, its longest recorded category II marine heatwave, with local anomalies up to 5 C in the central North Sea. records.title: North Sea sets record spring, summer and annual temperatures in 2025 and runs hot again in 2026
records.description: The German Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) reported the warmest North Sea spring (8.7 C), summer (15.7 C) and year (11.6 C) since its series began, with every month of 2025 above the long-term average. BSH says marine heatwaves are becoming longer and more frequent, and a September 2026 BSH-based report counts 66 marine heatwave days at its Helgoland station by early September 2026.

location.name: North Sea (German Bight to Norway and the Channel)
location.detail: BSH basin-wide analysis; largest anomalies off Norway and Denmark in spring, and in the western and southwestern North Sea up to the English Channel in summer (refs 1, 2).

records.layer_rationale: Record basin-wide sea temperatures are a physical climate signal.

notes.harm: BSH says marine heatwaves add pressure on marine ecosystems (ref 3) and NOC observed intense southern North Sea blooms in May 2025 (ref 5), but no mortality is documented, so potential harm.
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources reports a fishery or tourism restriction from the 2025 North Sea warmth (refs 1-5).
notes.scale: The BSH records cover the whole North Sea, a regional sea (refs 1-3).
notes.duration: Every month of 2025 was above the long-term average and the annual mean set a record (ref 3); a further heatwave is counted in 2026 (ref 4).
notes.significance: BSH, the German national agency, formally reported the records and the 11.6 C annual mean as the warmest since 1969 (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: North Sea annual surface temperature 11.6 C in 2025, the warmest since BSH measurements began in 1969, with June and December setting monthly records (ref 3).

signals: No economic loss figure appears in the cited sources.

records.title: Skagerrak marine heatwave in July 2025 equals the temperature record while kelp retreats along the coast
records.description: The Norwegian Meteorological Institute reported sea temperatures of 22-23 C, at least 5 C above normal, from Trondelag to Sweden and Denmark in July 2025. The Institute of Marine Research recorded 23.8 C at its Skagerrak station on 24 July, matching the 2008 record, while the Norwegian Environment Agency reported in October 2025 that kelp and large algae now grow at least 3 m shallower at over 40% of monitored Skagerrak stations.

records.layer_rationale: Heat extremes and warming-linked habitat decline on a coastal sea.

notes.harm: Okokyst monitoring found kelp and large algae growing at least 3 m shallower at over 40% of Skagerrak stations and algal condition worse in 60% of areas (ref 2); heat is one of several drivers named.
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or aquaculture restriction on the Skagerrak coast is reported; only a warning of stress to fish and a 2024 lice surge in northern Norway (ref 1).
notes.scale: The warm water ran from the Trondelag coast to Sweden and Denmark (ref 1) and the kelp decline spans the Skagerrak coast (ref 2), a regional sea.
notes.duration: The algae decline covers 2021-2024 (ref 2) and the heat event came in summer 2025 (ref 1), so recurring over years.
notes.significance: The Norwegian Environment Agency published the monitoring finding as a formal agency report and plans a 2025-summer impact analysis (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Northern Shelf cod: zero-catch advice for 2026 and again for 2027, with the southern substock below its critical limit since 2017
records.description: ICES advised zero catch of Northern Shelf cod (North Sea, Skagerrak, eastern Channel and west of Scotland) for 2026, and has now advised zero catch again for 2027. ICES says the Southern substock has been below its biomass limit since 2017 and the Northwestern substock is now also below it.

records.title: UK sandeel fishing closure in the North Sea upheld in Scottish waters and partly in English waters by EU-UK arbitration
records.description: On 26 March 2024 Scotland closed all its waters to sandeel fishing and the UK closed English North Sea waters through a licence condition. The EU challenged both closures under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. An arbitration tribunal ruling published on 2 May 2025 upheld the Scottish closure fully and found a procedural failure on proportionality in the English one; the UK says a new decision process completed in June 2025 resolves it and the closures remain. A three-member Permanent Court of Arbitration tribunal ruled in May 2025 that the UK's full closure of sandeel fishing in English waters breached the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement because it was not proportionate for EU vessels, but rejected the EU's other three claims, including on the Scottish closure and on scientific evidence. The UK said it was not legally obliged to reverse the closure of English waters. Danish industry says the ban costs it about 40 million pounds a year.

notes.livelihoods: The Scottish order closed all Scottish waters to sandeel fishing for all vessels, so the directed fishery there is ended (ref 2).
notes.scale: The closure covers the English and Scottish North Sea, a national-waters scale rather than the whole sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: Closures began on 26 March 2024 and remained in place after the June 2025 UK decision process (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: An arbitration tribunal issued a ruling on the EU's Trade and Cooperation Agreement challenge, published 2 May 2025 (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.description: In December 2025 the UK, EU and Norway agreed a long-term management strategy for North Sea autumn-spawning herring and set a 2026 TAC of 328,566 tonnes, a 20% lower advice than for 2025. records.title: Container ship Solong hit the anchored tanker Stena Immaculate off the Humber, releasing jet fuel and starting a fire that left one crew member presumed dead
records.description: On 10 March 2025 the container ship Solong collided with the anchored tanker Stena Immaculate, which carried 220,204.5 barrels of aviation fuel, 14 nautical miles north-east of Spurn Head. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) interim report says the collision breached the No.7 port cargo tank, the escaping fuel ignited and the fire spread to containers on Solong; 36 crew were recovered and one Solong crew member is presumed dead. The volume of fuel that reached the sea is not stated in the interim report, and the MAIB investigation was still listed as current on 2 October 2026. On 10 March 2025 the container ship Solong, making about 16 knots, struck the anchored tanker Stena Immaculate about 14 nautical miles north-east of Spurn Head, breaching a cargo tank and igniting aviation fuel and containers. The UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch's April 2025 interim report found neither ship had a dedicated lookout and that one Solong crew member is missing, presumed dead. The MAIB is also examining the use of the area as an anchorage for vessels waiting for the Humber; Wikipedia reports the Solong's master was convicted of gross negligence manslaughter in February 2026.

records.title: PFAS from the 3M Zwijndrecht plant polluted the Scheldt and Western Scheldt; Netherlands and 3M agreed compensation for affected businesses in December 2025
records.description: PFAS discharged for years into the Scheldt from the 3M plant at Zwijndrecht, Belgium, reached the Western Scheldt estuary in Zeeland, where RIVM advised eating as little as possible of several fish, crustacean and shellfish species. The Dutch state held 3M liable in May 2023, and in December 2025 the Dutch infrastructure ministry and 3M Belgium agreed compensation for affected businesses, with the amount kept confidential. Talks on Rijkswaterstaat's own costs, such as removing contaminated sludge, had not concluded.

records.title: OSPAR's 2023 assessment keeps the Scheldt, Meuse, Rhine, Ems and Elbe plumes, German Bight and Danish coast classed as eutrophication problem areas
records.description: OSPAR's Quality Status Report 2023, published on 13 September 2023, applied its eutrophication procedure to 2015-2020 and found eutrophic areas along the continental coast from France to Denmark. In the North Sea the Scheldt, Meuse, Rhine, Ems and Elbe plumes, German Bight Central, the outer German-Danish coastal area and the Eastern North Sea remain problem areas, with seafloor oxygen below 6 mg/l in the Eastern North Sea. Nutrient concentrations are falling, but OSPAR says its objective of no anthropogenic eutrophication has not been met.

records.title: About 1.3 million tonnes of munitions on the German North Sea floor are releasing explosive residues that accumulate in marine life
records.description: Germany's environment ministry (BMUKN) says about 1.3 million tonnes of unexploded munitions from two world wars lie in German North Sea waters, and about 1.6 million tonnes across the North and Baltic Seas combined. Explosive residues, some carcinogenic, are already accumulating in mussels and fish, and the ministry cites 25 percent more liver tumours in flatfish than in uncontaminated areas. A 100 million euro immediate action programme tested recovery technology in the Baltic in 2024 to 2025; no North Sea clearance results were opened.

records.title: Scottish court finds Rosebank and Jackdaw consents unlawful over omitted downstream emissions; fresh UK decisions pending
records.description: In January 2025 Scotland's Court of Session ruled that the UK consents for the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields were unlawful because their environmental impact assessments left out downstream (scope 3) emissions, as the UK Supreme Court's Finch judgment requires. The quashing was suspended, so preparatory work could continue but no oil or gas can be produced until consent is re-granted. A revised Rosebank assessment estimates about 254 million tonnes CO2e over the field's life, and government consultations on the two fields ran to August 2026 with decisions still to come.

records.title: North Sea CO2 storage begins: Northern Lights injects its first volumes and the UK permits the Endurance store
records.description: Northern Lights, owned equally by Equinor, Shell and TotalEnergies, reported its first CO2 stored in the Aurora reservoir about 2,600 m below the Norwegian North Sea seabed on 25 August 2025, with phase 2 to lift capacity to at least 5 million tonnes a year. records.title: Dutch government pays NAM 163 million euros to drop gas drilling plan under the Wadden Sea at Ternaard
records.description: NAM, owned equally by Shell and ExxonMobil, applied in 2019 and 2020 to extract gas from the Ternaard field, which lies largely under the Wadden Sea World Heritage area. records.title: Second-largest September oxygen depletion on record across Danish waters, 2024
records.description: Aarhus University's DCE reported that oxygen depletion in Denmark's inner waters covered about 11,000 km2 in mid-September 2024, the second-largest September extent on record after 2002. Bottom water was oxygen-free in many areas and toxic hydrogen sulphide was released, with dead lobsters, crabs and starfish in Limfjorden and dead fish in Lovns Bredning. Widespread depletion in the southern and central Kattegat had not been seen since 2008.

notes.scale: The 11,000 km2 affected area lies within Denmark's EEZ line, a national-waters extent that also reaches into German bays (ref 1).

records.title: Oxygen depletion in Danish waters for a third year, with hydrogen sulphide in fjords, 2025
records.description: Danish monitoring reported about 3,200 km2 of oxygen-depleted bottom water in August 2025 and just under 3,700 km2 in the second half of September, smaller than the 2024 peak but again with oxygen-free bottom water and toxic hydrogen sulphide at some sites. DCE's late-autumn note names Mariager Fjord and Flensborg Fjord as places where hydrogen sulphide was released. Greenpeace calls 2025 the third year running of severe depletion. Aarhus University's national centre DCE reported oxygen depletion in inner Danish waters between 31 October and 26 November 2025, including anoxic bottom water in several fjords and toxic hydrogen sulphide released from the seabed in Mariager Fjord and Flensburg Fjord. Denmark had its worst deoxygenation in 25 years in 2023, according to coverage citing the Danish Environmental Agency, and fertiliser nitrogen run-off is blamed for the fjords' decline.

records.title: Record hydrogen sulphide and a third of the Baltic Proper seabed hypoxic, 2023 to 2026
records.description: SMHI's preliminary figures show anoxia on about 18 percent and hypoxia on about 34 percent of Baltic bottom areas in 2024, with hydrogen sulphide at the highest levels ever recorded in the East Gotland Basin. SMHI research cruises in July and August 2025 and July 2026 still found hydrogen sulphide from 70 to 125 m and acute oxygen shortage from 60 to 90 m in the Gotland basins. A peer-reviewed study describes the 2016 to 2024 stagnation as unprecedented deoxygenation. SMHI's oxygen survey for 2024 found anoxia on about 18% and hypoxia (including anoxia) on about 34% of Baltic Sea bottom area, with hydrogen sulphide at record levels in all basins around Gotland. The agency says the severe conditions have persisted since a 1999 regime shift and that inflows have been too small to change the overall picture.

records.title: October 2023 storm surge: second-highest Baltic flood in 150 years on Germany's Schleswig-Holstein coast
records.description: The 20-21 October 2023 storm surge put Flensburg 2.27 m above mean water, the highest there since 1872, broke dikes at Arnis and elsewhere and was roughly a 200-year event at several gauges. Schleswig-Holstein damage was put at about EUR 200 million, more than 150 yachts sank, and Damp harbour is to be fully restored only by the 2028 season.

records.layer_rationale: Wind-driven storm surge flooding a coastline, the Baltic's highest since 1872 at Flensburg.

notes.harm: At least six regional dikes breached, 5.3 km of dike moderately and 6.7 km severely damaged, and about 600 m of dike collapsed at Geltinger Birk (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Damp harbour is to be fully restored only by the 2028 season and 48 boats sank at Kiel-Schilksee, taking berths out of use (ref 4, ref 3).
notes.scale: The surge hit the Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg coasts and reached Denmark, a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Reconstruction of harbours and coastal protection was still under way two years later, with 20% of boat damage unprocessed a year on (ref 3, ref 4).
notes.significance: Officials in Schleswig-Holstein's interior ministry warned of damage in the hundreds of millions and the state set up a special fund (ref 2, ref 3).

records.title: October 2023 storm surge: worst on Denmark's Baltic coasts since 1913
records.description: DMI reported the 20 October 2023 storm surge, which hit the western Baltic from Bornholm to the Little Belt, as the highest water measured in the Baltic since 1913 (2.31 m at Schleswig), with up to 2.39 m above normal at Hesnæs on Falster. Flooding hit southern Jutland, including Haderslev and Aabenraa, and DTU later put the socio-economic cost of the October 2023 event above DKK 1 billion.

records.description: BSH reported that the Baltic's 2025 mean surface temperature was 9.7 C, 1.1 C above the long-term average and the second-warmest year after 2020. In spring a marine heatwave at the Kiel lighthouse station lasted a record 55 days, from 28 March to 21 May, averaging 2.6 C above the 1991-2020 normal. BSH's summer 2026 report ranked that summer the seventh warmest, with June nearly 3 C above average.

records.title: Baltic Proper harbour porpoise stays critically endangered as the EU tightens control of net closures
records.description: The resident Baltic Proper harbour porpoise population is listed as Critically Endangered by IUCN and is estimated at fewer than 500 animals. A 2024 peer-reviewed review reports that bycatch, almost entirely in static nets, exceeds the sustainable limit of 0.7 animals a year and that the only abundance estimate dates from 2011 to 2013. In February 2026 the European Commission adopted a delegated act adding vessel-position and control requirements to the 2022 static-net closures.

records.layer_rationale: Documented bycatch and a very small population of a protected marine mammal in the Baltic Proper.

notes.harm: Estimated bycatch was 7 animals in 2017 against a potential biological removal of 0.7 a year, and at least 97% of recorded bycatch was in static nets (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The Commission states that 11 marine areas are closed to static nets under Delegated Regulation 2022/303, with mandatory pingers at two sites (ref 3).
notes.scale: The population ranges over the Baltic Proper offshore banks and coasts of Sweden, Poland, Germany and Denmark (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: IUCN has rated the population Critically Endangered since 2008 with no change in 16 years (ref 2); HELCOM says status is not good for any Baltic population (ref 4).
notes.significance: A Commission delegated act of 27 February 2026 adds control measures (ref 1), and the Commission sent Sweden a reasoned opinion in February 2024 (INFR(2020)4037, as reported in ref 2).

records.title: Baltic grey seal hunt quotas disputed: scientists disagree on whether about 3,000 seals a year is sustainable
records.description: Sweden, Finland and the Aland Islands allow a combined grey seal hunt of about 3,000 animals a year while the population is 55,000 to 57,000. A 2024 University of Gothenburg study judged that level unsustainable and put the maximum sustainable catch at 1,900, whereas a June 2026 University of Helsinki modelling study found about 3,050 viable but 3,600 raises extinction risk. Sweden has proposed 1,350 licensed plus 150 protective grey seals for 2026 to 2027, and Danish scientists warn this may delay recovery in Danish waters.

records.title: Finland raises Baltic ringed seal hunting quota to 425 while HELCOM rates southern populations as failing and ice-dependent
records.description: From 1 August 2025 to 31 July 2027 Finland allows ringed seal hunting only in the Bothnian Bay-Kvarken area, with the annual quota raised by 50 to 425. HELCOM's assessment found the Bothnian Bay population and the southern unit (Archipelago Sea, Gulf of Finland, western Estonia) fail good status and that milder winters make counts unreliable and threaten snow-lair breeding. A University of Helsinki-led study reported the Baltic ringed seal has grown about fivefold since the 1970s to roughly 25,000.

notes.harm: HELCOM expects no status improvement and says climate change threatens snow-lair breeding, with southern subpopulations at risk of extirpation (ref 3).

notes.scale: Subpopulations span the Gulf of Bothnia, Archipelago Sea, Gulf of Finland and western Estonia (ref 3).
notes.duration: Counts since 2012 are highly variable because of milder winters (ref 3), and HELCOM says shorter, warmer winters restrict suitable ice fields for ringed seal lairs (ref 4).

records.title: Puck Lagoon eelgrass has lost at least 69% and up to 99% of its cover since 1957, a 2025 mapping study finds
records.description: A Maritime Institute study published in November 2025 compares 2023 benthic maps with the 1957 baseline and finds eelgrass (Zostera marina) cover in Puck Lagoon fell by 84-99% depending on the model, or at least 69% after correcting for seasonal mismatch. records.title: Spring counts of Baltic-breeding common eiders at Hyllekrog fell 65% from 2009 to 2024
records.description: A 2026 Ornis Fennica study reports that standardised daily spring counts of migrating common eiders at Hyllekrog, Denmark, fell 65.2% from 404,845 in 2009 to 140,820 in 2024, with a 45.2% decline at Kaseberga in Sweden and a falling share of females. The authors cannot separate real decline from short-stopping in milder winters. The decline underlies the 2023-2032 AEWA International Single Species Action Plan for the Baltic, North and Celtic Seas population.

records.title: Round goby now established along most of the Baltic coast and is reshaping Swedish coastal fish communities
records.description: The non-native round goby, first recorded in the Gulf of Gdansk in 1990 and in Sweden's Karlskrona archipelago in 2008, now occupies most of the Baltic coastline and has reached Ornskoldsvik in the north. A 2025 PLOS One study of 17 to 23 years of monitoring data at four Swedish sites found higher perch, cyprinid and piscivore abundance and lower whitefish and flounder abundance after its arrival, with no clear effect on herring or sprat.

records.title: Eastern Baltic cod stays under zero-catch advice, with only by-catch quotas allowed
records.description: ICES advises zero catch of eastern Baltic cod for 2027 and 2028 (all catches from subdivisions 24 to 32), and zero-catch advice has stood for six years. The Council set a by-catch-only TAC of 430 tonnes for 2026 against the Commission's proposed 159 tonnes, and recreational cod fishing remains banned across the Baltic. The Commission's 2027 proposal says the stock has not improved despite measures since 2019 and proposes cutting the by-catch TAC by 51%.

notes.duration: Zero-catch advice has run six years (ref 4) and the Commission states the situation has not improved since 2019 (ref 5).

records.title: Bothnian Sea herring TAC cut 41% for 2026, but still above the legal safety rule, with a provisional TAC ending 31 October 2026
records.description: The Council cut the 2026 Gulf of Bothnia herring TAC by 41% to 39,108 tonnes, less than the 62% cut (25,560 tonnes) the Commission proposed, and made it provisional until the end of October 2026 with a three-month spawning closure. The Baltic Sea Centre says the Council TAC breaches the five percent rule in Article 4.6 of the Baltic multiannual plan, and the Commission said the Bothnian TAC is less likely to rebuild the stock. For 2027 the Commission proposes a 3% increase, saying the stock is larger than estimated but still below sustainable levels.

records.title: Baltic main basin salmon limited to by-catch, with five wild river stocks in very poor condition
records.description: ICES advises zero salmon catches south of the Aland Sea in 2026, and the Council cut the main basin TAC by 27% to 25,537 fish, by-catch only. The Thunen Institute reports five of 27 assessed wild river stocks, all in Assessment Unit 5, are in very poor condition, and that recreational trolling landings fell 77% across the Baltic between 2019 and 2024. The Commission said continued recreational fisheries for main basin salmon are less likely to support stock rebuilding.

location.detail: Atlantic salmon in ICES subdivisions 22 to 31, including the Rugen trolling grounds (Germany), Bornholm (Denmark), the south Swedish coast and Latvian rivers Salaca and Saka; Finland fishes the Gulf of Bothnia coastal quota.

records.layer_rationale: A migratory fish stock with weak wild river populations and a restricted fishery.

notes.harm: Five of 27 wild salmon stocks assessed by ICES are in very poor condition, and only the Salaca and Saka rivers in Latvia are expected to meet Rlim among the 12 Assessment Unit 5 rivers (ref 1).

records.title: Sweden moves the pelagic trawl limit out to 12 nautical miles in the central Baltic to protect coastal herring
records.description: From 1 February 2025 to 30 April 2027 Sweden bans pelagic trawling within 12 nautical miles of the coast in parts of the central Baltic, up from 4, as a scientific trial. SLU Aqua says coastal herring catches have fallen sharply and large fish have become scarce. The Swedish Pelagic Federation calls the ban a death blow to small-scale fishing, while a Stockholm University ecologist says it is unlikely to show results in so short a period and may shift pressure to sprat.

records.title: Baltic Proper nutrient input ceilings will not be met by 2030, HELCOM assessment finds
records.description: HELCOM's 2025 assessment of the Baltic Sea Action Plan found that nutrient inputs have fallen since 1997-2003 but that most countries will miss their 2030 nutrient input ceilings, with Denmark the only one on course. The largest remaining nitrogen gap lies in the Baltic Proper, where Poland and Lithuania carry the biggest shortfalls and the Vistula and Nemunas rivers meet neither their nitrogen nor their phosphorus ceilings. A German Environment Agency modelling report published in August 2026 found that even full delivery of the Action Plan targets would leave most western Baltic basins short of good eutrophication status.

location.name: Baltic Proper
location.detail: Baltic Proper including the Bornholm and Gotland basins; the largest remaining nitrogen and phosphorus reductions are owed by Poland, Lithuania and Latvia and by the Vistula, Nemunas and Oder rivers.

records.layer_rationale: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus inputs drive eutrophication and oxygen loss, a pollution pressure.

notes.harm: HELCOM reports nearly 77,000 t of further nitrogen cuts needed, 69,000 t of them in the Baltic Proper, and the Vistula alone owes 29,414 t of nitrogen and 3,032 t of phosphorus (ref 1); the UBA model finds only Kiel Bay reaching good status (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited HELCOM, Latvian ministry or UBA pages documents a fishery or tourism closure tied to these input shortfalls.
notes.scale: The ceilings gap spans a whole sub-basin of a regional sea, with eight coastal states owing reductions or reporting none (ref 1, Table 1).
notes.duration: Inputs have been above the ceilings since the 1997-2003 reference period and HOLAS 3 saw little to no improvement over 2016-2021 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A formal HELCOM Contracting Party assessment under Baltic Sea Action Plan Action E1 and the 2026 German Environment Agency report (refs 1, 3); no enforcement order.

records.title: Gulf of Finland and Gulf of Riga nutrient ceilings missed, with the Neva and Estonian loads furthest off
records.description: HELCOM's 2025 assessment shows that Estonia, Latvia and Finland will not meet their 2030 nitrogen or phosphorus ceilings for the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Riga, and that none of the nine transboundary rivers with ceilings meets its phosphorus ceiling. Russia, the Neva's catchment country, reported no information for the ceiling tables, although it did cut municipal phosphorus loads, mainly through better wastewater treatment in St Petersburg.

location.name: Gulf of Finland and Gulf of Riga
location.detail: Eastern Baltic gulfs; Estonia carries the largest nitrogen shortfalls (1,240 t Gulf of Finland, 4,348 t Gulf of Riga); Neva and Daugava river inputs.

records.layer_rationale: Nutrient inputs above agreed ceilings in two enclosed gulfs are a pollution pressure.

notes.harm: Estonia still owes 4,348 t of nitrogen to the Gulf of Riga and 1,240 t to the Gulf of Finland, and the Neva owes 15,027 t of nitrogen and 1,361 t of phosphorus (ref 1, Tables 1 and 3).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, beach or port restriction linked to these ceiling shortfalls appears in the cited HELCOM material.
notes.scale: Two sub-basins of the Baltic fed by five countries, so regional-sea scale (ref 1).
notes.duration: The shortfalls are measured against the 1997-2003 reference period and are projected to persist to 2030 (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal HELCOM assessment of Baltic Sea Action Plan commitments adopted by the Helsinki Commission in April 2025 (refs 1, 4); not an enforcement action.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Of nine transboundary rivers with ceilings, only the Daugava meets its nitrogen ceiling and none meets its phosphorus ceiling by 2030; Estonia's Gulf of Riga nitrogen gap is 4,348 tonnes (HELCOM 2025).

records.title: Dumped wartime munitions in the Bay of Lübeck and Kiel Bight leak explosives into the water
records.description: A GEOMAR study found about 3,000 kg of dissolved munition chemicals, including TNT, RDX and DNB, in the south-western Baltic, with TNT highest in Kiel Bay and RDX and DNB in Lübeck Bay. Germany ran a 100 million euro pilot recovery off Haffkrug, Pelzerhaken and Boltenhagen from 2024 to autumn 2025 and pledged 50 million euros a year for six years in July 2026.

location.name: Bay of Lübeck munitions
location.detail: Bay of Lübeck and Bay of Mecklenburg off Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern; about 300,000 t of munitions are estimated in the German Baltic.

records.layer_rationale: Leaking explosives and munition chemicals contaminate sea water and sediment.

notes.harm: GEOMAR found munition chemicals in nearly all 2017-2018 samples, mostly below health thresholds but some 'approaching critical levels' (ref 2); no standard exceedance is stated.
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited GEOMAR, idw or Yacht pages reports a fishery, beach or shipping restriction from the contamination.
notes.scale: A national coastline problem across the German south-western Baltic, estimated at 300,000 t of munitions (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Corrosion of the casings could continue for at least 800 years without recovery (ref 1).
notes.significance: Formal federal programme: a 100 million euro emergency pilot and a July 2026 pledge of 50 million euros a year for six years, with a federal centre of excellence planned in Rostock (ref 3); no court or treaty action.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Nord Stream blasts resuspended 250,000 tonnes of contaminated sediment near the Bornholm munitions dumpsite
records.description: A peer-reviewed assessment led by Aarhus University estimated that the September 2022 Nord Stream explosions resuspended about 250,000 tonnes of contaminated sediment, creating toxicological risk for fish and other biota in about 11 cubic kilometres of water for over a month. Tributyltin and lead drove most of the modelled toxicity, and the blasts lay close to a 1947 chemical-weapons dumpsite and the Bornholm Basin cod spawning ground. The figures are model-based.

notes.harm: Modelled resuspension of 250,000 t of sediment gave 'unacceptable toxicological risks' to fish and biota in 11 km3 of water, mostly tributyltin and lead, but no post-blast measurement is reported (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited paper and Scientific American flag possible effects on Eastern Baltic cod eggs and juveniles but document no fishery closure (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The affected water body is a single basin site around the four rupture points (ref 1).
notes.duration: Risk lasted more than a month after the 26 September 2022 blasts: 15 days (NS1) and 34 days (NS2) above the harm threshold in the preprint (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports, 14 November 2023, with no formal notice, listing or order attached (ref 1).

records.title: Disabled crude tanker Eventin with about 100,000 tonnes of oil held off Rügen since January 2025
records.description: The nearly 20-year-old Panama-flagged tanker Eventin lost power on 9 January 2025 with about 100,000 tonnes of Russian crude aboard and drifted into German waters before being towed to an anchorage off Sassnitz on Rügen. No spill occurred and officials said there was no immediate environmental risk, but the ship, later added to EU, UK and US sanctions lists, was reported still at anchor in January 2026 while courts reviewed the seizure of ship and cargo. The sanctions and court side belongs to the governance topic; this record covers the spill risk. The tanker Eventin lost power in the Baltic on 9 January 2025 and drifted into German territorial waters, and was towed to an anchorage near Sassnitz on Rügen where it remains detained. German customs ordered the oil cargo confiscated, but on 11 December 2025 the Federal Fiscal Court upheld a lower court's suspension of that order, so authorities cannot for now sell or use the ship or its roughly 100,000 tonnes of oil. A final ruling is pending.

notes.harm: About 100,000 tonnes of crude aboard a tanker that lost all power; officials reported no spill and 'no environmental risk' (ref 1, ref 3), so harm is potential only.
notes.livelihoods: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's tourism association called for safer shipping but no beach or tourism closure is reported (ref 3).
notes.scale: A single vessel at a single anchorage off Rügen (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Drifted on 9 January 2025 and still detained off Sassnitz in December 2025 and January 2026 (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: German customs detention and seizure orders and an 11 December 2025 Federal Fiscal Court ruling upholding the suspension of the confiscation (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Ageing shadow fleet tankers raise oil spill risk along the Primorsk to Skagen route
records.description: The Swedish Coast Guard, Finland's coast guard and Greenpeace-commissioned Hereon modelling all describe a growing oil spill risk from old, poorly insured tankers carrying Russian crude through the Gulf of Finland and the Danish straits. Greenpeace reports that the average age of crude tankers on the route rose from 8.9 years in 2021 to 16.6 in 2024, and a Hereon simulation of a 48,000 t spill showed long-term pollution from Finland to Poland. No spill from these ships is reported in the cited sources.

location.name: Baltic tanker route, Primorsk to Skagen
location.detail: Tanker route from Russian Gulf of Finland ports through the Baltic Proper and Danish straits to Skagen; Eagle S was held off Porvoo, Finland.

records.layer_rationale: A concentration of ageing, under-insured tankers is a standing oil pollution risk.

notes.harm: Greenpeace's analysis says the fleet 'presents a significant environmental danger'; the Swedish Coast Guard says these ships 'do not meet the safety standards that we regard as normal in this region' (refs 1, 2); harm is potential.
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or tourism restriction is reported in the cited sources; the Hereon simulation projects resort pollution only as a scenario (ref 3).
notes.scale: The route crosses a regional sea from the Gulf of Finland to Skagen and the Hereon scenarios reach coastal states from Finland to Poland plus Germany and Denmark (ref 3).
notes.duration: Concern runs from Greenpeace's September 2024 report through the Coast Guard's March 2025 statement to the Hereon study reported in February 2026 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: Formal statements and monitoring by the Swedish Coast Guard and Finland's coast guard, and Finnish and Estonian oil-pollution exercises (refs 2, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: A Hereon simulation commissioned by Greenpeace modelled a 48,000 t spill of Ural crude at eight sites along the Primorsk to Skagen route, spreading over 30 days.

records.title: Heavy fuel oil washes ashore on Estonia's north coast after attacks on Ust-Luga oil port
records.description: In late April 2026, lumps of heavy fuel oil washed up on beaches in Lääne-Viru County, including Suureliiva near Lahemaa National Park, and the Estonian Environmental Board linked it to Ust-Luga, where Ukrainian drone strikes set oil facilities on fire. Volunteers collected more than 760 kg, no large-scale spill and no harmed wildlife were reported, and officials also pointed to shadow fleet tankers anchored off Vaindloo.

notes.harm: Tests confirmed heavy fuel oil on several beaches, over 760 kg collected, but 'no reports of harmed wildlife' so far and no large-scale spill (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No beach closure or fishery restriction is reported; the Environmental Board only asked the public to report oiled animals on 1247 (ref 1).
notes.scale: A stretch of shoreline around Suureliiva and between Käsmu and Kunda (ref 2).
notes.duration: Oil was first seen in the week of 24 April 2026 and cleanup continued into the following week; reports end on 30 April 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Estonian Environmental Board confirmed the substance by laboratory test and led the cleanup with the Rescue Board (refs 1, 2).

records.title: PFAS in pike and perch from Helsinki's Vanhankaupunginselkä exceed EU limits and prompt a consumption warning
records.description: Surveys commissioned by the City of Helsinki found PFOS and total PFAS in pike and large perch caught in Vanhankaupunginselkä above the EU limit for fish used in foods for infants and small children. Helsinki recommends that risk groups avoid these fish, and the Finnish Food Authority separately limits Baltic perch, pike, large herring and wild salmon.

notes.livelihoods: Helsinki's consumption recommendation covers pike and large perch and notes fishers and sellers must keep batches within legal limits (ref 1).
notes.scale: The advice is for one bay, Vanhankaupunginselkä, though the Finnish Food Authority's wider advice covers Baltic fish nationally (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Sampling in autumn 2023 and spring 2024 and a recommendation that 'will remain in effect until further notice' (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal municipal recommendation, alongside the Finnish Food Authority's advice updated on 1 February 2025 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Lost fishing nets tangled on a sunken buoy off Rügen, with 10,000 more nets lost each year
records.description: Divers from the German group GRD recovered several hundred kilograms of old fishing nets from a sunken fairway buoy about eight kilometres off Rügen in late 2023, while several more tonnes remained snagged. GRD says it has retrieved more than ten tonnes of ghost nets from the Baltic since 2019 and estimates about 10,000 nets and net parts are lost each year. HELCOM published a report on preventing fishing gear loss in January 2026.

records.title: Microplastics in Gotland Basin sediments rise from the 1970s to up to 4,450 particles per kilogram
records.description: A Linnaeus University and Geological Survey of Sweden study of two sediment cores from the northern Baltic Proper and western Gotland Basin found microplastic accumulation starting in the 1970s-1980s and rising to the present, up to 4,450 particles per kg of dry sediment.
