records.title: Gulf of Finland microplastics: rivers supply 76% and most settle on the seabed, model shows
records.description: A TalTech modelling study published in January 2025 found that rivers deliver about 76% of microplastics entering the Gulf of Finland and wastewater plants the other 24%, with most particles accumulating inside the gulf rather than drifting to the Baltic Proper. Accumulation zones lie mainly between 28 and 30 degrees east near the Narva and Kymi rivers and the Neva-influenced eastern gulf, and about 75% settles on the seabed.

location.name: Gulf of Finland
location.detail: Eastern Gulf of Finland between 28 and 30 degrees east, near the Narva, Kymi and Neva river mouths.

records.layer_rationale: Modelled microplastic pathways and seabed accumulation are plastic pollution.

notes.harm: The model finds about 75% of microplastics settling on the seabed in the gulf (ref 1); it does not measure ecological harm.
notes.livelihoods: Neither the Frontiers paper nor the ERR report on a separate TalTech model mentions any fishery or beach effect (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The whole Gulf of Finland, shared by Finland, Estonia and Russia, is modelled (ref 1).
notes.duration: Most particles stay in the gulf and about 75% settles on the seabed, so the load accumulates rather than leaving (ref 1).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed Frontiers in Marine Science paper (20 January 2025) and a separate TalTech model in Ocean Dynamics, neither tied to a regulator (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Eagle S anchor drag cut Estlink 2 and telecom cables in the Gulf of Finland; Finnish jurisdiction case revived on appeal
records.description: On 25 December 2024 the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S was alleged to have dragged an anchor along the seabed of the Gulf of Finland, damaging the Estlink 2 power cable and several telecommunications cables between Finland and Estonia. The Helsinki District Court declined jurisdiction in October 2025, but on 27 August 2026 the Helsinki Court of Appeal ruled that Finland can try the three officers. The ruling can still be taken to the Supreme Court.

location.name: Gulf of Finland (Estlink 2 route)
location.detail: Seabed between Finland and Estonia in the Gulf of Finland. The damage was located in Finland's exclusive economic zone according to the reporting cited; exact cable positions are not given in the sources.

records.layer_rationale: Damage to energy and communications infrastructure on the seabed, now a jurisdiction and liability dispute in the courts.

notes.livelihoods: Estlink 2 returned to service only in late June 2025, about six months after the damage, and cable owners seek about EUR 105 million in repair costs and lost income (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: One anchor track of about 90 km across a single corridor of the Gulf of Finland, so a local, single-site incident (ref 1).
notes.duration: Incident of 25 December 2024; proceedings were still moving through the courts in August to September 2026, with a Supreme Court deadline of 26 October 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Helsinki Court of Appeal ruled on 27 August 2026 that Finland has jurisdiction, overturning the October 2025 district court dismissal (refs 2, 3).

key_measure.text: The Helsinki Court of Appeal held unanimously that Finland has jurisdiction to try three Eagle S officers over damage to Estlink 2 and four telecom cables (The Record, 27 August 2026).

records.title: Balticconnector gas pipeline and cables damaged by a ship anchor in October 2023, with criminal cases still open
records.description: On 8 October 2023 the Balticconnector gas pipeline between Finland and Estonia and nearby data cables were damaged in the Gulf of Finland. Finnish investigators traced an anchor found near the damage to the Hong Kong-flagged container ship Newnew Polar Bear; China has said the damage was an accident caused by a storm. In May 2025 the ship's captain appeared before a court in Hong Kong, and Finnish and Estonian investigations were reported as ongoing.

records.layer_rationale: Damage to cross-border energy infrastructure that became a multi-jurisdiction criminal and diplomatic matter.
secondary_drivers: Anchor strike by a merchant vessel

notes.harm: Pressure fell from 34.5 bar to 6 bar and the pipeline was shut; Finnish investigators described the damage as mechanical rather than an explosion, and no marine ecological harm is documented (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: The pipeline carrying gas between Finland and Estonia was out of use from 8 October 2023 until service resumed on 22 April 2024 (ref 3); repair cost was about EUR 35 million (ref 2).
notes.scale: A single pipeline corridor of the Gulf of Finland (ref 1).
notes.duration: Damage in October 2023; investigations and the Hong Kong case were still reported in 2025 and criminal trial is expected in early 2027 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The captain was brought before a Hong Kong court in May 2025 on marine-rule charges, and Finland and Estonia run a joint criminal investigation (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Yi Peng 3 anchor dragging cut two Baltic telecom cables in November 2024; Swedish probe inconclusive on intent
records.description: In November 2024 the Chinese-flagged bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 dragged its anchor for about 1.5 days over 180 nautical miles off south-east Sweden, cutting the Arelion Gotland-Lithuania cable and the C-Lion 1 cable linking Finland and Germany. Sweden's Accident Investigation Authority reported in April 2025 that it could not determine whether the cutting was deliberate, citing late and limited access to the ship.

records.title: Fitburg anchor drag damaged Finland-Estonia telecom cables on 31 December 2025; captain and boatswain on trial in Helsinki
records.description: On 31 December 2025 telecom operators Elisa and Arelion reported faults on cables between Finland and Estonia in the Gulf of Finland. Finnish police stopped the St Vincent and the Grenadines-flagged cargo ship Fitburg, which was carrying steel from St Petersburg, and drag marks consistent with its anchor were found. The captain and a boatswain went on trial at the Helsinki District Court in September 2026; both deny the charges and the defence disputes Finnish jurisdiction because the damage lay in Estonia's exclusive economic zone.

records.title: Baltic Sea cable and pipeline damage since 2023 and NATO's Baltic Sentry response
records.description: At least 11 Baltic Sea cables had been damaged between October 2023 and January 2025, according to the Associated Press. NATO announced Baltic Sentry on 14 January 2025 to deploy ships, aircraft and naval drones around undersea infrastructure. New incidents followed at the turn of 2026, including a Lithuania-Latvia cable damaged near Liepaja in early January 2026, which Latvian police linked to a ship that crossed it.

notes.livelihoods: The cited reports describe no lasting service closures across the region; the Lithuania-Latvia cable case reported services continuing normally (ref 3).
notes.scale: Incidents span the Gulf of Finland, the Baltic Proper and the Latvian coast, so a regional sea rather than a basin (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.duration: Incidents from October 2023 to January 2026, with the damage near Liepaja in January 2026 following a year with few reports (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: NATO announced the Baltic Sentry mission on 14 January 2025 and its planned initial duration was 90 days (ref 1).

records.title: Baltic and North Sea states begin insurance and port state checks on shadow fleet tankers in the Danish straits
records.description: In December 2024 nine European countries including Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Poland and Sweden confirmed plans to ask suspected shadow fleet tankers for proof of oil pollution insurance in the Danish straits and the Gulf of Finland. Denmark announced port state control of tankers anchoring at Skagen in February 2025, and in July 2025 Germany and Sweden began insurance checks on passing tankers. The checks are mainly for transparency and cannot compel vessels in the Danish straits to answer.

records.title: Record-high sea temperatures across UK waters in the 2026 marine heatwave, from the Channel to Liverpool Bay
records.description: Cefas WaveNet buoys recorded sea temperatures between May and August 2026 that were 3 to 4.5 C above the seasonal average at four highlighted sites, with several sites reaching their highest readings since monitoring began in 2002 and 2004. Readings included 21.7 C in Poole Bay, 21.4 C at Hastings, 21.1 C south-west of the Isles of Scilly and 22.3 C in Liverpool Bay. Cefas notes that heatwaves of this kind can raise the risk of harmful algal blooms, disease and non-native species, and scientists report octopus and unusual sharks in the south-west.

records.title: Northeast Atlantic and adjacent seas warming and acidifying faster than the global average, Copernicus Ocean State Report 9 finds
records.description: The ninth Copernicus Ocean State Report, published September 2025, finds that the northeastern Atlantic and adjacent seas are warming and acidifying at rates above the global average. It reports surface pH falling 0.017 units per decade from 1985 to 2023 and sea level rising 3.7 mm a year from 1999 to 2024. Around one-third of the region experienced severe-to-extreme marine heatwaves in 2023, and the Bay of Biscay is named among 2024 extreme heatwave areas.

location.name: Northeast Atlantic and adjacent seas
location.detail: The report chapter covers the northeastern Atlantic and adjacent European seas; the Faroe Plateau, Iberian coast and Celtic-Biscay Shelf are named as warming slower than the semi-enclosed seas but faster than the global average.

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale carbonate chemistry, temperature and sea-level change documented in a peer-reviewed ocean assessment.

notes.harm: The chapter says about 17 percent of cold-water corals and 50 percent of seagrass experienced extreme, long-lasting marine heatwaves in 2024, a potential rather than a measured loss (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: About 17 percent of shellfish farms on European coasts lay in seas with severe-to-extreme heatwaves in 2024, but no closure or loss is reported (ref 1).
notes.scale: The pH, temperature and sea-level trends are assessed for the whole northeastern Atlantic and adjacent seas, a basin-level region (ref 1).
notes.duration: The pH decline is measured over 1985 to 2023 and the warming trend over 1982 to 2024, so the change is multi-decadal (ref 1).
notes.significance: A scientific assessment report with no regulatory, treaty or court action attached (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Toconao plastic pellet spill from lost containers reaches beaches in Galicia, Asturias and Cantabria; criminal case dismissed in 2026
records.description: The container ship Toconao lost six containers about 80 km off Viana do Castelo, Portugal on 8 December 2023, one holding about 26 tonnes of plastic pellets in 1,040 sacks. Pellets reached Galicia from 13 December and Galicia raised an alert to level 2 on 9 January 2024. In January 2026 a Noia court permanently closed the criminal case, finding no crime and no toxicity, while the Xunta says it spent over 2.3 million euros on cleanup.

records.title: Sandymount Strand rated Poor for bathing after wastewater overflows in Dublin Bay, improving in 2025 as Dun Laoghaire Baths is rated Poor
records.description: The EPA classified Sandymount Strand in Dublin Bay as Poor in 2023 and 2024, with local authorities required to advise against bathing all season, citing wastewater overflows, dog fouling and misconnections. In 2025 it improved to Sufficient and the restriction was lifted, while Dun Laoghaire Baths was rated Poor on its first classification because of wastewater overflows. Ireland's largest treatment plant at Ringsend serves about 40 percent of national wastewater and was being upgraded.

records.title: Scotland to apply tighter seabed limit for sea-lice drug emamectin benzoate at salmon farms after evidence of harm to crustaceans
records.description: SEPA survey work in 2017 found emamectin benzoate near fish farms had a negative effect on crustacean abundance and richness at seabed concentrations well below the original 763 ng/kg standard. A new standard, recalculated in March 2023 to 272 ng/kg dry weight, replaces it, and the Scottish Government said in June 2024 it intends to direct SEPA to apply it at existing farms after 48 months. The industry warns of fewer treatment options for sea lice.

notes.livelihoods: The Scottish Government expects the standard to reduce the number of sea-lice treatments allowed per production cycle, and industry cites limited alternatives (ref 2).
notes.scale: The standard applies to all licensed Scottish marine finfish farms, a national coastline (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The issue dates from the 2016 review and 2017 SEPA interim restrictions and runs to a 48-month phase-in from 2024; the compound is persistent (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: UKTAG recommended a new environmental quality standard and Ministers intend a formal Direction to SEPA (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Shoreline retreat south of Figueira da Foz and at Costa Nova-Vagueira on Portugal's west coast prompts sand nourishment and breakwater studies
records.description: Portugal's environment agency APA reports the 3.5 km coast between Cova-Gala and Lavos south of Figueira da Foz retreated 14 m on average in 2018 to 2021 (5.5 m a year), with 52 percent of the stretch in extreme erosion. Further north, the Costa Nova to Areao coast retreated about 140 m on average from 1958 to 2021, though recent years show stabilisation. APA has prepared a beach nourishment project at Figueira da Foz and studied a detached breakwater off Vagueira.

records.title: Bay of Biscay winter fishing closures to stop common dolphin bycatch continue into a fourth year
records.description: Common dolphins and other small cetaceans are caught in fishing gear in the Bay of Biscay at rates ICES says exceed the limit for a favourable conservation status every year since 2018. After a French Conseil d'Etat order in March 2023, annual winter closures for vessels over eight metres were applied from 2024, and on 4 September 2026 the European Commission proposed extending the closure into winter 2027. The French observatory PELAGIS found 2025 bycatch mortality significantly lower than estimated before the closures.

notes.harm: The Conseil d'Etat found the maximum limit for favourable conservation status in the North-East Atlantic had been exceeded every year since 2018, citing ICES opinions (ref 1); EIA reports more than 110,000 common dolphins bycaught in the Bay since 1990 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: About 300 EU vessels over 8 m are affected by each closure and compensation is paid from the EMFAF or state aid (ref 4); IFAW cites a 30 million euro compensation package for the 2024 closures (ref 3).
notes.scale: The closure involves France, Spain, Portugal, Belgium and the Netherlands and covers the Bay of Biscay as a regional sea (ref 4).
notes.duration: Winter closures have run since January 2024 (ref 3) and the Commission proposed a fourth year on 4 September 2026 (ref 4); bycatch strandings have occurred in unprecedented numbers since 2016 (ref 3).
notes.significance: The Conseil d'Etat ordered the government to close fishing areas within six months on 20 March 2023 (ref 1) and the Commission is acting through a delegated act under the CFP (ref 4).

records.title: ICES advises zero catch for cod, haddock, whiting and Irish Sea plaice across the Celtic Seas
records.description: ICES advice for 2026, issued on 27 June 2025, recommended zero catch for Celtic Sea cod, haddock, whiting and herring, the first zero-catch advice ever for haddock. Advice issued in June 2026 for 2027 again recommends zero cod in the Irish Sea, Western Channel and southern Celtic Seas, zero haddock in the southern Celtic Sea and Western Channel and, for the first time, zero Irish Sea plaice. ICES calls the situation in the Celtic Sea and Irish Sea 'particularly concerning'.

records.layer_rationale: Commercial fish stocks in the Celtic Seas ecoregion are below biomass limits and recruitment has fallen.

notes.livelihoods: ICES warned zero-catch advice will have 'serious consequences' for fishing communities (ref 2); the Irish Sea plaice limit for 2026 was 614 tonnes and the Irish Sea haddock advice for 2027 is down 69% (ref 3).
notes.scale: The advice spans the Celtic Sea, Irish Sea and Western Channel stocks within one ecoregion, with ICES overviewing 48 demersal stocks from the North Sea to Iberia (ref 1).
notes.duration: Zero-catch advice was issued in June 2025 for 2026 (ref 1) and again in June 2026 for 2027 (ref 3), so two consecutive advice years.
notes.significance: ICES advice is a formal scientific recommendation, not an enforcement order; a Cefas assessment found most UK 2026 limits were not set in line with advice (ref 3).

records.title: Celtic Seas pollack: zero-catch advice cut the handline fishery to bycatch only, and advice for 2027 is reduced
records.description: ICES advised zero catch of pollack in subareas 6 and 7 (Celtic Seas and English Channel) for 2024 and 2025. In response the UK and EU agreed that pollack could only be caught as bycatch in 2024, and the Marine Management Organisation set up support for the affected fishers. ICES advice issued on 30 June 2026 allows total removals of up to 3,216 tonnes in 2027 but shows a 41 percent probability that spawning biomass falls below Blim in 2028.

records.title: Northeast Atlantic mackerel fished well above scientific advice by the coastal states
records.description: ICES advised a 77 percent cut in mackerel catches for 2026, yet its forecast of 2026 catches is about 398,000 tonnes, roughly 128 percent above that advice. Only the UK, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Iceland agreed a 299,010-tonne total for 2026, with the EU and Greenland outside the deal, and no internationally agreed TAC exists. ICES put spawning biomass at about 3.2 million tonnes, just above the critical limit of 3.07 million, and advised up to 352,938 tonnes for 2027.

location.detail: Widely distributed pelagic stock fished by coastal states including the UK, Norway, the Faroe Islands, Iceland and the EU;

records.layer_rationale: Shared stock whose catch limits are set unilaterally above advice because the coastal states have no sharing agreement.

notes.harm: ICES estimated 2026 spawning biomass at about 3.2 million tonnes, just above the 3.07 million tonne critical limit and below the 4.12 million tonne precautionary level, with a 33.2% probability of falling below the limit in 2028 (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: Mackerel, Atlanto-Scandian herring and blue whiting fisheries lost MSC certification more than five years ago and some European brands and retailers are switching to alternatives (ref 1).
notes.scale: The stock spans the Northeast Atlantic and several coastal states; the EU and Greenland sit outside the 2026 four-party arrangement (ref 3).
notes.duration: Total catch limits have exceeded scientific advice by 5% to 80% since 2009, and by 39% on average in 2020 to 2024 (ref 2).
notes.significance: ICES advice is formal but does not set national quotas, and the Marine Conservation Society downgraded midwater-trawled mackerel to rating 4 in April 2025 (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Iceland capelin: zero-catch advice in 2024, a tiny quota in 2025 and a sharp fall in autumn 2026 advice
records.description: Iceland's Marine and Freshwater Research Institute advised zero capelin catch for winter 2024/25 after the autumn 2024 survey, then 8,589 tonnes in February 2025. Advice recovered to 197,474 tonnes for 2025/26, but after the September 2026 survey came in well below expectations the new advice for the coming season is 105,773 tonnes, about 70 percent below the 358,044 tonnes proposed in June 2026. The institute says incomplete survey coverage means the stock is probably underestimated.

location.detail: Capelin stock surveyed in the Iceland-East Greenland-Jan Mayen area, off east Greenland and north of Iceland.

notes.harm: The autumn 2024 survey put spawning stock biomass at about 193,000 tonnes and found the harvest control rule's 95% probability of staying above Blim of 114,000 tonnes could not be met (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Zero catch was advised for winter 2024/25 and only 8,589 tonnes were advised in February 2025 (refs 1, 2), so almost no winter capelin catch was advised that season.
notes.scale: A single shared stock, the Iceland-East Greenland-Jan Mayen (IEGJM) capelin, is involved (ref 3).
notes.duration: Advice swung from zero (October 2024) to 8,589 t (February 2025), 197,474 t (January 2026) and 105,773 t (October 2026) across three seasons (refs 1 to 5).
notes.significance: The advice follows the harvest control rule agreed by the coastal states and was issued jointly with the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources (refs 1, 5).

records.title: Faroe Islands pilot whale and dolphin drive hunts killed more than 1,000 animals in 2025
records.description: Sea Shepherd counted 992 cetaceans killed across ten hunts in 2025 by 13 September, and Geographical reports more than 1,000 pilot whales and white-sided dolphins for the year, while the official count of the 13 September Fuglafjordur hunt was 285 pilot whales, excluding juveniles and foetuses. A further hunt near Sandavagur in early May 2026 killed more than 125 animals in the official toll, which excludes at least 15 foetuses and small juveniles. The hunt has no fixed quota and the UK-Faroe trade arrangements are due for review at the end of 2026.

records.title: Iceland fin whaling resumes in 2026 under a licence to 2029 as a bill to ban whaling is planned
records.description: Iceland granted Hvalur hf. a five-year licence in December 2024 to take up to 209 fin whales a year in 2025 to 2029, and its minke licence-holder 217 minke whales. Hvalur did not hunt in 2025 because Japanese meat prices were too low, but resumed in 2026, with 80 fin whales caught by 8 September against a quota of up to 150. The government says it will submit a bill in February 2027 that could permanently ban whaling.

records.title: Scottish salmon farms record more than 35 million officially reported deaths from 2023 to 2025
records.description: Scottish farms officially reported 35,867,788 salmon deaths between January 2023 and October 2025, according to freedom of information data obtained by Animal Equality UK. The Animal and Plant Health Agency inspected 21 of 213 active sites in that period, with two unannounced inspections, and none of the 20 sites with the most deaths. A Scottish Parliament committee criticised the government's slow progress on regulating salmon farming in January 2025.

notes.duration: Record mortality was reported in 2022 and 2023, a Mowi farm lost more than a million fish in October 2024, and 35.9 million deaths were reported over January 2023 to October 2025 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Galician shellfish beds collapse after low-salinity and heat events in the Rias Baixas
records.description: A December 2023 mass mortality reportedly killed about 95 percent of Galicia's cockles and 75 percent of Japanese clams after rainfall 127 percent above normal and salinity near 5 parts per thousand. Bivalve harvests in the Ria de Arousa fell from 2,700 tonnes in 2023 to 1,700 tonnes in 2024, and mussel production in 2024 was the lowest in 25 years. About 3,500 licensed shellfish gatherers remain, half as many as in 2001.

records.title: Iberian orcas keep damaging and sinking sailing yachts off Portugal and Galicia
records.description: A small group of endangered Iberian orcas has been striking the rudders of sailing yachts since 2020. A yacht with five people aboard sank off Fonte da Telha near Lisbon in September 2025, and on 24 July 2026 another yacht sank near Estaca de Bares, Galicia, with its two occupants rescued. More than 500 interactions have been recorded and Spanish authorities advise sailors in orca zones to follow official guidance.

records.title: Wester Ross maerl beds recover after a ten-year scallop dredging ban, with threats remaining
records.description: Scallop dredging was banned in 2016 across the 600 square kilometre Wester Ross Marine Protected Area, the world's largest for maerl, and a decade of citizen-science surveys and local reports describe recovering scallops and fish and more sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. The surveys also found damaged maerl in some places from illegal dredgers and invasive algal growth that scientists suspect is linked to salmon-farm nutrients. In June 2026 Environmental Standards Scotland found that Scottish Ministers had failed their legal duties to protect and restore the seafloor.

notes.livelihoods: Creel fishing, hand diving and prawn trawling in designated areas remain allowed, and local creel and dive fishers report better catches since the ban (ref 1).
notes.scale: The protection applies to one 600 sq km marine protected area (ref 1).
notes.duration: The dredging ban dates from 2016 and BHA has surveyed the maerl for ten years (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: ESS found Scottish Ministers non-compliant with the Marine Strategy Regulations 2010 on seafloor monitoring (ref 2).

records.title: First UK-wide bycatch analysis finds thousands of seabirds, cetaceans and seals killed each year
records.description: A June 2026 analysis by the Wildlife and Countryside Link coalition estimates that UK fishing boats catch over 10,000 seabirds, over 1,000 cetaceans, around 500 seals and over 120 tonnes of protected sharks, skates and rays every year. It says the totals are likely the tip of the iceberg because only a fraction of the fleet is monitored. A two-year Cornish trial found towed deterrents cut the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets by 59 to 71 percent.

location.name: UK waters, bycatch of protected species
location.detail: UK waters, spanning the North Sea and Atlantic seas; the gillnet deterrent trial involved Cornish fishing vessels.

records.layer_rationale: Incidental killing of protected species by fishing gear.

notes.harm: WCL's extrapolation is over 10,000 seabirds, over 1,000 cetaceans, around 500 seals and over 1,000 Atlantic salmon killed each year, plus six humpback and 30 minke whales found dead in Scottish creel ropes (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The report documents no fishery closure or loss of livelihood; it asks for remote electronic monitoring and mitigation, and trials in Filey Bay cut bycatch from 700 seabirds to four or five (ref 2).
notes.scale: The analysis spans UK waters across several seas and finds bycatch is a key reason the UK fails to reach good environmental status in some seas (ref 2).
notes.duration: The report says deaths have stayed 'stubbornly high' for decades despite known impacts (ref 1).
notes.significance: This is an NGO coalition analysis; Defra says it is acting through its Clean Catch programme and the Cornish trial results were published in Conservation Letters (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Every year fishing boats catch over 10,000 seabirds, over 1,000 cetaceans, around 500 seals, over 120 tonnes of protected sharks, skates and rays and over 1,000 endangered Atlantic salmon (WCL, June 2026).

records.title: Repeated SHEFA-2 subsea cable faults off Orkney cut broadband to Shetland for 11 and 25 days in 2025
records.description: The SHEFA-2 fibre cable linking the Faroe Islands, Shetland, Orkney and mainland Scotland was damaged twice in 2025 off Orkney, in July (a fishing vessel is believed responsible) and October (cause not determined at the time). Shetland News reported outages of about 11 days and about 25 days for customers of providers without a backup route. The operator told a parliamentary inquiry that the cable has suffered over 20 major breaks since 2007, and the Scottish Government has since committed to the pre-development phase of a second cable.

location.detail: Shallow-water sections of the SHEFA-2 cable about 1.5 to 9 km off Orkney's east coast, serving Shetland, Orkney and the Faroe Islands; Scotland, UK and Faroe Islands.

records.layer_rationale: Critical communications infrastructure on the seabed is repeatedly damaged, a governance and resilience question for coastal communities.
secondary_drivers: Tidal and current abrasion in shallow water

notes.harm: Households and businesses lost internet, card payments and some bank machines; no ecological harm is reported (refs 1, 3); human services disruption only, so scored as limited.
notes.livelihoods: The Toll Clock post office closed and shops asked for cash during the July outage (ref 2); Vodafone, Sky and TalkTalk customers lost service in October (ref 4).
notes.scale: Effects are confined to Shetland and Orkney and one cable system (ref 1).
notes.duration: Outages of about 11 days (July to August 2025, ref 3) and about 25 days (3 to 28 October 2025, ref 4); the operator cites over 20 major breaks since 2007 (ref 5).
notes.significance: A UK Parliamentary inquiry took evidence in February 2026 (ref 5) and the Scottish Government committed to a pre-development phase for another cable in September 2026 (ref 6); no enforcement order is reported.

records.title: China's coastal sea level stood 72 mm above average in 2023, rising 4.0 mm a year since 1993
records.description: China's 2023 Sea Level Bulletin reported coastal sea level 72 mm above the 1993 to 2011 average, with the Bohai 122 mm above, the Yellow Sea 74 mm and the East China Sea 43 mm. The rate of rise was 4.0 mm a year from 1993 to 2023, up from 3.5 mm a year over 1980 to 2023. records.title: Shanghai's typhoon flood extent could grow 80 percent by 2100 as the delta sinks and seas rise
records.description: A December 2025 One Earth study modelling Shanghai finds the inundation extent of a 200-year typhoon event could grow by up to 80% by 2100. Land subsidence accounts for 34% of the increase, sea level rise 29% and more intense tropical storms 37%. The authors warn of a 'polder effect' if defences fail and say raised defences and mobile barriers are likely to be needed.

records.description: A 2025 study of shallow inshore waters of the southeastern Yellow Sea off South Korea found the aragonite saturation state averaged 1.6 in February, with some areas below 1. records.title: Summer hypoxia off the Yangtze estuary reached about 11,600 km2 in the 2020 flood year
records.description: Studies of the East China Sea inner shelf find bottom hypoxia that expands when Changjiang (Yangtze) floods push nutrients farther offshore, reaching about 11,600 km2 with a minimum of 21 micromol/L oxygen in summer 2020. Modelling shows bottom water in the hypoxic zone losing about 1.2 mmol/m3 of oxygen a year, with river discharge explaining 73% of year-to-year variation. China's Ministry of Natural Resources lists estuarine hypoxia among the continuing marine ecological risks in its 2025 bulletin.

notes.scale: The zone spans the inner shelf from the Changjiang estuary south along the Zhejiang coast (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: Seasonal hypoxia recurs each summer, with oxygen declining about 1.2 mmol/m3 a year in the hypoxic zone (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Ministry of Natural Resources named estuarine hypoxia a continuing ecological risk in its formal 2025 monitoring bulletin (ref 1).

records.title: Korean fish farms lose a record 143 billion won to heat in 2024 and face repeat die-offs in 2025 and 2026
records.description: Korea's National Institute of Fisheries Science put 2024 aquaculture losses from extended extreme sea temperatures at 143 billion won, the largest since statistics began, including 25.82 million fish and shellfish dead on South Jeolla farms and a record 17.19 million on South Gyeongsang's south coast. Die-offs recurred in 2025 and again in summer 2026: 360,707 farmed fish had been reported dead nationwide by 3 August, about five times the same point in 2025, and by 4 September 13.533 million had died at 455 farms, with the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries at Serious Level I of its high-water-temperature alert. Response measures include liquid oxygen supply equipment, early harvest and emergency releases, and a South Chungcheong pilot that moves cage fish to a cooler heat refuge. The Korea Meteorological Administration reports marine heatwave days around Korea at 83.3 a year over the past decade against 22.6 on the long-term average.

location.name: Korean fish-farming coasts
location.detail: Cage and land-based farms along South Korea's south coast (South Jeolla, South Gyeongsang), Jeju and the west coast (Cheonsu Bay, South Chungcheong)

records.layer_rationale: Heat-driven mass mortality of farmed fish and shellfish.
secondary_drivers: Low dissolved oxygen in warm water

notes.harm: South Jeolla farms reported 25.82 million fish and shellfish dead in 2024 and South Gyeongsang's south coast a record 17.19 million (ref 1); 360,707 farmed fish were reported dead nationwide by 3 August 2026 (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: The Korea Maritime Institute reported rockfish shipments down 17.5% year on year in July 2025 and farm prices up 9.2% to 55.6% by region and fish weight (ref 2); farmers are being urged to harvest early, release stock and suspend feeding (ref 3); no farm closure figure is given.
notes.scale: Die-offs were reported in several provinces from Jeju to the west coast, a national coastline rather than one bay (refs 1, 3, 5).

records.title: Korea's coastal catch has fallen about 40% since the 1980s and squid landings to a tenth of their peak as seas warm
records.description: The Korean government reports that coastal fish catch fell from 1.51 million tonnes in the 1980s to about 910,000 tonnes over the past four years, and a 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science paper citing Statistics Korea shows common squid catch dropping from a peak of 250,000 tonnes in 1996 to roughly 23,000 tonnes in 2023. Korean waters warmed 1.60 C from 1968 to 2025, according to the National Institute of Fisheries Science as reported by Herald Business. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries' 2026-2027 plan widens total allowable catch limits to 19 species and 23 fishery types and aims to cover all coastal and offshore fisheries from July 2030.

Official figures cited by a Chinese think tank say the share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 64.6% in 2019, and the 2024 campaign investigated 9,770 violations.

records.title: Court cancels Saemangeum airport plan beside the Getbol World Heritage tidal flats, but backers keep pushing

records.title: Taiwanese white dolphin down to about 45-50 animals as Taichung Port expansion and offshore wind advance
records.description: A researcher at the National Museum of Marine Biology and Aquarium told a July 2025 press conference that only 45 to 50 Taiwanese white dolphins (Sousa chinensis taiwanensis) remain, down about 3% to 4% a year since monitoring began in 2002, with about 60% showing visible injuries. The IUCN Cetacean Specialist Group notes four offshore wind farms with 201 turbines operating on the west coast by end 2023 and calls for stricter noise rules.

records.title: Coral bleaching reported at Kenting, Little Liuqiu and Taiwan's offshore islands in the July 2024 heatwave
records.description: Environmental groups reported in mid-July 2024 that divers had found bleaching since June off Kenting and around Little Liuqiu, Orchid and Green islands, with water near Little Liuqiu at 30 to 32 C against a normal 28 to 29 C. Taiwan's Ocean Affairs Department said a coral conservation action plan was being drafted. Bleaching had previously been recorded in 2020 and in 2022, when the Ocean Conservation Administration issued level 2 alerts across southern waters.

notes.scale: Bleaching spans southern and eastern coastal waters, a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Bleaching was reported from June to mid-July 2024, a period of weeks to months (ref 1).
notes.significance: The reports come from environmental groups; the government response so far is a draft action plan (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Invasive cordgrass clearance on China's Bohai and Yellow Sea coast clears most of the Yellow River estuary while Jiaozhou Bay is still invaded
records.description: A remote-sensing study found that 4,816.35 hectares of invasive smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora) were cleared in the Yellow River estuary between September and December 2021, 92.81% of the species' area there. A 2025 Qingdao University study found the species still spreading in Jiaozhou Bay, with 338.75 hectares at the Yanghe River estuary, and Fujian's 2025 marine report says the cordgrass there was largely eradicated. IUCN also lists invasive Spartina among current threats to Korea's Getbol tidal flats.

location.name: Yellow River estuary and Jiaozhou Bay
location.detail: Salt marsh and tidal flats in Shandong (Yellow River estuary, Jiaozhou Bay at Qingdao) and Fujian on China's Bohai, Yellow and East China Sea coast

records.layer_rationale: An invasive plant displacing native tidal-flat habitat, with large-scale clearance under way.

notes.harm: Cordgrass covers hundreds of hectares in Jiaozhou Bay's Yanghe estuary alone (338.75 ha) and is linked to sewage outlets, rubber dams and aquaculture (ref 2); the sources give no native-habitat loss figure.
notes.livelihoods: The sources report no fishery or community disruption.
notes.scale: Clearance and invasion are documented across several provinces' coasts (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.duration: Clearance in the Yellow River estuary took place in 2021 and the Jiaozhou Bay study runs to 2025, with Fujian's report in 2026 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: Provincial and national control plans are cited as the basis for the clearance work (ref 1) and the Ministry of Natural Resources selected two Fujian restoration projects as models (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: 4,816.35 ha of Spartina alterniflora were cleared in the Yellow River estuary from September to December 2021, 92.81% of its area there (Journal of Remote Sensing).

records.title: China's offshore mariculture grew about 15% in 2018 to 2022, with most of it outside planned marine functional zones
records.description: A 2025 satellite study found China's offshore mariculture area rose from 1,203.62 square km in 2018 to 1,384.12 square km in 2022, shifting toward deeper, farther waters, with 61.79% of mariculture outside planned marine functional zones. Fujian and Liaoning grew fastest while Shandong and Jiangsu shrank slightly. A 2026 study of a Landsat dataset found 733,840 hectares of offshore mariculture nationwide in 2018, with Fujian alone at 183,025 hectares.

location.detail: Offshore farms from Liaoning and Shandong to Zhejiang and Fujian on China's Bohai, Yellow and East China Sea coast; national figures also include southern provinces

records.layer_rationale: Rapid offshore farm expansion that outpaces marine spatial planning.

notes.harm: The studies document spatial mismatch with zoning but no mortality, pollution or habitat-loss measurement (refs 1, 2); the 2025 paper notes high-density mariculture pressures in Shandong.
notes.livelihoods: No restriction or closure affecting farmers is reported in the studies.
notes.scale: The analysis spans China's coastal provinces, the national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: The trend covers 2018 to 2022 and continues with 28.2% growth of deep-sea and far-sea farm area in 2022 (ref 1).
notes.significance: These are academic findings with no regulatory action cited (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: In 2022 only 0.608% of designated functional zones were actually used for mariculture while 61.79% of mariculture activity lay outside planned zones (Remote Sensing, March 2025).

records.title: Chinese steel structures in the Korea-China Yellow Sea Provisional Measures Zone draw Korean objections
records.description: At least three large steel structures that China calls deep-sea aquaculture facilities stand in the Provisional Measures Zone (PMZ), where the Korean and Chinese EEZs overlap and only fishing and navigation are agreed. Seoul opposes the installations and fears they could support a sovereignty claim, while the Chinese embassy says they comply with domestic and international law. In 2025 a Korean survey ship was blocked from inspecting one, and in January 2026 China said it would withdraw the management facility.

location.name: Yellow Sea PMZ (Korea-China)
location.detail: Central Yellow Sea where the Korean and Chinese EEZs overlap; the cited articles give no coordinates for the structures

records.layer_rationale: A maritime-zone dispute over unilateral installations in a jointly managed area.

notes.harm: No environmental damage is documented; the Chinese embassy said the structures pose no risk to the marine environment or navigation, and Korea has begun its own environmental survey (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: China's Lianyungang maritime safety office declared three no-sail zones in the PMZ that overlapped Korea's EEZ for a five-day window in May 2025 (ref 1).
notes.scale: The PMZ is a bilateral zone in the central Yellow Sea, a regional-sea-scale area rather than a single site (ref 3).
notes.duration: Korean reporting dates China's installations to at least 2018, with two more in April and May 2024 and one in early 2025 (refs 2, 4).
notes.significance: Seoul's Foreign Ministry conveyed a firm position to China after the February 2025 standoff and the Blue House restated its consistent opposition in January 2026, which is a formal diplomatic notice, not an enforcement order (refs 2, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: China says it will withdraw the management facility; two aquaculture facilities remain in the PMZ, per President Lee Jae Myung (ref 4).

records.title: China Coast Guard patrols in Kinmen and Matsu restricted waters after the February 2024 speedboat deaths
records.description: Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration reported more than 60 entries by China Coast Guard vessels into waters near Kinmen in the year to March 2025, often in groups of four, and drove them out. China calls the patrols regular law enforcement and does not recognise Taiwan's restricted-water boundaries; Taiwan calls them grey-zone harassment. The pattern began after a Chinese speedboat capsized in February 2024 while evading a Taiwanese inspection, killing two men.

records.title: Anchor damage to Taiwan's subsea cables: Hong Tai 58 conviction and the Shunxin 39 case
records.description: In February 2025 the Togo-flagged Hong Tai 58 dragged its anchor across a no-anchor zone and cut Chunghwa Telecom's Taiwan-Penghu No. 3 cable, and on 12 June 2025 the Tainan District Court sentenced its Chinese captain to three years. In January 2025 Taiwan's coast guard also asked the Shunxin 39 to return to port after a cable off the north coast was cut; the owner denied involvement and China called such events common accidents. Taiwan counts 36 outside-force cable damage cases in 2019 to 2023 and five in 2025 up to June.

location.name: Taiwan-Penghu cable corridor, Taiwan Strait
location.detail: Cable between Taiwan's southwest coast and Penghu; a second January 2025 cut was off Taiwan's north coast

records.layer_rationale: Seabed infrastructure damaged by vessel anchors with legal and security consequences.

notes.harm: The Hong Tai 58 cut caused repair costs above NT$17 million; no ecological or injury harm is documented, so this is limited infrastructure harm (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cut disrupted telecom and internet services between Taiwan and Penghu, while the January 2025 north-coast cut did not affect service because backups were activated (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: Cases span Taiwan's northern and south-western waters, with 36 outside-force cases in 2019 to 2023 and five by June 2025 (ref 2).
notes.duration: The Matsu cuts of 2023, the January 2025 cut and the February 2025 cut show a recurring pattern over more than two years (ref 3).
notes.significance: The Tainan District Court convicted the captain and sentenced him to three years on 12 June 2025, described as Taiwan's first conviction of a seafarer in a cable-sabotage case (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Repeated subsea cable cuts isolate the Matsu Islands, from 2023 to the Dongyin case of 2026

records.title: Offshore wind cable works and exclusion zones hit oyster farmers and fishers off Fangyuan, Changhua
records.description: Rest of World reported in January 2026 that cable trenching for an offshore wind project off Fangyuan, Changhua, raised silt that killed nearly all of one farmer's oysters, and that yields fell for the area's more than 500 oyster farmers since work began around 2022. Roughly 600 fishers face reduced catches, and many have quit; compensation covers only licensed vessels and farms that cables cross. Taiwan's Energy Administration says developers must compensate fishers for construction losses and fund mitigation.

records.title: Korea plans to extend and enlarge Yellow Sea EEZ sand mining west of Gunsan over fishers' objections

records.title: MT Terranova fuel oil spill in Manila Bay: 41,849 fisheries claims collected and compensation under way
records.description: The Philippine tanker MT Terranova capsized and sank in Manila Bay on 25 July 2024 during Typhoon Gaemi while carrying 1,468,896 litres of intermediate fuel oil, polluting coasts in Bataan, Cavite and Manila. About 97 percent of the cargo was recovered and the wreck was removed on 21 September 2025, but claims are expected to exceed the owner's liability limits so the 1992 IOPC Fund is likely to pay; payments to Bataan fishers began in 2026.

notes.scale: Impact was confined to the east side of Manila Bay and adjoining coasts, a single bay (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: The spill began on 25 July 2024 and wreck removal ended on 21 September 2025, with claim assessment still running in March 2026 (ref 1).

records.title: Jakarta Bay coast sinking up to 4 m in four decades while the giant sea wall plan advances

A 20 km section of the planned 46 km coastal barrier exists and the government announced in March 2025 that the giant sea wall along Java's north coast would start, though researchers say groundwater extraction, the main driver, is not addressed.

records.title: Raja Ampat nickel mining: four permits revoked in June 2025 as sediment runoff clouds coastal waters
records.description: Indonesia revoked four nickel mining permits in Raja Ampat on 10 June 2025 after an Environment Ministry investigation found environmental violations, while PT Gag Nikel continues on Gag Island. A September 2025 report by Auriga Nusantara and Earth Insight documented sediment run-off turning waters murky brown and bleached coral near mining sites, and said post-mining rehabilitation is very poor. Nickel mining on the small islands of Raja Ampat in West Papua, inside the Coral Triangle, drew a government response in June 2025: four mining permits were revoked and the fifth operator, PT Gag Nikel, was allowed to continue under closer supervision. Officials and campaigners reported sediment runoff from the Manuran and Kawe island operations and large forest clearance, while the cited sources describe the risk to coral reefs as potential rather than a measured loss. In April 2026 campaigners said heavy machinery remained on the islands.

records.title: Supreme Court ruling opens Philippine municipal waters to commercial fishing
records.description: A Supreme Court First Division resolution, reported in December 2024, upheld a Malabon trial court decision in a petition by Mercidar Fishing Corp. that declared small fishers' preferential access to the 15-km municipal waters unconstitutional. The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources and the Department of Agriculture asked the Court to reconsider in January 2025, and fisherfolk groups, local governments and Oceana filed petitions and interventions. records.title: Philippine Supreme Court strikes down commercial fishing vessel tracking order FAO 266
records.description: The Philippine Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that voided Fisheries Administrative Order 266, which required commercial fishing vessels to carry tracking devices and report catches to curb illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. The decision, dated 21 January 2026 and announced on 3 August 2026, found the order failed the rational basis test; BFAR and the fisherfolk group Pangisda Pilipinas filed motions for reconsideration on 14 August 2026. records.title: Indonesia's quota-based fishing policy delayed amid stock and monitoring concerns
records.description: Indonesia introduced a quota-based measured fishing policy (PIT) in March 2023, capping total catch at 80% of estimated stock across six zones covering 11 fisheries management areas, but the start date was pushed to 2025. Mongabay reported that estimated stocks fell to 12 million tonnes and the share of management areas rated fully exploited rose to 53%, while scientists and the Ombudsman criticised the lack of updated stock data and monitoring capacity. A March 2026 study at Banda Aceh found limited port infrastructure and low fisher awareness.

records.title: Indonesia's mangrove restoration target slips to 2029 after a million hectares lost
records.description: Indonesia holds 3.44 million hectares of mangrove (2024 National Mangrove Map), about 20% of the global total, but has lost more than 1 million hectares over four decades. The Environment Ministry now targets rehabilitating 600,000 ha by 2029 under its enhanced NDC and identified 769,824 ha for rehabilitation, after the original 2024 goal was missed with about 150,000 ha restored by December 2024 according to the restoration agency. Funding, coordination and landowner resistance, including holdings kept for aquaculture, are named obstacles.

records.title: Indonesian shrimp farming hit by Cs-137 import alerts and US tariffs
records.description: US authorities detected radioactive caesium-137 in containers from Indonesia in August 2025, and FDA testing confirmed it in one frozen shrimp sample, leading to Import Alerts 99-51 and 99-52 that by October 2025 affected shrimp from Java and Lampung. Exports fell 54% year on year in October 2025 and January to June 2026 shipments were 14% below the same period of 2025. US tariffs of up to 32%, later cut to 15%, and antibiotic-residue concerns add pressure on pond farmers.

records.title: Ice-ice disease and epiphytes cut seaweed farm productivity in North Sulawesi
records.description: A peer-reviewed study at Nain Island in North Sulawesi found that ice-ice disease in farmed Eucheuma denticulatum was linked to epiphyte biofilm and thallus wounds, with warm, low-salinity water raising susceptibility. A farm without biosecurity lost 20% of productivity to 33 kg of epiphytes, and on-farm biosecurity cut disease effects by up to 83%. The paper also notes Indonesian eucheumatoid production fell about 20% from 2015 to 2022.

records.title: Plastic pellets from the sunken MSC Elsa 3 wash ashore along Kerala beaches
records.description: After the container ship MSC Elsa 3 capsized and sank off Kerala on 24-25 May 2025, plastic nurdles from its cargo came ashore along the state coast. Kerala reported hundreds of tonnes collected from beaches and six cetacean carcasses found, and a fishing ban out to 20 nautical miles was imposed. The Kerala High Court later ordered the shipping line to deposit compensation.

records.title: IMO committee warns attacks on shipping near Hormuz could cause large-scale marine pollution
records.description: Since late February 2026 attacks on commercial ships around the Strait of Hormuz have trapped dozens of large tankers in the Persian Gulf and raised the risk of major oil pollution. On 1 May 2026 the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee adopted a resolution warning of large-scale marine pollution in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea and asked the Secretary-General to monitor environmental effects. Slicks have been documented near Qeshm and Kharg, and no estimate of crude reaching the sea exists.

records.title: Karachi discharges about 425 million gallons a day of untreated sewage into the Arabian Sea
records.description: A Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation study estimates the city generates about 460 million gallons of sewage a day and treats only about 35 million, sending roughly 425 million gallons a day to the sea. Industrial and domestic wastewater flows through the Lyari River, and WWF-Pakistan's technical adviser says marine biodiversity around the Lyari and Malir river mouths has largely disappeared. The S-III treatment programme, started in 2014, has slipped to a December 2027 deadline.

records.title: Seawater has submerged more than 124 revenue villages in the Indus delta, a Dawn study finds
records.description: A Dawn study published in May 2025 found that over the past decade more than 124 dehs across six coastal talukas of Thatta and Sujawal districts have been submerged by the sea, with the total inundated area put at 1.2 million acres. Reduced freshwater flow below Kotri is cited as the main driver, with families leaving for Karachi. Further Dawn reporting in June 2025 describes rising sea levels, mangrove loss and displaced fishermen. Dawn's May 2025 analysis of Sindh revenue data found more than 124 dehs (revenue villages) across six coastal talukas of Thatta and Sujawal districts have been submerged by seawater in the past decade, after freshwater flows below Kotri Barrage fell. AFP reported in August 2025 that flows into the delta are down about 80 per cent since the 1950s, salinity has risen about 70 per cent since 1990 and fish, shrimp and crab stocks have suffered. Sindh runs a mangrove restoration programme, but reports say clearing for land grabbing and housing continues elsewhere in the delta.

records.title: Desalination brine raises salinity in parts of the Persian Gulf, modelling studies find
records.description: The Persian Gulf hosts about half of the world's seawater desalination capacity, and most plants discharge brine back into the Gulf. A 2019 modelling study found brine raised mean Gulf salinity by only 0.43 g/kg but by about 4.3 g/kg in the southwestern Gulf near the Arabian coast, and a 2020 follow-up found basin salinity resilient to present discharge. A 2019 global study attributed over half of world brine output to Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar, and an August 2026 analysis again flags hot, hypersaline effluent zones.

records.title: Severe coral bleaching at Lakshadweep's Kavaratti atoll in 2024 on top of a halving of live coral cover since 1998
records.description: ICAR-CMFRI researchers recorded severe bleaching of hard corals across Lakshadweep after marine heatwaves that began in October 2023, and a Lakshadweep Department of Science and Technology scientist put bleaching at Kavaratti atoll at 84.6 per cent in 2024, against 41.9 per cent in 2020. A peer-reviewed 24-year study published in July 2025 found live coral cover at 12 reef sites on Agatti, Kadmat and Kavaratti fell from about 37.2 per cent in 1998 to about 19.1 per cent in 2022, and that Lakshadweep has no formal reef management.

records.title: Endangered Arabian Sea humpback whales of about 80 animals face gillnet entanglement and ship strikes off Oman
records.description: A peer-reviewed health assessment found about two thirds of photographed Arabian Sea humpbacks bore scars consistent with entanglement in fishing gear and six had injuries consistent with vessel strikes. In February 2025 Oman's Environment Authority opened an investigation into a dead humpback found at Al Jazer in Al Wusta, and a June 2026 satellite-tagging study counted just over 80 whales in the Endangered population. A UN migratory species report said a regional conservation plan had not yet been agreed and the Concerted Action should be extended.

records.title: Masirah Island's loggerhead nesting population down 79 per cent, with about 2,000 caught in fisheries each year
records.description: Researchers reported a 79 per cent decline in the loggerhead nesting population on Masirah Island, Oman, one of the largest loggerhead nesting grounds in the world, based on about 30 years of data. The Environment Society of Oman estimates around 2,000 loggerheads are caught annually in local fisheries, and the population is listed Critically Endangered in the Northwest Indian Ocean. Oman's Environment Authority began a five-year nesting and hatching study in May 2022 under an agreement with the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or income loss is reported; the cited conservation work focuses on bycatch workshops and observers rather than restrictions (ref 1).
notes.scale: The decline is documented at one island, although the population is assessed across the Northwest Indian Ocean (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 79% decline rests on about 30 years of research and threats such as bycatch and beach driving are chronic (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The population is listed Critically Endangered in the Northwest Indian Ocean and Oman's Environment Authority runs a five-year study under an MoU with the US Fish and Wildlife Service (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Gwadar fishers report a collapse of local catches blamed on illegal deep-sea trawling in Balochistan's waters
records.description: A Dawn feature published in April 2025 reports that fishers in Gwadar, Balochistan, say illegal, unreported and unregulated deep-sea trawling, mostly by vessels from Sindh, is depleting the sea. Balochistan's Marine and Fisheries Department says the Mobula ray (karinj) is effectively extinct locally and sawfish have disappeared, and officials describe enforcement of the 12-nautical-mile trawler limit and the June to July breeding-season ban as difficult. Fishers also allege bycatch of turtles, dolphins and sharks and report intimidation, including a fatal incident on 28 May 2024.

records.layer_rationale: Overfishing and illegal trawling depleting small-scale fisheries and threatened species.

notes.harm: Balochistan's Marine and Fisheries Department says the Mobula ray is effectively extinct locally (17 sightings in 2021-2022) and the sawfish has disappeared, with sharp declines in sardines, mackerel, pomfret and shrimp reported (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Local fishers say 10 days of their work cannot match one trawler's day, and report attacks, detentions and intimidation, including a fatal incident on 28 May 2024 (ref 1).
notes.scale: The article covers the whole 750 km Balochistan coast, a national coastline rather than a single bay (ref 1).
notes.duration: Enforcement of the 1971 Balochistan Sea Fisheries Ordinance limits is widely described as ineffective and a dispute over trawlers at Gwadar port was reported in 2021, so the problem is chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Existing legal limits (12 nm trawler distance, June to July breeding-season ban) exist and a Balochistan fisheries official says enforcement across the large sea is hard, a formal-rule context, but no enforcement order or penalty is cited (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure; the article describes small-scale fishing communities in Gwadar and Pasni.

records.title: Kerala's sardine catch collapses from 3.9 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021 and stays volatile
records.description: Onmanorama reported in June 2024 that Kerala's sardine landings fell from 3.92 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021, recovered to 1.38 lakh tonnes in 2023, and that sardine prices had risen from about Rs 100 to over Rs 400 per kg while fishers expected a very poor 2024. A CMFRI study in Current Science, reported in October 2025, linked swings in small-sardine abundance to monsoon rainfall and upwelling and recommended species-specific warnings and local fishing restrictions. Kerala's annual 52-day monsoon trawling ban is in force.

location.detail: Kerala's Arabian Sea coast, India; fishers at Munambam and Vypeen quoted. Coordinates are those of Munambam.

records.layer_rationale: Fluctuating small pelagic stock under fishing pressure, warming and monsoon variability.

notes.harm: Sardine landings fell from 3.92 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021 before recovering to 1.38 lakh tonnes in 2023 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sardine prices rose from about Rs 100 to over Rs 400 per kg and a traditional fishers' leader warned the shortage would severely affect livelihoods, while a 52-day trawling ban restricts mechanised boats each monsoon (ref 1).
notes.scale: The impact covers Kerala's coast, with 3,800 mechanised boats and about 34,000 other boats registered in the state (ref 1).
notes.duration: The swing runs from 2012 through 2024 and CMFRI's 2025 study describes recurring fluctuation (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: CMFRI minimum legal sizes (10 cm for sardine) are being breached by catches of 7-8 cm fish, and a Current Science study proposes formal localised restrictions, a formal advisory-level signal (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: Nearly one lakh traditional fisherfolk are in Kerala per ref 1, but the number affected is not reported.

records.title: Abu Dhabi aerial survey puts dugongs at over 3,500 and sea turtles at about 8,000 in 2024 under a net ban and protected areas
records.description: The Environment Agency Abu Dhabi completed an aerial survey of more than 8,000 square kilometres of marine habitat and reported an estimated 3,500 dugongs in 2024, with mother-calf pairs making up 20 per cent of sightings, and about 8,000 sea turtles, roughly 30 per cent more than in 2015. The agency credits a fishing-net ban in the emirate's waters, nesting-site protection and marine protected area management. Abu Dhabi is described as the second-largest dugong habitat after Australia.

notes.harm: The survey reports growing dugong and turtle estimates and no mortality event, so harm is scored only as potential given the net ban implies fishing interaction risk (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The agency cites a fishing-net ban in the emirate's waters as a conservation measure, a restriction on fishers (ref 1).
notes.scale: The 8,000 km2 survey covers the emirate's waters, which is one habitat zone of the Gulf (ref 1).
notes.duration: EAD has run these aerial assessments since 2004 and the findings reflect a multi-year management programme, but no sustained harm is reported (ref 1).
notes.significance: The numbers are an official agency announcement and the net ban is a regulatory measure, which is a formal notice (ref 1).

records.title: UAE reefs on both coasts tested for heat tolerance as Abu Dhabi launches a 40,000-module coral restoration after the 2017 die-off
records.description: In January 2026 NYU Abu Dhabi's Mubadala ACCESS centre, with the Environment Agency Abu Dhabi and the Fujairah, Ras Al Khaimah and Sharjah environment authorities, reported a UAE-wide field heat-stress test of corals from western Abu Dhabi to Fujairah. A professor quoted said climate change is pushing even these hardy species to their limits. A secondary report says the 2017 bleaching event destroyed 73 per cent of Abu Dhabi's coral cover and that Abu Dhabi launched a Coral Gardens programme in May 2025 to deploy 40,000 artificial reef modules by 2030.

notes.significance: Four emirate environment authorities are acting on the findings and Abu Dhabi launched a formal restoration programme in May 2025 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Bombay duck (bombil) catches fall at Satpati-Dahanu from a record 40,065 tonnes in 1979 as boats and trawlers crowd the fishery
records.description: A People's Archive of Rural India report said the Satpati-Dahanu bombil catch peaked at 40,065 tonnes in 1979 and was recorded at 16,576 tonnes in 2018, while bombil boats at Satpati fell from 30 to 35 in the 1980s to 12 by mid-2019. A May 2025 Krishi Jagran article describes growing concern about overfishing, catching immature fish and habitat disruption in the Palghar to Valsad fishery. Fishers blame trawlers and purse seiners and industrial pollution.

notes.harm: The Satpati-Dahanu catch fell from 40,065 tonnes in 1979 to 16,576 tonnes in 2018, although PARI says it is unclear whether the latter figure covers the zone or the state (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Bombil boats at Satpati fell from 30 to 35 in the 1980s to 12 by mid-2019 and fisherwomen report falling incomes and borrowing (ref 1).
notes.scale: The documented decline is for one zone, although the fishery spans Palghar to Valsad (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The reported decline runs from 1979 to 2019 and concerns were still published in 2025, so the pattern is chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The sources are a journalism report and a trade article; no official notice, restriction or CMFRI figure is cited, so this scores as informal (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman disrupted by attacks since 28 February 2026
records.description: After US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman have been struck by projectiles and explosive-laden boats, and the IMO Secretary-General said in April that there was no safe transit anywhere in the strait. Lloyd's List Intelligence reported over 90 attacks on commercial ships by 30 September 2026 and a severe threat level, with weekly transits still far below normal. Mines were reported to have made the strait's traffic separation scheme unusable for evacuations.

records.layer_rationale: A security-driven closure of the world's key oil and gas shipping lane, handled through IMO and flag-state decisions rather than a pollution or habitat process.

notes.harm: The IMO Secretary-General said IMO had verified 29 attacks on vessels and at least 10 seafarer deaths by 24 April 2026 (ref 4), after at least seven deaths were reported in March (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: The IMO Secretary-General said on 24 April that there was no safe transit anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz, and Lloyd's List Intelligence said major container lines still avoid the area in late September (refs 4, 6).
notes.scale: Incidents were logged across the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf near Basra and UAE waters, and the Gulf of Oman north of Muscat, a regional sea rather than one site (refs 1, 5).
notes.duration: Attacks began on 28 February 2026 and Lloyd's List Intelligence still rated the threat severe with an attack on a Kuwaiti-managed tanker on 28 September, more than seven months on (refs 1, 6).
notes.significance: IMO convened its 36th extraordinary Council session in March and the Council met again in July, where the Secretary-General reported the evacuation of stranded vessels was paused because safety could not be assured (refs 3, 5).

records.title: Thousands of seafarers stranded in the Persian Gulf as IMO evacuation plan is paused
records.description: The IMO Secretary-General put about 20,000 seafarers on roughly 1,600 vessels inside the Persian Gulf in March and April 2026. An evacuation framework that began at the end of June moved 136 vessels and 2,900 seafarers by 8 July, then was suspended after ships were hit; about 6,000 seafarers were still reported trapped. The IMO said sea mines made the usual traffic separation scheme unusable.

notes.duration: Crews were reported stranded from March, still about 6,000 in July, a span of four months at the least on the cited pages (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: The IMO Council held an extraordinary session in March and heard the Secretary-General's update on 8 July during its 137th session, a formal international process rather than an enforcement order (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Sea of Japan surface waters hit record warmth in 2024 and stay far above normal in 2025
records.description: Japan's Meteorological Agency reports that sea surface temperature around Japan in 2024 was 1.44 degC above the 1991-2020 average, the highest since 1908, with the Sea of Japan well above normal for most of the year and its northern part the warmest on record for January 2025 (records start in 1982). A September 2024 marine heatwave lifted Sea of Japan surface temperatures up to 5 degC above average, and 2025 was the third-warmest year on record around Japan. Korea's fisheries institute reports the East Sea warmed 2.04 degC from 1968 to 2024, the fastest of the seas around Korea.

records.title: Noto Peninsula earthquake lifts the coast by 4 m or more and strands fishing ports
records.description: The 1 January 2024 magnitude 7.5 Noto earthquake raised parts of the peninsula's north coast by as much as 4 m in NASA's account, and a later measurement near Cape Saruyama in Wajima gave 5.2 m, exposing seabed and leaving some ports dry. NASA reports about 85 km of coastline affected, about 4.4 square km of new land and more than 15 fishing ports in Ishikawa with uplift. Damage was confirmed at 60 of 69 fishing ports in Ishikawa, and the Fisheries Agency's 21 March 2024 update listed 20 ports where catch could not be landed, with most ports in Wajima and Suzu considered unusable. By September 2025 the seabed around Wajima port had risen 1.5 to 2 m, boats moored in layers at temporary piers and large vessels used Kanazawa, about 90 km away. Main restoration of the Naoetsu port quay in Niigata was reported complete in March 2025.

location.name: Northern Noto coast, Wajima area
location.detail: Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan, Sea of Japan coast of the Noto Peninsula; Kaiso fishing port and the Port of Wajima are named in the sources.

records.layer_rationale: Tectonic uplift moved the shoreline seaward and drained harbours, a physical coastal change rather than a pollution event.

notes.harm: Uplift of 3.6 to 3.9 m at Kaiso fishing port lifted subtidal oysters, worm tubes and bivalves out of the water, and rocky-shore algae turned white as it dried (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: Seabed around the Port of Wajima rose 1.5 to 2 m, temporary piers were needed and large vessels moved to Kanazawa about 90 km away (ref 2).
notes.scale: The Geospatial Information Authority counted about 85 km of uplifted coastline and about 4.4 square km of exposed land (ref 1).
notes.duration: A September 2025 briefing to Wajima ama divers on the new seabed map and temporary piers still in use show the effects more than a year after the quake (ref 2).
notes.significance: Japan's Geospatial Information Authority measured the uplift and the Japan Hydrographic Association published a before-and-after seabed map of northern Noto (ref 1, ref 2).

population_affected.note: The cited sources describe coast and ports, not a count of fishing households.

key_measure.text: Some areas of the north Noto coast rose as much as 4 m (NASA); 5.2 m was later measured near Cape Saruyama (ref 2), shifting coastlines and leaving some ports dry (NASA Earth Observatory).

Ama divers have been resurveying changed fishing grounds since heavy rain in September 2024 (ref 2).

Temporary piers were built at Wajima and a reconstruction consultative panel was set up on 25 March 2024 (refs 1, 2).
The Umi-no-Chizu project resurveyed Noto waters in April and May 2024 to map the new seabed (ref 2).
Main restoration of the Chuo Futo quay at Naoetsu port was reported complete on 12 March 2025, with port facilities reopening in stages by September 2025 (ref 6).

The Korea Times reported that an underwater breakwater built in 2020 for the private Anin power plant project accelerated sand loss. records.title: Dissolved oxygen is falling from the Sea of Japan's deep water to its shelves, and the sea is projected to acidify fastest around Japan
records.description: Peer-reviewed studies document a long-term decline of dissolved oxygen in the Sea of Japan's deep and bottom water (Kim and colleagues, 1980 to 2015, ref 2) and, from 1960 to the 2000s, in the bank and shelf waters of the southern sea (Ono, ref 1), with part of the Tsushima Strait area projected to reach a sublethal oxygen threshold by the end of this century (ref 1). Japan's Meteorological Agency projects that the Sea of Japan will see the largest drop in surface pH of any sea region around Japan by 2081-2100 (ref 3).

location.name: Sea of Japan basin and southern shelves
location.type: Deep basin and shelf waters (oxygen and pH)
location.detail: Whole sea; the shelf study covers Yamato Bank, Wakasa Bay, off Awashima and east of the Tsushima Strait, with the deep-water model covering the East/Japan Sea.

records.layer_rationale: Warming-driven weakening of deep-water formation and rising carbon dioxide change the sea's oxygen and carbonate chemistry.

notes.harm: Oxygen declines are documented but no harm is; Ono projects a 134 micromol per kg sublethal threshold in part of the Tsushima Strait area by about 2100 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources reports fishery or coastal-economy disruption from oxygen or pH change (ref 1, ref 2, ref 3).
notes.scale: Kim and colleagues describe the decline across the deep (1500-2500 m) and bottom (2500-3500 m) layers of the whole East/Japan Sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: Ono analysed data from the 1960s to the 2000s and Kim and colleagues cover 1980 to 2015, a multi-decade chronic trend (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.significance: The sources are research papers and a JMA projection, with no formal notice, listing or enforcement (ref 1, ref 2, ref 3).

population_affected.note: Not a population-level finding.

key_measure.text: Oxygen below 300 m in the southern Japan Sea fell by 0.51 to 0.80 micromol per kg per year, comparable with earlier deep-water rates of 0.46 to 0.69 (Ono, Journal of Oceanography, 2021).

records.title: Sea of Japan autumn-spawning squid stock at a record low, with record-low 2025 quota and a small-boat suspension
records.description: Japan's Fisheries Research and Education Agency assessed the autumn-spawning Japanese flying squid stock, which lives mainly in the Sea of Japan, at a predicted record-low 145,000 tonnes of biomass for the 2024 fishing year, with a predicted spawning stock of 65,000 tonnes against the 255,000 tonnes at maximum sustainable yield. Trade press reported that the 2025 national quota was cut 76% to a record low and raised 34% mid-season, and in late 2025 small boats were ordered to stop after landing 2,039 tonnes over their allocation.

notes.duration: Biomass fell from 2016 to 2019, rebounded briefly in 2020 and has fallen again every year since 2021, while catch dropped from 374,000 t in 2006 to 28,000 t in 2023 (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Fisheries Agency set a record-low 2025 quota, raised it mid-season for the first time since 1998, and a Fisheries Policy Council subcommittee added 2,485 t of quota in December 2025 (refs 2, 3, 4).

records.title: Japanese flying squid has no international catch limit while foreign catches in the Sea of Japan are poorly known
records.description: The North Pacific Fisheries Commission's January 2026 species summary states that the measure then in force for Japanese flying squid sets no catch or effort limits and that the Commission has done no stock assessment, leaving management to domestic rules such as Japan's total allowable catch. A new measure, CMM 2026-11, entered into force on 1 June 2026: it asks members to refrain from expanding the number of authorised vessels until the Commission's Scientific Committee completes a stock assessment, but sets no catch limit. Japan's own assessment says Chinese and North Korean catches are not well known and assumes a Chinese catch of 150,000 tonnes a year over the 2004 to 2020 seasons, except in 2004, 2009 and 2013 when it judged catches to be small, drawing on a 2020 satellite study that counted over 900 Chinese vessels fishing in North Korean waters in 2017.

location.name: Japanese flying squid, Sea of Japan and NW Pacific
location.detail: Squid fished by Japan, Korea, China, North Korea and Russia in the Sea of Japan and adjoining waters; the NPFC covers the Pacific high seas

records.layer_rationale: The gap is in the management regime, with no shared catch limit or assessment.

notes.harm: The NPFC summary says no stock assessment has been conducted for the Convention Area and the autumn stock is recorded as at a record low in Japan's assessment (refs 1, 2), so harm is potential from unmanaged catch.
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources document no closure or restriction caused by the governance gap itself (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The Commission's measure covers several flag states in the North Pacific and the squid straddle Japanese, Korean, Russian and North Korean waters (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The 2020 satellite study reported Chinese fleets in North Korean waters in 2017 and 2018 (ref 3) and Japan's assessment assumes Chinese catches from 2004 (ref 2).
notes.significance: NPFC measure CMM 2026-11, in force from 1 June 2026, is a formal measure that freezes authorised vessel numbers pending an assessment but sets no catch limit for this species (refs 1, 5).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Korean east-coast minke whale bycatch trade and illegal whaling under scrutiny after DNA tests find protected whales on sale
records.description: A lawmaker and an environmental federation bought meat from 27 of 115 whale-meat restaurants, with results announced on 6 October 2026; DNA tests found 20 minke and seven protected whales (five Bryde's, one sei, one fin), all seven in Busan. Korea Coast Guard data cited by Kyunghyang Shinmun show 33 illegal-capture cases, 148 people and 52 whales from 2022 to August 2026, and Herald Business reports that a group was caught off Pohang in July 2026 over an estimated five minke whales. Bycatch minke whales may be sold legally; one fetched 71 million won at Ulsan in July 2026.

records.description: A 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science study cites Hokkaido Government figures that Steller sea lion conflict cost about 727 million yen in 2023 in lost catch and damaged gear, and interviewed 29 fishers in 12 villages on the Sea of Japan and Sea of Okhotsk coasts, 20 of whom supported population control. records.title: Mitsubishi quits two Akita offshore wind projects in the Sea of Japan and Japan postpones its fourth auction
records.description: On 27 August 2025 a Mitsubishi-led consortium confirmed it would not proceed with three round 1 projects totalling about 1.7 GW, including Yurihonjo (819 MW) and Noshiro-Mitane-Oga (479 MW) off Akita, citing cost increases. The Economy Minister called the decision deeply regrettable, the government plans to re-auction the sites, and round 4 including two Hokkaido zones at Matsumae and Hiyama was postponed from 14 October 2025. In August 2026 offshoreWIND.biz reported that the government had moved to re-tender the three round 1 areas, without giving dates.
