records.title: Median hard coral cover across Red Sea and Gulf of Aden reefs fell from 36.9% to 21.0% between 2021 and 2024 after extreme heat stress
records.description: The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network's 2025 regional chapter, written by PERSGA, Egyptian, Saudi and UNDP authors, reports modelled median hard coral cover falling by 15.9 percentage points between 2021 and 2024, a relative decline of 43.1%. Cover in the southern Red Sea fell to 13.1% in 2024, while northern Red Sea reefs stayed comparatively stable. The Gulf of Aden has no monitoring data after 2017.

location.detail: Reefs in the exclusive economic zones of nine countries, 12,590 km2 of reef in four subregions from the northern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden (ref 1).

notes.duration: Extreme heat stress peaked in 2023 and 2024 and declined in 2025, so the documented loss is months to about two years of stress (ref 1).
notes.significance: It is a formal regional status assessment by PERSGA, Egypt's EEAA, Saudi Arabia's SHAMS and UNDP authors within the GCRMN report, not an enforcement action (ref 1).

records.title: Fuel oil from two wrecked tankers fouls the Kerch Strait, Anapa and Crimea coasts, and a federal emergency follows
records.description: Two Russian fuel-oil tankers, Volgoneft-212 and Volgoneft-239, wrecked in the Kerch Strait on 15 December 2024 and spilled about 2,400 tonnes of fuel oil according to Russia's Transport Ministry. Fuel oil reached the Anapa and Temryuk coasts and Crimea, regional and federal emergencies were declared, and Rospotrebnadzor declared 141 Anapa beaches and nine in Temryuk district unsuitable for recreation. By August 2026 pumping of fuel oil from the sunken tanker sections was reported complete, 111 Anapa beaches had received Rospotrebnadzor approval documents, Rosprirodnadzor put the environmental damage at about 84.9 billion rubles in claims against the two owners, of which a Kuban court ordered 49.46 billion rubles to be paid for the Volgoneft-212 in August 2025. After two tankers were damaged in a storm in the Kerch Strait on 14 December 2024, the Delfa Dolphin Rescue and Research Center reported 32 dolphin deaths it said were most likely related to the fuel-oil spill, most of them endangered Azov harbour porpoises. Russian authorities said up to 200,000 tons of soil may have been contaminated, and Rospotrebnadzor declared 141 Anapa beaches unfit for recreation, a status its head said still applied in February 2026. Local reports in March 2026 described dead birds and dolphins left uncollected on Anapa beaches.

records.title: Fuel oil clots from the Kerch Strait tanker spill wash up on the Odesa coast
records.description: In late January 2025 Ukrainian environmental inspectors found fuel oil clots of 0.5 to 5 cm on the Odesa region coast, including a 1.5 km line at Katranka where a sand sample held 10.5% petroleum hydrocarbons by mass, and a petroleum film in Odesa port. The pollution was traced to the Russian tankers wrecked in the Kerch Strait on 15 December 2024. Collection of the clots began on 29 January and the environment ministry asked for wider monitoring and an assessment of risks to coastal nature reserves.

records.layer_rationale: Fuel oil from a distant tanker wreck contaminating a national coast.

notes.harm: A sand sample at Katranka contained 10.5% petroleum hydrocarbons by mass (105 g/kg) along a 1.5 km oiled line (ref 1), and about 5,000 dead jellyfish on 2 km of shore were linked to the fuel oil by a Tuzly park biologist (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited reports documents a beach closure, fishing restriction or port stoppage on the Odesa coast; a petroleum film in Odesa port on 28 January is the only port-related finding (ref 1).
notes.scale: Findings are a few shoreline stretches within one oblast, from Katranka to Mykolaivka (ref 1), and on 8 January 2025 the Odesa coast had not been considered at risk (ref 2).
notes.duration: Fuel oil was found from 24 to 30 January 2025 and clean-up started on 29 January, with monitoring ongoing three weeks later (refs 1, 3): weeks.
notes.significance: The Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection ordered stronger monitoring, wider zones and a risk analysis for reserves, and the oblast safety commission met in extraordinary session (refs 1, 3): a formal notice.

records.title: Record Black Sea marine heatwave in 2024 with anomalies above 4.6 C and events lasting over 30 days
records.description: A Copernicus Marine Ocean State Report chapter published in September 2026 found that the Black Sea and Mediterranean both had record marine heatwave intensities and durations in 2024, with anomalies above 4.6 degrees C along the Anatolian coast and events lasting over 30 days. Turkish marine scientists reported surface water near 27 C in September 2024 against a normal of about 22 C, and Copernicus Climate Change Service recorded record annual sea-surface temperatures for the Black Sea in 2024.

notes.harm: A Turkish ecologist estimated warming may have raised the spread of Mediterranean alien species in Turkish seas by 5 to 6 times and warned warm surface water can reduce oxygen (refs 3, 5), but no mortality event is documented in these sources.
notes.livelihoods: A Karadeniz Technical University professor said anchovy fishing practices should be reconsidered (ref 2), but no closure or catch loss is documented.
notes.scale: The whole Black Sea is affected, with strong events covering more than 80% of the basin in the CMCC analysis (ref 1), which scores as a regional sea.
notes.duration: Events lasted over 30 days and moderate events were detected on more than 125 days in 2024 (ref 1), after a record-hot July 2023 reported by Turkish researchers (ref 5).
notes.significance: The Copernicus Marine Ocean State Report and the Copernicus Climate Change Service report record temperatures (refs 1, 4); no emergency or enforcement action.

records.title: Sea snot returns to the Sea of Marmara in 2024 as most promised wastewater plants are still unbuilt

Türkiye's environment ministry says almost 80% of the 169 advanced biological wastewater plants municipalities pledged under the 22-item Marmara action plan were not fully established, and fined four municipalities about TL 9 million in one month in January 2025.

records.title: Romanian Black Sea waters remain eutrophic, with falling oxygen and rising Noctiluca blooms
records.description: A 2024 assessment of the Romanian exclusive economic zone for 2020 to 2022, based on 68 stations and 617 water samples, found coastal waters carry higher nutrient levels and more algal blooms than offshore water. A 2025 analysis of 1960 to 2023 data on the Romanian coast found rising seawater temperature, falling oxygen and a rising nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio linked to more Noctiluca scintillans blooms.

location.name: Romanian Black Sea coast and EEZ
location.detail: Romanian coast and exclusive economic zone including Danube Delta transitional waters and the northwestern shelf, assessed by the Grigore Antipa institute in Constanța.

records.layer_rationale: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus drive blooms and oxygen loss in coastal water.

notes.harm: Coastal waters need roughly 38% less phosphorus and 37% less nitrogen to reach good environmental status, and the 1960-2023 record shows falling oxygen and more Noctiluca blooms (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Neither peer-reviewed paper reports a fishery or beach restriction tied to the eutrophication findings.
notes.scale: The assessment covers the Romanian EEZ and coast, 68 stations in 2020 to 2022 (ref 1), a national coastline rather than the whole sea.
notes.duration: Eutrophication has affected the Black Sea since the 1980s and the Romanian record runs from 1960 to 2023 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Two peer-reviewed assessments by the national marine institute; no formal notice, listing or enforcement is reported in the opened abstracts (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Romanian coastal waters need about 38% less phosphorus and 37% less nitrogen, and Danube Delta transitional waters about 55% and 43%, to reach good environmental status (Lazar et al., Sustainability, June 2024).

records.title: Romanian Black Sea coast and Danube Delta erode by up to 8 m a year as beach works run over budget
records.description: Reporting by the Balkans and Caucasus observatory OBCT in August and September 2025 says 43% of Romania's coastline is highly sensitive to erosion and 37% is already receding, with the Danube Delta losing up to 8 m a year and peaks of 20 m. A coastal protection programme launched in 2013 with over 840 million euros of EU funding has added beaches and breakwaters between Mamaia and Eforie, and Apele Române defends the shift from nature-based solutions to breakwaters and nourishment.

location.name: Romanian coast and Danube Delta
location.detail: Romanian Black Sea coast of about 250 km: the southern resorts (Mamaia, Eforie, Costinești, Mangalia) and the Danube Delta coast, which is over 160 km and 65% eroding.

records.layer_rationale: Coastline retreat from sea-level rise, subsidence and reduced Danube sediment.

notes.harm: 37% of the Romanian coastline is already receding, with up to 8 m a year lost in the Danube Delta (ref 1) and 65% of the delta coast eroding (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Beaches have shrunk each year at Mamaia, Eforie and Saturn-Mangalia, which receive over eight million visitors, but no closure or economic loss figure is documented (ref 1).
notes.scale: The Romanian national coastline of about 250 km is affected, not the whole sea (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The programme started in 2013 and the Danube now carries about a third of its former sediment, so retreat is long-running and chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A national Master Plan from 2012 and EU-funded protection programme are formal action, and Apele Române is the responsible agency (refs 1, 2); no enforcement order.

records.title: Plastic dominates litter on Bulgarian and Turkish Black Sea beaches, with none meeting the EU threshold in Bulgaria
records.description: A 2023 survey of 45 Bulgarian beaches found 753 litter items per 100 m on average, down 48% from 1,462 in 2021, with plastics dominating and none of the beaches meeting the EU threshold of 20 items per 100 m. A 2025 study of 37 stations on the Turkish Black Sea shoreline recorded 29,610 items at 0.80 items per square metre, 88.2% of them plastics, with the highest pollution in the east and hazardous items such as syringes and broken glass at some sites.

records.title: Dozens of dead porpoises wash up on the Tuzly Lagoons coast of Odesa Oblast in 2026, with a criminal ecocide case open
records.description: Researchers at Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park recorded 63 dead harbour porpoises on the Odesa Oblast coast between 18 May and early July 2026. The park's research head attributes the deaths to oil pollution and underwater noise from explosions, sonar and missile strikes, while the cited report says the precise causes have not been conclusively established. A specialised environmental prosecutor in Odesa Oblast is investigating the deaths within a criminal case into alleged ecocide.

records.title: Attacks on merchant ships and ports in the Odesa region and the Black Sea, including the July 2026 strike on the Golden Leo
records.description: A Black Sea Strategic Studies Institute monitoring group counted 22 Russian attacks on ships in Odesa-region ports and the Black Sea in 2025, damaging 39 vessels. In July 2026, Ukraine's navy said Russia hit the corn-carrying Golden Leo with three cruise missiles off Odesa, and the seaports authority reported 10 dead; Reuters reports both sides are escalating strikes on shipping, and Ukraine says it hit Russian vessels. Reuters sources say Ukrainian attacks forced Russia to restrict shipping in the Sea of Azov.

records.title: Anaklia deep-sea port on Georgia's Black Sea coast moves to state-led dredging after the Chinese consortium drops out
records.description: Georgia's prime minister said on 5 August 2026 that construction of the Anaklia port had entered an active phase, with the first stage due in 2029 and the Belgian firm Jan De Nul dredging the seabed to 17.5 m. Eurasianet reported in July 2026 that Georgia would develop the port under a state-owned landlord model after talks with a China Communications Construction Company consortium ended. The cited reports give no environmental assessment for the dredging.

location.detail: Planned deep-water port at Anaklia on the Black Sea coast of western Georgia, with seabed dredging and a planned 1.38 km breakwater.

notes.livelihoods: No fishing, shipping or tourism restriction is reported (refs 1, 2, 3).

notes.duration: The project dates from 2016 and first-stage completion is set for 2029 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A government contract with Jan De Nul and a cabinet decision for a state-owned model are formal government actions (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.title: Black Sea Commission chairmanship blocked at the October 2024 session while the war stalls the Bucharest Convention
records.description: At the 44th session of the Commission on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution on 16 October 2024, Ukraine prevented the chairmanship from passing from Romania to Russia, with Ukraine's First Deputy Environment Minister arguing Russia cannot chair the body while at war with Ukraine. Carnegie Europe commented in February 2025 that the Bucharest Convention's trajectory has been negative since the early 2010s and that engagement with Russian authorities is unlikely in the short term.

location.name: Bucharest Convention and Black Sea Commission
location.detail: Intergovernmental commission of the six Black Sea parties to the Bucharest Convention.

records.layer_rationale: The regional sea convention's chair rotation is blocked by a party-state dispute.

notes.harm: Carnegie says the war has accelerated marine degradation and notes low oxygen in nearly 90 percent of the sea's waters, so the lapse is a potential harm (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or port restriction follows from the chair dispute in the cited sources (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The convention covers all six Black Sea coastal states, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: The chair dispute dates from October 2024 and Carnegie dates a negative trend to the early 2010s (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The 44th Commission session on 16 October 2024 did not pass the chairmanship to Russia, a treaty-body outcome (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The Commission's chairmanship did not pass from Romania to Russia at its 44th session on 16 October 2024.

records.title: Turkish Black Sea anchovy fishery under a 400,000-tonne quota amid volatile catches and expert warnings of depletion
records.description: Turkiye introduced a quota system for anchovy from the 2024 season with a catch limit of 400,000 tons, according to Daily Sabah. Turkish Minute reported in April 2025 that Turkiye's anchovy catch swung from 125,980 tons in 2022 to 273,915 tons in 2023 and began importing Russian anchovy, with experts citing climate change, pollution and overfishing. A 2022 Hurriyet Daily News interview quotes an Ordu University professor describing the stock as depleted.

location.detail: Anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) fishery along Turkiye's Black Sea coast and towards the Georgian border.

records.layer_rationale: Fishing pressure and a small-fish catch on a shared stock.

notes.harm: Experts cited by Turkish Minute say overfishing reduced average fish size and nutritional value, and Prof. Aydin said the stock was depleted in 2022 (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: A 400,000-ton quota and seasonal bans restrict fishing and Turkiye began importing Russian anchovy in 2025 (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The fishery spans Turkiye's Black Sea coast to the Georgian border (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Catch swings from 96,452 tons in 2019 to 273,915 tons in 2023 show a multi-year pattern (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Agriculture Ministry set the quota regulation for the 2024 season and will monitor compliance (ref 1).

records.title: Women fishers protest a planned 12,000-tonne cage farm at Zelek, Rize, as Black Sea marine aquaculture expands
records.description: BirGun reported on 30 August 2026 that Black Sea marine aquaculture rose from 13,000 to over 80,000 tonnes in seven years, almost all of it rainbow trout sold as Turkish salmon, and that women fishers have held a vigil at Zelek harbour in Pazar district, Rize against a planned cage farm of 12,000 tonnes capacity. A 2025 review found that reported Turkish aquaculture mortality and escape incidents roughly doubled between 2010-2015 and 2020-2024.

records.title: Invasive blue crab spreads along the Turkish and Bulgarian Black Sea coasts, with egg-bearing females recorded
records.description: A 2024 monitoring study from Taskana Cape (Unye) to the Georgian border recorded the invasive blue crab Callinectes sapidus from 2017 to 2024, including two egg-bearing females and the easternmost record in Rize, and the authors suggest a possibly self-sustaining population. A 2025 ZooNotes paper reports a male caught near Cape Shabla, Bulgaria on 26 April 2024 and asks for monitoring of reproduction.

A March 2026 peer-reviewed study by Istanbul Technical University authors says the project may pose notable environmental challenges, including wastewater pollution in the Marmara Sea, salinisation risks and marine damage from dredging and spoil disposal.

records.title: Marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent across the Gulf of Guinea, peer-reviewed analysis finds
records.description: A peer-reviewed analysis of satellite and buoy temperatures from 1991 to 2020 found about two marine heatwave events a year in the eastern tropical Atlantic, with frequency rising, most sharply on the northern Gulf of Guinea coast. The longest events lasted roughly 47 to 49 days (2019) and anomalies above 2 C were strongest off the Congo-Gabon coast. A 2025 conference abstract by the same group extends the work to coastal ecosystems in Cote d'Ivoire's Grand-Bereby Marine Protected Area.

location.name: Gulf of Guinea, eastern tropical Atlantic
location.detail: Three zones analysed: northern Gulf of Guinea coast, the equator, and the Congo-Gabon coast; Grand-Bereby MPA (Cote d'Ivoire) used as a coastal case study.

records.layer_rationale: Recurring marine heatwaves are a physical ocean-warming signal.

notes.harm: The paper does not measure ecosystem damage; it notes heatwaves can cause habitat loss, bleaching and harmful blooms generally, so harm is potential only (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or income loss is documented; the authors only note that the Gulf of Guinea supports Atlantic tuna fishing and upwelling-driven food webs (ref 1).
notes.scale: The analysis covers the whole eastern tropical Atlantic and Gulf of Guinea, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: Frequency has risen since about 2015 and the longest equatorial and Congo-Gabon events in 2019 lasted roughly 47 to 49 days, a recurring pattern over decades (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Peer-reviewed paper and a conference abstract only; no agency notice or enforcement (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Recurrent Sargassum influxes strand on the northern Gulf of Guinea coast and disrupt fishing
records.description: Satellite-based studies show Sargassum biomass in the northern Gulf of Guinea rose significantly from 2011 to 2022, peaking around September with a smaller peak in March to May. A 2026 study finds strandings arrive twice a year, mostly advected from the eastern tropical Atlantic and pushed ashore by winds after Cape Palmas. In Ghana, Sargassum-entangled nets reduce catches and communities have turned to food rationing and loans.

location.name: Northern Gulf of Guinea coast (Sierra Leone to Ghana)
location.detail: Ghana is the documented impact case; Sierra Leone is where spring biomass builds up offshore and Cape Palmas (Liberia) is the entry point for onshore transport.

records.layer_rationale: Floating macroalgal bloom influx linked to sea-surface temperature, salinity and river inputs.

notes.harm: The Phycology study reports no measured ecological damage; stranded biomass is flagged as an unquantified risk and beached Sargassum creates odour and aesthetic nuisance, so harm is potential (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: In Ghana, Sargassum-entangled nets reduce catches at peak months and communities use food rationing, loans and alternative income (ref 1).
notes.scale: The influx affects the northern Gulf of Guinea coast across several countries, a regional-sea scale (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Strandings recur every year since the 2011 influx, with peaks in March to May and September to November (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Peer-reviewed paper and a preprint only; no government notice or emergency declaration is cited (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: The studies describe affected fishing communities in Ghana but give no count.

key_measure.text: Monthly floating Sargassum biomass in the northern study area reached roughly 2.7 million metric tons at its highest, with a significant rising trend from 2011 to 2022.

records.title: Nigeria records at least 589 oil spills in 2024 as fresh leaks hit Nembe Creek and Bukuma

In the Niger Delta, NOSDRA confirmed a leak on the Nembe Creek Trunk Line in June 2024, and a gas leak at NNPCL's Well 8 on Bukuma Island, Degema, in January 2025 where investigators found stressed mangrove vegetation near the well-head.

records.title: Niger Delta legacy oil pollution: $12 billion Bayelsa clean-up estimate as Shell exits onshore, London trial set for 2027
records.description: The Bayelsa State Oil and Environment Commission estimated that cleaning up Bayelsa would cost $12 billion, well above Shell's projections. Shell concluded the sale of its onshore Nigerian assets to Renaissance Africa Energy in March 2025, and on 17 July 2026 the Federal High Court in Bayelsa dismissed a suit by the Ekpetiama monarch seeking to halt the divestment as premature and statute-barred. In London, the High Court ruled on 20 June 2025 that the Bille and Ogale claims against Shell can proceed to a four-month full trial from March 2027; Shell says most spills were caused by third parties such as oil thieves and saboteurs.

records.title: Dakar's Hann Bay is contaminated by sewage and industrial effluent while a EUR 184.5 million clean-up nears completion
records.description: A marine specialist (Amidou Sonko, AFP via eNCA) found E. coli at 13 to 100 times the permitted limit in Hann Bay, plus salmonella, microplastics and aluminium, chromium and zinc above standards, with factories, a tannery and sewage pipes discharging directly. A treatment plant for 26,000 cubic metres a day is reported 95 percent complete, but the sea outfall has not started pending extra financing. The minister says the project could be finished by 2027 if efforts continue.

records.title: The sea has swallowed Fuveme and other Keta-coast villages as World Bank-backed sea defences stay at design stage
records.description: Ghana News Agency reported in 2023 that the sea had overtaken three fishing communities in Keta Municipality (Kporkporgbor, Gbakpeygbor and Fuveme) with eight more at risk. After tidal waves hit Fuveme and Blekusu in April 2026, the President said the $150 million WACA sea-defence project had finished feasibility studies, is at design stage and had stalled in 2024. Erosion is also pushing the sea to open a second estuary at Fuveme, threatening the Keta Lagoon and fisherfolk.

records.title: Ghana suspends licences of four trawlers for one year over saiko transshipment, juvenile fish and restricted-zone fishing
records.description: In April 2025 Ghana's Fisheries Commission and the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture suspended the licences of four Ghana-flagged trawlers (Meng Xin 10, Florence 2, Long Xiang 607 and Long Xiang 608) for one year. The violations cited were unauthorised transshipment at sea (saiko), dumping, fishing in restricted zones and harvesting juvenile fish. The Environmental Justice Foundation estimates that Chinese corporations own at least 90% of Ghana's industrial trawlers, and artisanal fishers report incomes down by as much as 40% per canoe over about 15 years.

notes.harm: The Environmental Justice Foundation's Steve Trent said saiko is 'precipitating the collapse of Ghana's staple fish stock' and the vessels were cited for harvesting juvenile fish and dumping (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Artisanal fishers' average annual income has fallen by as much as 40% per canoe over roughly 15 years, and more than 100,000 artisanal fishermen are affected (ref 1).
notes.scale: The enforcement covers one country's industrial fleet and EEZ, and the article puts IUU losses to Ghana at $14.4 million to $23.7 million a year (ref 2).
notes.duration: The article describes a roughly 15-year income decline for canoe fishers (ref 1) and notes a five-year EU yellow card for Ghana (ref 2).
notes.significance: Ghana's Fisheries Commission and Ministry suspended four licences for one year in April 2025, an administrative enforcement action (ref 1).

A Business and Financial Times headline on the report states that 94% of fishers register declining catches.

records.title: Senegal lets its EU fisheries agreement lapse after the European Commission's IUU yellow card
records.description: The European Commission issued Senegal a yellow card on 27 May 2024 over shortcomings in monitoring, control and surveillance, including weak controls on foreign vessels in the port of Dakar. The 2019 EU-Senegal fisheries agreement expired on 17 November 2024 and was not renewed, and European vessels stopped fishing in Senegal's EEZ. Senegal's prime minister's office says the government chose not to renew in order to better protect fish resources.

records.title: EU Court of Justice confirms annulment of the EU-Morocco fisheries agreement as applied to Western Sahara waters
records.description: On 4 October 2024 the Court of Justice of the EU confirmed the annulment of the EU-Morocco fisheries and agricultural agreements, finding they were concluded without the consent of the people of Western Sahara. The fisheries protocol expired on 17 July 2023 and fishing activity has been suspended since. Morocco's Foreign Ministry says it is not a party to the case and describes the ruling as containing obvious legal errors and political bias.

records.title: Saint-Louis fishers say Greater Tortue Ahmeyim LNG exclusion zone has cut access to fishing grounds
records.description: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim LNG project off Senegal and Mauritania loaded its first cargo on 17 April 2025, with the floating LNG vessel about 10 km offshore. A July 2026 DeSmog investigation reports that an agreement sets a 500 m limit around the facilities but that fishers say navy patrols keep them more than six kilometres away, and an analyst doubts fishers will be compensated. Kosmos says the safety zone protects mariners and that fishing outside it is not prohibited.

notes.duration: Production began at the end of 2024 per ref 1 (first gas flow on 31 December 2024 per ref 2) and the first cargo was loaded on 17 April 2025, with the issue still reported in July 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: An OECD complaint against BP and Kosmos was found by the UK National Contact Point in February 2026 to merit further examination, and the case is ongoing (ref 1).

records.title: Mauritania cuts fishmeal licences and bans sardinella use as small pelagic stocks decline
records.description: Mongabay reported in January 2026 that Mauritania had 44 authorised fishmeal plants in 2021 and has since withdrawn licences, banned certain species from fishmeal and cut output to 59,158 tonnes in 2024 from 128,789 tonnes in 2020. Scientists cited by Mongabay found round sardinella declined rapidly from 2018 and flat sardinella, a banned species, still made up about 15 percent of 2024 fishmeal inputs. The fisheries ministry says industrial vessels were cut from over 70 to fewer than 15, and artisanal fishers describe empty seas.

location.type: Fishmeal industry and small pelagic fishery

records.layer_rationale: Reduction fisheries for fishmeal pressure small pelagic stocks used for food.

notes.harm: Round sardinella declined rapidly from 2018 and flat sardinella shows signs of overexploitation, per scientists cited by Mongabay; scientists call for a 60% cut in fish mortality (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: A Nouadhibou fisherman says 'there is nothing in the sea now' and fishing supports up to 300,000 jobs (ref 2).
notes.scale: Plants operate at Nouadhibou, PK28 and Port Tanit, covering Mauritania's national waters (ref 1).
notes.duration: Regulation tightened from 2015, with a May 2021 decree and a November 2022 small pelagics management plan adopted as law; flat sardinella was still about 15% of fishmeal inputs in 2024 (ref 1).
notes.significance: A May 2021 decree banned certain species from fishmeal and a November 2022 small pelagics management law bars fishmeal fishing within 12 nautical miles; the ministry has withdrawn the licences of six of 30 Nouadhibou plants (ref 1).

records.title: ICJ rules Equatorial Guinea holds title to Mbanie, Cocotiers and Conga islands in dispute with Gabon
records.description: On 19 May 2025 the International Court of Justice found by 13 votes to two that the title to the islands of Mbanie, Cocotiers and Conga is the one held by Spain on 12 October 1968, to which Equatorial Guinea succeeded. It found by 14 votes to one that the Bata Convention relied on by Gabon is not a treaty with the force of law. The waters around the islands are described by Reuters as potentially rich in oil, and Gabon must withdraw its soldiers from Mbanie.

records.layer_rationale: A maritime boundary and island sovereignty dispute settled by the ICJ.

notes.harm: No environmental harm is documented in the cited reports, which concern title to the islands (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The sources describe the islands as mostly uninhabited and report no fishery or port restriction (ref 1).
notes.scale: The dispute concerns three small islands and the boundary starting from the 1900 Convention terminus (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The dispute dates from Gabon's army driving out Equatorial Guinea's soldiers from Mbanie in 1972; both countries agreed in 2016 to let the ICJ decide, and the case was brought to the Court in 2021 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The ICJ delivered a final and binding judgment on 19 May 2025 (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Studies document large mangrove loss in Nigeria's Niger Delta, with oil spills and invasive nypa palm as drivers
records.description: A University of Galway study reported in February 2025 estimates about 5,644 hectares of Niger Delta mangrove are lost to oil spills each year. A 2025 study led by Fatoyinbo puts Nigeria's 2023 mangrove area at 957,747 hectares, with 4.5% lost since 1990, at least 37% of the loss directly caused by oil spills, and invasive nypa palm covering almost 10% of mangroves. A Land journal study reports a 54% fall in mangrove area across the Niger Delta region between 1986 and 2024, and a January 2026 analysis links mangrove loss to higher coastal vulnerability.

records.description: Sierra Leone's Fishermen's Union says average artisanal catches are down about 40% in recent years and alleges trawlers come close to shore at night and cut lines and damage nets. Under the 2018 Fisheries and Aquaculture Act, industrial vessels found in the inshore exclusion zone face fines starting at $1.5 million. A Ministry of Fisheries director disputed the corruption allegation, saying all international vessels must carry tracking transponders and are checked often.

records.title: Recurrent marine heatwaves off Salvador, Bahia, with a record event in March 2024
records.description: A peer-reviewed study of a coastal buoy off Salvador found 42 marine heatwave events between August 2019 and April 2024, including a particularly significant event in March 2024 with a maximum sea-surface temperature anomaly of 2.61 C. A separate 2025 study of 40 years of NOAA temperature records at 33 South Atlantic reef sites, mostly off Brazil and Africa, reports that heat-stress episodes rose to 81 in 2010-19 and 75 in 2020-24.

records.title: Petrobras drills the Morpho exploration well off Amapá after a contested Ibama licence and a drilling-fluid discharge
records.description: Ibama licensed Petrobras to drill the Morpho well in block FZA-M-59 in the Foz do Amazonas basin on 20 October 2025, about 175 km off Amapa, after refusing a licence in 2023; Ibama's technical staff were reported divided after the August 2025 emergency simulation, and the licence required a revised wildlife plan, tested in a new simulation during drilling, and a second wildlife care centre at Oiapoque. Drilling stalled for weeks after an 18.44 m3 discharge of synthetic drilling fluid on 4 January 2026, which Ibama fined at R$ 2.5 million; the ANP later let drilling resume under safety conditions. Petrobras announced oil discoveries on 14 August and 2 October 2026, and Ibama has amended the licence to allow three contingent wells. Federal prosecutors and civil-society groups contest the licence, citing reef, spill-modelling and consultation concerns; the Amapa federal court dismissed the prosecutors' suit on 23 September 2026 and fined them for bad-faith litigation, and they appealed to the TRF1 on 28 September. Petrobras says it met all of Ibama's requirements.

records.title: 19 Foz do Amazonas oil blocks sold in the ANP auction of 17 June 2025 over prosecutors' and NGOs' objections
records.description: In the ANP permanent-offer auction of 17 June 2025, 19 of the 47 blocks offered in the Foz do Amazonas basin were sold to Petrobras with ExxonMobil and to Chevron with CNPC, for R$ 844 million. records.title: Oil export terminal and floating LNG plans in Golfo San Matías draw a UNESCO request to suspend works near Península Valdés
records.description: The Vaca Muerta Oil Sur pipeline (437 km) is to end at an oil terminal at Punta Colorada, Río Negro, and a consortium plans floating LNG vessels in the same gulf. At its 48th session in Busan in July 2026, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, as reported by Argentine media, asked Argentina to suspend works on the pipeline and terminal until studies show no harm to Península Valdés, about 30 km away, citing tanker traffic, whale collisions, noise, lighting and spill risk, and set an updated-report deadline of 1 February 2027. Argentina told UNESCO the project has an impact assessment, mitigation measures and a spill contingency plan, which the Committee found insufficient. A 2025 NOAA GNOME spill model run by WCS Argentina for the Foro para la Conservación del Mar Patagónico found that oil would reach the coast within 6 to 8 days in every scenario.

records.title: Avian influenza killed about 97% of southern elephant seal pups at Península Valdés in 2023; the colony fell about 61%
records.description: The 2023 H5N1 avian influenza epidemic killed about 97% of the southern elephant seal pups born that year at Península Valdés, Chubut, and an uncertain number of breeding adults. A WCS Argentina census of October 2024, reported in September 2025, estimated 19,871 animals older than one year, down about 61% from roughly 60,000, with annual pup production of 5,677 against 14,427 in 2022. In April 2026 the IUCN moved the southern elephant seal globally from Least Concern to Vulnerable, citing avian-flu declines (WCS Argentina, July 2026), and WCS plans a full census in spring 2026. A Marine Mammal Science study projects recovery to 2022 levels by 2029 to 2051 if only pups were affected, and around 2091 if breeding females were also affected.

records.title: Brazil's 2024 coral bleaching event was the most severe on record, with high mortality on northeast reefs
records.description: Bleaching began in March 2024 on reefs at Tamandaré (Pernambuco) and Sergipe and spread across the northeast. A Ministry of Environment and Climate Change presentation by Prof. Beatrice Padovani Ferreira (UFPE) to ICRI describes 2024 as the most extreme event on record, with over 90% bleaching at Tamandaré, Maragogi and Fernando de Noronha and mortality of 50 to 90% at Maragogi and Sergipe. The Coral Vivo project's 2024 report says it was Brazil's second major bleaching episode after 2019. A Coral Reefs study of 18 reef systems monitored from August 2023 to December 2024, reported by Diario de Pernambuco, found that 88% of coral cover disappeared at Maragogi.

records.title: Foreign squid fleets gather at the edge of Argentina's 200-mile line each season, while Chinese capital grows in the national fleet
records.description: Argentina's Prefectura Naval reported in December 2025 that 148 foreign vessels were already heading to the 200-mile line ("Milla 201"), with about 500 expected, mostly from China, South Korea and Taiwan, to fish Illex argentinus. Argentina can enforce inside its EEZ but has limited tools beyond it.

records.title: Cape Town's three marine sewage outfalls face a permit appeal, a flow-limit suspension and an ActionSA challenge
records.description: Cape Town discharges screened but otherwise untreated sewage into the Atlantic through marine outfalls at Green Point, Camps Bay and Hout Bay, under permits issued in 2019 and 2022 to 2023. ActionSA and others appealed the permits, the environment minister suspended the daily flow limits in August 2024 pending appeals, and the appeal was still before an independent panel in December 2025. The City's monitoring reports about 99% of samples within guidelines and says the outfalls do not affect Blue Flag beaches; ActionSA disputes that the permits are being met.

records.title: MV Ultra Galaxy wreck spills more than 500 tonnes of fuel and fertiliser cargo on the West Coast
records.description: The Panama-flagged cargo ship MV Ultra Galaxy grounded near Doringbaai in July 2024 and broke up in storms, and SAMSA said only about 8 tonnes of marine gas oil was removed before the rest of its fuel and fertiliser cargo was lost to the sea. Oil reached mining beaches, Papendorp and Strandfontein, and about 180 people in 12 teams were cleaning a 40 km stretch of coast in February 2025 while the wreck was removed. Oiled wildlife was limited to one dead Cape gannet and one oiled plover in the sources opened.

notes.livelihoods: Oil reached ramps 3, 4 and 7 of the Tormin mineral sands mine and parts of the Transhex area, and clean-up crews of about 180 worked a 40 km coastline (ref 4).
notes.scale: Oiling was patchy along a roughly 40 km section of the West Coast (ref 4), a local rather than regional extent.
notes.duration: The ship grounded in early July 2024 (ref 3), oil re-emerged during wreck removal that began in December 2024, and clean-up was still under way on 7 February 2025 (ref 4).
notes.significance: SAMSA activated its national oil spill contingency plan and the ship's insurer tendered the wreck removal, with removal of material from the seabed under way by February 2025 (refs 2, 3, 4).

records.title: Repeated oil incidents in Algoa Bay and along the Eastern Cape coast oil seabirds and wash up tar balls
records.description: A spill in Algoa Bay on 7 September 2024, with the MSC Apollo named as the likely source, oiled penguins at St Croix Island, and SAMSA investigated. In January and February 2026, two fishing vessels burned off Gqeberha and St Francis Bay carrying 14 and 2 tonnes of diesel, and tar balls of unidentified origin were reported on beaches in Algoa Bay, the Garden Route and Struisbaai. Algoa Bay also saw ship-to-ship bunkering spills before 2024, which led South Africa to suspend fuelling there.

records.title: Mass die-offs of octopus, lobster and fish along the Swakopmund and Walvis Bay coast, with low oxygen suspected
records.description: In April 2025 thousands of dead and dying octopuses, crustaceans and small fish washed up between Swakopmund and Walvis Bay, after a similar event near Henties Bay about two months earlier. Residents and the reporting suspected low oxygen from river runoff, sulphur eruptions or a Benguela Nino, but no official cause was reported. Namibia's most recent major red tide was in January 2024, and UCT research describes unpredictable low-oxygen events in the southern Benguela upwelling system (ref 6).

notes.scale: The die-offs cover a stretch of the central Namibian coast from Henties Bay to Walvis Bay, a local to coastal extent (ref 1).
notes.duration: A major red tide struck in January 2024 (ref 2), a similar die-off occurred about February 2025 south of Jakkalsputz and the April 2025 event followed (ref 1), so episodes recur over more than a year.
notes.significance: Only press reports and an advocacy-group article exist; the cited pieces contain no ministry statement or formal notice (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Lagoon Beach at Milnerton closed to swimming for chronic Diep River and lagoon pollution
records.description: In September 2024 the City of Cape Town said Lagoon Beach at Milnerton remained closed to swimming because of chronic pollution in the Diep River, with warning signs in place. The campaign group Rethink the Stink said raw sewage regularly flows into the lagoon near Milnerton High School with no plans to fix it, and that the City's plans for recreational areas will not be completed until 2028. City samples of 17 September 2019, reported in December 2019, found E. coli up to 300 times the guideline in the lagoon area, in a stormwater channel at Bayside Mall.

records.title: Namibia grants an environmental clearance for the Sandpiper seabed phosphate dredging project; the agriculture minister appeals
records.description: Namibia's environment commissioner issued an environmental clearance certificate on 5 August 2026 to Namibian Marine Phosphate for the Sandpiper project, which would dredge phosphate-rich seabed sediments on a concession off Walvis Bay. The fishing federation CNFA opposes the project, and the agriculture minister appealed against the decision in its entirety (lodged on 1 September and confirmed by the ministry on 2 September 2026). The company says active mining will not start immediately and depends on further permits and an oversight committee.

notes.duration: The High Court barred physical mining without a clearance certificate in 2021 after early trial mining (ref 1) and the certificate followed on 5 August 2026, so the permitting dispute has run at least five years.
notes.significance: The High Court ruled in 2021 that no physical mining could occur without a clearance certificate (ref 1), and the clearance issued on 5 August 2026 is under a ministerial appeal against the decision in its entirety, lodged 1 September 2026 (ref 2).

records.title: West Coast rock lobster stock at 1.4% of pristine abundance as the 2025/26 catch limit rises to 800 tonnes
records.description: South Africa raised the West Coast rock lobster total allowable catch by 58.4% to 800 tonnes for 2025/26 after an assessment showed signs of recovery, while GroundUp reports the stock is still at 1.4% of pristine abundance. The scientific working group warned that poaching remains very high, and the department kept the season to four months to limit effort. Illegal trade is estimated at at least twice the annual catch limit.

records.title: Rabies established in Cape fur seals along the South African and Namibian coasts
records.description: WOAH reports more than 100 confirmed rabies cases in Cape fur seals in South Africa and Namibia since 2024, the first known establishment of rabies in a free-ranging marine mammal population, with more than 145 human exposure incidents by May 2026. Mongabay reports that retrospective testing found cases back to 2021 and 2022, and that a July 2025 workshop judged the disease likely endemic and no longer eradicable. No human rabies case from a seal has been recorded by the national institute.

location.name: Cape fur seal colonies, Cape Town to Namibia
location.detail: Western, Northern and Eastern Cape coasts of South Africa and the Namibian coast; Cape Town sites include Kommetjie, Simon's Town, Fish Hoek, Duiker Island and Seal Island.

records.layer_rationale: A new wildlife disease in a coastal marine mammal with human health spillover.

notes.harm: More than 100 seals have tested positive and more than 145 human exposure incidents had been reported by May 2026 (ref 1); Cape Town recorded 73 bite injuries from 135 aggressive seal incidents since 2021 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited reports describe no fishery or beach closure, and no economic disruption is documented (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Cases are confirmed along the coasts of two countries, from the Northern Cape to the Eastern Cape and in Namibia (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Retrospective testing found positives from 2021 and a Kommetjie seal from July 2022, and cases continue to 2026 (ref 2).
notes.significance: WOAH issued a formal statement on 17 July 2026 and a South African government report of October 2024 judged mass vaccination not feasible (refs 1, 2).

records.title: House mice attack adult wandering albatrosses on Marion Island as the eradication timeline moves to 2029
records.description: A 2025 study reports that house mice are wounding adult wandering albatrosses across Marion Island, with 11 injured adults among nests surveyed in 2024 and lower breeding success at affected nests. A May 2026 update to the albatross and petrel agreement ACAP says the Mouse-Free Marion eradication is now targeted for 2029, subject to funding and approvals, after a larger aerial baiting trial planned for 2027.

notes.livelihoods: The island is a nature reserve and no fishery or community disruption is reported in the cited sources (refs 1, 2).

notes.significance: The ACAP Population and Conservation Status Working Group received an information paper dated 25 May 2026, and the island is part of the Prince Edward Islands Special Nature Reserve (ref 2).

records.title: Record 2024 marine heat stress across the Western Indian Ocean, with more than 20 degree heating weeks for the first time
records.description: El Nino, a positive Indian Ocean Dipole and record global ocean temperatures built heat stress across the region from late 2023. CORDIO East Africa reported more than 8 degree heating weeks by February 2024 and over 12 by April, with pockets in Seychelles reaching 16. The 2026 GCRMN regional chapter states that 93% of the region's reefs passed 4 degree heating weeks in 2024-2025 and that values above 20 were documented for the first time.

location.name: Western Indian Ocean reef waters
location.detail: Heat stress mapped from the equator to about 20 S, strongest on the East African coast, the Seychelles and the Mascarenes; Mozambique Channel and southwest Madagascar saw less heat stress in 2024.

records.layer_rationale: A basin-scale thermal event driven by ENSO, the Indian Ocean Dipole and long-term warming.

notes.harm: CORDIO East Africa found about 80% of observed locations bleached and 40% with moderate to extreme mortality, and GCRMN reports more than 20 degree heating weeks for the first time (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources documents a fishery closure or advisory tied to the heat stress itself; Down To Earth only flags tuna-route concern in 2026 (ref 4).
notes.scale: The heat stress spans the regional sea from the equator to about 20 S rather than a single reef (ref 1).
notes.duration: Record global temperatures from April 2023 and heat stress through 2024-2025 mean a year or more of exposure (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A regional CORDIO report and the GCRMN Status of Coral Reefs 2025 chapter formally assess the event, but no emergency declaration is cited (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: The cited reports give reef and observation counts, not people affected.

records.title: A third of Kenya's coast rated highly vulnerable to sea-level rise, with Mombasa and Kilifi-Malindi most exposed
records.description: A national coastal vulnerability index published in Frontiers in Marine Science in May 2026 placed 31.7% of 7,555 shoreline segments in the High or Very High class, with the Kilifi-Malindi corridor and the Mombasa urban core most vulnerable. All nine heritage sites among the 46 heritage sites, hotels and biodiversity areas inventoried fell in the High or Very High class. A July 2025 Daily Nation report on an IPCC authors' meeting in Mombasa described sinking land, brackish wells and erosion on the city's coast.

location.detail: Kenya's 640 km coastline; hotspots on Mombasa Island and the Kilifi-Malindi corridor.

records.layer_rationale: Sea-level rise and shoreline change are physical climate hazards to the coast.

notes.livelihoods: The Daily Nation cites a KALRO estimate of about USD 12 million per year in lost coastal agricultural productivity, a loss of income but not a closure (ref 2).
notes.scale: The assessment covers Kenya's whole 640 km coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Shoreline erosion, land subsidence of up to 5 mm per year in parts of Mombasa and a trend in sea level make this chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Mombasa's Climate Action Plan 2023-2050 is cited by its governor as the formal city response, but no enforcement action or emergency declaration appears (ref 2).

records.title: Rising seas and erosion breach sea walls and shrink Tanzania's Mafia, Unguja and Pemba coasts
records.description: Tanzania's environment minister told Parliament in April 2024 that sea level at Dar es Salaam has risen by an average of 6 mm a year since 2002, with erosion, loss of beaches and saltwater intrusion. The Citizen documented walls breached at Kilindoni on Mafia Island and a 2019 Zanzibar survey listing severely eroded sites on Unguja and Pemba. In September 2026 the Vice President told a UN General Assembly meeting that erosion, saltwater intrusion and flooding are growing risks, and a July 2026 journal review examines flood vulnerability and governance constraints on the Tanzanian coast.

records.description: A 2020 Oxford and Seychelles Islands Foundation study estimated about 513 tonnes of marine litter remain on Aldabra, a UNESCO World Heritage atoll, after a 2019 clean-up removed 25 tonnes. In October 2025 Plastic Odyssey, UNESCO and the Seychelles Islands Foundation mapped over 40 km of coastline by drone and recorded 115 geolocated points. The partners plan a large clean-up on Grande Terre from late 2027.

records.title: Severe 2024 mass coral bleaching across the Western Indian Ocean erases two decades of hard coral gain
records.description: CORDIO East Africa's regional report found that 2024 heat stress, driven by El Nino and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, caused widespread bleaching and mortality on reefs from Kenya and Tanzania to Seychelles, Mauritius, Madagascar and the Comoros. The 2025 GCRMN regional chapter models regional hard coral cover falling from 33.9% in 2023 to 25.9% in 2024, comparable to 1999 levels, and reports 66% cumulative coral mortality at Mayotte after the bleaching and Cyclone Chido.

notes.livelihoods: The cited sources describe reef dependence of coastal communities (ref 2) but report no fishery or tourism closure tied to the 2024 bleaching, so no disruption is scored.
notes.scale: Bleaching was reported from eight countries and heat stress above 12 Degree Heating Weeks spanned the equator to 20 degrees S (ref 1), a regional-sea scale.
notes.duration: The GCRMN chapter calls 2024 to 2025 the most severe regional heat stress event and states 93% of reefs exceeded 4 DHW, with recovery outlook uncertain (ref 2).
notes.significance: A regional bleaching report by the GCRMN regional coordinator (ref 1) and the 2025 GCRMN chapter (ref 2) are formal assessments, but no enforcement or legal action applies.

records.title: Chagos treaty ratification stalls as the future of the 640,000 km2 marine protected area stays undecided
records.description: The UK and Mauritius signed a treaty on 22 May 2025 recognising Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, with Mauritius committed to create its own marine protected area and the UK support terms left to a separate instrument. In April 2026 a Loughborough University legal expert reported the UK had shelved the implementing legislation after the US withdrew support, and Mauritius said it was exploring legal avenues.

records.title: IOTC adopts yellowfin catch limits for 2027 to 2028 while the 2024 stock assessment stays contested
records.description: At its 30th session in the Maldives in May 2026 the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission adopted Resolution 26/01 on interim catch limits for yellowfin tuna, reported by industry body Europeche as a 436,867 tonne total allowable catch for 2027 and 2028 against current catches of 489,742 tonnes. The 2024 assessment found the stock not overfished with an 86% probability of Kobe Green, but the Commission recorded important data uncertainties, and an NGO submission says objecting fleets, notably Oman, expanded catches sharply.

notes.livelihoods: Resolution 26/01 sets catch limits and quotas that constrain fleets, and a Galmudug State fisheries minister estimated USD 300 million a year is lost to IUU fishing in Somalia (refs 2, 3, 4).
notes.scale: The IOTC area of competence is the whole Indian Ocean basin and the stock is fished by over two dozen members (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Yellowfin was declared overfished in 2015 and interim plans have run since then, with the Commission deferring yellowfin proposals in 2024 and 2025 (refs 1, 2, 5).
notes.significance: Resolution 26/01 was adopted by the Commission on 11 to 15 May 2026 and binds members from 19 September 2026 unless objections are lodged (ref 3).

records.title: Four vessels hijacked off Somalia in April and May 2026 as the IMB reports a persistent piracy threat
records.description: The ICC International Maritime Bureau's mid-year report for January to June 2026 recorded four hijackings in the Somali region between April and May 2026, with further attacks continuing in June. The IMB attributes 94% of crew taken hostage worldwide in the period to Somali pirates. On 2 October 2026 the IMO Secretary-General said five seafarers died during the 29 September rescue of the hijacked HONOUR 25 in Somali waters, and that 44 seafarers were freed from three vessels (HONOUR 25, SEAMULL (SIBU 1) and EUREKA) seized between April and August 2026; 22 seafarers remained held on the ASANA.

records.layer_rationale: Piracy is a security and governance risk to commercial shipping and fishing vessels, not a pollutant or habitat issue.

notes.harm: Five seafarers died during the 29 September 2026 HONOUR 25 rescue and several were seriously injured (ref 3); the IMB recorded 67 crew taken hostage worldwide in January to June 2026 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The IMB urged ships transiting the Somali coast and Gulf of Aden to stay alert and report all incidents promptly, and credits Best Management Practices with preventing further boardings (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The four hijackings and further attacks span the Somali coast and the Gulf of Aden and Western Indian Ocean, a regional sea (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: The IMB says the risk remains serious despite the lowest mid-year piracy total since 1992, with Somali hijackings in April and May and attacks continuing in June, and the IMO says the vessels were seized between April and August 2026 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: The IMB issued a formal mid-year advisory on 9 July 2026 (ref 1) and the IMO Secretary-General issued a public statement on 2 October 2026 calling for renewed resolve and resources against piracy (ref 3).

records.title: Mozambique LNG restarts at Afungi while resettled fishing villages remain about 10 km from the sea
records.description: TotalEnergies and Mozambique announced the full restart of the USD 20 billion Mozambique LNG project at Afungi on 29 January 2026 after a force majeure that began in 2021, with first LNG targeted for 2029. Mongabay reports that critics say land compensation is unresolved and that several fishing villages moved about 10 km inland, far from their fishing grounds, and Reuters describes the site as an enclave reachable only by sea or air.

records.title: Zanzibar seaweed farmers report heat-driven losses as yields fall and women turn to sponge farming
records.description: Zanzibar has nearly 25,000 seaweed farmers, about 90% of them women, and the Citizen reported in August 2024 that seaweed production fell 47% between 2002 and 2021. A peer-reviewed survey of 183 farmers in Micheweni, Pemba, found average household yields fell from 4,480 kg in 2016 to 2,422 kg in 2020, attributed to heat stress and winds, and AFP reported in November 2025 that some farmers are switching to sponge cultivation.

records.title: Distant-water fleet fishes the Saya de Malha Bank with little tracking as protection calls continue
records.description: The Outlaw Ocean Project reported in March 2025 that more than 200 distant-water vessels, mostly from Sri Lanka and Taiwan, have gathered along the deeper edge of the Saya de Malha Bank between Mauritius and Seychelles, and that virtually no one tracks or polices them. The bank, about 40,000 km2, is described in the reporting as one of the world's largest seagrass meadows and a candidate for protection, while the extent of seagrass there is not settled in the sources opened.

records.title: Record 2024-25 marine heatwave along more than 1,500 km of Western Australia's coast
records.description: The WA Coral Bleaching Group, convened by the Australian Institute of Marine Science, reported that the 2024/25 marine heatwave was the longest, largest and most intense on record for Western Australia. Surface temperatures reached up to 4 degrees C above average and heat stress peaked in December 2024 to January 2025 and again in March to April 2025 before receding in May. Heat stress reached 20 degree heating weeks at central Ningaloo and up to 30 at some Pilbara reefs, with bleaching and mortality following; coral outcomes are covered separately.

location.name: Northwest and west coast of WA (Kimberley to Ningaloo)
location.detail: Western Australia, from the Kimberley and Rowley Shoals south through the Pilbara to Ningaloo; heat spread along more than 1,500 km of coastline (ref 1).

records.layer_rationale: A prolonged thermal anomaly in coastal waters, with the physical heat event itself as the primary issue.
secondary_drivers: Absence of monsoonal storms and cyclones

notes.harm: Surveys found coral bleaching and death from medium (11-30%) to extreme (over 90%) across systems up to 1,500 km apart, including 61-90% death at Rowley Shoals' Mermaid and Clerke Reefs in April 2025 (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources describe no closure, restriction or advisory tied to the heatwave itself, so no livelihood disruption is scored.
notes.scale: Heat affected seas along more than 1,500 km of the Western Australian coast, a national coastline rather than a single site (ref 1).
notes.duration: AIMS partners began monitoring in September 2024 and temperatures only began to recede in May 2025, roughly eight months of heat stress (ref 2).
notes.significance: Scientists and managers of the WA Coral Bleaching Group formally described it as the longest, largest and most intense on record for the state, but no enforcement or emergency declaration is cited (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Heat stress reached 20 degree heating weeks at central Ningaloo and a maximum of 30 at central Pilbara reefs; 4 DHW is where bleaching is likely (AIMS scientist, The Conversation, 12 Aug 2025).

measures.note: Heatwave and bleaching spanned more than 1,500 km (ref 1).

measures.note: Up to 4 C above average in places (ref 1).

trend.note: Heat receded from May 2025; the source warns temperatures will keep rising in coming years (ref 1).

records.title: Prolonged Karenia algal bloom kills marine life along South Australia's gulf and island coasts
records.description: A harmful algal bloom dominated by Karenia species was first detected off the Fleurieu Peninsula in March 2025 during a marine heatwave and had spread across Gulf St Vincent, Kangaroo Island, Yorke Peninsula and parts of Spencer Gulf. The SARDI chief said it affected about 30 per cent of the state's coastline; it caused mass deaths of marine life, foam on Adelaide beaches, respiratory irritation and fishing and tourism losses. A government report released in July 2026 concluded that floodwater nutrients, a coastal upwelling and the marine heatwave together created the conditions, and by February 2026 the main activity had moved to south-western Yorke Peninsula.

location.name: Gulf St Vincent, Fleurieu, Yorke and Kangaroo Island coasts
location.detail: South Australia; Gulf St Vincent, Fleurieu Peninsula, Kangaroo Island, Yorke Peninsula and parts of Spencer Gulf and the Eyre Peninsula coast.

records.layer_rationale: A nutrient-fuelled harmful algal bloom in coastal waters, with nutrient input, upwelling and marine heat as drivers.

notes.harm: AAP reported hundreds of reports of marine deaths including sharks, penguins, flathead, squid, crabs and rock lobsters, and OzFish counted more than 200 species killed (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Commercial fishing catches dwindled (ref 2) and the SA government has restricted commercial scalefish and blue crab fishing in the Gulf St Vincent and Kangaroo Island zone from 1 November 2025 and committed 48 million dollars to coastal communities and businesses (ref 3, ref 6).
notes.scale: SARDI's chief estimated the bloom affected about 30 per cent of the state's coastline, roughly 1,500 km, across two gulfs and several peninsulas (ref 2).
notes.duration: First detected in March 2025, still present in January 2026 with a hotspot on south-western Yorke Peninsula, and described as lasting over 12 months by July 2026 (refs 3, 5).
notes.significance: SA Health issued advice for people with asthma, the state and federal governments funded response packages and the SA government released a SARDI peer-reviewed drivers report in July 2026, but no emergency declaration is cited (refs 4, 6).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Sri Lanka's Supreme Court orders US$1 billion for the X-Press Pearl disaster; first payment not made
records.description: The container ship X-Press Pearl burned and sank off Colombo in 2021, releasing an estimated 70 to 75 billion plastic nurdles plus chemicals and bunker oil along Sri Lanka's west coast. On 24 July 2025 the Supreme Court held the owner, operator and local agent jointly liable and ordered an initial US$1 billion in compensation in instalments within a year. X-Press Feeders said it was unable to pay the first US$250 million due on 23 September 2025, and the local agent told the court it lacked the resources.

location.name: Off Colombo and Sri Lanka's west coast
location.detail: Wreck off Colombo; nurdles and chemical contamination reached about 80 km of the west coast initially, spreading to an area about 750 km from Negombo north to Mannar (ref 5). Coordinates are Colombo city.

records.layer_rationale: Release of hazardous chemicals, resins, bunker oil and plastic pellets from a burned and sunk container ship.

notes.harm: The Court described the environmental impact as immeasurable and found the release of billions of nurdles, hazardous chemicals and bunker oil caused widespread contamination and destroyed marine life (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: A year-long fishing ban hit the affected coastline and the Diplomat estimated about 20,000 Negombo-area families abandoned fishing (refs 3, 5).
notes.scale: Initial contamination covered an 80 km stretch of the west coast, later spreading across about 750 km, a national coastline (ref 5).
notes.duration: The 2021 spill is still producing contamination and litigation in 2026; beach cleaning in Negombo was continuing four years later (ref 5).
notes.significance: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka judgment of 24 July 2025 in SC/FR 168/2021 and connected cases ordered US$1 billion, a compensation commission and further investigations (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: Families the Diplomat estimated had abandoned fishing after nurdle pollution and fishing bans around Negombo (ref 5); not a court figure.

key_measure.text: The Supreme Court ordered the X-Press Pearl group to pay an initial US$1 billion, with a first US$250 million instalment due by 23 September 2025, which X-Press Feeders said it was unable to pay.

records.title: Maldives reclamation boom: over 4,000 hectares of new land raises reef and flooding concerns
records.description: A peer-reviewed study published in May 2026 mapped 109 community land reclamation projects on inhabited Maldivian islands between 2000 and 2024, adding at least 4,198 hectares, with a peak of 25 projects started in 2023. Reclamation is promoted as protection against sea-level rise, but the study and earlier reporting say it disrupts reef systems and sediment flows and can raise wave energy, erosion and flood exposure. Human Rights Watch, quoted in 2023, said projects were often rushed and cited buried mangroves and damaged reefs at Addu.

location.name: Hulhumalé and inhabited islands, Maldives
location.type: Atoll reclamation and artificial island coast
location.detail: Maldives; 109 projects on inhabited islands, 71% of reclaimed land in the Central Region and over half in Kaafu Atoll, including Hulhumalé (ref 1). Coordinates are Hulhumalé.

records.layer_rationale: Coastal adaptation to sea-level rise that may itself raise flooding and erosion risk.

notes.harm: Human Rights Watch, quoted by AFP, said 70 per cent of mangroves on Kulhudhuffushi were buried by an airport reclamation and a project at Addu damaged coral reefs (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The same AFP report said the Addu reclamation damaged coral reefs that fishermen depended on, and local critics say the new land has not met economic needs (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: Projects span the national archipelago, with 109 projects across inhabited islands and 4,198 hectares reclaimed (ref 1).
notes.duration: Reclamation has been continuous since 2000 and 19 projects were still ongoing when the study was compiled (ref 1).
notes.significance: Human Rights Watch published a formal report criticising unenforced environmental rules, and a peer-reviewed national assessment followed, but no enforcement action is cited (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: About 100,000 people live on reclaimed Hulhumalé (ref 2); not a count of people harmed.

key_measure.text: At least 4,198 hectares reclaimed across 109 projects on inhabited islands between 2000 and 2024, a conservative estimate (MJET, 28 May 2026).

records.title: Coastal erosion eats Sri Lanka's west and south coast, from Colombo to Kalutara
records.description: Sri Lanka's Coast Conservation Department told The Morning in September 2025 that more than 30 acres of land had been lost around Kalutara, with the worst west-coast erosion at Abrew Road and Waskaduwa, and Colombo's Kinross Club damaged. Civil society links the sand loss partly to Colombo Port City dredging and beachfront construction; the department names no single cause. The department said it would spend Rs 303.5 million on protective structures in 2025.

location.detail: Sri Lanka west and south coast; Wellawatte, Moratuwa, Kalutara and Galle area beaches named in the cited reports.

records.layer_rationale: Shoreline retreat from waves, storms, sea level and coastal works.

notes.harm: The Coast Conservation Department calculated over 30 acres of land lost in the Kalutara area, partly from river-mouth flooding, and the Kinross Club boundary collapsed (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Low-income communities at Moratuwa live at the edge of the sea fearing loss of homes and tourism beaches are threatened, but no closure or displacement is documented (ref 1).
notes.scale: Erosion is reported across the west, south, east and north-west coasts of the country (ref 1).
notes.duration: Colombo beach sand has been washing away and not replenishing since 2020, and Kalutara outlet eroded about 30 m from 2017 to 2023 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Coast Conservation Department has officially assessed and budgeted protective structures, a formal agency response without enforcement or an emergency order (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Plastic debris keeps washing onto Cocos (Keeling) Islands beaches
records.description: A 2019 study estimated 414 million plastic items weighing 238 tonnes on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands. Sea Shepherd Australia's 2024 clean-up, its fifth consecutive year, removed 9.3 tonnes from about 10 km of coastline on five islands, including more than 700,000 pieces of lightweight plastic and 2.7 tonnes of ghost gear. Sea Shepherd said the islands burn waste openly because of biosecurity rules and shipping costs.

notes.harm: The 2019 survey estimated 414 million items and 238 tonnes of plastic with about 93% buried to 10 cm, and Sea Shepherd found hermit crabs using plastic lids as shells and wildlife trapped in containers (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources report no beach closure or fishery disruption; tourism is the islands' main income source but no loss is documented (ref 2).
notes.scale: The pollution is concentrated on a small island group, scored as a single site rather than a regional sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: Sea Shepherd has returned five consecutive years since 2020 and removed over 49 tonnes, showing chronic recurrence (ref 1).
notes.significance: Evidence is a 2019 scientific study and an NGO clean-up report; no notice, listing or order is cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Plastic pellets found on all nine surveyed Sri Lankan west-coast beaches in 2025
records.description: A survey of nine west-coast beaches over 13 weeks from July to September 2025, presented in June 2026, found nurdles at every site, from about 15 to more than 3,000 per standardised search. The authors could not attribute the pellets to the May 2025 MSC Elsa 3 sinking off Kerala because no pre-spill baseline exists, and older X-Press Pearl pellets may be resurfacing. Environmental groups told The Diplomat that nurdles believed to come from the MSC Elsa were also reaching Sri Lanka's north and west coasts.

notes.scale: The nine beaches span the western coastline of the country (ref 1).
notes.duration: Nurdles have been found on Sri Lankan beaches continuously since the 2021 X-Press Pearl spill and weekly counts in 2025 kept fluctuating (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The evidence is a conference-presented preliminary assessment and news reports, with no regulatory notice or order cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Record marine heatwave bleaches and kills corals along 1,500 km of Western Australia's reefs, including Ningaloo and the Rowley Shoals
records.description: The Western Australian Government's conservation department (DBCA) and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) report high levels of coral bleaching and mortality across the north-west atolls, Kimberley, Pilbara and northern Gascoyne coasts after a marine heatwave that began around December 2024. AIMS describes it as the longest, largest and most intense marine heatwave on record for the state, and DBCA says follow-up surveys continue through 2025 and into 2026 to establish the full impact.

location.name: WA north-west reefs: Ningaloo to the Kimberley
location.detail: Western Australia: Ningaloo Marine Park, Exmouth Gulf, Montebello and Barrow Islands, Dampier Archipelago, Rowley Shoals, Kimberley coast

records.layer_rationale: Habitat loss on reefs driven by prolonged marine heatwave heat stress.

notes.harm: DBCA reported a 60 per cent decline in coral cover at long-term sites in the Montebello and Barrow Islands reserves and very high mortality at shallow Dampier Archipelago sites (ref 1); AIMS-reported mortality of 61-90 per cent at the Rowley Shoals monitored sites (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or restriction is documented in the cited pages; a Exmouth glass-bottom boat operator said the loss of about 90 per cent of coral in some patches had potential to affect his business (ref 3), so this is scored 0 pending evidence of an actual restriction.
notes.scale: Bleaching and mortality were reported along a 1,500 km stretch of the WA coast (refs 3, 4), a national coastline rather than a single reef.
notes.duration: Heat stress ran from about December 2024 (ref 2) and DBCA still described high bleaching and mortality almost 12 months later, with surveys planned through 2026 (ref 1); AIMS estimated reefs may need 10-15 years to recover (ref 4).
notes.significance: DBCA and AIMS published formal monitoring findings and the AIMS-led WA Coral Bleaching Group documented the event as the worst on record for the state (refs 1, 3); no enforcement or treaty action applies.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: AIMS: the 2024-25 marine heatwave was the longest, largest and most intense on record for WA, with bleaching and mortality reported across a 1,500 km area (ABC, 12 Aug 2025).

records.title: Maldives suspends coastal dredging during 2024 coral bleaching; central atoll reefs show uneven recovery in 2025 survey
records.description: The Maldives Marine Research Institute reported localised bleaching in March 2024 and the Environmental Protection Agency suspended major coastal development, such as dredging and reclamation, over the bleaching window. A Reef Check partner report on October 2025 surveys in Ari, South Male and Vaavu atolls says the archipelago escaped a mass bleaching event in 2025 after severe thermal stress in 2024 but shows uneven recovery, with inner lagoon reefs recovering more slowly than outer slopes.

notes.duration: Localised bleaching was reported from 17 March 2024 (ref 2) and the October 2025 survey still found uneven recovery (ref 3), spanning more than a year.

records.title: Woodside's Browse gas development near Scott Reef remains in WA and federal environmental assessment after the 2025 amended proposal
records.description: Woodside Energy's proposed Browse development would drill for gas in the Torosa reservoir, about 425 km north of Broome, around Scott Reef. The WA Environmental Protection Authority has assessed the state-waters component since 2019, accepted an amended proposal in August 2025 after more than 17,700 submissions, and has yet to publish its recommendation in the sources reviewed. records.title: Western Australia closes West Coast demersal fishing to commercial fishers and bans recreational boat fishing for dhufish and snapper to 2027
records.description: After stock assessments showed several demersal species including WA dhufish under severe threat, the State Government announced in December 2025 that the West Coast bioregion (Kalbarri to Augusta) will not reopen to boat-based recreational demersal fishing until spring 2027 and is permanently closed to commercial demersal fishing from 1 January 2026, with a licence buyback. Other regions get catch reductions and new limits under a $29.2 million package.

records.title: Sewage-derived debris balls wash up on Sydney, South Coast and Central Coast beaches from October 2024
records.description: Black and grey debris balls, mostly marble-sized, washed up on Sydney's Eastern Suburbs beaches from October 2024, then on the South Coast, the Northern Beaches (January 2025) and Central Coast beaches (August 2025). NSW EPA analysis found hair, waste cooking oil, faecal material and hydrocarbons, and in April 2025 named Sydney Water's land-based sewage system as the most likely source, narrowing it to the Malabar system in October 2025. The EPA issued Sydney Water a Preliminary Investigation Notice; the EPA page lists no confirmed reports since August 2025.

records.title: Deep oxygen falls below guideline range in Macquarie Harbour, home of the endangered Maugean skate
records.description: The Tasmanian EPA reports that dissolved oxygen in Macquarie Harbour held steady in the top 15 to 20 metres between July 2025 and June 2026 but declined below that, falling under the interim guideline range in the central and south-east segments. The decline coincided with the wettest spring and summer since 1998 and weaker ocean recharge, and the regulator required the three salmon producers to offset 10.3 tonnes of oxygen demand a day. The harbour is the only place the Maugean skate, listed Endangered since 2004, is now found.

records.title: Total nitrogen exceeds guideline values across Storm Bay as salmon farming expands under a staged nitrogen limit
records.description: Storm Bay's 2023/24 broadscale monitoring report (May 2023 to April 2024) found total nitrogen above default guideline values at multiple sites over multiple months in one region, continuing a high-nitrogen trend recorded since 2021. The report, prepared for Tassal and Huon Aquaculture, attributes the pattern to a regional signal such as shifting boundary currents or river inputs, with no clear link to distance from the leases, and found no broad-scale change in sediments or seabed animals. The EPA set a Stage 1 Total Permissible Dissolved Nitrogen Output of 1,747 tonnes for the Storm Bay Regional Area from 1 January 2025.

records.title: Derwent Estuary reports nutrient enrichment, summer low oxygen and legacy metals despite sewage upgrades
records.description: The Derwent Estuary Program's State of Timtumili Minanya/Derwent 2025 report summarises Hobart's estuary as under pressure from elevated nutrients, localised algal growth, seasonal low dissolved oxygen in the upper estuary, and legacy metal contamination. Sewage plants supply most of the dissolved inorganic nitrogen and total phosphorus, and total nitrogen rose in the upper estuary. A TasWater plant closure and upgrade is expected to cut nutrient loads by up to 58% for nitrogen and 42% for phosphorus.

records.title: Moa Point wastewater plant failure sends untreated sewage into Cook Strait off Wellington's south coast
records.description: Flooding on 4 February 2026 knocked out power and treatment at the Moa Point Wastewater Treatment Plant, and untreated wastewater has since discharged into Tarakena Bay and out the long outfall into Cook Strait. Tarakena Bay is a no-go area and people are told not to collect or eat kaimoana from Ōwhiro Bay to Breaker Bay. Tiaki Wai says the Crown Review found no single point of failure, Greater Wellington Regional Council has filed court charges (announced 1 October 2026), and the plant is due to resume treatment in November 2026 with full operations expected by February 2027.
