records.title: Hauraki Gulf report finds 1,793 dry-weather sewage overflows in a year and sediment above guideline rates
records.description: The Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf 2026 report rates the Gulf as under pressure, recording 1,793 uncontrolled dry-weather wastewater overflow events across 19 Auckland catchments in 2024/25. More than a third of monitored intertidal sites accumulate sediment above guideline rates, and nutrient enrichment, microalgal blooms and reduced dissolved oxygen are becoming more evident in parts of the Gulf. Network separation and Watercare's Central Interceptor, planned for mid-2026, aim to cut wet-weather overflows to the Waitemata Harbour.

records.title: Marine heatwaves reach Tasmania, Bass Strait and the NSW coast in summer 2024-25, with a salmon die-off and a NSW fish kill
records.description: A peer-reviewed review of the 2024/25 season reports localised marine heatwaves off south-east Tasmania from late November 2024, covering most of the state by March 2025 and reaching southern Victoria and Bass Strait by late March. Impacts included salp, Noctiluca and moon jellyfish blooms, reduced little penguin returns, and a salmon bacterial disease outbreak causing mass mortality of farmed Atlantic salmon in southern Tasmania. Off the NSW south coast, short moderate-to-strong heatwaves preceded a mid-March fish kill of thousands of threadfin leatherjacket after temperatures dropped 4 to 6 C in 48 hours.

records.layer_rationale: Sustained warm-water anomalies are a physical ocean change that drove biological impacts.

notes.harm: Thousands of threadfin leatherjacket died off the NSW south coast in March 2025 after a 4 to 6 C fall in 48 hours, and warm water was associated with mass mortality of farmed Atlantic salmon in southern Tasmania (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: A rickettsia outbreak linked to warm water caused mass mortality of farmed Atlantic salmon in southern Tasmania, and an abalone mortality at an NSW processing facility was attributed to heat-stressed stock or handling (ref 1).
notes.scale: The heatwaves covered most of Tasmania, Bass Strait, southern Victoria and the NSW south coast (ref 1).
notes.duration: Localised heatwaves began in late November 2024 and extended to most of Tasmania by March 2025, while NSW events lasted under 20 days each (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Tasmanian Government issued a marine heatwave information sheet and a response plan, and researchers ran national marine climate briefings advertised by the Fisheries Research and Development Corporation (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Bass Strait runs warm through 2025 and into 2026, with the warmest months of a ten-year record in two regions
records.description: AFMA's Bass Strait scallop climate reports say the strait was average or anomalously warm through the year to June 2025, with moderate marine heatwaves since January 2025. records.title: New Zealand waters warming 0.2 to 0.3 C a decade, fastest off the east coast and in the Tasman Sea
records.description: An Earth Sciences New Zealand report for Fisheries New Zealand, released in October 2025, finds average sea surface temperatures around New Zealand warmed 0.2 to 0.3 C per decade from 1982 to 2022, with trends especially pronounced off eastern New Zealand, in the Tasman Sea and over the Chatham Rise. Some recent marine heatwaves have already exceeded historic baselines by 5 C and could exceed them by 10 C by 2100 under high emissions. The 2026 State of our Gulf report links Hauraki Gulf heatwaves to temporary kelp loss and seabird breeding stress.

notes.scale: The warming spans New Zealand's coastal waters, the offshore Tasman Sea and the Chatham Rise (ref 1).
notes.duration: The trend covers 40 years, 1982 to 2022, at 0.2 to 0.3 C per decade at the surface (ref 1).

records.title: New Zealand coastal flood losses to infrastructure projected to nearly double by 2075
records.description: A study by Earth Sciences New Zealand for Te Waihanga, the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, projects that under a high-emissions scenario coastal flooding losses to infrastructure grow from about $165 million a year in 2025 to $325 million in 2075. Hawke's Bay faces the largest increase relative to its network size, rising from $43 million to about $89 million a year across inland and coastal flooding. The commission says sea levels are rising and communities and networks designed for yesterday's conditions face greater pressure.

records.title: Taranaki seabed iron-sand mining bid declined in draft by the Fast-track panel, then withdrawn in 2026
records.description: Trans-Tasman Resources applied under the Fast-track Approvals Act to extract up to 50 million tonnes of seabed sediment a year in the South Taranaki Bight. In February 2026 the expert panel issued a draft decision to decline, citing credible risk of harm to Maui dolphins, kororā (little penguins) and fairy prions, and the company then withdrew its application. Opponents say the withdrawal leaves open a possible new application, and the company said the panel misunderstood key foundations of its case.

notes.harm: The panel found a credible risk of harm to Maui dolphins, kororā and fairy prions, but no mining has taken place so the harm is potential (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or lost income is reported in the cited sources; the panel cut the applicant's job estimates, which concern the project's benefits (refs 2, 3).

records.description: The endangered Maugean skate lives only in Macquarie Harbour on Tasmania's west coast, where salmon farms operate. records.title: Tasmanian salmon farms lose about 20,000 tonnes of fish to mortality in 2025
records.description: Atlantic salmon mortality data published by the Tasmanian EPA show at least four million fish died prematurely at Tasmanian farms in 2025, a total of 20,133 tonnes, with losses rising in the last three months of the year. Earlier government data obtained by a campaign group showed about 1,100 tonnes died in Macquarie Harbour between September 2023 and March 2024. The industry body says mortality is part of normal production. An unprecedented salmon mortality event ran from February to early May 2025 in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel, where Huon Aquaculture and Tassal farm. Congealed fish oil from dead salmon washed up at Verona Sands, Randalls Bay, Roaring Bay, Drip Beach and western South Bruny Island beaches, which the EPA treats as a loss of containment of a controlled waste. Over 5,500 tonnes of salmon mortality waste was received in February, some oil globules held oxytetracycline residues, and the EPA directed both companies on 6 March 2025 to remove dead fish.

records.title: Hauraki Gulf Marine Protection Act 2025 protects part of the Marine Park but leaves most bottom trawling in place
records.description: New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Act took effect in October 2025, extending two marine reserves, creating high protection areas and five seafloor protection areas where trawling, Danish seining and dredging are banned. Greenpeace and LegaSea say bottom trawling remains allowed across much of the Gulf, and the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries rejected the proposed trawl-corridor restrictions in May 2025. records.title: Ex-Typhoon Halong storm surge floods Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta villages, setting a record at Kipnuk and Kwigillingok
records.description: On 12 October 2025 the remnants of Typhoon Halong drove a Bering Sea storm surge and winds of more than 50 mph onto the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta in western Alaska. The state counted 208 homes destroyed and 471 with major damage, about 1,600 people were displaced, and nearly all residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok were evacuated. The National Weather Service put the surge at Kipnuk at 6.6 feet above the normal highest tide, above the 4.7-foot record set in 2000.

location.name: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta coast
location.detail: Southwest Alaska, United States: Kipnuk and Kwigillingok hardest hit; 49 to 52 communities reported damage

records.layer_rationale: Storm surge on a very low-lying coast, with the University of Alaska noting the delta lies within about 1.6 feet of the high tide line.

notes.harm: The state surveyed 3,472 homes and found 208 totally destroyed and 471 with major damage, with one confirmed death and two people missing in October reports (refs 2, 4).
notes.livelihoods: About 1,600 people were displaced, nearly all of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok were evacuated by air, and stored subsistence food was lost (refs 1, 4, 6).
notes.scale: The University of Alaska counted 49 communities with damage across the Y-K Delta and Norton Sound coasts, a regional stretch of the Bering Sea coast, not a single bay (ref 1).
notes.duration: Residents were still waiting to return in July 2026, nine months after the storm, and the region had flooded in summer 2024 as well (refs 9, 3).
notes.significance: The governor declared a state disaster on 9 October 2025 and the University of Alaska fact sheet records a federal disaster declaration approved on 23 October (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Estimated number displaced, from the University of Alaska fact sheet (ref 1); other reports use 1,000 to 1,800 depending on date.

key_measure.text: The surge at Kipnuk reached 6.6 feet above the normal highest tide mark, against a previous record of 4.7 feet in 2000 (ref 2); 208 homes destroyed and 471 with major damage statewide (ref 4).

records.title: Kipnuk and Kwigillingok vote to relocate to higher ground after Halong, but no federal route funds a move

Kwigillingok also voted to move. The state plans to rebuild in place to pre-disaster condition and says recovery funds cannot pay for whole-community relocation.

notes.duration: Residents had been displaced for nine months by July 2026 and Kipnuk faced a second federal declaration after August 2024 flooding (refs 4, 5).

records.title: Newtok abandoned to erosion as the last residents move to Mertarvik, with the Ninglick River cutting about 70 feet a year
records.description: Newtok on the Ninglick River lost nearly half a dozen homes and half its school to erosion and thawing permafrost, and the village council voted in August 2024 to shut down all critical infrastructure after the last residents chose to leave. About 230 residents had moved to Mertarvik from 2019 and the last 71 followed in 2024, but a June 2025 report found housing shortages and strained utilities at the new site. The move has cost about $160 million.

notes.duration: Relocation has been underway for more than 30 years, with the last residents leaving in fall 2024 and the move still unfinished in June 2025 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The village council voted unanimously in 2024 to shut down critical infrastructure, and Newtok was among six communities a GAO report deemed imminently threatened (refs 2, 1).

Shaktoolik, on a gravel spit where Merbok washed away the protective cobble berm, has a relocation estimate of about $290 million, and a new storm surge of 3 to 5 feet was forecast for the southern Seward Peninsula in October 2026.

records.title: Aleutian waters stay among the warmest on record after the Bering Sea heatwave years
records.description: NOAA's ecosystem status reports found Aleutian winter sea surface temperatures in 2022-23 were the warmest since 1900 and those of 2023-24 were among the ten warmest, while the eastern Bering Sea cooled to average conditions after record warmth in 2014 to 2021. NOAA reports poor groundfish condition in the Aleutians since 2012 and that Pacific cod eggs hatch only within a 3 to 6 degree range, which has been exceeded. NOAA did not update the eastern Bering Sea and Aleutian reports in 2025.

notes.livelihoods: Several Bering Sea crab stocks kept declining, forcing disruptive harvest closures (ref 3).
notes.scale: Conditions span the whole Aleutian chain of about 1,100 miles and the eastern Bering Sea shelf (ref 3).
notes.duration: Aleutian winters were record-warm in 2022-23 and still among the ten warmest in 2023-24, after eastern Bering Sea heatwave conditions in 2014 to 2021 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: NOAA Fisheries issues these formal annual ecosystem status reports to the North Pacific fishery managers (refs 1, 2, 4).

records.title: Ocean acidification linked to Bristol Bay red king crab decline in a 2025 NOAA study
records.description: A study led by Mike Litzow at NOAA's Kodiak Lab found that rising acidity explained about 21 percent of the Bristol Bay red king crab's variability in 1980 to 2023 and about 45 percent since 2000, while warming had little effect. NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program says acidification may be partly responsible for the 2021-22 and 2022-23 fishery closures. The authors stress that the result is a correlation, not proven causation.

records.title: Fuel and hazardous-material spills from Halong flooding hit Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta villages
records.description: Flooding from ex-Typhoon Halong damaged bulk fuel storage in western Alaska villages, with fuel drums floating through Nightmute and a sheen on the water. The Coast Guard reported a light sheen on 13 October 2025 and the state later reported a hazardous materials spill at Nightmute with a boil-water notice for traditional outdoor water sources. A February 2026 report lists heating oil, diesel and sewage among the substances released.

notes.livelihoods: A boil-water notice stayed in effect for Nightmute's traditional outdoor water sources, and concern was raised over subsistence fish and game (refs 3, 2).
notes.scale: The spills are reported in a handful of villages (Nightmute, Chevak and others), a local rather than regional effect (refs 2, 4).
notes.duration: Reported from 12 October 2025, with the state still working with the Coast Guard on the Nightmute spill in mid-November (ref 3).
notes.significance: The Coast Guard assessed the fuel storage facilities and the state and Coast Guard response is formal, but no enforcement order is cited (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Bering Strait traffic nearly doubled to 665 transits in 2024, raising oil spill risk on both sides
records.description: The Oil Spill Recovery Institute reports that 665 vessels transited the Bering Strait in 2024, 362 on the Russian side and 303 on the U.S. side, close to double the traffic of 15 years earlier. records.title: Bering Sea snow crab fishery rebuilds slowly after the heatwave collapse, with the 2026-27 quota cut about 45%
records.description: NOAA scientists report that more than 10 billion snow crab disappeared from the eastern Bering Sea after 2018, and the fishery was closed for two consecutive seasons from October 2022. It reopened in 2024-25 at 4.72 million pounds, rose to 9.3 million pounds in 2025-26, and Alaska announced 5.1 million pounds for 2026-27. A December 2025 NOAA study attributes the collapse to warm water and crowding that limited the crabs' energy reserves, and calls recovery fragile.

records.title: Council recommends a 45,000-fish Western Alaska chum bycatch limit for the Bering Sea pollock fleet
records.description: In February 2026 the North Pacific Fishery Management Council recommended a limit of 45,000 Western Alaska chum salmon for the Bering Sea pollock fishery, with a corridor closure if a sector reaches its share. The recommendation goes to the Secretary of Commerce and National Marine Fisheries Service before it can take effect. Tribal groups link repeated Yukon and Kuskokwim closures to weak chum runs, while industry groups say hard caps risk early fishery shutdowns.

notes.harm: The council says about 17% of chum caught over the past decade were bound for Western Alaska rivers and that declines across the North Pacific appear driven largely by warm water, so bycatch harm is partial (refs 1, 5, 6).
notes.livelihoods: Tanana Chiefs Conference testified that closures over six years cost its region about $27 million in direct income, and a Kuskokwim commission official said there is no more commercial fishing income (ref 1).
notes.scale: The issue spans the southeastern Bering Sea pollock grounds and the Western Alaska river systems the salmon return to (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Dozens of Yukon communities were in their sixth year of near-total salmon fishing closures in June 2025, and chum bycatch peaked above 500,000 fish in 2021 (ref 5).
notes.significance: The council made a formal recommendation to the Secretary of Commerce in February 2026, but it is not yet a federal rule (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Appeals court reinstates ringed and bearded seal critical habitat reaching the central Bering Sea
records.description: On 25 March 2026 the Ninth Circuit reversed a 2024 district court ruling and reinstated NOAA's 2022 critical habitat for threatened ringed and bearded seals, nearly 160 million acres from the central Bering Sea to the Beaufort Sea. The State of Alaska says the designation is unlawfully broad and will keep objecting. NOAA closed a 2018-2019 ice seal die-off investigation that recorded 284 stranded seals and a preliminary cause of ecosystem changes in the Bering Sea.

records.layer_rationale: Habitat protection for ice-dependent seals was reinstated by a court after sea-ice loss and prey changes affected the species.

notes.harm: Both species are listed as threatened because of sea-ice dependence, and NOAA's closed unusual mortality event recorded 284 stranded ice seals in 2018-2019, though that event has ended (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Critical habitat adds a layer of review for federally permitted activities such as oil development, and Alaska says it burdens resource development and fisheries (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The designation spans the central Bering, Chukchi and Beaufort seas, a multi-sea region (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The species were listed in 2012 and the habitat dispute has run from the 2022 designation through the 2024 and 2026 rulings (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Ninth Circuit ruled on 25 March 2026 in State of Alaska v. National Marine Fisheries Service, reversing the 2024 district court decision (refs 1, 2, 4).

records.title: Western Steller sea lions keep declining in the central and western Aleutian Islands while the wider population is stable
records.description: NOAA Fisheries says the endangered western distinct population segment of Steller sea lions has increased slowly overall since 2003 but continues to decline in the central and western Aleutian Islands. NOAA's 2025 survey summary, published 24 September 2025, reports the 15-year non-pup trend changed from increasing to stable, with a modeled 38,911 non-pups and 12,762 pups for the western stock in Alaska.

notes.significance: The western DPS is listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act and depleted under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (ref 1).

records.title: Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area leasing withdrawal has been revoked, reinstated and extended across three administrations
records.description: Executive Order 13754 created the Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area in December 2016 and closed parts of the northern Bering Sea and Norton Sound to oil and gas leasing. A 2017 executive order revoked it, and Executive Order 13990 reinstated it in 2021. A presidential memorandum of 6 January 2025 withdrew the area's remaining parts from leasing without an expiration date. A law firm analysis says whether a future president can revoke an OCSLA withdrawal is legally unsettled.

location.type: Offshore oil and gas leasing withdrawal area
location.detail: Norton Sound, St. Lawrence Island and northern Bering Sea shelf, Alaska, US

notes.harm: No spill or contamination is documented; the sources concern leasing protection and existing leases are unaffected (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No disruption is documented; the withdrawal prevents new leasing only, and existing leases are unaffected (ref 1).
notes.scale: The area spans the northern Bering Sea shelf including Norton Sound and St. Lawrence Island waters (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The area was created in 2016, revoked in 2017, reinstated in 2021 and extended in January 2025, a status that has shifted for a decade (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: A presidential memorandum under OCSLA section 12(a), published in the Federal Register on 17 January 2025, withdrew the remaining areas indefinitely (ref 1).

population_affected.note: The sources name tribal groups that advocated for the area but give no population figure.

key_measure.text: The 6 January 2025 memorandum withdrew the remaining areas of the Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area from oil and gas leasing for a time period without a specific expiration (ref 1).

signals: The opened sources give no lease-sale or revenue figures for the northern Bering Sea.

records.title: Trans-Ecuadorian pipeline rupture sends crude down the Esmeraldas River toward the Pacific coast
records.description: A landslide ruptured the SOTE crude pipeline at El Vergel (Quinindé) on 13 March 2025 and oil travelled down the Esmeraldas River system toward its mouth at the Pacific. Authorities declared an environmental emergency and temporarily closed three Esmeraldas beaches, and Ecuadorian press reported oil reaching Pacific waters and the Atacames shoreline. Petroecuador was ordered to contain and clean up; the volume spilled was not published in the sources opened.

notes.livelihoods: The environment ministry temporarily closed the Las Palmas, Camarones and Las Piedras beaches (ref 3).

notes.duration: A biologist estimated impacts on smaller rivers could last about three years; the sources opened date only from the first week (ref 1).
notes.significance: The national emergency committee declared an environmental emergency on 16 March 2025 and the International Charter was activated on 20 March 2025 (refs 2, 4).

records.title: Hundreds of boats sunk by Hurricane Otis still pollute Acapulco Bay with fuel and batteries
records.description: Hurricane Otis (25 October 2023) sank hundreds of boats in Acapulco Bay. Eighty days later divers and biologists reported an iridescent hydrocarbon film, metals and lead or lithium batteries leaching from the wrecks, and in May 2026 a volunteer group said it was still removing wreck fragments and estimated 700 to 1,000 tonnes of waste remained on the seabed. Counts of sunken vessels differ widely between sources.

notes.duration: Reports run from January 2024 (ref 1) to May 2026, when removal work was still under way (ref 3).
notes.significance: The reports cite volunteer and environmentalist accounts and no official notice or enforcement; the removal group said authorities did not respond (ref 3).

records.title: Galapagos beaches receive mostly imported plastic: 80 tonnes removed by park rangers in six years
records.description: A report by the Galapagos Conservation Trust and the Galapagos National Park Directorate (September 2024) says rangers removed 80 tonnes of plastic from the archipelago's beaches over six years, with more than 95% likely originating outside the Galapagos Marine Reserve. It reports plastic exposure in 52 species and attributes at least 40% of plastic pollution to maritime sources such as fishing fleets.

notes.livelihoods: The cited material reports no fishery or tourism closure (ref 1).
notes.scale: Debris affects the coastline of an archipelago marine reserve across several islands (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: The Plastic Pollution Free Galapagos programme started in May 2018 and rangers removed 80 tonnes over six years (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal report co-produced with the National Park Directorate documents the problem, without an enforcement order (ref 1).

records.title: Repeated fuel oil pipeline spills at Salina Cruz refinery reach four Pacific beaches
records.description: Between 9 and 21 June 2026 five pipeline leaks between the Salina Cruz refinery and Pemex's marine terminal sent heavy fuel oil through city streets, and a spill on 29 July 2026 affected four beaches. Local environmentalists count at least 66 spills in the corridor since 2022; Semar joined a coastal contingency committee and cleanup began on 29 July.

records.title: IATTC shortens eastern Pacific tuna purse seine closure to 64 days but leaves FAD reforms unfinished
records.description: At its 103rd meeting in September 2025 the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission reduced the purse seine closure by eight days to 64 days for one year, citing healthy bigeye, yellowfin and skipjack stocks, and expanded the requirement to keep satellite FAD buoys transmitting south of 10 degrees S and west of 100 degrees W. The ISSF notes that broader FAD reforms such as a register were not addressed; the IATTC page for 2026 lists 64-day closures and 10 to 22 extra days for vessels above the 1,200 t bigeye limit. At its September 2026 meeting in Lisbon the IATTC reached no consensus on new tropical tuna measures, so the 2025 measure stays in force; NOAA Fisheries says the United States opposed proposed increases in purse seine capacity, members rolled over the "fins naturally attached" shark measure and adopted the Commission's first management procedure, for Pacific bluefin tuna.

notes.significance: The Commission adopted Resolution C-25-01 at its 103rd session, a treaty-body decision (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Naval incidents in the Gulf of Fonseca in 2025 and 2026 test the Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua boundary
records.description: In September 2025 Honduras' armed forces accused Salvadoran coast guard vessels of entering Honduran waters in the Gulf of Fonseca during a joint patrol with Nicaragua, and declared maximum alert; the Salvadoran government had issued no statement when the reports were published. On 4 June 2026 El Heraldo reported that Honduras' Pacific naval commander was arrested after handing seized boats over in what the paper says were Salvadoran waters, and that the Foreign Ministry opened diplomatic channels.

records.title: Costa Rica's oil and gas exploration ban still rests on a 2002 decree as a bill to make it law stalls and the climate pledge drops it
records.description: Costa Rica's ban on oil and gas operations dates from a 2002 presidential decree, which Human Rights Watch calls a fragile legal foundation, and bill 23.579 to declare the country free of oil and gas exploration and extraction received a favourable committee report in February 2024 but faced 128 motions from the Nueva República caucus. On 14 November 2025 the government removed a pledge to make the moratorium law from its updated climate commitment, and President Chaves has floated exploration.

records.title: Coral bleaching across Eastern Tropical Pacific reefs from April 2023: 38 of 72 monitored sites severely bleached
records.description: A reef ecologist of the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network reported on 17 April 2024 that bleaching had been confirmed in Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica, Panama and Colombia since April 2023, and that of 72 sites monitored since mid-2023, 38 showed severe bleaching and 20 had some coral death; some reefs were recovering. Separately, researchers reported cold-water bleaching and mortality on Clipperton Atoll's deep reefs, with bleached and dead coral about 70% of coral surveyed at 32 m.

records.title: Peru's official El Niño Costero alert extends into 2027 as forecasts rise to extraordinary magnitude
records.description: Peru's multisectoral ENFEN commission declared an El Niño Costero alert in February 2026 and has kept it active; by its 14 September 2026 statement the highest probability for September 2026 to January 2027 in the Niño 1+2 region was extraordinary magnitude, up from a weak event forecast in February. The commission expects anchoveta to stay deep and nearer the coast and warns of heavy rain on the north coast from November.

location.detail: Peru's whole Pacific coast, with the strongest rainfall risk forecast for the north coast; ENFEN reports on the Niño 1+2 region off Peru and Ecuador.

notes.harm: ENFEN forecasts that north-central anchoveta will stay deep and move closer to the coast and that warm-water species persist, a limited ecological shift with no mortality reported (ref 5).

notes.scale: The alert covers Peru's national coastline and the Niño 1+2 region rather than a single bay (ref 3).
notes.duration: The alert opened in February 2026 for an event expected from March and, by the September statement, to run to about May 2027, more than a year (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: ENFEN's formal 'Alerta de El Niño Costero' status has been maintained through communiques 03, 07, 09 and 14-2026 (refs 1, 2, 4, 6); no emergency declaration is cited.

records.title: Marine heatwaves on Chile's coast and Northern Humboldt build into an El Niño in 2025-2026
records.description: The SPRFMO 2025-2026 ecosystem status report counts six marine heatwaves totalling 179 days off northern Chile, including a 109-day event in early 2026, with the first events already in late 2025. By August 2026 sea-surface anomalies reached +3.17 °C in the Northern Humboldt region off Peru and +1.77 °C off northern Chile as El Niño developed. A Mercator Ocean bulletin from November 2025 flagged a heatwave forming off northern Chile.

notes.harm: The report documents heatwave days and weaker coastal upwelling but no mortality or habitat loss, so harm is limited to potential ecological stress (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources links these heatwaves to a Chilean fishery or farm closure, so no disruption is scored here (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Heatwaves were detected across five regions spanning northern Chile, Peru's Northern Humboldt and the oceanic Southeast Pacific, a regional-sea footprint (ref 1).
notes.duration: The longest northern Chile event ran 109 days in early 2026 and the 179 heatwave days were spread over late 2025 to mid-2026, a span of months (ref 1).
notes.significance: The sources are a scientific status report, an operational bulletin and a thesis, none an advisory or enforcement action (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.title: Central Chile's urban beaches erode faster as swells intensify, with Reñaca and Santo Domingo among the worst
records.description: A Universidad Católica study by the Observatorio de la Costa tracked 66 beaches between Arica and Chiloé and found retreat accelerating between 2023 and 2024, with Santo Domingo at 5.7 m a year and Hornitos at 5.2 m a year. records.title: Mass intoxications of schoolchildren around Quintero Bay in 2025 leave the cause unidentified
records.description: From late September 2025, odours of gas and chlorine around Quintero Bay coincided with hydrocarbon loading operations and sent 127 students and teachers, then nearly 200 people, to health centres, with over 100 diagnosed with T59 toxic-gas intoxication. AIDA and Greenpeace filed a protection action on 8 November 2025 in Valparaíso asking for automatic industrial shutdowns and full compliance with the 2019 Supreme Court ruling. The cause had not been identified in the sources opened.

location.detail: Quintero and Puchuncaví communes, Valparaíso region, around the Quintero Bay industrial and port complex that also includes Concón.

records.layer_rationale: Toxic-gas exposure episodes tied to an industrial and hydrocarbon port complex on the bay.

notes.harm: More than 100 of nearly 200 people attending health centres were diagnosed with T59 intoxication, mostly minors, across nine schools (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: A health alert was in force in the Concón, Quintero and Puchuncaví industrial belt and schools were affected, an advisory rather than a closure of fishing or ports (ref 1).
notes.scale: The episodes centre on two communes and one bay, a local site (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: Episodes in 2018, 2022, 2023 and again from September 2025 show recurring exposure over years (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A 2019 Supreme Court ruling ordered preventive and corrective measures that the November 2025 protection action says are unmet, and an Inter-American Commission petition (P-1800-25) was sent to Chile in February 2026 (refs 4, 5).

population_affected.note: Almost 200 people attended health centres between late September and mid-November 2025, mostly minors (refs 3, 4).

records.title: Chile extends its red tide health alert for Los Lagos and Aysén to April 2027
records.description: Chile's health ministry extended by decree 50 of 7 April 2026, published 30 April, the red tide health alert for Los Lagos and Aysén to 30 April 2027, the latest renewal since the alert began in April 2022. The decree recalls paralytic shellfish poison at 14,018 µg per 100 g in Aysén against an 80 µg limit, a fatality, and six cases in Los Lagos including the death of a child under three. A thesis finds marine heatwaves can trigger Alexandrium catenella blooms when nutrients suffice.

location.name: Los Lagos and Aysén fjords and channels
location.detail: Shellfish-harvesting waters of Chile's Los Lagos and Aysén regions, including Estero Quiltralco in Aysén and Canal Quihua in Los Lagos named in the decree; a red tide was also found in Tongoy Bay, Coquimbo, in summer 2026.

records.layer_rationale: Harmful algal blooms that contaminate shellfish with toxins, fed by warm, calm, nutrient-rich water.

notes.harm: The decree records paralytic poison at 14,018 µg/100 g against the 80 µg limit at Estero Quiltralco, one death there and six cases in Los Lagos with a child's death (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Semanario Local describes sanitary closures halting extraction of clams, mussels, razor clams and other filter feeders, hurting fishing, aquaculture and tourism (ref 2).
notes.scale: The alert covers two regions of southern Chile, and a 2026 bloom also appeared in Tongoy Bay, a regional footprint (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The alert began on 6 April 2022 and has been extended seven times, now to 30 April 2027 (ref 1).
notes.significance: Decree 50 of 7 April 2026 is a ministerial health-alert order with extraordinary powers, an enforcement-level instrument (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Six poisoning cases in Los Lagos in April 2022 cited in the decree, one fatal; a further death is recorded in Aysén in March 2022 (ref 1). No 2025-2026 case count was opened.

key_measure.text: Paralytic shellfish poison reached 14,018 µg per 100 g in Estero Quiltralco, Aysén, against a limit of 80 µg per 100 g (ref 1).

trend.note: The alert has been renewed every year since 2022 because toxins keep recurring; the decree cites ENSO-neutral and dry conditions as favourable to blooms (ref 1).

records.title: Mejillones Bay, a Chilean 'sacrifice zone', carries heavy metals and coal-port spills with fishers in decline
records.description: An AFP report of February 2024 says a 2019 regional study found significant heavy metals and organic matter in Mejillones Bay, linked to industrial waste and wastewater, and that about half of some 300 local fishers have left. A 2020 coal spill of about six tonnes at a port terminal came with more than ten similar spills in two years, and a 2019 Environment Ministry study found anoxic conditions. Chile plans to close the eight Mejillones coal plants before 2040.

notes.scale: The problem is one bay and port, a single site (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Spills and contamination are described across 2018 to 2020 and still in 2024, a chronic condition (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: The SMA gave the port company 72 hours for a remediation plan after the 2020 spill and Congress used the sacrifice-zone term in a July 2022 memorandum, formal notices rather than a court order (refs 1, 3).

records.description: The Científicos de la Basura survey run with Universidad Católica del Norte sampled 179 beaches in ten Latin American countries in 2024 and found Peru had the most polluted beaches, followed by northern Chile, with Antofagasta the worst in Chile. records.title: Peru ends its 2026 first anchoveta season at about a quarter of the lowest quota in a decade, citing warm anomalous waters and juvenile fish
records.description: Produce opened the north-centre first anchoveta season with a total permissible catch of 1,914,049 tonnes, the lowest first-season limit in a decade apart from 2023 according to Infobae. After IMARPE's Eureka LXXVIII survey on 15 to 18 August 2026 found juveniles made up 65% of fish by number amid anomalous warm conditions, Produce closed the season from 21 August; a later ministerial resolution says it reached about 24.61% of its limit and exempted shipowners from the usual catch obligation.

location.detail: Peru's coast from the northern limit of its maritime domain to 16 degrees S, the north-centre anchoveta zone managed by Produce and IMARPE.

notes.harm: IMARPE's Eureka LXXVIII survey found juveniles were 65% of specimens by number and 48% by weight and that somatic condition and fat content were low (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: Produce closed the season from 21 August 2026 and the fleet reached only about 24.61% of its limit, per the technical report cited in the ministerial resolution (refs 3, 4).
notes.scale: The measure covers the whole north-centre coast of Peru, a national fishery zone (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 2023 first season was never held, the 2025 first season closed early at 81.92% of a 3 million tonne limit, and the 2026 season ended in August (refs 2, 5, 3).
notes.significance: Produce issued a ministerial resolution authorising the season, a closure order, and a one-time exemption resolution published 15 September 2026 (refs 1, 3, 4).

records.title: Several hundred Chinese-flag squid vessels fish at the edge of Peruvian, Chilean and Ecuadorian waters as the jumbo squid stock sits in the red zone
records.description: Mongabay reports that China's own figures put its distant-water squid fleet at 528 vessels around the Ecuadorian, Peruvian and Chilean EEZs in 2024, and that 2024 jumbo squid catches fell to about 601,500 tonnes with the stock in the red zone of the Kobe diagram in four analysed cases. Chilean outlets reported 117 Chinese vessels detected off Chile in 2025 against 8 in 2024, and in July 2026 the Chilean Navy called a stationary concentration of about 370 Chinese-origin vessels near its territorial sea unusual; in Peru, artisanal fishers struck over a cut in the 2025 jumbo squid quota to 42,000 tonnes.

location.name: High seas beside the Peru, Chile and Ecuador EEZs
location.detail: Jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) grounds on the high seas adjoining the South American EEZs; the fleet moves between Chile, Peru and Ecuador through the year.

records.layer_rationale: An unregulated high-seas fishery for a stock reported in the red zone, with effects on coastal artisanal fleets.
secondary_drivers: No catch limit on the high seas

notes.harm: Mongabay Latam reports the stock in the Kobe red zone in four analysed cases and a 52% fall in catches in 2024 (ref 1); no mass mortality is documented.
notes.livelihoods: Peru's Produce cut the 2025 artisanal jumbo squid quota to 42,000 tonnes by RM 00323-2025-PRODUCE and guilds said more than 5,000 artisanal boats were affected, prompting a strike in Piura (ref 5).
notes.scale: The fleet fishes along three national EEZ boundaries and the Chilean Navy opened a surveillance operation using C-295 aircraft in July 2026 (refs 1, 4).
notes.duration: Mongabay says the Chinese fleet roughly doubled from 2014 to 2024, with a stock assessment still lacking in the fifth year of disagreement (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The SPRFMO Commission adopted a squid measure in March 2026 and Chile's Sernapesca told a November 2025 forum that it inspects all foreign vessels in its EEZ but sees regulatory gaps (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure appears in the cited sources.

records.title: SPRFMO caps squid vessels at 651 and starts monitoring in 2027, but no catch limit is set and Peru's buffer-zone proposal is not approved
records.description: At its 14th meeting in Panama City on 2 to 6 March 2026 the SPRFMO Commission adopted a consolidated jumbo flying squid measure, electronic-monitoring standards and port-inspection amendments, and set a 2026 jack mackerel total allowable catch. According to Mongabay the vessel ceiling falls from 766 to 651, observer coverage starts at 5% of fishing days on 1 September 2027, the Scientific Committee again failed to agree a stock assessment, and Peru's proposed no-fishing buffer outside South American EEZs was not approved; Pew called the change insufficient.

notes.scale: The measure applies to the whole SPRFMO high-seas squid fishery adjoining several national EEZs, a regional-sea scale (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Chile's Law 21.752 reallocates catch shares between artisanal and industrial fleets in 20 fisheries through 2040
records.description: Law 21.752, signed on 19 June 2025 and published in the Diario Oficial on 25 June 2025, fixes a new artisanal-industrial split of catch quotas to 31 December 2040. For jumbo squid the artisanal share starts at 90% within a 90 to 80% range, for anchoveta and Spanish sardine in the north at 55% with a 55 to 85% range, and for common hake at 45% up to 35,020 tonnes, with excess quota going to the artisanal fraction up to a 50% cap.

records.title: Fukushima Daiichi treated water still flowing into the Pacific in its fourth year, with China's seafood ban only partly lifted
records.description: Japan began releasing ALPS-treated water from the Fukushima Daiichi plant on 24 August 2023 under a roughly 30-year plan. By the start of the 21st round on 6 July 2026, about 157,000 tonnes had been discharged, and the IAEA's on-site analysis has found tritium far below the 1,500 Bq per litre operational limit. China banned all Japanese seafood in 2023 and partly lifted the ban on 29 June 2025, still excluding Tokyo, Fukushima and eight other prefectures. On 5 October 2026 TEPCO began its sixth release of fiscal 2026, the 24th since August 2023, about 7,800 tonnes due to finish by 23 October, with measurements reported well below national regulatory limits.

records.layer_rationale: Controlled release of tritiated water from a damaged nuclear plant into the sea, with trade and monitoring consequences.

notes.harm: The IAEA found tritium in the diluted water far below the 1,500 Bq per litre operational limit, so no exceedance is documented, but each round releases about 1.3 trillion Bq of tritium (refs 1, 4).
notes.livelihoods: Japanese seafood exports to China fell 99.3% year on year in September 2023 from a pre-ban value of about JPY75bn, and Tokyo, Fukushima and eight other prefectures remain excluded after the June 2025 partial lifting (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: Discharges run from one plant on the Fukushima coast but affect national fishery markets and regional trade, which we score as a national coastline (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: Releases began on 24 August 2023 and continue under a roughly 30-year plan, with eight rounds and about 62,400 tonnes planned for fiscal 2026 (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: China's customs authority imposed a blanket import ban on release day and Russia joined the restrictions; the IAEA monitors every batch and a China-Japan monitoring accord followed in September 2024 (refs 1, 2, 5).

records.title: Kuroshio Extension meander gave Japan's Sanriku coast two years of record warming, about 6 degrees C above normal
records.description: Sea surface temperature off the Sanriku coast ran about 6 degrees C above normal from February 2023 to January 2025 while the Kuroshio Extension meandered far north, which the University of Tokyo's Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute calls the most intense warming in the world's oceans. Warm-water fish appeared off Miyagi for the first time and fishers report poor catches, and Japan's Meteorological Agency declared the larger Kuroshio meander over in August 2025.

location.name: Sanriku coast and Kuroshio Extension
location.detail: Pacific coast of Tohoku (Aomori, Iwate, Miyagi), reaching south to the Boso and Kanto coasts

records.layer_rationale: Persistent marine heatwave driven by a shifted western boundary current.

notes.harm: Warm-water cardinalfish and southern yellowtail were confirmed off Miyagi for the first time, the warming reached about 700 m depth, and kombu harvests are declining sharply (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Mie Gaiwan fishers report mackerel catches at 20 to 30 percent of ten years ago, and Sanriku salmon and saury became harder to catch, but no closure is documented (ref 2).
notes.scale: The anomaly covered the Pacific coast of Japan's Tohoku region and the Kuroshio Extension, a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Temperatures stayed about 6 C above normal from February 2023 to January 2025, and marine heatwave conditions were present almost daily from April 2023 to August 2024 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Japan Meteorological Agency formally declared the large meander ended in August 2025 and linked the ocean state to record 2023 summer heat, backed by a peer-reviewed study (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Runit Dome nuclear waste cap on Enewetak Atoll exposed to rising seas, GAO and DOE reports find
records.description: The Runit Dome in the Marshall Islands holds contaminated soil and debris from US nuclear weapons tests in an unlined crater under a non-load-bearing concrete cap. GAO reported in January 2024 that Marshallese officials fear rising seas may affect contaminated sites and that DOE has struggled to explain its view that the health risk is low, and DOE's July 2024 report to Congress found storm surge with sea-level rise would matter most. A March 2026 report describes cracks in the cap and groundwater entering the crater.

notes.harm: DOE's modelled doses stay below 0.1 mrem per year with the dome intact and below 0.2 mrem per year after a hypothetical failure, so harm is potential; a 2026 report notes groundwater already enters the unlined crater (refs 2, 3).

notes.scale: The dome is a single containment structure on one island, although lagoon sediments across the atoll hold most of the long-term radioactivity (ref 2).
notes.duration: The dome was built in the late 1970s and DOE's study projects conditions to 2090 with 62 cm of sea-level rise, so the exposure is chronic (ref 2).
notes.significance: GAO issued formal report GAO-24-104082 whose communication recommendation remained open in July 2026, and DOE delivered a statutory report to Congress (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Open North Pacific acidifying faster below the surface near Hawaii and steadily across the western subtropical gyre
records.description: A University of Hawaii study of 35 years of Hawaii Ocean Time-series data at Station ALOHA, about 60 miles north of Oahu, found that acidification is faster below the surface than at the surface for every indicator, from the surface to nearly 3 miles deep. Japan's Meteorological Agency reports surface pH falling about 0.02 per decade along 137E and 165E, close to the global rate, and 0.016 to 0.029 per decade in the interior at 150 to 800 m.

records.layer_rationale: Absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide is changing seawater carbonate chemistry across the water column.

notes.scale: JMA's sections span 3N to 35N along 137E and 165E and the Hawaii record covers the whole water column, a basin-scale signal (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The Station ALOHA record is 35 years, JMA's 137E series starts in 1985 and its 165E series in 1996, and trends continue (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.significance: These are research and agency monitoring results without a formal notice, listing or enforcement, so the score is 0 (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.title: Great Pacific Garbage Patch holds about 100,000 tonnes of plastic over 1.6 million sq km, and cleanup has removed a fraction
records.description: The Ocean Cleanup estimates the patch between Hawaii and California covers about 1.6 million square kilometres and holds about 100,000 tonnes of plastic, mostly fishing gear. By April 2024 it had verifiably removed over 345,000 kg in 18 trips, about a third of a percent, and in July 2026 it said it would test drone-guided steering in the patch on a six-week expedition.

location.name: Great Pacific Garbage Patch
location.detail: North Pacific subtropical gyre between Hawaii and California, centred on average near 32N 145W

records.layer_rationale: Floating plastic concentrated by the gyre's circulation.

notes.harm: The Ocean Cleanup estimates about 1.8 trillion pieces and about 100,000 tonnes of plastic, of which fishing nets were 46% of the mass in 2018, but no mortality count is given in these pages (refs 1, 4).
notes.livelihoods: The cited pages describe no fishery, shipping or tourism restriction from the patch (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: The patch spans about 1.6 million square kilometres of the high seas in the North Pacific subtropical gyre, which is basin scale (ref 4).
notes.duration: Plastic has accumulated since the 2018 survey and the first cleanup extraction in 2019, with removal continuing through 2026 (refs 1, 2, 4).

records.title: Apra Harbor, Guam, logged a record 77 high-tide flood days in 2025-26, and Hawaii's Kawaihae and Hilo 44 each
records.description: NOAA's 2026-27 outlook review reports that Apra Harbor, Guam, set a station record of 77 high-tide flood days in the 2025-26 meteorological year against a predicted 4 to 11, which NOAA attributes to elevated regional sea levels. records.title: Pacific saury stock stays far below past levels as the NPFC trims quotas by only 5% for 2026
records.description: Japan's saury landings fell from about 300,000 tons until 2009 to about 18,000 tons in 2022. records.title: HMNZS Manawanui wreck and diesel spill on the reef off Upolu, Samoa
records.description: The New Zealand Navy survey ship HMNZS Manawanui grounded on the reef off Upolu's south coast on 5 October 2024 and sank the next day with an estimated 900,000 or more litres of diesel aboard. Local authorities estimated about 200,000 litres leaked in the first week, salvors later removed more than 300,000 litres of diesel and the wreck remains on the reef, with a court martial and an environmental assessment still pending in 2026.

notes.harm: About 200,000 litres of diesel leaked in the first week and the ship travelled about 400 yards over the reef; Safata village leaders say shores, reef and mangroves were damaged, although SROS tests found seawater uncontaminated (refs 2, 4, 6).
notes.livelihoods: A precautionary fishing zone was imposed after the sinking and later lifted, but a no-go zone around the wreck still blocks fishing, and one resident says about 80% of locals depend on the sea for food (refs 2, 4).

notes.duration: The grounding was in October 2024 and the wreck was still on the reef, with the environmental report under stakeholder review, in October 2025 and a fuel sheen checked in February 2026 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: A Navy court of inquiry blamed human error, Samoa's Cabinet decided the wreck stays, New Zealand agreed compensation, and charges were laid in the Court Martial of New Zealand on 2 March 2026 (refs 1, 4, 6).

records.title: Funafuti reclamation races rising seas as over half of Tuvalu is forecast to flood regularly by 2050
records.description: Sea levels around Tuvalu rose about 15 cm in the three decades to 2023, roughly twice the global average, according to NASA researchers cited by Reuters in October 2026. Donor-funded work worth about US$50 million is building sea walls and raising land on Funafuti, with about 21 hectares planned, while NASA flood maps project that areas with fewer than five high-tide flood days a year could average 25 by the 2050s.

notes.livelihoods: The cited sources document no closure or displacement; they describe sea walls and barriers to protect schools, clinics and crops from storm surges (ref 2).

notes.duration: The 15 cm rise accumulated over the three decades to 2023 and the reclamation programme spans phases from 2023 to a 2026 target (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: NASA ran the flood analysis at the request of Tuvalu and Kiribati with the US State Department, and donor-funded adaptation works are formally under way, but no enforcement action applies (refs 3, 1).

records.title: Serua Island, Fiji: king-tide flooding and erosion leave a chiefly village facing relocation
records.description: WMO's 2025 South-West Pacific report describes how, since 2000, higher king tides and seawater intrusion have destroyed Serua Island's seawall, submerged homes and killed food crops, and on two occasions the island could be crossed by boat. Fiji's government has offered relocation support, but most of the roughly 150 residents are choosing to stay because of ties to ancestral land.

location.detail: A small island about a five-minute boat ride off Viti Levu, the traditional residence of the paramount chief of Serua Province; coordinates are the province, not the island.

records.layer_rationale: Sea-level rise and coastal erosion are removing the habitable land of a village.

notes.harm: Over two decades erosion and flooding destroyed the seawall, submerged homes and let seawater kill food crops and wash away fertile soil (ref 1, ref 2).

records.title: Lomaiviti Princess II sinks in Suva Harbour and leaks oil as 17 derelict vessels await removal
records.description: The abandoned passenger ferry Lomaiviti Princess II capsized and sank in Suva Harbour in early June 2025 after being towed from Narain Jetty, releasing oil that responders contained with booms and dispersants. A joint maritime committee found its owner had not defuelled it despite removal notices, and Fiji has funded a multi-phase clean-up of 17 high-risk derelict vessels expected to run into 2026.

notes.duration: The vessel had been abandoned since 2019, the spill response was set for four to eight weeks, and the derelict clean-up is expected to run into 2026 (refs 3, 5).
notes.significance: The Joint Maritime Environment Committee found breaches of the Maritime Transport Act 2013 (section 129) and the minister ordered a full investigation, with penalties of up to FJ$1 million or three years cited, and Cabinet approved a review of the MSAF Act (refs 1, 3, 5).

records.title: Moruroa and Fangataufa nuclear test atolls: lagoon contamination and compensation remain disputed
records.description: France tested 193 nuclear devices at Moruroa and Fangataufa from 1966 to 1996 and dumped an estimated 3,200 tonnes of radioactive waste in Polynesian waters. France says continuing sampling shows no abnormalities and that IAEA experts saw no need for remediation, while a January 2026 National Assembly amendment states that lagoon sediments still show elevated contamination and the atolls remain defence nuclear installations.

location.name: Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls (PF)

records.layer_rationale: Residual radioactive contamination of lagoon sediments and dumped waste at former nuclear test sites.

notes.harm: An IAEA estimate put about 5 kg of plutonium in Moruroa's lagoon sediments and plutonium remains in the soil, but France reports samples without abnormalities, so contamination above a standard is disputed (refs 1, 2, 5).
notes.livelihoods: The opened sources document no fishery closure at the atolls; the compensation dispute concerns health claims (refs 3, 4).
notes.scale: Dumping sites between Hao and Moruroa across French Polynesian territorial waters extend beyond the two atolls (ref 2).
notes.duration: Testing ended in 1996 and the issue persists, with France sampling annually since 1998 and a deputies' amendment on it in January 2026 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: The atolls are formally classified as defence nuclear installations (INID) and France reported to the UN under General Assembly Resolution 78/240 (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Extreme high tides and record rain flood Tongatapu's low-lying coast in October 2024

records.title: ITLOS Seabed Disputes Chamber orders the ISA to observe due process in its inquiry into Nauru- and Tonga-sponsored contractors NORI and TOML
records.description: On 18 July 2026 the Seabed Disputes Chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea unanimously prescribed provisional measures in two cases (Cases 34 and 35) brought by Nauru Ocean Resources Inc. (NORI) and Tonga Offshore Mining Ltd. (TOML) against the International Seabed Authority. The Chamber did not suspend the Authority's inquiry into possible contractual non-compliance; it ordered the Authority to act within the legal framework, including due process, in the inquiry and in the extension of NORI's exploration contract, and to clarify procedures and questions to the contractor. The Nauru government reported that the ISA Council approved a five-year extension of NORI's contract on 20 July 2026.

notes.scale: Two contracts sponsored by two Pacific states (Nauru and Tonga) are in dispute, with implications for the wider ISA contractor regime (refs 1, 5).
notes.duration: The inquiry stems from a Council decision of 21 July 2025 and reached the Chamber in June 2026, so it has run for about a year (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Chamber delivered unanimous provisional-measures orders on 18 July 2026 in its first contentious proceedings, which is a tribunal ruling (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Cook Islands extends seabed minerals exploration to 2032 as a NOAA survey, US and China ties and public opposition shape the mining debate
records.description: The Cook Islands government says no decision to mine has been made, and Cook Islands News reported in November 2025 that exploration would be extended five years, pushing any mining decision to at least 2032. Five-year exploration licences issued in 2022 went to Moana Minerals, Cook Islands Cobalt and Cobalt Seabed Resources, and a 2026 NOAA expedition reported dense nodule fields. A Cook Islands News poll found more than 50% of voters opposed seabed mining, while a local environmental group criticised a new US exploration partner and growing US and Chinese involvement (refs 7, 8).

notes.harm: A July 2026 report cited by Cook Islands News warns of unaddressed radioactive-contamination risks, while the Seabed Minerals Authority says there is currently no evidence of severe toxic effects, so harm is potential (ref 5).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or lost income is reported; Cook Islands News says opponents warn of effects on food security and culture (ref 1).
notes.scale: The licences and nodule fields cover the national EEZ, estimated at 6.7 billion tonnes of nodules by Cook Islands News, which is a national-waters issue (ref 1).
notes.duration: Exploration licences date from 2022 and were extended in November 2025 to at least 2032, so the issue is chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The government formally extended exploration and licences remain active, a formal licensing step short of an enforcement order (ref 2).

records.title: Pacific Islands Forum leaders keep a member-led approach to deep-sea minerals as Fiji and French Polynesia press for a pause and civil society warns of sponsor liability
records.description: At their September 2026 meeting in Palau, Forum leaders endorsed a member-led regional approach and a regional repository of deep-sea mineral data, and PINA reports that members still hold differing views. Fiji describes a 10-year precautionary pause on commercial mining in its waters while still licensing exploration, French Polynesia's president called in September 2025 for a regional moratorium, and Cook Islands, Nauru and Tonga are exploring or sponsoring activity. Pacific civil society groups warn that sponsoring states could carry long-term liability.

records.title: High Seas Treaty is in force, but Nauru, the Cook Islands and Niue have signed without ratifying as the first Conference of the Parties nears
records.description: The Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction entered into force on 17 January 2026, and the first Conference of the Parties must meet by 17 January 2027. The UN Treaty Collection record shows Fiji and Tuvalu ratified on 9 June 2025, Kiribati on 9 December 2025, Tonga on 7 July 2026 and Samoa on 14 September 2026, while Nauru, the Cook Islands and Niue have signed with no ratification recorded. No high seas marine protected area exists yet under the treaty.

records.title: Pacific tuna stocks are reported healthy, but El Niño, warming-driven stock shifts and surveillance gaps put island access-fee revenue at risk
records.description: The Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency's 2024-25 annual report says skipjack, yellowfin, bigeye and albacore in the Western and Central Pacific are all assessed as not overfished, and that illegal fishing losses have fallen by more than 50% since 2016. The Secretariat of the Pacific Community has warned that overshooting 1.5 degrees C could shift tuna east out of island zones and cut access-fee revenue by up to US$90 million a year, and a strong El Niño is forecast to disrupt fishing into 2027. Only about 15% of tuna caught in the region is processed onshore, and Pacific ministers want more surveillance investment.

location.detail: Exclusive economic zones of Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency members and adjacent high seas in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean (refs 1, 2).

records.layer_rationale: Stock-status reports are positive, with climate redistribution and illegal fishing as the stated pressures on a managed tuna fishery.

notes.harm: No overfishing is reported, so harm is potential: the SPC projects tuna moving out of island EEZs if warming overshoots 1.5 degrees C (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The El Niño report notes fishing effort fell in some areas and shifted to the high seas and Kiribati and Tuvalu waters after the FAD ban, with no closure or income loss quantified (ref 4).
notes.scale: The fishery spans the Western and Central Pacific, which produces about 60% of the world's tuna according to PINA (ref 8).
notes.duration: The surveillance and processing challenges are chronic, with illegal-fishing losses tracked since 2016 and new measures adopted in December 2025 (refs 1, 6).
notes.significance: The Forum Fisheries Committee ministers issued a formal communique in July 2026 and WCPFC22 adopted an albacore management procedure in December 2025 (refs 6, 7).

population_affected.note: No population figure applies to the fishery-level risks reported.

records.title: FFA report links tuna fishing and supply chains to cocaine smuggling, with packages washing onto Pacific reefs and large seizures near Fiji and French Polynesia
records.description: The Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency's latest Trade and Industry News report says criminal networks are using tuna shipments, fishing vessels and offshore refuelling to move cocaine from South America across the Pacific. It cites packages washing onto reefs in the Marshall Islands and 26 kg on a reef at Mitiaro in the Cook Islands, and a 2.6 tonne seizure in north-west Viti Levu, Fiji, in early 2026. RNZ separately reported a Cook Islands fisherman's account of finding a package on the Mitiaro reef.

notes.scale: The report describes a South Pacific transit route with landfalls from the Marshall Islands to the Cook Islands, a regional-sea scale (ref 1).
notes.duration: The report notes drug vessels drifting ashore since 2024 and seizures dating from 2023, so the problem is recurring (ref 1).

records.title: NOAA confirmed mass coral bleaching across Fiji, Tuvalu, Kiribati, Samoa and French Polynesia in the fourth global event, which it now judges ended in mid-2025
records.description: NOAA announced on 15 April 2024 that the world was in its fourth global coral bleaching event and said mass bleaching had been confirmed across large areas of the South Pacific, including Fiji, Tuvalu, Kiribati, Samoa and French Polynesia. In June 2026 NOAA said bleaching-level heat stress ran from early 2023 to mid-2025, reached about 84% of the world's reef area and was documented in at least 83 countries and territories. NOAA's outlook warns that a developing El Niño could bring widespread bleaching back, with the highest probabilities in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

notes.scale: NOAA says about 84% of global reef area had bleaching-level heat stress, spanning the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans (ref 2).
notes.duration: Heat stress ran from early 2023 to mid-2025, about two and a half years, according to NOAA (ref 2).
notes.significance: NOAA formally confirmed the fourth global bleaching event on 15 April 2024 and declared it likely ended in June 2026 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Inquiry into the loss of HMNZS Manawanui off Upolu finds an autopilot error, training gaps and 12 contributing factors, with the wreck still on the reef in April 2025
records.description: The New Zealand Defence Force's Court of Inquiry found that HMNZS Manawanui, conducting a hydrographic survey, grounded on 5 October 2024 near Sinalei Reef south of Upolu, Samoa, and sank on 6 October after the failure to disconnect the autopilot. The final report found 12 contributing factors, including training and qualification gaps and inadequate risk management. As of April 2025 the navy said it had removed diesel and other pollutants and that no decision had been taken on removing the wreck.

Scientists warned of serious consequences for the reef, and the International Surfing Association said it would not support new construction on the reef. The tower was to be dismantled after the Games, and locals planned a reef check using monitoring tools from the Mega Lab.

records.title: Cook Islands announces a 400,000 km2 Ra'ui To'ora corridor to protect migrating, endangered Oceania humpback whales
records.description: At the UN Ocean Conference in June 2025 Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown announced a zone spanning over 400,000 square kilometres to protect the migratory corridors of the endangered Oceania humpback whale, applying the traditional ra'ui practice at ocean scale. Tonga's Princess Angelika Tuku'aho separately called for legal rights for whales, and in 2026 the Pacific Islands Forum acknowledged Tonga's concerns about migratory humpbacks. The legal status of the Cook Islands zone is not shown in the sources.

location.name: Cook Islands Ra'ui To'ora whale corridor
location.detail: Migratory corridors of Oceania humpback whales across Cook Islands waters, linked to Tonga's whale sanctuary (refs 1, 2).

records.layer_rationale: A protection zone announced for an endangered whale population's migratory routes.

notes.harm: RNZ describes the Oceania humpback as endangered and the whale declaration as seeking to grow dwindling populations, so harm is potential and not quantified (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery restriction is described in the announcement, and Tonga's whale watching guides say they will protect whales (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The zone covers over 400,000 square kilometres, within a national EEZ but linked to a proposed transboundary corridor (ref 1).
notes.duration: The zone was announced in June 2025 and Forum leaders noted Tonga's concerns in September 2026, a period of more than a year (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A head-of-government announcement at a UN conference and a Forum Leaders' acknowledgement are formal statements, though no gazetted order was found (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Record North Atlantic sea-surface temperatures and near-basin-wide marine heatwaves in 2023 and 2024
records.description: Copernicus Marine and Mercator Ocean report that the North Atlantic (0 to 60 N) averaged a record 22.91 C in 2024, 0.6 C above the 2023 record, with 98.8% of the basin hit by a marine heatwave. NOAA Climate.gov noted record North Atlantic surface temperatures from March 2023 through mid-2024. In 2025 the eastern North Atlantic again saw record months, while the basin average ranked lower than in 2023 and 2024.

location.name: North Atlantic basin, 0 to 60 N
location.detail: Basin-wide open-ocean finding covering the subtropical and subpolar North Atlantic; coastal impacts fall in the NEATL, NWATL, CAR and GOM records.

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale surface heat anomalies and marine heatwave coverage measured by ocean-monitoring services.
secondary_drivers: Weak Azores High and low winds in 2023

notes.harm: Climate.gov reported the 2024 marine heatwave caused heat stress across nearly all of the Atlantic tropical reef areas, a potential rather than quantified ecological harm (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited assessments documents a fishery closure, advisory or port restriction tied to the basin heat itself (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.scale: Mercator reports marine heatwaves over 98.8% of the North Atlantic from 0 to 60 N in 2024 and 99.6% in 2023, a whole-basin extent (ref 1).
notes.duration: Record surface temperatures ran from March 2023 into mid-2024 (ref 2) and the eastern basin set record months again in 2025, up to eight in a row at some locations (ref 4).
notes.significance: These are agency monitoring reports and press releases with no notice, listing or enforcement attached (refs 1, 4, 5).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The North Atlantic (0 to 60 N) recorded its highest sea surface temperature on record in 2024, averaging 22.91 C, 0.6 C above the 2023 record (Copernicus Marine / Mercator Ocean).

measures.note: Warmest June in the ERA5 record, about 0.5 C above 2010 (ref 3).

measures.note: Sixth-warmest August on record; 18% of the basin had strong or higher marine heatwave conditions (ref 6).

signals: Climate.gov linked the 2024 heat to above-normal Atlantic hurricane-season forecasts and heat stress on tropical reef areas (ref 2).

trend.note: The 2024 mean broke the 2023 record, then 2025 ranked lower for the basin (June 2025 third-warmest, August 2025 sixth-warmest) while the eastern basin set record months (refs 4, 5, 6).

records.title: Near-record warm Atlantic main development region fuels Hurricane Beryl to the earliest Category 4 and 5 on record
records.description: NOAA reported that the main development region of the tropical Atlantic was near record warm in late June 2024, with temperatures closer to those typical of mid-September, and Beryl intensified rapidly over it. The National Hurricane Center report records Beryl as the earliest Category 4 (30 June) and Category 5 (2 July) Atlantic hurricane on record, with 35 direct deaths. The storm formed near 8.9 N 39.6 W; its landfalls and damage are recorded in the Caribbean and Gulf records.

location.name: Tropical Atlantic main development region
location.detail: Beryl formed about 1,200 n mi east of Barbados and became a hurricane near 49.3 W, the farthest east a June Atlantic hurricane had formed in the tropics; coordinates are the best-track position at its first Category 4 intensity.

records.layer_rationale: Record-warm tropical Atlantic surface water acted as the fuel for rapid intensification of an unusually early major hurricane.

notes.harm: The NHC report attributes 35 direct deaths to Beryl, including 3 in Grenada, 8 in St. Vincent and the Grenadines and 14 in the United States (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The NHC report records over $7 billion of property damage in the United States and 99% of buildings damaged on Carriacou, but these impacts fall in the Caribbean and Gulf, so only restrictions are scored here (ref 1).
notes.scale: Climate.gov describes the main development region of the tropical Atlantic as near record warm, a regional-sea extent rather than a single site (ref 2).
notes.duration: Beryl lasted from 28 June to 9 July 2024 and its Category 5 peak was brief (ref 1), although record warmth persisted before and after (ref 3).
notes.significance: NHC issued advisories and the tropical cyclone report certifies records for earliest Category 4 and 5 hurricanes in the Atlantic (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Beryl became the earliest Category 5 hurricane of record in the Atlantic basin, reaching 145 kt at 0600 UTC on 2 July 2024 (NHC Tropical Cyclone Report).

measures.note: NHC report, amended version of 1 May 2025 (ref 1).

measures.note: 1800 UTC 29 June to 1800 UTC 30 June, tied record for an Atlantic named storm so early in the year (ref 1).

signals: Economic losses documented by the NHC fall in the US, Grenada and other Caribbean states, not at the open-ocean site (ref 1).

trend.note: A single storm; the 2024 and 2025 warm-ocean context is described in the basin record (ref 3).

responsible_bodies.role: Tropical cyclone forecast and warning agency

records.title: Subpolar North Atlantic cold blob south of Greenland tied to a weakening Atlantic overturning circulation
records.description: Two 2025 studies attribute the long-term cooling of the subpolar North Atlantic south of Greenland, the "cold blob", to a weakening Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC); a June 2026 Geophysical Research Letters study led by the Potsdam Institute reaches the same conclusion. Fan and co-authors find an atmospheric radiative pathway and ocean heat transport contribute about equally, and Liu and Li estimate AMOC weakening of 1.01 to 2.97 Sverdrups per century over 1900 to 2005. Direct AMOC measurements cover only about 20 years.

location.name: Subpolar gyre south of Greenland
location.type: Open-ocean cooling region (North Atlantic warming hole)
location.detail: The Liu and Li study places the cold zone between 40 N and 65 N south of Greenland, with cooling and freshening to about 3,000 m depth.

records.layer_rationale: A persistent ocean-circulation signal in the surface temperature field that contrasts with global warming.
secondary_drivers: Colder, drier air above the cold blob

notes.harm: The studies describe a risk to the climate system but document no measured ecological or human harm from the cooling itself (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or coastal restriction is documented in the cited studies or press coverage (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: The cold zone spans 40 N to 65 N south of Greenland and the AMOC is an Atlantic-wide circulation (ref 2).
notes.duration: Earth.com reports the cold spot has persisted for over 100 years, and Fan and co-authors describe cooling over the 20th century (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Peer-reviewed research and press coverage only, with no agency notice or treaty action (refs 1, 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Liu and Li estimate the AMOC weakened by 1.01 to 2.97 Sverdrups per century from 1900 to 2005, using temperature and salinity fingerprints (Communications Earth & Environment, per Earth.com).

measures.name: AMOC weakening, 1900 to 2005
measures.note: Range of 1.01 to 2.97 Sv per century estimated from fingerprints in six sea-surface temperature and three salinity datasets and 94 climate models (ref 2).

measures.name: Modelled cooling trend
measures.note: Up to 0.3 C per century in models with a weakening AMOC (ref 2).

trend.note: Euronews (June 2026) describes the blob as the place on Earth that keeps getting colder, citing a study led by the Potsdam Institute (ref 3).

responsible_bodies.name: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)

records.public_contact: PIK press office via pik-potsdam.de.
corrective_actions: No management response is documented; the AMOC is monitored by the RAPID array and other observing programmes, which the sources do not detail.

records.title: Canary Islands marine heatwave of 2023: sea temperature 2.3 C above normal through the summer and still above normal at year end
records.description: Spanish Institute of Oceanography data reported in August 2023 showed Canary Islands surface water at 24.32 C on 8 August, 1.56 C above average. A University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria study presented at the EGU General Assembly 2024 found the heatwave ran from mid-May to late summer 2023, averaged 2.3 C above normal and stayed above normal for the rest of the year. Weak winds are the proposed driver, and the authors note satellite data may understate how deep the anomaly runs.

records.layer_rationale: A months-long surface thermal anomaly driven by low winds and reduced heat loss.
secondary_drivers: Collapse of wind speeds in May and June 2023

notes.harm: The sources document temperatures and wind anomalies but no mortality, bleaching or other measured harm around the Canaries (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, tourism or beach restriction is reported in either source (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The anomaly covers the Canary Islands archipelago waters, a national coastline rather than a single site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The heatwave ran from mid-May through the summer of 2023 and temperatures remained above normal for the rest of the year (ref 2).
notes.significance: A press report on IEO monitoring and a conference abstract; no agency notice or listing (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Forty years of Sargasso Sea acidification, warming and oxygen loss at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study site
records.description: The longest sustained ocean acidification record, from the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study and Hydrostation S, shows surface pH down by about 0.1 units since 1983, with hydrogen-ion concentration up more than 30%. Surface water warmed by about 1 C, dissolved oxygen fell by 12.5 umol/kg (about 6%), and calcification conditions have become less favourable. The authors report that ocean chemistry in the 2020s is outside the range observed in the 1980s.

location.name: Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study site
location.detail: BATS is about 80 km south-east of Bermuda in the Sargasso Sea; Hydrostation S is about 25 km south-east of the island.

records.layer_rationale: Long-term carbonate chemistry, oxygen and temperature change in subtropical gyre surface water.

notes.harm: The authors conclude that calcification conditions have become less favourable, a potential effect on calcifiers rather than documented mortality (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The paper reports no fishery or coastal-economy disruption at the site (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The station represents Sargasso Sea and subtropical gyre surface water, a regional sea, with no basin-wide measurement in the paper (ref 1).
notes.duration: The record spans 1983 to 2023, forty years, with no slowing in the rates of change (ref 1).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study with an OA-ICC news item, but no notice or treaty action (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.
