records.title: Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt sets a record in 2025 and a second-highest year in 2026
records.description: University of South Florida scientists report that 2025 set a record for sargassum across the tropical Atlantic and 2026 ranked second-highest in the satellite record, with the Caribbean and Gulf both at record regional totals in June 2026. NASA Earth Observatory, citing USF, gives June 2026 totals of 3.6 million tonnes in the western Caribbean, 9 million in the eastern Caribbean and 5 million in the Gulf. The cause is still being investigated, with ocean warming and multiple nutrient sources suggested.

location.name: Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt
location.detail: A near-continuous belt of mats from West Africa across the tropical North Atlantic to the Gulf; the Caribbean and Gulf beachings are recorded in the CAR and GOM findings.

records.layer_rationale: A marine algal bloom linked to nutrient sources and warming, with beach inundation as the main impact.

notes.harm: USF and WGCU describe beach inundation and rotting seaweed but give no measured ecological or health harm figure (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: WGCU reports beaching continued in July 2026 across southeast Florida, the Caribbean and Lesser Antilles, with problems for resorts, officials and beach towns (ref 3).
notes.scale: NASA describes the belt as stretching nearly continuously from West Africa to the Gulf, an Atlantic-wide feature (ref 2).
notes.duration: The bloom began in 2011 and USF says total Atlantic sargassum has more than doubled about every five years since (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: USF and NASA monitoring and a NOAA-funded research programme, but no formal notice or declaration in the cited pages (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Plastic on every one of 46 monitored beaches across Macaronesia, with Canary Islands highest and five new hotspots
records.description: A 2020 to 2023 monitoring study of 46 beaches on 19 islands in four Macaronesian archipelagos found plastic on every beach, with the Canary Islands showing the highest concentrations. Researchers collected 271,203 plastic items in 430 field expeditions and identified five new plastic arrival hotspots. Beaches facing north-west to east received more plastic, which the authors link to the North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre.

notes.harm: Plastic was present on all 46 beaches, averaging 1,760 microplastic items per square metre, but the abstract reports no mortality or health outcome (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The abstract mentions no beach closure or tourism restriction (ref 1).

notes.duration: Seasonal monitoring ran 2020 to 2023 across 430 expeditions, and earlier Azores surveys found the same pattern in 2018 and 2020 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed academic study, with no regulatory notice or treaty action (ref 1).

records.title: North American lobster-gear plastic tags washing up on Faial and Pico beaches in the Azores
records.description: University of the Azores researchers found more than 1,500 items on Faial and Pico beaches between 2017 and 2025, many of them lobster-fishing gear traced by tag numbers to the United States and Canada, more than 3,000 km away. Among legible tags, 63% came from the US and 37% from Canada, and most tags were 7 to 13 years old, the oldest dating from 1983. Marine litter group head Christopher Pham says the pieces entered the sea many years ago and that knowing the origin would let action be taken at source.

records.title: Fuel-oil spill during bunkering at the Port of La Luz closes Telde beaches and triggers a regional marine pollution emergency
records.description: About 3,000 litres of fuel fell into the sea on the evening of 4 September 2024 during a bunkering operation at the Port of Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, and the slick reached Las Palmas and Telde. The Canary Islands government declared a regional-level marine pollution emergency, activated phase 1 of the National Maritime Plan, and five Telde beaches were closed to bathing. Port officials said the source had been stopped and that most of the fuel remained on the two ships involved.

location.detail: Spill at the Virgen del Pino pier in the Port of Las Palmas; the slick drifted to the Telde coast, including La Restinga, Bocabarranco, Barranquillo, Palos and San Borondon beaches. Coordinates are the centre of Telde.

records.layer_rationale: Fuel-oil release during ship bunkering affecting beaches.

notes.harm: Fuel oil entered the sea and a slick about 2 km long and 400 m wide formed, with port officials saying most fuel remained on the two ships and only small residues were on the water, and no mortality is reported (refs 1, 2).

notes.scale: The slick affected Las Palmas and Telde on one coast of Gran Canaria, a local site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The spill occurred on the evening of 4 September 2024 and cleanup began on 6 September, a matter of days (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Canary Islands government declared a regional-level marine pollution emergency and the National Maritime Plan was activated at phase 1 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Sewage leak from a blocked outfall pipeline clouds coastal water near the Garajau Nature Reserve, Madeira
records.description: A video posted on 18 April 2025 by the environmental project Agua Salgada showed cloudy seawater and a strong sewage smell between Reis Magos and Atalaia on the Caniço coast of Madeira, near the Garajau Nature Reserve. The regional environment authority DRAM said the cause was a major blockage in an underwater pipeline connected to the Caniço wastewater treatment station and issued an urgent order to the Santa Cruz council to repair it. DRAM said the inspection chamber has blocked repeatedly and earlier alerts had not stopped the problem.

records.title: Bermuda government study finds about 2,130 buildings at risk from sea level rise and storm surge, after Hurricane Ernesto
records.description: Bermuda's Minister of Home Affairs told the House of Assembly in November 2024 that the Smith Warner International study "Bermuda and Climate Change: Impacts from Sea Level Rise and Changing Storm Activity" found about 2,130 buildings (roughly 6%) at some level of risk, 326 of them highly exposed, and that 96% of coastal reserves require protection. Hurricane Ernesto struck in August 2024 with a dangerous storm surge, leaving about 26,100 of 36,000 utility customers without power. The government will create an expanded climate task force and a National Action Plan.

records.title: Azores 30% marine protected area network takes effect after a vote to keep fishing out of the fully protected half
records.description: The Azores Marine Protected Areas Network, approved in October 2024 and in force from 1 January 2026, covers about 287,000 km2, or 30% of Azorean waters, split between fully and highly protected areas. On 15 January 2026 the regional parliament kept the ban on all fishing in the fully protected areas but allowed tuna pole-and-line fishing in highly protected areas. The Azores Fisheries Federation says it is disappointed and that EUR 10 million of compensation falls short of the sector's annual revenue of EUR 42 million.

notes.livelihoods: Fishing is banned in the fully protected half and restricted in the highly protected half; the Fisheries Federation says compensation of EUR 10 million over three years falls short of EUR 42 million in annual sector revenue (ref 1).

notes.duration: The law was approved in October 2024 (ref 2) and the dispute over fishing in no-take areas ran from March 2025 to the January 2026 vote (ref 1), more than a year.
notes.significance: A regional law is in force since 1 January 2026 and parliament voted on 15 January 2026 to uphold the no-fishing rule (ref 1).

records.title: Bermuda and the UK draft the Hamilton II Declaration to seek high seas protection for the Sargasso Sea under the new High Seas Treaty
records.description: The Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026. Bermuda and the UK held a civil society consultation on 20 March 2026 on a draft Hamilton II Declaration that would build political support for a collective proposal to protect the Sargasso Sea's high seas areas, ahead of the first Conference of the Parties due before 17 January 2027. In a House of Lords debate on 6 July 2026 the UK minister said the measures still need to be negotiated and did not commit to the highest level of protection.

records.layer_rationale: The finding concerns a treaty process that decides whether a high seas area gains area-based protection.

notes.harm: No specific harm is documented in the sources; the protection effort is precautionary and the Lords debate named industrial fishing only as an activity that could be banned (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or restriction exists yet; the level of protection is still to be negotiated (ref 2).
notes.scale: The Sargasso Sea is a regional ocean area with Bermuda as its only land territory (ref 1), so a regional-sea scale.
notes.duration: The draft declaration has been in preparation and consultation since early 2026 (ref 1), and Greenpeace called for a proposal ahead of the first COP in May 2025 (ref 4), so months of process.
notes.significance: A draft political declaration and a consultation are formal steps, but no area has been designated; the treaty entered into force on 17 January 2026 (ref 3).

records.title: North Atlantic shortfin mako remains an overfished stock while ICCAT's 2025 shark measures target other stocks
records.description: NOAA Fisheries describes the North Atlantic shortfin mako as overfished and reports that ICCAT adopted a rebuilding measure in 2021 with a two-year retention ban. At its November 2025 meeting ICCAT completed a full stock assessment of Atlantic shortfin mako and adopted a new maximum mortality objective of 1,000 t for the South Atlantic stock, but its press release lists no new measure for the North Atlantic stock. NGOs said mako bycatch needs urgent mitigation.

notes.livelihoods: ICCAT's 2021 measure included a two-year retention ban on North Atlantic mako, a restriction on fishers (ref 1).
notes.scale: The stock spans the North Atlantic basin and is managed by an ocean-wide body (refs 1, 2).

notes.significance: ICCAT adopted a binding recommendation in 2021 (ref 1); the 2025 meeting adopted a measure for the South Atlantic stock only (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Ship collisions push Canary Islands sperm whales toward local extinction, researchers warn
records.description: In May 2025 researchers at the Canary Islands Oceanographic Centre (IEO-CSIC) and the University of La Laguna said two more sperm whales had died after ship strikes off Tenerife and that ship collisions are driving the species toward local extinction; they report that abundance has roughly halved. In October 2025 the regional minister told parliament the Canary stranding network recorded 1,358 dead cetaceans from 2000 to 2023, with 93 showing signs of ship collision, 53 of them sperm whales. OceanCare and the researchers call for mandatory speed limits.

records.title: NAMMCO advises zero catch of narwhal and beluga in East Greenland after quotas diverged from earlier advice
records.description: At its meeting in Nuuk on 24 to 26 March 2026, the North Atlantic Marine Mammal Commission endorsed its Scientific Committee's advice for a zero-catch limit for narwhal and beluga in East Greenland, citing a small narwhal stock and low beluga numbers. In 2022 Polar Journal reported that the Greenland government set 2023 quotas of 50 narwhals and 30 belugas for the east coast, different from NAMMCO's recommendation of a longer hunting pause. The Council also flagged pollution, shipping, cruise tourism and military activity as added pressures.

records.layer_rationale: A small marine mammal stock is hunted at levels that scientific advisers say should stop.

notes.livelihoods: Hunters and community leaders in Tasiilaq and Ittoqqortoormiit want higher quotas for meat and narwhal skin, so a catch ban would affect subsistence use (ref 2).
notes.scale: The advice concerns one regional stock complex on the east coast (ref 1), a site to regional scale.
notes.duration: NAMMCO and a 2019 working group had already questioned the quotas by 2022 (ref 2), and the advice was repeated in March 2026 (ref 1).
notes.significance: NAMMCO's Council formally endorsed zero-catch advice, which is advisory rather than binding on the Government of Greenland (ref 1).

records.title: Portugal enacts a seabed mining moratorium to 2050 while three ISA exploration contracts cover the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
records.description: Portugal's parliament passed a law on 14 March 2025 halting deep-sea mining in Portuguese waters until at least 2050 and committing Portugal to advocate a global ban, after an Azores regional assembly resolution in April 2023. Seabed around the Azores is thought to hold manganese, cobalt and nickel. Beyond national jurisdiction, the International Seabed Authority lists Poland, Russia and France (Ifremer) as holders of polymetallic sulphide exploration contracts on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

records.title: Canary Islands fishers petition the European Parliament over offshore wind rollout
records.description: In October 2025 the Canary Islands government asked Madrid for a dedicated offshore wind auction for the archipelago. On 2 March 2026 the shipowners and fishers association Miracanarias filed Petition 0620/2026 alleging Spanish failure to apply EU law in offshore wind to the detriment of fisheries; on 27 August 2026 the Petitions Committee asked the Commission for a preliminary investigation. The Committee has not ruled on the claims.

records.title: Bermuda petrel (cahow) fledges 78 chicks in 2025, the second-highest on record, as nest sites run short
records.description: The Nonsuch Expeditions programme reports that 78 cahow chicks fledged in 2025, second only to 79 in 2021. The species now has 165 established breeding pairs on the original islets and about 40 on Nonsuch Island, up from 53 pairs in 2000. Managers describe competition for burrows, tropicbird intrusions and sea-level rise and storm flooding on the low islets as continuing pressures.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery or community disruption is reported.

notes.duration: Recovery management has run since the 1950s rediscovery of 17 to 18 pairs and continues (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Critically endangered angelshark depends on the Canary Islands as its stronghold while a fisheries decree is drafted
records.description: The Angel Shark Project says the Canary Islands are the critically endangered angelshark's unique stronghold in Europe, where it has been on the Spanish endangered species list for Canary waters since 2019. Its January to March 2025 report counts 277 reported angelsharks on all eight islands, including the largest recorded aggregation, over 60 animals off Fuerteventura. The project asked to take part in public consultation on a new Canary fisheries decree and flagged recreational fishing impacts. The outcome of the consultation was not found.

records.title: Sea Lion oil field north of the Falklands reaches final investment decision after a contested environmental review
records.description: Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration took a final investment decision on the Sea Lion field in December 2025, after the Falkland Islands Government approved the field development and production programme. Phase 1 plans 11 subsea wells tied to a redeployed FPSO with first oil targeted for 2028. Falklands Conservation told the 2024 environmental consultation that the Environmental Impact Statement was not fit for purpose, citing carbon offsets, wildlife data gaps and spill and decommissioning risk. On 13 October 2026 Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea for provisional measures against the project, which the UK rejects; the Buenos Aires Times reports drilling is set to begin in early 2027 and that some oil-services providers, including Halliburton, have withdrawn amid Argentine sanctions threats.

records.title: Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal for provisional measures against the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands
records.description: Argentina filed a request for provisional measures with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea on 13 October 2026 in a dispute with the United Kingdom over hydrocarbon exploitation in the South-West Atlantic, ITLOS listed it that day. Argentine President Javier Milei had announced Annex VII arbitration on 28 September and set a two-week ultimatum; press reports say the UK rejected the arbitration on 30 September and defends the activity under Falklands law. Argentina's requests include preventing the start or continuation of production at Sea Lion. In early September Milei had also announced a sanctions bill covering suppliers, shareholders and directors. ITLOS would not rule on sovereignty.

records.title: Hundreds of distant-water squid jiggers fish the unregulated high seas at Argentina's mile 201 edge
records.description: Reports from 2025 and 2026 describe 300 to 600 foreign vessels, mainly Chinese, Korean and Taiwanese, fishing Illex squid just outside Argentina's 200-mile zone with no catch limits. The Environmental Justice Foundation found Chinese fishing hours rose 85% between 2019 and 2024 and that pressure outside the zone is over four times that inside it, alongside labour abuses on board. Argentine and Spanish industry voices warn of stock collapse.

location.name: Mile 201, high seas beyond Argentina's EEZ
location.detail: High seas of the south-west Atlantic along the outer edge of the Argentine 200-nautical-mile zone; the Argentine EEZ itself is covered under BRA.

records.layer_rationale: Intensive unregulated fishing of a keystone squid stock on the high seas.

notes.harm: EJF testimonies from 169 workers report up to five deaths aboard four Chinese vessels, beatings and 14 to 18 hour days, and crews describing the deliberate killing of South American fur seals (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Argentine industry and Spanish shipowners warn that high-seas fishing could deplete Illex and depress prices; no formal closure exists (refs 4, 5).
notes.scale: The fleet works the outer edge of the Argentine zone across the south-west Atlantic, a regional sea (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: The foreign fleet operates five or six months a year (ref 3) with effort rising 2019 to 2024 and reports repeated in 2025 and 2026 (refs 1, 4, 5).
notes.significance: Only NGO reports, industry statements and Argentine naval monitoring are cited; no regional fisheries body or enforcement order covers these waters (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Falklands Loligo squid seasons closed early for a third straight year as biomass falls, and Illex catch drops
records.description: The Falklands Fisheries Department closed the 2025 winter Loligo season after biomass estimates fell from 29,735 to 14,722 tonnes, and in August 2026 closed the second season again three days after a two-week pause, calling biomass "very low". The Illex season ended on 22 June 2026 with catches about 30% below the ten-year average. Officials cite squid movements out of the area, rising hake predation and heavier fishing power.

records.title: H5N1 avian flu kills penguin chicks and adults on Falklands colonies and keeps recurring
records.description: In January 2024 the Falkland Islands Government confirmed H5N1 in gentoo penguins on Sea Lion Island, with more than 200 chicks and some adults found dead and Steeple Jason also closed. An expedition operator page updated in July 2026 says the virus reached South Georgia in late 2023 and the Antarctic Peninsula in February 2024, and that a small number of Peninsula landing sites have at times switched to zodiac cruising only; it describes the Peninsula, not the Falklands.

records.title: Record August 2025 sea surface temperatures in the Kara Sea and up to 7 C above normal across Arctic Atlantic-sector seas
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card essay on sea surface temperature reports that the Arctic Ocean's mean August 2025 temperature was the second warmest on record, behind only August 2007, and that Kara Sea values were the warmest on record for the month. Parts of the Barents, Kara and Laptev seas ran roughly 1 to 4 C above the 1991-2020 mean, with local anomalies near 7 C. The authors note that Arctic marine heatwaves are a concern for already stressed ecosystems and that warming surface waters accelerate sea-ice loss.

records.title: Atlantification now reaches the central Arctic Ocean, weakening the halocline that shielded sea ice from ocean heat
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card 2025 essay by Polyakov, Ingvaldsen and Bluhm reports that an influx of warmer, saltier Atlantic water and biota now reaches the central Arctic Ocean, with a signal in the western Amerasian Basin moving toward Alaska. In the eastern Eurasian Basin the Atlantic Water layer has shoaled from about 150 m in the early 2000s to as shallow as 70 m, and sea-ice thinning linked to the process spans the central Arctic. The essay suggests the Atlantic water entering the Arctic from the Barents Sea has warmed more strongly than that through Fram Strait.

records.description: Tuktoyaktuk, a hamlet on the Beaufort Sea coast, is losing shoreline to storm waves and thawing permafrost. records.title: Greenland ice sheet and Arctic glaciers keep adding to global sea level rise in the 2024-25 season
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card 2025 reports that the Greenland Ice Sheet lost 129 Gt of ice in the 2025 mass balance year (September 2024 to August 2025), less than the 2003-24 average loss of 219 Gt but part of net loss every year since the late 1990s. Arctic glaciers and ice caps outside Greenland lost 151 Gt in 2023/24, adding about 0.42 mm to sea level, and Svalbard glaciers had severe losses. Meltwater from these ice masses raises sea level at coasts worldwide, including Arctic shorelines already eroding.

notes.scale: Greenland and pan-Arctic glaciers contribute to global mean sea level, so the scale is global (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Greenland has had net ice loss every year since the late 1990s and glaciers lost 181 Gt per year on average since 2002 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Aragonite-undersaturated water thickens in the Canada Basin, the open-ocean region most susceptible to acidification
records.description: A 2025 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans found that aragonite-undersaturated water in the Canada Basin thickened from none at the surface in 2003 to 19 m in 2019, and from 94 m to 136 m in the subsurface layer. The undersaturated share of the 0 to 250 m water column rose from 38% to 62%. The authors say surface thickening was driven by freshening until 2012 and by anthropogenic CO2 uptake after 2012, and warn that a weaker Beaufort Gyre could bring undersaturated water shallower, potentially affecting marine life.

records.title: Microplastic fluxes recorded over 21 months at the HAUSGARTEN observatory in Fram Strait, with high levels in sea-ice algae
records.description: An Alfred Wegener Institute study published online in December 2024 measured microplastics in sediment traps at the HAUSGARTEN observatory in Fram Strait from September 2019 to July 2021. Fluxes ranged from 0 to 2.9 particles per square metre per day, peaked in April 2020 and April 2021, and all particles were under 300 micrometres. An earlier pilot study found microplastics in all samples of the sea-ice alga Melosira arctica, up to 5.7 x 10^4 particles per cubic metre.

records.title: Plastic dominates litter on Svalbard beaches, with debris traced to more than 25 countries
records.description: Alfred Wegener Institute researchers working with expedition-cruise tourists collected more than 23,000 items weighing 1,620 kg on 14 remote Spitsbergen beaches between 2016 and 2021, about 80% of it plastic. Debris traced to more than 25 countries, led by Russia (32%), Norway (16%) and Germany (8%), and more than a third of the plastic came from outside the Arctic. A separate 2023 study found particles of 1 mm or more in only 2 of 53 beach sediment samples but warned that this likely underestimates microplastic contamination.

records.title: Sunken nuclear submarines K-27 and K-159 remain on the Kara and Barents Sea floors as Russia funds a lifting plan
records.description: Two Soviet nuclear submarines lie on the Arctic seabed: K-27, scuttled in Stepovoy Bay off Novaya Zemlya in the Kara Sea, and K-159, which sank in the Barents Sea in 2003 with about 800 kg of spent nuclear fuel. The Barents Observer reported on 20 October 2025 that Russia's draft 2026 budget and 2027-2028 plan include about 30 billion rubles for planning and lifting them, with preparations in 2026 and funding from 2027. Bellona, on 4 November 2025, judged raising them in the foreseeable future highly improbable and said no concrete plan is public.

records.title: Cargo ship Ruby with 20,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate sheltered off Tromsø in September 2024
records.description: The Maltese-flagged cargo ship Ruby, carrying 20,000 tons of ammonium nitrate from Kandalaksha, Russia, bound for Las Palmas, asked Norway for shelter on 26 August 2024 because of storms and anchored near Vannoya. It then docked at Breivika in Tromsø, where police ordered it to leave, and on 4 September 2024 it departed with two tugs to anchor about 30 nautical miles north of the city. records.title: IMO Arctic heavy fuel oil ban in force since July 2024 but waivers and exemptions allow continued use until 2029
records.description: IMO's MARPOL Annex I regulation 43A bans the use and carriage of heavy fuel oil as fuel by ships in Arctic waters from 1 July 2024, but ships with protected fuel tanks are exempt and Arctic coastal states can waive the rule for their flagged ships until 1 July 2029. The Clean Arctic Alliance, citing ICCT analysis, says 74% of Arctic shipping can continue as before and that HFO use and carriage may rise between 2024 and 2029. Russia told the IMO the amendments would not enter into force for it, and Canada said it intends to comply.

In early December 2025 a budget agreement dropped the first licensing round, and Parliament voted on the pause on 5 December 2025; Mongabay reports no round before 2029 while the Energy Ministry says its policy and regulatory framework are unchanged.

records.title: Baffinland iron ore shipping through Milne Inlet narwhal habitat: Phase 2 rejected in 2022, 6 Mt extension suspended and 4.2 Mt limit for 2025
records.description: Baffinland's Mary River mine ships iron ore from Milne Port through Milne Inlet, which crosses the Tallurutiup Imanga National Marine Conservation Area, described by Nunatsiaq News as sensitive habitat for narwhals and seabirds. The federal government rejected the 12 Mt Phase 2 plan in 2022; in 2024 the company shipped about 6 Mt on 70 ore carriers, then suspended its application to extend 6 Mt shipping and said it would return to the 4.2 Mt limit in 2025 while developing the Steensby rail and port route. records.title: Svalbard seabirds in decline: Brunnich's guillemot, ivory gull and kittiwake monitoring to May 2026
records.description: The Norwegian Polar Institute's May 2026 monitoring pages report the Svalbard breeding population of Brunnich's guillemot falling about 4% a year since the mid-1990s, probably by a third in the last decade at Bjornoya and western Spitsbergen, and the ivory gull falling about 7% a year over 2015 to 2025. Black-legged kittiwake numbers have turned more negative since about 2021, with avian influenza likely explaining at least part of it. A 2022 SEAPOP study of western Spitsbergen found colony declines linked with sea-ice loss.

records.title: Western Hudson Bay polar bears: 2021 survey counted 618 bears, down from 842 in 2016, as harvest consultations continued in 2024

Nunavut's Department of Environment says that when Western and Southern Hudson Bay are pooled the difference between 2016 and 2021 was one bear, and that part of the decline reflects movement across the subpopulation boundary. records.title: Western Mediterranean has its hottest summer on record in 2026, with 158 marine heatwave days and a 33.02 C buoy reading off Mallorca
records.description: The Balearic Islands coastal observation system Socib reported on 6 October 2026 that the western Mediterranean had its hottest summer since its records began in 1982, with 158 days of marine heatwaves from January to September and a record 33.02 C at a Dragonera buoy. Copernicus Marine data showed anomalies of about 6 C in the Gulf of Lion on 13 August, and Copernicus-based analyses put the Mediterranean basin mean at a record 28.6 C on 14 August.

notes.livelihoods: None of the opened reports describes a fishery, beach or port closure caused by the heat (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: Anomalies of about 6 C were mapped in the Gulf of Lion and above 5 C off Iberia, spanning a regional sea sector rather than one site (ref 2).
notes.duration: The western Mediterranean logged 158 marine heatwave days between January and September 2026, with the sea above 30 C for 42 consecutive days at Pollenca port (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: The evidence is observational reporting by a regional coastal observatory and Copernicus Marine imagery; no warning, order or listing is cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Greenpeace divers find necrosis and die-offs to 40 m in Ustica marine protected area after the 2026 heatwave
records.description: Greenpeace Italia divers and marine biologists surveyed four coralligenous sites in the Ustica Marine Protected Area on 10 and 11 September 2026 and found necrosis, bleaching and die-offs down to 40 m, which Greenpeace calls the first time impacts were this clear at that depth. Its Mare Caldo thermometers recorded a +4.54 C surface anomaly at Ustica, and bleaching of Posidonia oceanica was documented for the first time in the project.

location.detail: Island of Ustica off northern Sicily in the Tyrrhenian Sea; sites include Punta Galera, Punta San Paolo and Capo Falconiera

records.layer_rationale: Heat-driven mortality of habitat-forming corals, gorgonians and seagrass is damage to a benthic habitat.

notes.harm: Divers found Cladocora caespitosa colonies completely dead at Punta Galera and advanced necrosis of Paramuricea clavata at 40 m, the worst deep damage since the project began in 2019 (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Copernicus Ocean State Report 10: record ocean heat in 2025, sea level rising 4.2 mm a year and ocean 17% more acidic since 1985
records.description: The 10th Copernicus Ocean State Report, published on 30 September 2026, says total heat stored in the ocean reached its highest level on record in 2025 and the ocean became about 17% more acidic between 1985 and 2025. It also finds that since 1999 about 65% of small island developing states' ocean territory has been exposed to accelerating sea-level rise.

location.name: Global ocean

notes.duration: Global sea level rose 3.8 mm a year from 1999 to 2025 and 4.2 mm a year from 2012 to 2025, a multi-decade trend (ref 2).
notes.significance: A formal annual assessment by the Copernicus Marine Service produced by 125 specialists, but not a treaty action or order (ref 3).

population_affected.note: The summaries give exposed ocean area, not population.

records.title: IMO Net-Zero Framework for shipping still unadopted: vote resumes 4 December 2026 after a year of delay
records.description: The IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee postponed adoption of the Net-Zero Framework, a global fuel-intensity standard with emissions pricing for large ships, in October 2025. At MEPC 84 (27 April to 1 May 2026) countries agreed to take the original framework forward as the basis for further work and set up an intersessional working group; the resumed extraordinary session is scheduled for 4 December 2026, after MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December). The same session also adopted a North-East Atlantic Emission Control Area and extended the underwater noise experience-building phase to the end of 2028.

location.name: Global shipping (IMO, MARPOL Annex VI)
location.detail: Applies to ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage under the proposed MARPOL Annex VI amendments; negotiated at the IMO in London.

records.layer_rationale: A treaty process on shipping emissions whose adoption has been delayed.

notes.harm: Shipping accounts for more than 2% of global emissions and is not covered by the Paris Agreement, so delay leaves potential climate harm unaddressed (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or restriction results; the framework would price fuel intensity from 2028, with a fund expected to raise $10-15bn a year in early years (ref 2).
notes.scale: The framework would apply worldwide to large ocean-going ships (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Adoption was adjourned for one year in October 2025 and is now not expected before December 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: MEPC 84 produced a formal committee outcome carrying the framework forward without adopting it, and 57 countries backed the October 2025 adjournment (refs 1, 2).

key_measure.text: Resumed second extraordinary MEPC session scheduled for 4 December 2026, subject to MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December) (ref 1).

measures.note: Carbon Brief (ref 2).

records.title: Extra-polar sea surface temperature sets a September record of 21.05 C as the Nino 3.4 region reaches an all-time high
records.description: Copernicus Climate Change Service reports that the September 2026 average sea surface temperature of the extra-polar ocean (60S to 60N) was 21.05 C, the highest on record for the month and above the 20.92 C of September 2023. The monthly Nino 3.4 value reached an all-time high of 29.70 C, above the peaks of the 1982/83, 1997/98 and 2015/16 El Ninos, and the bulletin reports record September temperatures along the Atlantic coast of Europe and in the western Mediterranean.

location.detail: Extra-polar world ocean with the equatorial Pacific Nino 3.4 region, and European Atlantic and western Mediterranean waters.

notes.livelihoods: The cited bulletin and article report temperatures only and describe no closure or restriction tied to this reading (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The record covers the whole extra-polar ocean from 60S to 60N, with the Nino 3.4 region also at an all-time high (ref 1).
notes.duration: The monthly record follows a record August for the extra-polar ocean at 21.07 C and El Nino is still intensifying and expected to last into 2027 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Copernicus Climate Change Service issued its formal monthly bulletin on 12 October 2026 reporting the record (ref 1).

records.title: IUCN lists the emperor penguin and Antarctic fur seal as Endangered and the southern elephant seal as Vulnerable
records.description: On 9 April 2026 the IUCN Red List moved the emperor penguin from Near Threatened to Endangered, projecting its population to halve by the 2080s, and the Antarctic fur seal from Least Concern to Endangered after a fall from about 2,187,000 mature seals in 1999 to 944,000 in 2025. records.title: Southeast Alaska summer Dungeness crab season closed three weeks early after the lowest early catches in over 30 years
records.description: Alaska Department of Fish and Game closed the 2026/27 Southeast Alaska summer commercial Dungeness season on 25 July, three weeks early, because the harvest estimate was the lowest in at least 25 years. ADF&G said it is not sure why so few legal-size males were available, and that a fall season will be held.

location.name: Southeast Alaska Dungeness crab fishery
location.detail: Inside waters of Southeast Alaska, managed by the State of Alaska (refs 1, 2).

records.layer_rationale: A commercial shellfish stock producing record-low early catches, forcing closure.
secondary_drivers: Sea otter predation (reported by fishermen and ADF&G)

notes.harm: ADF&G said it is unsure why legal-size males were scarce; no stock assessment result is cited (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The summer season closed on 25 July, three weeks early, after 40 fishing days (ref 1); the 2025-26 season was valued at $8.6 million (ref 2).
notes.scale: The closure applies to commercial Dungeness fishing across Southeast Alaska (ref 1).
notes.duration: This is the fifth early closure since 2000 and last year's summer season also closed six days early (ref 2).
notes.significance: ADF&G issued a formal closure announcement on 29 June 2026 with gear removal by 1 August (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No participant count in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: About 388,000 pounds were landed in the first seven days against a 10-year average of about 860,000 pounds, and ADF&G projected about 1.5 million pounds for the season (ref 2).

measures.name: First-seven-day landings
measures.note: Versus 10-year average of about 860,000 lb (ref 2).

measures.name: Projected season harvest
measures.note: ADF&G projection from first-week data (ref 2).

measures.note: Season closed 25 July, three weeks early (ref 1).

signals: Season closed three weeks early (ref 1).
2025-26 season valued at $8.6 million (ref 2).

trend.note: Early closures in 2025 (six days) and 2026 (three weeks) (ref 2).

responsible_bodies.name: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries

records.public_contact: ADF&G Division of Commercial Fisheries, Southeast Region offices (published on adfg.alaska.gov).
corrective_actions: Early summer closure on 25 July 2026; a fall season is planned, details to be announced (ref 2).

records.title: Oil slick and shoreline fuel oil after the 6 October drone attack on the tanker Rio put Krasnodar's Black Sea coast on alert
records.description: After a naval drone attack set the Liberian-flagged Aframax tanker Rio on fire off Sochi on 6 October 2026, satellite monitoring showed a slick spreading along the Krasnodar coast as far as Anapa. Fuel oil was found along about 500 metres of shoreline at Novorossiysk and oiled birds were recovered, and the governor ordered heightened alert for Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk. Regional emergency officials say only small amounts reached the shore and that these did not come from the tanker, while Greenpeace and satellite projects tie the slick to the attack.

location.name: Sochi to Novorossiysk and Anapa coast
location.detail: Krasnodar Krai Black Sea coast between Sochi, Gelendzhik, Novorossiysk Bay (near the CPC offshore loading facilities) and Anapa

records.layer_rationale: Bunker fuel and possibly cargo oil released into coastal waters from a tanker hit in a drone attack.
secondary_drivers: Attack on a tanker at sea

notes.harm: Fuel oil was found along about 500 m of coast at Novorossiysk and 10 oiled birds had been found by 12 October, three with chemical burns taken to a rescue centre in Anapa; the amount of oil released is not reported (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Sochi and Sirius beaches were closed after the 6 October attack and reopened on 8 October, and a volunteer beach clean-up was requested in the Abrau-Dyurso district; no fishery closure is reported (ref 1).
notes.scale: Greenpeace measured about 8 km2 on 7 October and about 25 km2 on 8 October; later imagery shows patches along the coast to Anapa, within one stretch of one country's coast (ref 2).
notes.duration: The attack was on 6 October and the shoreline reports run to 14 October, about eight days, so the event is still in its first weeks (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Governor Veniamin Kondratyev's order of 13 October raised the alert level for Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk and warned of a potential emergency, a formal notice short of an emergency declaration (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Greenpeace satellite analysis: a slick of about 8 km2 on 7 October growing to about 25 km2 on 8 October 2026; fuel oil found along about 500 m of Novorossiysk shoreline (Novorossiysk rescue chief).

measures.name: Slick area, 7 October (Greenpeace, satellite)
measures.note: Trail near Lazarevskoye, about 50 km from the fire site (ref 2).

measures.name: Slick area, 8 October (Greenpeace, satellite)
measures.note: After the tanker passed Tuapse (ref 2).

measures.name: Shoreline with fuel oil at Novorossiysk
measures.note: Figure given by Novorossiysk's chief rescue official (ref 1).

measures.name: Oiled birds found
measures.note: As of 12 October, per Meduza (ref 2).

signals: Sochi and Sirius beaches were temporarily closed after the attack (ref 1).
Oil traces were reported near the CPC offshore loading facilities and Novorossiysk Bay (refs 1, 2).

trend.note: Imagery from 10 and 12 October showed the slick breaking into patches; authorities reported small amounts ashore on 14 October (refs 1, 2).

responsible_bodies.name: Krasnodar Krai administration and regional emergency headquarters

records.public_contact: Krasnodar Krai administration public enquiries (see published website)
corrective_actions: Governor Kondratyev's order of 13 October asks for more environmental monitoring and tells the regional Marine Rescue Service to prevent oil reaching the shore (ref 1).
Krasnodar's emergency headquarters says shoreline clean-up is under way (ref 2).
Volunteers were asked to help clean a beach in the Abrau-Dyurso district and oiled birds were taken to a rescue centre in Anapa (refs 1, 2).

sources.title: Russia's Krasnodar Region Raises Alert as Oil Washes Ashore on Black Sea Coast
Greenpeace reports another huge oil slick in the Black Sea following an attack on a tanker off Sochi's coastline

history.note: New record from the global sweep; latest source dated 15 October 2026.

conflicts.note: Authorities and Greenpeace differ: Russian officials said the fire caused no pollution and that oil on the Novorossiysk shore did not come from the tanker, while Greenpeace and the Transparent World project link the slick to the 6 October attack (refs 1, 2).
The tanker's cargo is disputed: one report says it carried crude from Novorossiysk to India, another says it was empty; Greenpeace believes mainly bunker fuel burned (ref 2).

records.title: USGS study finds seafloor sulfide rocks from Escanaba Trough spontaneously combusted during lab processing, raising a mining safety question
records.description: A USGS-led study in Scientific Reports reports that some metal sulfide rocks from Escanaba Trough on the southern Gorda Ridge off the US West Coast spontaneously combusted during laboratory processing. The combusting rocks were mainly nanocrystalline marcasite, and the authors recommend dedicated risk assessments and engineering controls for seafloor massive sulfide mining. The study does not show that all such deposits will combust.

location.name: Escanaba Trough, southern Gorda Ridge
location.detail: Hydrothermal area along the southern Gorda Ridge off the US West Coast, named in the OceanMiningIntel report of the USGS study.

records.layer_rationale: The finding concerns a safety and risk-assessment question for seafloor sulfide mining.
secondary_drivers: Interest in seafloor copper and zinc deposits

notes.harm: Rocks from Escanaba Trough spontaneously combusted during laboratory processing, a potential hazard if such material is brought to the surface (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No mining operation or closure is described; the report covers a laboratory finding only (ref 1).
notes.scale: The study documents the behaviour in particular Escanaba Trough rocks and notes each deposit's mineralogy matters (ref 1).
notes.duration: A single study reported on 8 October 2026 with no ongoing event (ref 1).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed research paper with no regulatory action reported (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited source.

key_measure.text: Some metal sulfide-rich rocks from Escanaba Trough spontaneously combusted during laboratory processing; the combusting rocks were mainly nanocrystalline marcasite (ref 1).

records.public_contact: USGS published general contact channels at usgs.gov.
corrective_actions: The researchers recommend dedicated risk assessments for seafloor massive sulfide deposits and engineering controls to reduce self-heating and spontaneous combustion (ref 1).

sources.title: USGS Study Flags Spontaneous Combustion Risk in Seafloor Massive Sulfide Mining
